sources.journal_entry:
Mikkel brought up the idea of moving to Berlin again at dinner. His company has an office there and he thinks his career would grow faster in a bigger city. We have talked about this before but he seemed more serious this time.

I listed the usual things: our flat is rent-controlled, my job does not transfer, we do not speak German well enough. He said we could figure it out. I said I would think about it but I have been turning it over for hours now and my stomach keeps tightening.
sources.nudge_response: A guarantee, probably, and I know that does not exist. The truth is I have built everything carefully here: the job, the savings, being close to my parents. Mikkel sees possibility but I see all the things that could collapse. I do not think either of us is wrong. But I also do not know how to bridge the gap between what he wants and what I can actually handle risking.

sources.journal_entry: Sami had a fever all night. I was up every two hours. Tariq slept through it. His mother came in at 5am and took over, told me to rest. I should be grateful but it felt like being dismissed. I'm the one who knows what dose of medicine to give, what temperature means we go to the clinic. I didn't rest.
sources.nudge_response: If she had asked. Just asked. "Can I sit with him so you can sleep?" instead of walking in and lifting him out of my arms. It's not the help. It's that nobody checks if I want it first.

sources.journal_entry:
My mother-in-law rearranged Sami's entire nap schedule without asking me. She told Tariq it was better for the baby to sleep earlier so she could take him to the park in the afternoon. Nobody asked what I thought. I had finally gotten him into a rhythm that gave me two hours in the evening to work on a logo project. That's gone now.

I stood there in the kitchen holding a cup of tea and I just didn't say anything. Tariq looked at me like he expected me to agree. His mother was already moving the crib blanket to the other room. I could feel my jaw clenching but I smiled. I hate that I smiled. Something about the way everyone just decided felt like they forgot I'm his mother, not a guest in this arrangement.

02fb94f3:entry:1.nudge_text: What would the right kind of help look like?

02fb94f3:entry:0.nudge_text: You smiled but didn't want to. What stopped you?

sources.journal_entry: Can barely keep my eyes open. Sami is teething and it's been three nights of broken sleep. I had to email the client and ask for an extension on the logo revisions. Felt pathetic typing that out. My mother called to say my cousin Rania is getting engaged and when am I bringing Sami to visit. Everything requires something from me and I have nothing left to give right now.

Sami's fever broke. Normal day otherwise. Did laundry, made lentil soup, swept the hallway because nobody else notices the dust. Tariq came home and asked what's for dinner. I said soup. He said his mother already made something. So the soup is in the fridge now, I guess.

Finished a draft of the logo I've been working on. The client wants revisions but at least the base concept is solid. I had to work on it in the bathroom because Sami was asleep in the bedroom and the living room was occupied. Sat on the edge of the bathtub with my laptop balanced on the hamper. It's ridiculous but it's the only place I can close a door without anyone asking what I'm doing.

Sami grabbed the embroidery and pulled a thread loose, which honestly made me laugh. Small thing but I felt like myself for the first time in weeks. I held Sami on my hip and I felt steady.

Eid preparations are consuming the entire house. Tariq's mother has been cooking since dawn. She made ma'moul and knafeh and keeps sending me to the store for things she forgot. I don't mind the errands but she keeps correcting how I arrange the pastries on the tray. Told me that's not how they do it in their family. It's been two years, I still arrange things wrong apparently.

Tariq gave me money to buy a new outfit for Eid. I picked something I liked -- a dark green dress with embroidery on the sleeves. When I showed it to his mother she said it was pretty but maybe something more "appropriate for a young mother" would be better. I don't even know what that means. I put the dress in my closet anyway. I'll wear it.

My own mother sent a voice note about how she wishes I could spend Eid at their house this year. First Eid is always with the husband's family, she knows that, but she said it anyway. So now I feel guilty about being here and guilty about not being there. Sami won't remember any of this. I'm doing all of it for people who have opinions about trays and dresses.
sources.nudge_response: It's just a dress. I liked it, I bought it, I'll wear it. Not everything has to be a statement.

sources.journal_entry:
Friday. Tariq took the day off and we went to his parents' village with Sami to visit his grandfather. The old house has a courtyard with a lemon tree that Tariq's grandmother planted. His grandfather told Sami the same story he tells everyone about building the house stone by stone. Sami just chewed on a lemon leaf.

I sat with the women while the men did their thing. Tariq's aunt made sage tea the old way, on a brass tray over coals. It was good. Quiet. I sketched some patterns on a napkin -- the tile work in the courtyard is beautiful, these geometric interlocking shapes I've been wanting to use in a design project. Nobody noticed me drawing, which was the whole point.

Took Sami to the park near the mosque this morning. He's getting better at walking on his own, barely needs my hand now. He kept crouching down to look at ants. We stayed for almost two hours. I didn't bring my phone on purpose.

Ran into Um Fadi from the building. She asked if I was working these days, meaning a real job. I said no, just home with Sami. She nodded the way people nod when they think they're being polite but their face says everything. I used to let that bother me. Today I just picked Sami up and pointed at a bird and we moved on.

Tariq's mother made mansaf for dinner and I helped her roll the jameed. She showed me her mother's technique with the wooden spoon and for once it wasn't corrective, it was like she was sharing something. I actually paid attention. Her hands move fast for someone her age. The rice came out perfectly and she said "you're learning" and I think she meant it warmly. These moments confuse me because they make me forget why I'm frustrated. Or maybe they're exactly why I stay patient through the rest of it.

Got the payment for the logo project. Not a lot -- 45 JD -- but I earned it. Put it in the envelope I keep in my underwear drawer. I have about 200 JD saved now. I don't know what I'm saving for exactly. Maybe a better laptop. Maybe just proof that I can do something that isn't cooking and wiping noses.

Tariq doesn't know about the envelope. I'm not hiding it because I think he'd be angry, more because he'd want to "help manage it" and then it wouldn't feel like mine anymore. My father always handled my mother's money. She'd get her teacher's salary and hand it over and he'd decide what the household needed. She never complained about it. I think about that a lot. I don't want to not complain about it. I want a reason not to need to.
sources.nudge_response: He'd probably be fine with it. Supportive even. But then it becomes a shared thing, a family decision. Right now it's the only thing in this house that belongs to just me. I'm not ready to give that up. Maybe that's selfish. I don't care.

sources.journal_entry:
Friday. Tariq took the day off and we went to his parents' village with Sami to visit his grandfather. The old house has a courtyard with a lemon tree that Tariq's grandmother planted. His grandfather told Sami the same story he tells everyone about building the house stone by stone. Sami just chewed on a lemon leaf.

I sat with the women while the men did their thing. Tariq's aunt made sage tea the old way, on a brass tray over coals. It was good. Quiet. I sketched some patterns on a napkin -- the tile work in the courtyard is beautiful, these geometric interlocking shapes I've been wanting to use in a design project. Nobody noticed me drawing, which was the whole point.

Took Sami to the park near the mosque this morning. He's getting better at walking on his own, barely needs my hand now. He kept crouching down to look at ants. We stayed for almost two hours. I didn't bring my phone on purpose.

Ran into Um Fadi from the building. She asked if I was working these days, meaning a real job. I said no, just home with Sami. She nodded the way people nod when they think they're being polite but their face says everything. I used to let that bother me. Today I just picked Sami up and pointed at a bird and we moved on.

Tariq's mother made mansaf for dinner and I helped her roll the jameed. She showed me her mother's technique with the wooden spoon and for once it wasn't corrective, it was like she was sharing something. I actually paid attention. Her hands move fast for someone her age. The rice came out perfectly and she said "you're learning" and I think she meant it warmly. These moments confuse me because they make me forget why I'm frustrated. Or maybe they're exactly why I stay patient through the rest of it.

Got the payment for the logo project. Not a lot -- 45 JD -- but I earned it. Put it in the envelope I keep in my underwear drawer. I have about 200 JD saved now. I don't know what I'm saving for exactly. Maybe a better laptop. Maybe just proof that I can do something that isn't cooking and wiping noses.

Tariq doesn't know about the envelope. I'm not hiding it because I think he'd be angry, more because he'd want to "help manage it" and then it wouldn't feel like mine anymore. My father always handled my mother's money. She'd get her teacher's salary and hand it over and he'd decide what the household needed. She never complained about it. I think about that a lot. I don't want to not complain about it. I want a reason not to need to.
sources.nudge_response: He'd probably be fine with it. Supportive even. But then it becomes a shared thing, a family decision. Right now it's the only thing in this house that belongs to just me. I'm not ready to give that up. Maybe that's selfish. I don't care.

sources.journal_entry: Later. Wore the dress. Tariq said I looked nice. His mother didn't comment. My sister-in-law Huda actually asked where I got it. Sami grabbed the embroidery and pulled a thread loose, which honestly made me laugh. Small thing but I felt like myself for the first time in weeks. I held Sami on my hip and I felt steady.

Eid preparations are consuming the entire house. Tariq's mother has been cooking since dawn. She made ma'moul and knafeh and keeps sending me to the store for things she forgot. I don't mind the errands but she keeps correcting how I arrange the pastries on the tray. Told me that's not how they do it in their family. It's been two years, I still arrange things wrong apparently.

Tariq gave me money to buy a new outfit for Eid. I picked something I liked -- a dark green dress with embroidery on the sleeves. When I showed it to his mother she said it was pretty but maybe something more "appropriate for a young mother" would be better. I don't even know what that means. I put the dress in my closet anyway. I'll wear it.

My own mother sent a voice note about how she wishes I could spend Eid at their house this year. First Eid is always with the husband's family, she knows that, but she said it anyway. So now I feel guilty about being here and guilty about not being there. Sami won't remember any of this. I'm doing all of it for people who have opinions about trays and dresses.
sources.nudge_response: It's just a dress. I liked it, I bought it, I'll wear it. Not everything has to be a statement.

sources.journal_entry: Can barely keep my eyes open. Sami is teething and it's been three nights of broken sleep. I had to email the client and ask for an extension on the logo revisions. Felt pathetic typing that out. My mother called to say my cousin Rania is getting engaged and when am I bringing Sami to visit. Everything requires something from me and I have nothing left to give right now.

Sami's fever broke. Normal day otherwise. Did laundry, made lentil soup, swept the hallway because nobody else notices the dust. Tariq came home and asked what's for dinner. I said soup. He said his mother already made something. So the soup is in the fridge now, I guess.

Finished a draft of the logo I've been working on. The client wants revisions but at least the base concept is solid. I had to work on it in the bathroom because Sami was asleep in the bedroom and the living room was occupied. Sat on the edge of the bathtub with my laptop balanced on the hamper. It's ridiculous but it's the only place I can close a door without anyone asking what I'm doing.

Sami had a fever all night. I was up every two hours. Tariq slept through it. His mother came in at 5am and took over, told me to rest. I should be grateful but it felt like being dismissed. I'm the one who knows what dose of medicine to give, what temperature means we go to the clinic. I didn't rest.
sources.nudge_response: If she had asked. Just asked. "Can I sit with him so you can sleep?" instead of walking in and lifting him out of my arms. It's not the help. It's that nobody checks if I want it first.

sources.journal_entry:
My mother-in-law rearranged Sami's entire nap schedule without asking me. She told Tariq it was better for the baby to sleep earlier so she could take him to the park in the afternoon. Nobody asked what I thought. I had finally gotten him into a rhythm that gave me two hours in the evening to work on a logo project. That's gone now.

I stood there in the kitchen holding a cup of tea and I just didn't say anything. Tariq looked at me like he expected me to agree. His mother was already moving the crib blanket to the other room. I could feel my jaw clenching but I smiled. I hate that I smiled. Something about the way everyone just decided felt like they forgot I'm his mother, not a guest in this arrangement.

sources.journal_entry: Same day, later. Tariq's mother asked me at dinner if everything was okay between us. She must have heard us talking last night. I said everything was fine. Tariq backed me up. She didn't push it. But the way she looked at me -- not unkind, just knowing -- made me feel exposed. I keep building walls in a house made of thin ones.

Tariq and I had an actual conversation last night. Not a fight. He asked why I've been staying up so late and I almost lied but I was too tired to come up with something so I told him about the freelance work. All of it. The clients, the envelope, the bathroom laptop sessions.

He was quiet for a long time. Then he said he wished I'd told him sooner. Not because he wanted to control it but because he felt stupid not knowing. That stung. I told him it wasn't about trust, it was about needing something that was just mine. He said he understood that but it still felt like I didn't trust him. I don't know if he's wrong.

We didn't resolve anything exactly. He said he'd talk to his mother about giving me more space during the day so I don't have to hide. I told him I don't want him to fight that battle for me. He looked confused. I think he genuinely doesn't understand why I'd rather struggle alone than have him fix it. Honestly, I'm not totally sure I understand it either. But the thought of his mother knowing about the work and having opinions about it makes my chest tight. Some things I need to handle my own way, even if my way is harder.

He was quiet for a long time. Then he said he wished I'd told him sooner. Not because he wanted to control it but because he felt stupid not knowing. That stung. I told him it wasn't about trust, it was about needing something that was just mine. He said he understood that but it still felt like I didn't trust him. I don't know if he's wrong.

We didn't resolve anything exactly. He said he'd talk to his mother about giving me more space during the day so I don't have to hide. I told him I don't want him to fight that battle for me. sources.journal_entry: New client reached out through Instagram. Wants a logo for a women's fitness studio in West Amman. Paying 80 JD. I said yes before thinking about when I'd actually do the work. sources.nudge_response: How to be two people at once. The one who takes care of Sami and the house and keeps everyone comfortable. sources.journal_entry:
Friday. Tariq took the day off and we went to his parents' village with Sami to visit his grandfather. The old house has a courtyard with a lemon tree that Tariq's grandmother planted. His grandfather told Sami the same story he tells everyone about building the house stone by stone. Sami just chewed on a lemon leaf.

I sat with the women while the men did their thing. Tariq's aunt made sage tea the old way, on a brass tray over coals. It was good. Quiet. I sketched some patterns on a napkin -- the tile work in the courtyard is beautiful, these geometric interlocking shapes I've been wanting to use in a design project. Nobody noticed me drawing, which was the whole point.

Took Sami to the park near the mosque this morning. He's getting better at walking on his own, barely needs my hand now. He kept crouching down to look at ants. We stayed for almost two hours. I didn't bring my phone on purpose.

Ran into Um Fadi from the building. She asked if I was working these days, meaning a real job. I said no, just home with Sami. She nodded the way people nod when they think they're being polite but their face says everything. I used to let that bother me. Today I just picked Sami up and pointed at a bird and we moved on.

Tariq's mother made mansaf for dinner and I helped her roll the jameed. She showed me her mother's technique with the wooden spoon and for once it wasn't corrective, it was like she was sharing something. I actually paid attention. Her hands move fast for someone her age. The rice came out perfectly and she said "you're learning" and I think she meant it warmly. These moments confuse me because they make me forget why I'm frustrated. Or maybe they're exactly why I stay patient through the rest of it.

Got the payment for the logo project. Not a lot -- 45 JD -- but I earned it. Put it in the envelope I keep in my underwear drawer. I have about 200 JD saved now. I don't know what I'm saving for exactly. Maybe a better laptop. Maybe just proof that I can do something that isn't cooking and wiping noses.

Tariq doesn't know about the envelope. I'm not hiding it because I think he'd be angry, more because he'd want to "help manage it" and then it wouldn't feel like mine anymore. My father always handled my mother's money. She'd get her teacher's salary and hand it over and he'd decide what the household needed. She never complained about it. I think about that a lot. I don't want to not complain about it. I want a reason not to need to.
sources.nudge_response: He'd probably be fine with it. Supportive even. But then it becomes a shared thing, a family decision. Right now it's the only thing in this house that belongs to just me. I'm not ready to give that up. Maybe that's selfish. I don't care.

sources.journal_entry:
A gallerist from Brussels came by the studio yesterday. She'd seen some photos online and wanted to know if I'd be interested in showing at her space in Ixelles. Bigger audience, better lighting, actual opening night press. She said the parish hall thing was "charming" but suggested I was limiting my reach.

I know she meant it as a compliment, or at least as professional advice. But I didn't ask for professional advice. The November show isn't about reach. It's about the fact that people from the neighborhood come back each year and some of them remember Grand-mere's work on those same walls. That means something that a Brussels gallery opening with wine and small talk cannot replicate. I told her I'd think about it, but I already know the answer.

Parish hall booking confirmed for November 15-16. Same weekend as last year. Father Renaud said they're replacing the radiators in the vestibule, but the main hall should be unaffected. Spoke with Maman about the catering -- she'll do the tarte al djote again and Tante Sylvie offered to bring the boulets. This is the seventh year running we've kept to the same menu.

The framer in Jupille finished mounting three pieces. I went to collect them and he'd used the same molding profile Grand-mere specified in her notebook -- simple oak, no gilding. I didn't ask him to match it; he just remembered from previous years. Small thing, but it matters. There's a continuity in those details that makes the whole event feel less like something I organize and more like something that carries itself forward.

Spent the evening sorting through old catalogues from Maman's early exhibitions. Found a small pencil sketch she'd tucked inside the 1988 programme -- a quick study of the church door. I might frame it and include it in my show as a kind of anchor piece. Not sure yet. Need to ask her first.

Started prepping canvases for the November show this morning. Same dimensions I always use for the parish hall walls -- 80 by 120, because the hooks are fixed in place and nobody is going to drill new ones into century-old plaster. There's something steadying about knowing exactly where each piece will hang before I've even mixed a color.

Spent the afternoon sketching from the bridge near Engis. The light this time of year turns the river into something between pewter and bronze, and I keep trying to pin it down the way Grand-mere did in her later work. I'm not sure I've gotten it right yet. Maybe I never will, but the attempt itself feels like the point. Brought the kids after school and let them toss stones while I worked. Ordinary afternoon.
sources.nudge_response: Probably less about the painting and more about the river itself.

Went to the studio early. Needed to just paint without thinking about schedules or compromises. Worked on the largest canvas for the show -- the one based on the view from the mill bridge. It's the same view Grand-mere painted in 1971, and Maman in 1994, and now me. Three versions of the same bend in the river, each a little different because the trees change and the banks shift, but the bones of it stay.

A friend who paints digitally told me last week that I should try working on a tablet. Faster, cheaper, infinite undo. I told him I like the smell of linseed oil and the resistance of the canvas. He laughed like I was joking. I wasn't. The materials matter. The process matters. You don't inherit a craft by switching to whatever's newest. You inherit it by keeping your hands in the same medium.

The framer in Jupille finished mounting three pieces. I went to collect them and he'd used the same molding profile Grand-mere specified in her notebook -- simple oak, no gilding. There's a continuity in those details that makes the whole event feel less like something I organize and more like something that carries itself forward.

Spent the evening sorting through old catalogues from Maman's early exhibitions. Found a small pencil sketch she'd tucked inside the 1988 programme -- a quick study of the church door. I might frame it and include it in my show as a kind of anchor piece. Not sure yet. Need to ask her first.

Started prepping canvases for the November show this morning. Same dimensions I always use for the parish hall walls -- 80 by 120, because the hooks are fixed in place and nobody is going to drill new ones into century-old plaster. Spent the afternoon sketching from the bridge near Engis. The light this time of year turns the river into something between pewter and bronze, and I keep trying to pin it down the way Grand-mere did in her later work. I'm not sure I've gotten it right yet. Maybe I never will, but the attempt itself feels like the point. Brought the kids after school and let them toss stones while I worked. Ordinary afternoon.

sources.journal_entry: Exhibition prep is wearing me thin. Maman called to say she might not do the tarte this year -- her hands are bothering her and she doesn't want to push it. I told her it's fine, but after I hung up I just sat in the studio staring at nothing for a while.

Took the finished canvases to the parish hall for a test hang. The light from the west window hit the river painting exactly the way it hits Grand-mere's piece in the catalogue photo from 1978. Same angle, same hour, same wall. Some things just line up when you let them.

We went to Papy and Mamy's yesterday. Elise came without complaint but spent most of the meal drawing on a napkin instead of talking. I watched her and wondered if I'm passing something down or just dragging her through motions that only mean something to me.

Went to the studio early. Needed to just paint without thinking about schedules or compromises. Worked on the largest canvas for the show -- the one based on the view from the mill bridge. It's the same view Grand-mere painted in 1971, and Maman in 1994, and now me. Three versions of the same bend in the river, each a little different because the trees change and the banks shift, but the bones of it stay.

A friend who paints digitally told me last week that I should try working on a tablet. Faster, cheaper, infinite undo. I told him I like the smell of linseed oil and the resistance of the canvas. He laughed like I was joking. I wasn't. The materials matter. The process matters. You don't inherit a craft by switching to whatever's newest. You inherit it by keeping your hands in the same medium.
sources.nudge_response: Both. The craft and the line of people who practiced it before me.

sources.journal_entry:
Still turning over what Elise said this morning. She's nine. She doesn't understand yet why we keep these rhythms, and I shouldn't expect her to. But the question caught me off guard because I've never had to justify it before. To anyone. Not even to myself.

My partner mentioned, gently, that maybe the Sunday lunches could shift to every other week. That the kids are getting older and their schedules are filling up. He wasn't attacking anything -- he was being practical. But it felt like the start of something eroding. If we skip one week, then two, then the meal becomes a monthly obligation that people rearrange their calendars around rather than something that simply is.

I know that's not rational. Things have to bend sometimes. I just don't want to be the one who let them break. Three generations of Sunday lunches in that kitchen. My grandfather built the long table specifically because he wanted everyone to sit together. It wasn't incidental. It was a decision, and decisions like that deserve to be honored even when they stop being convenient.

Stayed late at the lab again. Got home after the kids were asleep. Dina didn't say anything but I could tell from the way she left my dinner on the counter instead of the table. That's her signal.

sources.journal_entry:
Second time writing today which is unusual. Just got back from putting the kids to bed. Layla wanted me to read to her and I did three chapters of that Junie B. Jones book she's obsessed with. Omar fell asleep on my lap halfway through. Small thing but I needed it.

Dina and I actually talked after. Not about logistics for once. She told me about this cooking class she wants to take on Saturdays, Palestinian dishes from her grandmother's recipes. Her eyes lit up describing it. I told her she absolutely should and I'd handle the kids Saturday mornings. She looked surprised, like she wasn't expecting me to just say yes. That bothered me a little because it means she's gotten used to me being unavailable.

But I said yes and I meant it. Saturday mornings are mine with the kids and hers for the class. This is something I can actually hold onto. The dissertation won't collapse because I take three hours on a Saturday. And Dina deserves to have something that's just for her, same way the PhD is my thing. Though calling the PhD "my thing" feels strange when it's supposed to be for all of us. Whatever, the point is tonight felt right. I was present and it didn't cost me anything I'll regret.

Monday again. Advisor meeting at 10, went fine I think, he wants the literature review chapter revised by Friday which is tight but manageable. Spent the afternoon in the lab calibrating the shake table sensors. Boring but necessary work, nobody else was going to do it.

Dina took Omar to the pediatrician because he's had this cough for two weeks. She texted me the update: nothing serious, probably allergies, they gave him a prescription. I should've gone with her but Mondays are impossible with the advisor meeting and the TA prep for Tuesday's section. She handled it fine. She always handles it fine. That's partly the problem I guess, she's so capable that I lean on her for everything outside the lab and at some point that stops being partnership and starts being something else.

Called my mother in the evening. She asked when I'm defending. When I said probably next spring she went quiet then started talking about my cousin Faisal who just got promoted to department head at the ministry back home. He's two years younger than me. She didn't say it outright but the comparison was loud. Told her I had to go because Omar needed a bath, which was true but also convenient.
sources.nudge_response: Just imbalance I think. Not worth spiraling about right now.

Apologized to Dina this morning properly. Not just a mumbled sorry but sat down with her during the kids' cartoons and told her I knew I was being unfair. She said she knows the pressure I'm under but she needs me to not take it out on her. Fair. Completely fair.

Made pancakes for everyone after. Layla put chocolate chips in hers in the shape of a smiley face. Omar ate his with his hands and got syrup everywhere. Normal family morning and I was actually there for it instead of hunched over my laptop. Advisor can wait until tomorrow.

Pulled two all-nighters this week to get the chapter revision done. Submitted it at 4am. Body is wrecked. Dina asked if I was okay and I snapped at her, said I was fine when I obviously wasn't. Feel awful about that. She doesn't deserve my stress dumped on her.
sources.nudge_response: Guilty. Because she was being caring and I resented it somehow. Like her concern reminded me I'd been neglecting everything that wasn't the dissertation.

New month. Advisor approved the revised chapter with minor edits. Felt good to get that confirmation after the crunch. Started outlining the methodology chapter, should be more straightforward since it's describing work I've already done.

Dina started her Saturday cooking class last week. She came home with maftoul and it was better than my mother's, which I will never say to my mother. The kids and I went to the park while she was gone. Taught Layla to pump on the swing by herself. Omar mostly ate sand. Standard Saturday. This arrangement is working and I want to protect it.

Apologized to Dina this morning properly. Not just a mumbled sorry but sat down with her during the kids' cartoons and told her I knew I was being unfair. She said she knows the pressure I'm under but she needs me to not take it out on her. Fair. Completely fair.

Made pancakes for everyone after. Layla put chocolate chips in hers in the shape of a smiley face. Omar ate his with his hands and got syrup everywhere. Normal family morning and I was actually there for it instead of hunched over my laptop. Advisor can wait until tomorrow.

Pulled two all-nighters this week to get the chapter revision done. Submitted it at 4am. Body is wrecked. Dina asked if I was okay and I snapped at her, said I was fine when I obviously wasn't. Feel awful about that. She doesn't deserve my stress dumped on her.
sources.nudge_response: Guilty. Because she was being caring and I resented it somehow. Like her concern reminded me I'd been neglecting everything that wasn't the dissertation.

sources.journal_entry:
Second time writing today which is unusual. Just got back from putting the kids to bed. Layla wanted me to read to her and I did three chapters of that Junie B. Jones book she's obsessed with. Omar fell asleep on my lap halfway through. Small thing but I needed it.

Dina and I actually talked after. Not about logistics for once. She told me about this cooking class she wants to take on Saturdays, Palestinian dishes from her grandmother's recipes. Her eyes lit up describing it. I told her she absolutely should and I'd handle the kids Saturday mornings. She looked surprised, like she wasn't expecting me to just say yes. That bothered me a little because it means she's gotten used to me being unavailable.

But I said yes and I meant it. Saturday mornings are mine with the kids and hers for the class. This is something I can actually hold onto. The dissertation won't collapse because I take three hours on a Saturday. And Dina deserves to have something that's just for her, same way the PhD is my thing. Though calling the PhD "my thing" feels strange when it's supposed to be for all of us. Whatever, the point is tonight felt right. I was present and it didn't cost me anything I'll regret.

Monday again. Advisor meeting at 10, went fine I think, he wants the literature review chapter revised by Friday which is tight but manageable. Spent the afternoon in the lab calibrating the shake table sensors. Boring but necessary work, nobody else was going to do it.

Dina took Omar to the pediatrician because he's had this cough for two weeks. She texted me the update: nothing serious, probably allergies, they gave him a prescription. I should've gone with her but Mondays are impossible with the advisor meeting and the TA prep for Tuesday's section. She handled it fine. She always handles it fine. That's partly the problem I guess, she's so capable that I lean on her for everything outside the lab and at some point that stops being partnership and starts being something else.

Called my mother in the evening. She asked when I'm defending. When I said probably next spring she went quiet then started talking about my cousin Faisal who just got promoted to department head at the ministry back home. He's two years younger than me. She didn't say it outright but the comparison was loud. Told her I had to go because Omar needed a bath, which was true but also convenient.
sources.nudge_response: Just imbalance I think. Not worth spiraling about right now.

sources.journal_entry:
Stayed late at the lab again. Got home after the kids were asleep. Dina didn't say anything but I could tell from the way she left my dinner on the counter instead of the table. That's her signal.

The thing is I know I should've been home earlier. Layla had her first swimming lesson and I told her this morning I'd try to make it. "Try" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. I didn't try. I got pulled into running another simulation batch and the hours just disappeared. And now my kid learned to float without me there and I can't get that back. I keep telling myself the PhD is for them, for our future, but some of these moments don't wait for dissertations to be finished.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly all of them. But the ones where they stop asking me to come. That's what scares me.

Spent the morning reviewing proposals from two potential investors. One offers more capital but wants a board seat and quarterly reviews. The other is smaller but completely hands-off. Everyone keeps telling me the bigger check is the obvious choice. But I keep thinking about three years ago when I walked away from a salary that would make most people's eyes water, all because I couldn't stand someone else dictating my calendar.

Maybe I'm being naive. Maybe smart founders take the bigger check and learn to play the game. But every time I imagine sitting in those quarterly reviews, justifying my decisions to people who've never built anything themselves, something in my chest tightens.
sources.nudge_response: It's the same feeling I had in my last corporate job. Before I quit. Like I'm slowly being boxed in. When I was younger I thought I'd outgrow it, learn to compromise. But if anything it's gotten stronger. I think that feeling is my compass now—when it shows up, I know I'm about to betray something important about how I want to live.

sources.journal_entry:
My mother called from Tehran today. She wanted to know when I'm getting married, when I'm having children, when I'm going to "settle down and stop playing." I'm almost forty. I've heard these questions my whole adult life. Usually I brush them off. Today it got under my skin more than usual.

I think it's because part of me wonders if she has a point. Not about marriage specifically—I'll figure that out when I figure it out. But about what I'm building toward. I work hard, yes, but I also make sure to enjoy the fruits of that work. Weekends in Oman. Good wine. A nice apartment. She sees all of that as frivolous, as avoiding responsibility. In her world, you sacrifice everything for family, for the future, for some distant reward.

But I've watched people sacrifice their entire lives for that distant reward and then die before they get there. Or they get there and realize they forgot how to enjoy anything. I don't want that. I refuse that. And yet—today, after we hung up, I sat on my balcony for an hour just staring at the water, wondering if my version of a good life will leave me alone at sixty with nothing but nice memories.
sources.nudge_response: The one where I'm present. Where I'm actually living my days instead of deferring them. I've tried the other way—grinding through miserable weeks for some hypothetical payoff. It made me sick, literally. Migraines, insomnia. My body rejected it. So I know what's true for me. I just wish knowing made it easier to hear my mother's disappointment.

sources.journal_entry:
We went to Muscat for three days. Left my laptop at home—Layla's one condition. First day I was restless, kept reaching for my phone. By the third day I had forgotten what I was even anxious about.

We hiked to this natural pool in the mountains. Cold water, complete silence except for birds. I floated on my back and watched clouds move and thought: this is why I built my own thing. Not for the money, not for the status. For moments like this, whenever I want them. The ability to disappear for three days without asking permission.

I need to protect this. The business should serve the life, not the other way around.

Layla and I got into it last night. She thinks I work too much. I think that's rich coming from someone who doesn't understand what it takes to run your own thing. When you're employed, you clock out and your problems stay at the office. When it's YOUR company, it follows you everywhere.

But then—I don't know. She made this comment about how I used to be more fun. More spontaneous. And it stung because she's not wrong. The last few months I've been grinding harder than usual, trying to prove to myself that taking the smaller check was the right call. Trying to show I can grow this thing without giving up control.

I hate that I'm becoming the person I swore I wouldn't become. The one who's always "busy."
sources.nudge_response: I don't want to think about that right now. I just needed to get this out. I know what I need to do—I need to take her somewhere nice for the holidays and actually be present. That's the plan.

sources.journal_entry:
Turned down the Bahrain project. Explained that I could consult remotely but wouldn't relocate. They accepted, which surprised me. I expected them to walk away. Maybe I've been underestimating my leverage. Maybe I've been saying yes to things out of scarcity when I could afford to negotiate.

Layla was relieved. She said, "You're finally acting like someone who knows what he wants." I think she's right. For years I was running from things—from my old career, from expectations, from boredom. Now I'm starting to run toward something specific. A life that actually fits. It's a subtle shift but it feels significant.

We're planning another trip for March. Somewhere new. The reward for good work isn't more work—it's more life.

Funny thing happened today. One of my clients—a resort chain—asked if I'd relocate to Bahrain for six months to oversee an opening. Great money, interesting project. My immediate reaction was no. Not because of the work, but because I imagined six months without my Thursday dinners at that Lebanese place, without my morning runs along the creek, without the routines that make my life here feel like mine.

Then I caught myself and thought—wait, am I becoming rigid? I built this life precisely so I could be flexible. So I could say yes to adventures. But now I'm protecting routines like they're sacred.

Or maybe routines are sacred. Maybe I've earned the right to build a life I don't want to escape from. Maybe flexibility isn't about saying yes to every opportunity but about having the freedom to say no.

I don't know. I told them I'd think about it over the weekend.

My old colleague Faisal reached out. He's now a VP at a big consulting firm, wanted to know if I'd consider coming back to corporate. "Senior role, name your salary, you'd have a team of twenty."

I said no, obviously. But then he made this comment—"You're still doing the solo thing? I thought that was a phase." And I felt this flash of anger. Like I needed to justify myself. Started listing my clients, my revenue, my growth numbers. Trying to prove I wasn't some hobbyist.

Later I wondered why I cared so much. Why his opinion mattered. I left that world for a reason. I don't owe anyone an explanation.
sources.nudge_response: Maybe the fear that I'm fooling myself. That everyone else sees something I don't—that I gave up a real career to play entrepreneur, and one day it'll all fall apart and I'll have nothing to show for it. I know that's not rational. My business is healthy. But there's this voice that sounds a lot like my father, saying I'm not serious enough. That real men build empires, not lifestyles. I thought I'd silenced that voice. Apparently not.

Three days into building my own pipeline and I'm already behind on coursework. Stayed up until four last night debugging tokenizer issues that would've been solved if I'd just used the lab's existing toolkit. My officemate Nina asked if I wanted help and I said no before I even thought about it. That was stupid. She's good at this stuff and she wasn't going to steal the project.

I keep doing this — refusing help because I need it to be entirely mine, and then drowning quietly. The fellowship application is due Friday and I haven't started the personal statement because every time I open it I think about how I'm supposed to frame myself as a team player. I don't know how to write that without it feeling like a lie, but I also don't know how to explain that I work better alone without sounding like a problem.

People keep asking why I turned down Professor Hecht's placement like I owe them an explanation. It was a bad fit. I don't need to justify building something from scratch when the alternative is tweaking someone else's framework for two years. My project, my call.

sources.journal_entry:
Weird day. Started normal — coffee, standup, tickets. Then around lunch Pieter from platform team pinged me about a side project he's been hacking on, this internal tool for tracking deployment health across services. He wanted to know if I'd help build the backend. Not sanctioned work, just something he thinks would be useful and wants to pitch to leadership once it's built.

First thought was yes obviously, this is the kind of thing I actually want to spend time on, building something new without twelve layers of sign-off. Second thought was that Martijn would not love me spending cycles on an unsanctioned project right when he's evaluating me for lead. Third thought was that Pieter didn't ask anyone else, he asked me, and that felt good in a way I don't fully understand. Like someone saw the part of me that wants to just build.

Her dad asked about the promotion and I gave the standard answer — it's in progress, I'm grateful for the opportunity, etc. He seemed pleased. Then on Sunday I stayed up way too late working on Pieter's tool and got completely absorbed refactoring the data ingestion layer. Noor asked what I was doing and I said "just work stuff" which wasn't really a lie but wasn't the whole truth either. I don't know why I didn't just explain it. Maybe because explaining it would mean admitting how much more alive that project makes me feel, and then someone might ask what that says about everything else.

sources.journal_entry:
Weird day. Started normal — coffee, standup, tickets. First thought was yes obviously, this is the kind of thing I actually want to spend time on, building something new without twelve layers of sign-off. sources.journal_entry:
Same day, later. Parents were thrilled, mum teared up a little. Had a glass of wine with Noor and she kept saying she knew it would happen. Everyone's reaction confirmed that this was the right move, or at least the expected one, and those two things feel like they should be different but tonight they're the same and I'm too tired to untangle it.

I keep coming back to something small. When Martijn told me, my first feeling wasn't excitement. It was relief. Relief that it's done, that I don't have to hold the performance anymore, that I can stop wondering and just be in the role. Maybe excitement comes later. Or maybe relief is enough. I genuinely don't know and I'm going to stop thinking about it and go to bed.
Got the tech lead offer. Accepted on the spot because that's what you do. Texted Noor and she sent about fifteen celebration emojis. Calling my parents tonight.

Martijn pulled me aside after standup. Apparently someone mentioned to him that I've been spending time on Pieter's tool and he wanted to know if it was affecting my sprint commitments. It isn't — I've been keeping my velocity up — but the way he framed it made it sound like a warning. "Just want to make sure your priorities are clear," he said.

I told him it wouldn't be an issue and that the tool is now being folded into the platform roadmap anyway, so it's legitimate work. He nodded and dropped it. But I've been replaying the conversation all afternoon. The rational part of me knows he was just doing his job. The other part feels like I got caught doing something I wasn't supposed to enjoy. I hate that I felt the need to justify it. I hate more that I did justify it, immediately, without pushing back at all.
sources.nudge_response: Saying something like "I'm delivering on everything you've asked, so what I do with my remaining time is my call." Which is true. But I keep imagining how that would land — confrontational, difficult, not a team player. So I default to the smooth version. And then I'm annoyed at myself for it later, which is its own kind of exhausting.

sources.journal_entry: Presented the deployment health tool to Pieter's skip-level manager today. She liked it. Asked if we'd want to bring it under the platform roadmap officially. Said yes without hesitating.
sources.nudge_response: Some things don't need overthinking.

sources.journal_entry:
Team drinks after work. Everyone was congratulating me about the shortlist like it's already decided. I kept saying it wasn't confirmed yet but nobody listens. Devika made a joke about me being her future boss and I laughed but it sat wrong with me for the rest of the evening.

I don't think I'm being fake about it. I genuinely want to do well, and the role comes with better pay, more visibility, things that matter. But there's this gap between how I talk about it to other people and what actually runs through my head at 11pm when I'm staring at Pieter's repo. Not sure what to do with that. For now I'm doing both, which is sustainable enough.

Martijn officially put me on the lead shortlist. Two candidates, me and someone from the other squad. I thanked him and said I'd put my best foot forward. Which I will. Whatever doubts I have aren't anyone else's problem to carry.

Noor and I went to dinner with her parents in Rotterdam on Saturday. Her dad asked about the promotion and I gave the standard answer — it's in progress, I'm grateful for the opportunity, etc. He seemed pleased. On the train back Noor said she was proud of me and I felt genuinely good about it. Like I'm on a track that makes sense to the people I care about.

Then on Sunday I stayed up way too late working on Pieter's tool and got completely absorbed refactoring the data ingestion layer. Noor asked what I was doing and I said "just work stuff" which wasn't really a lie but wasn't the whole truth either. I don't know why I didn't just explain it. Maybe because explaining it would mean admitting how much more alive that project makes me feel, and then someone might ask what that says about everything else.
sources.nudge_response: Probably nothing bad. She'd understand. I think the issue is more that saying it out loud makes it real — that the path everyone's excited about for me isn't the one that lights me up. And then I'd have to figure out what to do with that.

sources.journal_entry:
Told Pieter I'd help with the tool. We set up a repo and I spent an hour last night after Noor went to sleep scaffolding the API layer. Felt more engaged in that hour than I have all sprint on the actual work.

Today was back to normal though — reviewing PRs, answering Slack threads, sitting through a planning session where half the decisions had already been made before we walked in. The usual. I'm not complaining, it's fine. I just noticed the contrast, that's all.
sources.nudge_response: Yeah. It's work, it doesn't all have to be exciting.

sources.journal_entry:
Weird day. Started normal — coffee, standup, tickets. Then around lunch Pieter from platform team pinged me about a side project he's been hacking on, this internal tool for tracking deployment health across services. He wanted to know if I'd help build the backend. Not sanctioned work, just something he thinks would be useful and wants to pitch to leadership once it's built.

First thought was yes obviously, this is the kind of thing I actually want to spend time on, building something new without twelve layers of sign-off. Second thought was that Martijn would not love me spending cycles on an unsanctioned project right when he's evaluating me for lead. Third thought was that Pieter didn't ask anyone else, he asked me, and that felt good in a way I don't fully understand. Like someone saw the part of me that wants to just build.

I told Pieter I'd think about it over the weekend. Which is code for "I want to do it but I need to figure out if I'm allowed to want to do it." That sounds ridiculous written down. I'm a grown man deciding whether to write some code on the side. But it feels more loaded than that right now.

Sprint retro got a bit heated. Devika suggested we rethink the approval flow for deployments because she thinks it slows us down. She's right, technically — it does add a half-day lag. I had a whole alternative sketched in my head while she was talking, a lighter-weight check that would still catch the critical stuff.

Didn't say it though. The senior architects set up the current flow and they were in the call. Felt like bringing up a redesign right there would come across as me trying to show off, especially with the tech lead thing floating around. So I just nodded and said I could look into Devika's point offline. She seemed a bit deflated that nobody backed her up more directly. I get it.

Long week. Spent most of it pairing with the new hire, walking her through the codebase and our deployment pipeline. Didn't get to touch my own backlog at all but she's ramping up faster than the last person we onboarded so I'll take it.

Had the tech lead conversation with Martijn today. He laid out what the role would look like — running standups, making architecture calls, representing the team in cross-department meetings. I said I was interested, which is true, but the whole time I was thinking about how I'd actually handle it. I build things well when people leave me alone to think. That's not what this role is.

But I also know I did the right thing saying yes. Everyone on the team expects it, Noor would think I was insane to turn it down, and frankly it would look odd to pass on a promotion you're being handed. I can figure out the rest as I go. Probably.

sources.journal_entry:
Thinking more about the board thing from yesterday. Turned it down this morning. Polite email, said maybe next year. But now I'm sitting with this feeling like I just closed a door I shouldn't have. My buddy Jake from college is VP of Operations at a company half our size. He's thirty-two. He's on two industry boards, he did that leadership program at Northwestern, and every time I see his LinkedIn I feel this pull in my chest like I'm falling behind some invisible race.

I know comparison is poison. I know that. But it's hard when the scoreboard is right there on your phone. Jake doesn't have a grandfather who spent fifty years building something with his name on it. Jake doesn't sit at a dinner table every Sunday hearing about how things were done the right way. Jake just has a title and a trajectory and nobody asking him to preserve anything.

Meanwhile I'm trying to grow this company AND keep it feeling like the company it's always been. Like those two things are the same direction. Most days they are. But days like today they feel like opposite ends of a rope and I'm standing in the middle.

Had a call with the regional HVAC association about their young leaders program. They want me to apply for the board. On paper it's a great opportunity — good network, visibility in the industry, looks sharp on a resume. But the meetings are every other Thursday evening, which is when I do my site walkthroughs with the install crews.

Those walkthroughs aren't required. Nobody would notice if I stopped. But Grandpa drilled it into me when I started: you show up where the work happens, you shake the hands of the guys turning the wrenches. It's how you earn trust. Feels wrong to swap that out for a conference call with people trading business cards. But then I look at some of the other managers my age who are on three boards and speaking at conferences while I'm in a crawlspace checking ductwork.
sources.nudge_response: The walkthroughs. No question. I'd never forgive myself otherwise.

sources.journal_entry:
Sunday dinner. Grandpa wasn't feeling well so it was just Mom, Dad, and me. Without Grandpa at the table the whole energy was different. Dad talked about maybe expanding into the residential solar market. I've been thinking about it too — the margins are there, the demand is growing, it's a natural fit. But when I brought it up to Grandpa last month he said "we're heating and cooling people, that's what we do."

I didn't push it. How do you push it with an eighty-year-old man who built the thing from nothing? He earned the right to say no. But tonight Dad said something that's been rattling around in my head since — he said "your grandfather doesn't run the company anymore, Ryan. You do." And I know that's technically true. My name is on the decisions. But it doesn't feel true. It feels like I'm managing a museum and every choice I make is either a restoration or a renovation and I can never tell which one the family wants.

I keep going back to that nod at his birthday party. What was he passing to me exactly? The company as it is? Or the company as whatever I can make it? I genuinely don't know. And I'm scared to ask because what if the answer is something I can't live with.
Danny used the new scheduling software today. Without being asked. Came in, saw the tablet on the wall, and just started putting jobs in. Didn't say a word about it. I didn't either.
sources.nudge_response: Relief. Like I finally got permission to move forward.

sources.journal_entry:
Performance reviews this week. Had to sit down with each of my crew leads and go through their numbers. Most of the conversations went fine but Danny — he's been with us nineteen years, started under Grandpa — pushed back when I talked about the new scheduling software. Said it was "a solution looking for a problem" and that the whiteboard system works fine.

I wanted to snap at him. The whiteboard system loses us hours every week in double-bookings and missed follow-ups. I have the data. But instead I heard myself saying "let's give it a trial run and see how it goes, no pressure." Which is exactly what Grandpa would have done — never force it, bring people along. But part of me thinks Grandpa could afford to be patient because he had decades. I don't feel like I have decades. sources.journal_entry:
Had a weird moment today. Was driving back from a site visit and passed the old Whitfield Heating building — the original one on Division Avenue that Grandpa worked out of before we moved to the new place in '02. It's a laundromat now. The sign is gone, the awning's different, there's nothing left of what it was. Just a building someone else uses for something else. I pulled over and sat there for a minute. Not because I was sad exactly. More like I was looking at the future.

Someday the new building will be something else too. Someday the name on the trucks will change, or the trucks will be gone, or the whole industry will be different. Nothing I do is permanent. Nothing Grandpa did was permanent. The only thing that lasts is whether you did it right while you were doing it.

Something shifted sitting in that parking lot. Like maybe I've been so focused on holding everything together exactly as it is that I forgot the point was never the building or the sign. It was how you treated people, how you showed up, whether you left things better than you found them. Grandpa didn't preserve his father's business — he built his own. Maybe that's what the nod meant. Not "keep this the same." Just "do it right." I'm still not sure about solar. But I'm less afraid of the question now.
sources.nudge_response: I stopped seeing it as either/or. It was never about furnaces.

sources.journal_entry:
Fourth of July at the lake house. The whole family thing — burgers, fireworks, Uncle Bill doing his annual speech about "what this country was built on." I usually tune it out but this year he looked at me during the part about "carrying the torch" and I realized he wasn't just talking about America.

Cousin Travis was there again. This time he asked how the company was doing and I gave him the numbers — up fourteen percent year over year, best Q2 since 2019, retention above ninety percent. He nodded and said "so it's doing well?" and I said yes. Then he asked "but are YOU doing well?" and I didn't have an answer. I said something about being busy, which is true but not what he was asking. The honest answer is I don't separate the two. The company does well, I'm doing well. The company struggles, I struggle. I don't know if that's dedication or if it's a problem.
sources.nudge_response: I honestly don't know. That's what scares me.

sources.journal_entry:
Sunday dinner. Grandpa wasn't feeling well so it was just Mom, Dad, and me. Without Grandpa at the table the whole energy was different. Dad talked about maybe expanding into the residential solar market. I've been thinking about it too — the margins are there, the demand is growing, it's a natural fit. But when I brought it up to Grandpa last month he said "we're heating and cooling people, that's what we do."

I didn't push it. How do you push it with an eighty-year-old man who built the thing from nothing? He earned the right to say no. But tonight Dad said something that's been rattling around in my head since — he said "your grandfather doesn't run the company anymore, Ryan. You do." And I know that's technically true. My name is on the decisions. But it doesn't feel true. It feels like I'm managing a museum and every choice I make is either a restoration or a renovation and I can never tell which one the family wants.

I keep going back to that nod at his birthday party. What was he passing to me exactly? The company as it is? Or the company as whatever I can make it? I genuinely don't know. And I'm scared to ask because what if the answer is something I can't live with.
Danny used the new scheduling software today. Without being asked. Came in, saw the tablet on the wall, and just started putting jobs in. Didn't say a word about it. I didn't either.
sources.nudge_response: Relief. Like I finally got permission to move forward.

sources.journal_entry:
Performance reviews this week. Had to sit down with each of my crew leads and go through their numbers. Most of the conversations went fine but Danny — he's been with us nineteen years, started under Grandpa — pushed back when I talked about the new scheduling software. Said it was "a solution looking for a problem" and that the whiteboard system works fine.

I wanted to snap at him. The whiteboard system loses us hours every week in double-bookings and missed follow-ups. I have the data. But instead I heard myself saying "let's give it a trial run and see how it goes, no pressure." Which is exactly what Grandpa would have done — never force it, bring people along. But part of me thinks Grandpa could afford to be patient because he had decades. I don't feel like I have decades. The market is moving and if we don't modernize the ops side we'll be the company that did great work in the '90s and couldn't keep up.
sources.nudge_response: His respect. And every guy on the floor who remembers Grandpa.

sources.journal_entry:
Grandpa's 80th birthday party Saturday. The whole family came — uncles, cousins, people I haven't seen since I was a kid. Mom put together a slideshow with photos from when he first started the company. There's one of him standing in front of his first van, WHITFIELD HEATING hand-painted on the side. He was twenty-six in that picture. Three years younger than I am now.

Uncle Bill gave a toast about how the company was built on handshakes and showing up. Everyone raised their glasses. I watched Grandpa's face and he was trying not to cry. He looked at me across the table at one point and nodded, this small nod like he was passing something forward. I can't explain why that hit so hard.

Later that night I went out to the driveway to get some air and my cousin Travis followed me out. He works in tech in Seattle, does well for himself. He asked me if I ever thought about doing something else, something that was just mine. I told him the company IS mine. He kind of shrugged and said "you know what I mean." I do know what he means. But I also think he doesn't understand what it feels like to be part of something that started before you were born and will keep going after you're gone. There's weight to that. Some days it's an anchor. Other days it's the only thing keeping me steady.

Just realized I wrote twice in one day. Whatever. Came home and Jake posted about keynoting some supply chain conference. Good for him. I'm going to go prep my Q2 numbers because at least those are mine.
sources.nudge_response: That I actually built something real. Forty-three paychecks.

sources.journal_entry:
Thinking more about the board thing from yesterday. Turned it down this morning. Polite email, said maybe next year. But now I'm sitting with this feeling like I just closed a door I shouldn't have. My buddy Jake from college is VP of Operations at a company half our size. He's thirty-two. He's on two industry boards, he did that leadership program at Northwestern, and every time I see his LinkedIn I feel this pull in my chest like I'm falling behind some invisible race.

I know comparison is poison. I know that. But it's hard when the scoreboard is right there on your phone. Jake doesn't have a grandfather who spent fifty years building something with his name on it. Jake doesn't sit at a dinner table every Sunday hearing about how things were done the right way. Jake just has a title and a trajectory and nobody asking him to preserve anything.

Meanwhile I'm trying to grow this company AND keep it feeling like the company it's always been. Like those two things are the same direction. Most days they are. But days like today they feel like opposite ends of a rope and I'm standing in the middle.

Had a call with the regional HVAC association about their young leaders program. They want me to apply for the board. On paper it's a great opportunity — good network, visibility in the industry, looks sharp on a resume. But the meetings are every other Thursday evening, which is when I do my site walkthroughs with the install crews.

Those walkthroughs aren't required. Nobody would notice if I stopped. But Grandpa drilled it into me when I started: you show up where the work happens, you shake the hands of the guys turning the wrenches. It's how you earn trust. Feels wrong to swap that out for a conference call with people trading business cards. But then I look at some of the other managers my age who are on three boards and speaking at conferences while I'm in a crawlspace checking ductwork.
sources.nudge_response: The walkthroughs. No question. I'd never forgive myself otherwise.

sources.journal_entry: Closed the Meyer Medical Group contract today — biggest commercial deal we've landed this quarter. Stayed late to call Grandpa and tell him before the rest of the family heard. He said "that's my boy" and I don't think I've smiled like that in a month.

Dad brought up the Hendricks thing at Sunday dinner. In front of everyone. Said maybe I should have driven out there in person instead of sending a proposal over email. Like I haven't been running seventy hours a week already.
sources.nudge_response: That he might be right. Grandpa would've driven out there.

sources.journal_entry: Long day. Lost the Hendricks account because their new facilities guy wants to go with a national chain. Grandpa built that relationship in '89 and I just watched it walk out the door.

Got an email from my cousin Faris today, forwarding photos from his daughter's first birthday party back in Amman. The whole family was there — uncles, aunts, my mother holding the baby with that particular look she gets. I was not invited to skip it; I just was not there. No one said anything pointed but the group chat went quiet for a while after the photos dropped and I could feel the space where my name should have been.

Nothing happened, really. I ate leftover lentil soup, re-read a paper on morphological parsing, tried to focus. My flatmate Callum asked if I wanted to go to a pub quiz and I said no, then sat there wishing I had said yes.
sources.nudge_response: It is not that they are angry. It is that they have stopped expecting me to show up. That is worse, I think. Like I have been reclassified from "absent" to "gone."

Second entry today because my brain will not shut off. After the call with my mother I went for a walk up Arthur's Seat. Halfway up I got this rush of clarity — or maybe it was just adrenaline — where I started thinking about what it would look like to pivot my thesis entirely. Not the careful narrowing Dr. Keane wants. Something bigger. Cross-linguistic transfer models for under-resourced dialects. Levantine, Gulf, Maghrebi. My heart was actually racing on the hill and it was not from the climb.

Then I sat on the bench at the top and the wind hit me and I thought about what pivoting would mean. Another meeting with Keane where I contradict what I said three days ago. My mother asking again when I will finish. My uncle Hisham, who helped fund the first year, shaking his head at another delay. Everyone back home already thinks this PhD was an impulsive detour, and changing direction again would prove them right.

So I walked back down, made tea, opened the narrowed proposal draft. Still sitting here with it. The cursor is blinking at the end of paragraph three and I have not typed anything in forty minutes.

Friday call with my mother went well for once. She asked about the thesis and I described the morphological analysis angle in simple terms — how computers learn to break Arabic words into their root pieces. She said it sounded useful, which from her is high praise.

I felt like myself on that call. Not performing, not deflecting her questions about when I am coming home. Just explaining something I actually care about to someone who wanted to listen. She even asked a follow-up about how the root system works differently in dialects. Small thing, but it settled something in me.

Library until six. Drafted the introduction for the narrowed thesis proposal, which took longer than it should have because I kept second-guessing paragraph transitions. Callum and I walked to the chippie on Clerk Street after.

Supervisor meeting. Dr. Keane asked me to commit to one research question by next Friday and I heard myself say yes, absolutely, no problem. Walked home and could not stop thinking about the three other directions I had sketched out last month.
sources.nudge_response: Because pushing back feels like making a scene, and I do not make scenes. My father never raised his voice in a meeting in his life. But I keep wondering if the question I pick will be the one that bores me by October.

sources.journal_entry:
Department social last night at The Pear Tree. I went because Dr. Keane mentioned it would be good to show face, and I know what that means in academic circles — it means attendance is optional in the way that prayer is optional at a family gathering. So I went.

Ended up in a long conversation with Priya from the NLP group. She is working on code-switching detection in Hindi-English tweets and the way she talked about it — with this specific, focused energy — made me jealous. Not of the topic. Of the certainty. She has her question, her method, her timeline. She did not seem to need a detour.

I told her about the dialect transfer idea. She said it sounded fascinating and asked why I was not doing it. I said timing, funding, the usual. She shrugged and said "those are real constraints" in a way that felt like she was politely letting me off the hook. I appreciated it and hated it at the same time.
sources.nudge_response: Something like "do it anyway." Or "those are excuses." Someone outside the family orbit giving me permission to be reckless. Which is ridiculous because I am thirty-eight years old and should not need permission from a colleague I barely know.

sources.journal_entry:
Second entry today because my brain will not shut off. After the call with my mother I went for a walk up Arthur's Seat. Halfway up I got this rush of clarity — or maybe it was just adrenaline — where I started thinking about what it would look like to pivot my thesis entirely. Not the careful narrowing Dr. Keane wants. Something bigger. Cross-linguistic transfer models for under-resourced dialects. Levantine, Gulf, Maghrebi. My heart was actually racing on the hill and it was not from the climb.

Then I sat on the bench at the top and the wind hit me and I thought about what pivoting would mean. Another meeting with Keane where I contradict what I said three days ago. My mother asking again when I will finish. My uncle Hisham, who helped fund the first year, shaking his head at another delay. Everyone back home already thinks this PhD was an impulsive detour, and changing direction again would prove them right.

So I walked back down, made tea, opened the narrowed proposal draft. Still sitting here with it. The cursor is blinking at the end of paragraph three and I have not typed anything in forty minutes.

Friday call with my mother went well for once. She asked about the thesis and I described the morphological analysis angle in simple terms — how computers learn to break Arabic words into their root pieces. She said it sounded useful, which from her is high praise.

I felt like myself on that call. Not performing, not deflecting her questions about when I am coming home. Just explaining something I actually care about to someone who wanted to listen. She even asked a follow-up about how the root system works differently in dialects. Small thing, but it settled something in me.

Library until six. Drafted the introduction for the narrowed thesis proposal, which took longer than it should have because I kept second-guessing paragraph transitions. Callum and I walked to the chippie on Clerk Street after.

Supervisor meeting. Dr. Keane asked me to commit to one research question by next Friday and I heard myself say yes, absolutely, no problem. Walked home and could not stop thinking about the three other directions I had sketched out last month.
sources.nudge_response: Because pushing back feels like making a scene, and I do not make scenes. My father never raised his voice in a meeting in his life. But I keep wondering if the question I pick will be the one that bores me by October.

sources.journal_entry:
Got an email from my cousin Faris today, forwarding photos from his daughter's first birthday party back in Amman. The whole family was there — uncles, aunts, my mother holding the baby with that particular look she gets. I was not invited to skip it; I just was not there. No one said anything pointed but the group chat went quiet for a while after the photos dropped and I could feel the space where my name should have been.

Nothing happened, really. I ate leftover lentil soup, re-read a paper on morphological parsing, tried to focus. My flatmate Callum asked if I wanted to go to a pub quiz and I said no, then sat there wishing I had said yes.
sources.nudge_response: It is not that they are angry. It is that they have stopped expecting me to show up. That is worse, I think. Like I have been reclassified from "absent" to "gone."

Went to the Edinburgh Farmers' Market at Castle Terrace this morning, mostly for the za'atar bread from the Lebanese stall. Ran into Priya and her partner. We talked about the summer conference circuit and she mentioned a workshop on low-resource NLP in Copenhagen in September. She looked at me when she said it, like she knew.

I came home and emailed Dr. Keane asking for a meeting next week. Just to discuss, I wrote. I did not say what about. But I printed out the dialect transfer outline and put it in my bag. Maybe I will bring it, maybe I will not. It is in the bag though. That feels like enough for today.
sources.nudge_response: Because I need to know it is there. Like a door I have not walked through yet but I can see. If I leave it at home it is just a file on my laptop. In the bag it is something I chose to carry. I think I am going to show it. I think I have been working up to this for weeks and I just did not want to admit it because admitting it means it matters, and if it matters then Keane saying no will actually hurt.

sources.journal_entry:
My uncle Hisham called today. Not the usual Friday family call — a separate, pointed call. He asked how the PhD was going and I told him I submitted the proposal. He said good, asked about the timeline, and then said he hoped I was not "chasing new rabbits" — his phrase, not mine. Apparently my mother mentioned something about dialect research and he connected dots.

I told him everything was on track, the proposal was submitted, Dr. Keane was happy. All true. I did not mention the outline document from last night. It is not lying. It is managing information. People share what is relevant and I shared what was relevant.

Submitted the narrowed thesis proposal to Dr. Keane this morning. Forty-two pages, bibliography cleaned up, research questions scoped to morphological segmentation for Modern Standard Arabic. Felt like handing in a homework assignment I had done properly rather than one that kept me up at night, but there is something to be said for finishing.

Callum and I cooked mansaf tonight — or my version of it, which involves Greek yogurt because Edinburgh does not have decent jameed. He kept asking questions about the spices and I caught myself explaining things the way my mother does, with small corrections and zero patience. Made me laugh.

After dinner I sat with my laptop and, almost without thinking about it, opened a blank document and started outlining the dialect transfer idea. Not as a thesis. Just notes. No one has to see it. I wrote for an hour and it was the most alive I have felt in front of a screen in weeks.

values.user_phrase: Making the world a fairer, better place
values.approved_definition: Understanding, appreciation, tolerance, and protection for the welfare of all people and for nature. Derives from survival needs that become apparent when people recognize that failure to accept those who are different and treat them justly will lead to strife, and when people become aware of the scarcity of natural resources.

sources.journal_entry:
Slow day for orders so I worked on a logo draft for this small tofu shop near Mullae. The owner is from Gyeongsang-do, reminds me of my dad a bit, stubborn about everything but generous when it matters. He wants the logo to look "clean and honest," which is vague but I kind of get it. Spent two hours on it at the cafe near my place.

Between that and three deliveries I made maybe 40,000 won today. Rent is due next week. I keep doing the math and it never quite adds up but somehow it always works out. My friend Eunji keeps telling me to just take the full-time position at her company's marketing team. Stable salary, benefits, the whole package. But every time I think about sitting in an office doing campaign graphics for some supplement brand I feel this weight in my chest.
sources.nudge_response: Feeling trapped doing work I don't care about for money.

sources.journal_entry: Spent all afternoon in the heat doing deliveries and my last drop-off was to this grandmother living alone in a rooftop unit with no AC. She tried to give me a banana milk from her fridge. Took it, thanked her properly the way my mom taught me, and biked home feeling like at least one interaction today was real.
