Sunday. Woke up late, made doenjang-guk with leftover vegetables. Sat by the window eating and watching the pigeons on the building across the street. One of them kept trying to land on a ledge that was too narrow and sliding off, over and over. Kept at it though.

Went grocery shopping after. The ajumma at the market stall I always go to asked about my mom, which she does every time. I buy too many spring onions from her because I can never say no when she bundles in extras. Walked around Mapo for a while after, no real destination. Passed by the old bookstore on the corner and picked up a used copy of a Murakami novel I've already read twice. Something about the cover design on this edition was different and I liked it.

Called my mom in the evening. She was watching a cooking competition show and narrating the whole thing to me like I could see it. She does this. I mostly just listened. She asked if I'm eating properly and sleeping enough, the standard questions. I told her yes to both, which is half true. She told me my cousin Hyunwoo got promoted at his bank job and I said that's great. She didn't compare us, she never does, but I could hear her thinking about it. Or maybe that's just me projecting. Hard to tell sometimes.

I've been thinking about the annual vendor review coming up next month and I already know I'm going to let the Guangdong supplier pass without flagging the labor stuff. It's not that I don't care. I do. But raising it means a formal review process, means Kwon gets involved, means I have to justify the cost difference all over again, and last time I brought up anything remotely like this he looked at me like I was wasting his time. So I'll probably just sign off on the renewal and move on.

The thing is, I know exactly what the right thing to do is. Or at least what I think is right. It's not even ambiguous. But the gap between knowing and doing keeps getting wider and I can feel it. Like there's a version of me that would've already drafted the memo and cc'd everyone and not cared about the politics. And then there's the version of me that's sitting here at midnight writing about it in a journal instead.

values.user_phrase: Seeking new experiences and challenges
values.approved_definition: Excitement, novelty, and challenge in life. Derives from the organismic need for variety and stimulation in order to maintain an optimal, positive, rather than threatening, level of activation. This need probably relates to the needs underlying Self-Direction values.

sources.journal_entry: Spent the morning organizing my savings spreadsheet. I have enough for eight months of expenses if something goes wrong. That number used to make me feel safe. Today it just felt like a number. Had coffee with my sister. She mentioned a colleague looking for a roommate, assuming I might want to save on rent. Didn't correct her assumption.
sources.nudge_response: I think I realized I've been saving for an emergency that might never come. Or maybe saving so I'd have an excuse not to take risks. "Can't leave, I'm building my safety net." But the net is built. So now what?

sources.journal_entry:
Winter break finally started and I should be relieved. Instead I feel this strange hollowness. My cousin Rania announced her engagement yesterday at the family gathering—everyone was so happy, talking about wedding dates and apartments and furniture. I smiled and hugged her but inside I was somewhere else entirely.

I keep thinking about that email from my old friend Amir. He's starting an educational nonprofit in Morocco and asked if I'd consider joining for six months. Six months. The thought makes my chest tight in two directions—terrified of leaving my position, my apartment, my carefully built routine. But also something like hunger.

My mother would never understand. She still talks about how "irresponsible" Malaysia was. But I was 24 then. I'm 29 now. At what point do I stop blaming responsibility for my fear and fear for my responsibility?

I keep thinking about that email from my old friend Amir. He's starting an educational nonprofit in Morocco and asked if I'd consider joining for six months. Six months. The thought makes my chest tight in two directions—terrified of leaving my position, my apartment, my carefully built routine. But also something like hunger.

My mother would never understand. She still talks about how "irresponsible" Malaysia was. But I was 24 then. I'm 29 now. At what point do I stop blaming responsibility for my fear and fear for my responsibility?

sources.journal_entry: Commission is done but I hate it. The client wanted "bold and colorful" and I gave them exactly that and now it's sitting in their corporate lobby looking like a very expensive screensaver. Got paid though.

Applied to a residency in New Mexico. Three months in the desert with studio space and a stipend. Deadline was today. Spent all morning putting together the application materials. Portfolio, artist statement, project proposal.

For the proposal I wrote about wanting to explore the relationship between geological time and human impermanence using found desert materials. It sounds pretentious when I read it back but that's what they want to hear. The real reason I want to go is simpler: I'm bored here. Same coffee shop, same studio, same loop of galleries on First Thursday. I think I work better when everything around me is unfamiliar.

Started tallying up my applications this year. Fourteen residencies, eight group shows, three grants. Got into two group shows and one residency that I ended up turning down because it conflicted with a commission. That's a fifteen percent success rate if you're generous about the math. Industry standard is apparently around ten percent so I guess I'm doing okay. But okay isn't what I'm aiming for.

Still thinking about yesterday. Couldn't sleep so I went back through my old sketchbooks from freshman year. Forgot how much I used to draw just for myself back then, weird little creatures and impossible architecture, no thought about whether it would sell or fit a gallery theme. Somewhere around junior year I started thinking about everything in terms of what it could become, what door it might open.

Worked my gallery shift today. It was dead, which meant I had hours to just sit there and stare at the current exhibition. These stark minimalist paintings that all look almost identical to me, just slight variations in shade and proportion. The artist is represented in galleries across the country. People pay five figures for those canvases. And I genuinely don't know if I'm jealous or horrified.

The owner came in toward closing and we got to talking. She said something that stuck with me: "The artists who last aren't the ones who burn brightest, they're the ones who find something they can sustain." I nodded like I understood but I'm not sure I do. What if I'm just not built for sustainability? What if I need the burn to keep going?

Got rejected from another group show today. Third one this month. I know my work is good, the feedback from the last curator even said my pieces were "visually compelling" but "lacked cohesion with the exhibition theme." I keep telling myself that I need to find the right fit, but sitting here surrounded by half-finished canvases and a pile of rejection emails, it's hard not to question everything.

The worst part is I was so bored with my last series that I started experimenting with metalwork halfway through. Now my portfolio looks like three different artists made it. Maybe that's the problem. Everyone keeps saying to develop a "signature style" but the thought of making the same kind of work for years makes me want to throw my brushes in the trash.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly? It feels like a cage. Like agreeing to draw the same box over and over because galleries can sell it easier. But maybe I'm also scared that if I pick one thing, I'll find out I'm not actually great at it. Easier to be "promising" in five directions than mediocre in one.

sources.journal_entry:
Got the email this afternoon. I'm in. New Mexico residency, three months starting in March. I read the acceptance twice and then I just sat there staring at my screen for a while. Not jumping up and down, not immediately texting everyone I know. Just this weird quiet feeling, like something clicking into place.

Called my mom to tell her. She's worried about me being alone in the desert, which is funny because I'm alone in my studio most of the time anyway. But she's excited too. She asked if I was going to use this to "focus on one style finally" and I managed not to sigh into the phone. I told her I'm going to use it to make the best work I've ever made, whatever form that takes.

Started planning what to bring. Limited luggage means I have to choose which materials matter most. I'm thinking oil paints, my good brushes, sketchbooks, and nothing else. Let the desert fill in the gaps. Maybe that's what I've been missing, not a signature style but just enough constraint to push against. Every time I've made something I was proud of, it was because I had a problem to solve, not unlimited options. Something to think about.

My success rate for applications this year ended at nineteen percent. Still not where I want to be. But for once the math feels less important than what's actually happening. I'm going to make art in the desert. That's real.
sources.nudge_response: Maybe they're not as different as I thought. A signature style doesn't have to mean repetition, it could be a set of constraints I choose for myself rather than ones galleries or clients impose. The desert residency is forcing me to pick only essential materials, and I'm actually looking forward to that limitation. If I could do the same thing with my artistic approach, choose my own boundaries instead of resisting all boundaries, maybe that's the middle ground. Still figuring it out.

sources.journal_entry: Spent ten hours in the studio today working on a new piece. Lost track of time completely. My back hurts and I forgot to eat lunch but there's something on the canvas now that wasn't there this morning and that's enough.

Commission is done but I hate it. The client wanted "bold and colorful" and I gave them exactly that and now it's sitting in their corporate lobby looking like a very expensive screensaver. Got paid though.

Applied to a residency in New Mexico. Three months in the desert with studio space and a stipend. Deadline was today. Spent all morning putting together the application materials. Portfolio, artist statement, project proposal.

For the proposal I wrote about wanting to explore the relationship between geological time and human impermanence using found desert materials. It sounds pretentious when I read it back but that's what they want to hear. The real reason I want to go is simpler: I'm bored here. Same coffee shop, same studio, same loop of galleries on First Thursday. I think I work better when everything around me is unfamiliar.

Started tallying up my applications this year. Fourteen residencies, eight group shows, three grants. Got into two group shows and one residency that I ended up turning down because it conflicted with a commission. That's a fifteen percent success rate if you're generous about the math. Industry standard is apparently around ten percent so I guess I'm doing okay. But okay isn't what I'm aiming for.

Still thinking about yesterday. Couldn't sleep so I went back through my old sketchbooks from freshman year. Forgot how much I used to draw just for myself back then, weird little creatures and impossible architecture, no thought about whether it would sell or fit a gallery theme. Somewhere around junior year I started thinking about everything in terms of what it could become, what door it might open.

Worked my gallery shift today. It was dead, which meant I had hours to just sit there and stare at the current exhibition. These stark minimalist paintings that all look almost identical to me, just slight variations in shade and proportion. The artist is represented in galleries across the country. People pay five figures for those canvases. And I genuinely don't know if I'm jealous or horrified.

The owner came in toward closing and we got to talking. She said something that stuck with me: "The artists who last aren't the ones who burn brightest, they're the ones who find something they can sustain." I nodded like I understood but I'm not sure I do. What if I'm just not built for sustainability? What if I need the burn to keep going?

Got rejected from another group show today. Third one this month. I know my work is good, the feedback from the last curator even said my pieces were "visually compelling" but "lacked cohesion with the exhibition theme." I keep telling myself that I need to find the right fit, but sitting here surrounded by half-finished canvases and a pile of rejection emails, it's hard not to question everything.

The worst part is I was so bored with my last series that I started experimenting with metalwork halfway through. Now my portfolio looks like three different artists made it. Maybe that's the problem. Everyone keeps saying to develop a "signature style" but the thought of making the same kind of work for years makes me want to throw my brushes in the trash.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly? It feels like a cage. Like agreeing to draw the same box over and over because galleries can sell it easier. But maybe I'm also scared that if I pick one thing, I'll find out I'm not actually great at it. Easier to be "promising" in five directions than mediocre in one.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a one-on-one with my manager today where he brought up the new "technical design review board" they're implementing. Starting in January, any architectural change needs to go through a committee of three senior engineers before we can even start coding. I nodded along and said it made sense for quality control, but inside I was thinking about how this is the third approval layer they've added this year.

Part of me gets it. We've had incidents. There's regulatory pressure. The team has grown from 12 to 45 people and you can't have everyone doing their own thing. But I miss the days when I could just have an idea, prototype it over a weekend, and ship it by Wednesday if it worked.

sources.journal_entry:
Sunday dinner at Maja's parents' place. Her father asked me about work and I gave the usual "it's going well, keeping busy" response. What I didn't mention was that I've been quietly looking at job postings this week. Nothing serious, just... looking. There's a startup in Gothenburg that's hiring senior engineers and their tech blog posts suggest they actually let people build things without eighteen layers of review.

But then I think about what leaving would mean. We bought this apartment two years ago specifically because it's close to Maja's parents and the kids' school. My in-laws help with pickup three days a week. The kids have their friends, their routines. And honestly, the current job pays well, has good benefits, and the people are mostly nice. It's just the bureaucracy that gets to me.

Over dinner, my father-in-law started talking about how his generation valued loyalty to employers and how job-hopping is "a young person's disease." I just smiled and nodded and said something about stability being important. Maja caught my eye across the table and I could tell she knew something was off, but we didn't talk about it in the car ride home. The kids were tired and there wasn't space for that conversation.
sources.nudge_response:
Uncomfortable, if I'm being honest. I'm not sure if I was lying to him or to myself. Part of me does believe in loyalty - I've given this company seven years and I've built things I'm proud of. But another part of me wonders if loyalty is just another word for being afraid to rock the boat.

The thing is, I don't actually know if I'd be happier somewhere else, or if I'd just find new things to be frustrated about. Maybe the startup in Gothenburg would turn into the same bureaucratic mess in three years. Maybe the problem is that I want to do things my way and the world doesn't work like that when you're part of a team. I haven't figured that out yet.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent the entire morning in back-to-back meetings about the new microservice architecture. Everyone has opinions, nobody wants to make a decision, and we ended up exactly where we started. I finally just said "look, why don't I build a proof of concept this week and we can evaluate from there?" My tech lead looked uncomfortable and reminded me we need to follow the new process.

The thing is, I know the process exists for good reasons. Last year Tomas pushed that caching change without proper review and it took down production for three hours. But there's got to be a middle ground between chaos and paralysis. Came home irritated and Maja asked what was wrong. I said "nothing, just work stuff" because I didn't want to vent about the same complaints again.
sources.nudge_response: Probably more than I should. It's just that she's heard the same story before - Erik is frustrated at work, Erik thinks things should be different. At some point it starts to feel self-indulgent. She has her own stress with the kids' schedules and her job. I don't want to be the guy who comes home every day complaining about meetings and processes. So I just... keep it to myself, put the kids to bed, then tinker with my side projects until midnight. It's fine. It works.

Submitted my first technical design document to the new review board today. It took me two hours to write up something I could have just built in four. Three diagrams, a risk assessment matrix, rollback procedures. The whole thing. And you know what? They approved it in the meeting with almost no changes. The tech lead even said it was "exactly the kind of thorough documentation we need."

I should feel vindicated but mostly I just feel tired. I did the thing. I followed the process. And now I get to actually code, which is what I wanted to do a week ago. Maybe this is just what being a senior engineer at a growing company looks like. You learn to work within the system instead of against it. On the way home I stopped to pick up the kids from football practice and my daughter asked if I could help her build a website for her school project. I said yes immediately. I finally just said "look, why don't I build a proof of concept this week and we can evaluate from there?" My tech lead looked uncomfortable and reminded me we need to follow the new process.

The thing is, I know the process exists for good reasons. Last year Tomas pushed that caching change without proper review and it took down production for three hours. But there's got to be a middle ground between chaos and paralysis. Came home irritated and Maja asked what was wrong. I said "nothing, just work stuff" because I didn't want to vent about the same complaints again.
sources.nudge_response: Probably more than I should. It's just that she's heard the same story before - Erik is frustrated at work, Erik thinks things should be different. At some point it starts to feel self-indulgent. She has her own stress with the kids' schedules and her job. I don't want to be the guy who comes home every day complaining about meetings and processes. So I just... keep it to myself, put the kids to bed, then tinker with my side projects until midnight. It's fine. It works.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a one-on-one with my manager today where he brought up the new "technical design review board" they're implementing. Starting in January, any architectural change needs to go through a committee of three senior engineers before we can even start coding. I nodded along and said it made sense for quality control, but inside I was thinking about how this is the third approval layer they've added this year.

Part of me gets it. We've had incidents. There's regulatory pressure. The team has grown from 12 to 45 people and you can't have everyone doing their own thing. But I miss the days when I could just have an idea, prototype it over a weekend, and ship it by Wednesday if it worked.

sources.journal_entry:
Could not sleep after writing that last note. The 10 PM meeting is bothering me more than it should. Back when I managed the retail lending division, if someone scheduled a meeting for 10 PM, there had better have been an emergency — a systems failure, a regulatory audit, something serious. These kids treat it like nothing.

I know I am supposed to adapt. That is the whole point of coming back to school — proving I can learn new ways of working. But there is a difference between adapting and abandoning every standard you spent a career developing. I ran teams. I built processes. I had an executive assistant who managed my calendar. Now I am asking a twenty-three-year-old named "Brayden" how to download an app on my phone.

The worst part is that I smiled and thanked him. What else was I supposed to do? Throw a tantrum about how things used to be? I have seen those people. They become cautionary tales whispered about in break rooms. So I will show up to the 10 PM meeting and I will contribute my ideas and I will be pleasant about all of it. That is the only path forward.

But I am writing this at 11:47 PM because I cannot stop replaying the moment when Brayden said "it's super easy, here let me show you" with that patient voice you use for elderly relatives who cannot work the remote control.

Group project assigned today. I was placed with three twenty-somethings who immediately started a WhatsApp thread I had to ask them to explain how to join. They scheduled our first meeting for 10 PM on a weeknight.

Orientation session today. Sat in the back row out of habit, then realized I was the only one over forty in the entire lecture hall. The program coordinator kept talking about "building your professional foundation" and I wanted to raise my hand and say that some of us already had a foundation, thank you, before it was demolished without warning.

I kept my mouth shut. That is what you do. You do not embarrass yourself by complaining about circumstances nobody asked about. But walking back to my apartment afterward, I felt it — that heaviness in my chest. I am not sure if this was the right decision. Forty thousand dollars a year to be lectured about organizational behavior by someone who has never actually run an organization.
sources.nudge_response: A title that commands respect again. A role where people come to me for guidance, not the other way around. I suppose I want to walk into a room and have people assume I belong there, the way they used to.

sources.journal_entry:
Interesting development. The group used my outline almost word for word. Brayden presented it in class as "our collaborative framework" and the professor praised the "clear structure and practical grounding." Nobody mentioned that I wrote it. I did not correct them.

Here is the thing though. I felt something shift when I saw the professor nodding along. That familiar feeling from the old days — when you put something together that works and people respond to it. The recognition does not need to be public. I know what I contributed. The professor knows the quality improved dramatically between our brainstorm and our deliverable.

Maybe this is how it works now. You do the work, you let other people take the stage, you build influence through competence rather than title. I am not sure I like it. But I am starting to see that there might be a way to operate here that is not completely foreign to who I am.

My ex-wife used to say I cared too much about getting credit. She meant it as criticism. Maybe she had a point, or maybe she did not understand what it is like to have your competence be the only thing you can rely on. Either way, the work got done. That matters.
sources.nudge_response: I suppose I was testing something. Whether I could let go of the credit and still feel like myself. And I did, mostly. But there was also this — if I had spoken up, I would have been the old man demanding acknowledgment. I have seen how quickly people dismiss that. Better to let the work speak and see who notices.

sources.journal_entry:
Sunday afternoon. First time in weeks I do not have something due tomorrow. Went to a coffee shop near campus and just sat for a while. Watched the students come and go with their laptops and their confidence and their entire futures stretching out in front of them.

I remember that feeling. Not the specifics — I was not a coffee shop person at twenty-five — but the sense that time was on my side. That I could make mistakes and recover. That every door led to another door. Now I feel like I am running out of doors. Or maybe I already picked one and the rest all closed behind me.

Here is what I have been circling around for weeks: I came back to school because I could not stand being unemployed. Being introduced at parties as "Harold, he's figuring out his next chapter." The pity. The sudden availability of career advice from people who had never managed anyone. An MBA gave me something to say when people asked what I was doing. A credential that signals I am still in the game.

But sitting here today, I wonder if that is enough of a reason. If I am just collecting another piece of paper to avoid facing the question of what I actually want from whatever time is left.

Group presentation today. I suggested we rehearse beforehand but was outvoted. "We'll figure it out live," Brayden said. So we went in unrehearsed and it showed — stumbling over transitions, contradicting each other on key points. Professor Chen gave us a B-minus and commented that our "individual insights were strong but integration was lacking."

I wanted to say something afterward but held back. What would be the point? They would just see me as the cranky old guy who cannot roll with informality. Better to take the grade and move on. But it grates. I built my reputation on preparation. On never walking into a room without knowing exactly what I was going to say and why. Watching twenty years of professional instincts get overridden by committee feels like swallowing glass.

Midterm grades posted. I received the highest score in the section on my case analysis. Professor Chen left a comment: "Exceptional integration of theory and practice." I printed it out and put it in my desk drawer.
sources.nudge_response: Evidence. Proof that I was not imagining things — that I do know what I am doing, even in this environment. On the days when I feel like an artifact, I can open that drawer and see that someone with credentials agrees I have something to offer.

sources.journal_entry:
Career services appointment today. The counselor — probably thirty years old at most — asked me what kind of "pivot" I was hoping to make. I explained that I am not pivoting, I am rebuilding. She looked confused.

I walked her through my background and she said the market is "challenging" for candidates my age but that I have "transferable skills." Transferable. As if thirty years of leadership is a foreign currency that needs to be exchanged for something more useful. I thanked her for her time and left with a folder of job search resources I will probably never open.

Interesting development. The group used my outline almost word for word. Brayden presented it in class as "our collaborative framework" and the professor praised the "clear structure and practical grounding." Nobody mentioned that I wrote it. I did not correct them.

Here is the thing though. I felt something shift when I saw the professor nodding along. That familiar feeling from the old days — when you put something together that works and people respond to it. The recognition does not need to be public. I know what I contributed. The professor knows the quality improved dramatically between our brainstorm and our deliverable.

Maybe this is how it works now. You do the work, you let other people take the stage, you build influence through competence rather than title. I am not sure I like it. But I am starting to see that there might be a way to operate here that is not completely foreign to who I am.

sources.journal_entry: End of semester. Submitted my last paper at 11:58 PM. Overall GPA: 3.7. I should feel accomplished. Mostly I feel relieved that I can stop pretending to be something I am not for three months. The consulting project starts Monday.

Email from a former colleague today. She is now VP at a regional credit union and asked if I would be interested in consulting on a branch optimization project over the summer. The pay is modest but the work is exactly what I know how to do.

I said yes immediately, then spent an hour wondering if I should have negotiated. Old habits. But the truth is I would have done it for free just to be back in a room where people want my opinion, not because of an assignment but because I have answers they need. That probably sounds desperate. Maybe it is.
sources.nudge_response: That I need to matter somewhere. The MBA is about credentials, about what looks right on paper. But this — someone calling because they remembered I knew what I was doing — that is about actually being useful. I suppose I have been confusing the two.

sources.journal_entry:
Sunday afternoon. First time in weeks I do not have something due tomorrow. Went to a coffee shop near campus and just sat for a while. Watched the students come and go with their laptops and their confidence and their entire futures stretching out in front of them.

I remember that feeling. Not the specifics — I was not a coffee shop person at twenty-five — but the sense that time was on my side. That I could make mistakes and recover. That every door led to another door. Now I feel like I am running out of doors. Or maybe I already picked one and the rest all closed behind me.

Here is what I have been circling around for weeks: I came back to school because I could not stand being unemployed. Being introduced at parties as "Harold, he's figuring out his next chapter." The pity. The sudden availability of career advice from people who had never managed anyone. An MBA gave me something to say when people asked what I was doing. A credential that signals I am still in the game.

But sitting here today, I wonder if that is enough of a reason. If I am just collecting another piece of paper to avoid facing the question of what I actually want from whatever time is left.

Group presentation today. I suggested we rehearse beforehand but was outvoted. "We'll figure it out live," Brayden said. So we went in unrehearsed and it showed — stumbling over transitions, contradicting each other on key points. Professor Chen gave us a B-minus and commented that our "individual insights were strong but integration was lacking."

I wanted to say something afterward but held back. What would be the point? They would just see me as the cranky old guy who cannot roll with informality. Better to take the grade and move on. But it grates. I built my reputation on preparation. On never walking into a room without knowing exactly what I was going to say and why. Watching twenty years of professional instincts get overridden by committee feels like swallowing glass.

Midterm grades posted. I received the highest score in the section on my case analysis. Professor Chen left a comment: "Exceptional integration of theory and practice." I printed it out and put it in my desk drawer.
sources.nudge_response: Evidence. Proof that I was not imagining things — that I do know what I am doing, even in this environment. On the days when I feel like an artifact, I can open that drawer and see that someone with credentials agrees I have something to offer.

sources.journal_entry:
Career services appointment today. The counselor — probably thirty years old at most — asked me what kind of "pivot" I was hoping to make. I explained that I am not pivoting, I am rebuilding. She looked confused.

I walked her through my background and she said the market is "challenging" for candidates my age but that I have "transferable skills." Transferable. As if thirty years of leadership is a foreign currency that needs to be exchanged for something more useful. I thanked her for her time and left with a folder of job search resources I will probably never open.

Interesting development. The group used my outline almost word for word. Brayden presented it in class as "our collaborative framework" and the professor praised the "clear structure and practical grounding." Nobody mentioned that I wrote it. I did not correct them.

Here is the thing though. I felt something shift when I saw the professor nodding along. That familiar feeling from the old days — when you put something together that works and people respond to it. The recognition does not need to be public. I know what I contributed. The professor knows the quality improved dramatically between our brainstorm and our deliverable.

Maybe this is how it works now. You do the work, you let other people take the stage, you build influence through competence rather than title. I am not sure I like it. But I am starting to see that there might be a way to operate here that is not completely foreign to who I am.

My ex-wife used to say I cared too much about getting credit. She meant it as criticism. Maybe she had a point, or maybe she did not understand what it is like to have your competence be the only thing you can rely on. Either way, the work got done. That matters.
sources.nudge_response: I suppose I was testing something. Whether I could let go of the credit and still feel like myself. And I did, mostly. But there was also this — if I had spoken up, I would have been the old man demanding acknowledgment. I have seen how quickly people dismiss that. Better to let the work speak and see who notices.

sources.journal_entry: The 10 PM meeting went until midnight. Brayden talked for forty-five minutes about "leveraging synergies" without saying anything concrete. I drafted the entire project outline afterward because someone had to. Submitted it to the group chat at 2 AM.

Professor Chen called on me in class today and I gave a detailed answer drawing on my experience restructuring our branch network in 2019. She nodded politely and said "that's one perspective, but let's look at what the research shows." Then proceeded to present a case study that contradicted half of what I said.

I stayed after class to discuss it further and she said my "practitioner insights are valuable" but that academic rigor requires us to "question our assumptions." I am not sure what assumptions she thinks I have. I was there. I saw what worked. The branch network I restructured is still operational — or it was until the whole bank got acquired.

My daughter texted me later asking how school was going. I told her it was fine.
sources.nudge_response: She has her own problems to deal with. My job is to handle mine.

sources.journal_entry:
Could not sleep after writing that last note. The 10 PM meeting is bothering me more than it should. Back when I managed the retail lending division, if someone scheduled a meeting for 10 PM, there had better have been an emergency — a systems failure, a regulatory audit, something serious. These kids treat it like nothing.

I know I am supposed to adapt. That is the whole point of coming back to school — proving I can learn new ways of working. But there is a difference between adapting and abandoning every standard you spent a career developing. I ran teams. I built processes. I had an executive assistant who managed my calendar. Now I am asking a twenty-three-year-old named "Brayden" how to download an app on my phone.

The worst part is that I smiled and thanked him. What else was I supposed to do? Throw a tantrum about how things used to be? I have seen those people. They become cautionary tales whispered about in break rooms. So I will show up to the 10 PM meeting and I will contribute my ideas and I will be pleasant about all of it. That is the only path forward.

But I am writing this at 11:47 PM because I cannot stop replaying the moment when Brayden said "it's super easy, here let me show you" with that patient voice you use for elderly relatives who cannot work the remote control.

Group project assigned today. I was placed with three twenty-somethings who immediately started a WhatsApp thread I had to ask them to explain how to join. They scheduled our first meeting for 10 PM on a weeknight.

Orientation session today. Sat in the back row out of habit, then realized I was the only one over forty in the entire lecture hall. The program coordinator kept talking about "building your professional foundation" and I wanted to raise my hand and say that some of us already had a foundation, thank you, before it was demolished without warning.

I kept my mouth shut. That is what you do. You do not embarrass yourself by complaining about circumstances nobody asked about. But walking back to my apartment afterward, I felt it — that heaviness in my chest. I am not sure if this was the right decision. Forty thousand dollars a year to be lectured about organizational behavior by someone who has never actually run an organization.
sources.nudge_response: A title that commands respect again. A role where people come to me for guidance, not the other way around. I suppose I want to walk into a room and have people assume I belong there, the way they used to.

Told Noor this morning she should accept the scholarship. She cried. I cried. We sat at the kitchen table for a long time not saying much. She kept saying she'd come back every summer, and I told her she should come back when she wants to, not because she feels she has to.

Spent the rest of the day reorganizing the pantry because I needed to do something with my hands. Found a jar of Samira's pickled turnips behind everything, must be from Hana's last batch. Put it on the counter where I can see it. The house is the same but it already feels like it's shifting.

Eid preparations started today and the house was full. Hana brought her husband and the baby, Tariq came with sweets from that bakery on Rainbow Street, even Walid video-called from Dubai to wish us well. Noor was in the kitchen all morning helping me roll grape leaves. For a few hours it felt exactly right, all the noise, the food, children running through every room. This is what I stayed home for.

But then after everyone left and it was just Noor and me cleaning up, she said quietly that she'd been offered a partial scholarship. She wasn't asking permission, not exactly, more like she was letting me know it was real now. I didn't say anything. I just kept drying the dishes and stacking them slowly.

I know I need to talk to her. I know what I'm leaning toward. But saying it out loud makes it final in a way I'm not ready for. The house will be so quiet without her.

Still thinking about the mansaf. The thing that keeps coming back to me is that she learned all of it here, in this kitchen, from watching me. Which means even if she's somewhere else, she carries it. I don't know why that's so hard for me to trust.

My father never let any of us leave Amman until we were married. I accepted that. But I also remember the years I spent wondering what it would have been like to study abroad when I had the chance. I told myself it didn't matter because I had responsibilities. Maybe it didn't matter. Or maybe I just never forgave myself for not pushing harder, and now I'm doing the same thing to her.
sources.nudge_response: Maybe I'm afraid her thriving proves I didn't need to sacrifice everything.

sources.journal_entry:
Still thinking about the meeting. I called Diego's mother after I got home because I wanted her to know he's been improving. She sounded tired but grateful. She asked if he was causing problems and I had to reassure her that no, he's doing well, he just needs to believe in himself more.

It made me think about recognition again. Sofia gets constant validation at home - her mother tracks every grade like it's a stock portfolio. Diego gets overlooked. His wins don't have an audience. So I try to be that audience for him. But sometimes I wonder if that means I'm spreading myself too thin.

The department head position pays more and would look better on my resume. Rojas said it's a stepping stone to curriculum development, which is where real change happens. She's not wrong. If I had more influence, maybe I could redesign the system so students like Diego don't fall behind in the first place.

But if I take that job, who runs the after-school program? Who calls Diego's mom at 9pm to tell her he's doing okay?
sources.nudge_response: I don't know. Time, mostly. I already don't have enough of it. Maybe I'm overthinking this.

sources.journal_entry:
The parent meeting tonight was exhausting. Fourteen families showed up, which is more than usual, so I should feel good about that. Most came because their kids are struggling with the history essay unit. I spent two hours explaining the rubric and offering to meet with students individually before the deadline.

What bothers me is that Sofia's mother cornered me afterwards to ask why her daughter got a B+ instead of an A on the last exam. I showed her the grading breakdown, explained exactly where Sofia lost points, and she still looked unsatisfied. Said something about how Sofia works so hard and deserves better recognition. I wanted to say that hard work doesn't automatically mean top marks, but I didn't. I just nodded and promised to look at the essay draft again.

Meanwhile, Diego from the after-school program wasn't there because his mom works double shifts and couldn't make it. He's the one who actually needs the support. But his parents never show up to these things because they can't. The system is set up for families who already have resources.

I don't know why I'm defending myself. Nobody accused me of anything.
sources.nudge_response: Probably myself. I keep second-guessing whether I'm spending my energy in the right places. Sofia's mom made me feel like I'm failing her daughter, but I know Diego needs me more. It's just hard when the parents who show up are the ones asking for more.

sources.journal_entry:
Rojas sent an email today. The deadline for the department head application is next week. She said she wants to recommend me but needs to know I'm interested first. I read it three times and then closed my laptop.

I keep thinking about what she said - that curriculum development is where real change happens. She's probably right. The current history curriculum barely mentions indigenous perspectives, and the standardized assessments are biased toward students with test prep resources. If I were in that role, maybe I could push for changes that would help hundreds of students, not just the twenty in my after-school program.

But that's a hypothetical. The students in front of me right now are real. Diego is real. The other kids who come every Tuesday and Thursday because they have nowhere else to go - they're real too. I don't know how to weigh a certain present impact against a possible future one.

My colleague Andres told me I'm being stubborn. He said I could hire someone to run the program if I got the department head salary. Maybe he's right. But it took me three years to build trust with those families. That's not something you can transfer to a new person overnight.

I'm tired of people acting like this is simple.
sources.nudge_response: I don't know. Someone who actually cares, I guess. It's not about the logistics.

sources.journal_entry:
Saturday morning, sitting with coffee in the kitchen. The house is quiet. Ingrid went to the market early which means she is buying too much cheese again and I will pretend to be surprised when she gets back.

I made a decision last night. I am going to pass on the Lisbon deal. Not because the numbers are wrong or because the founder is not impressive but because I realized I was looking for a feeling, not a business case. The feeling of the leap. That rush of committing to something uncertain and then having to make it work. I know that feeling well and it has served me, but I do not think chasing it right now is the responsible move.

We have the reserves in a good place. The studio has three portfolio companies that need attention. Ingrid and I are in a solid rhythm. I do not need to blow that up to feel alive. At least that is what I am telling myself this morning. Ask me again next week when I am bored.

Valentine's dinner last night, the Italian place near Erasmusbrug. We had a good time, actually managed to not talk about business for most of it. Ingrid brought up taking a trip to Gotland this summer to visit her mother, maybe staying a few weeks. I said yes immediately, genuinely meant it.

But then on the walk home I caught myself thinking about the Lisbon timeline and whether a few weeks in Sweden would slow down onboarding if we signed the deal. I did not say that out loud. I wonder when I started splitting like this, one half of me wanting to just be present and the other half always running the next scenario.
sources.nudge_response: That is the problem, they both do. The planning half is not some unwanted intruder, it is the part that built everything we have. But the part that wanted to just walk along the water with Ingrid without calculating anything, that felt real too. I think they used to be the same thing but somewhere along the way they started pulling in different directions.

sources.journal_entry:
Call with the Lisbon founder again today, third one this week. She pitched the expansion roadmap and honestly it is ambitious but not reckless. I ran the downside scenarios on a napkin while she was talking, which is a habit Ingrid would recognize and roll her eyes at. Worst case we lose about what I spent on that sailboat restoration three years ago, so it is recoverable.

Ingrid asked over dinner if I had decided. I said not yet. That is technically true but I think she could tell from my tone that I have already half-committed in my head. She did not push back, just said "make sure you are not chasing the feeling again." I told her I did not know what she meant, which was a lie.

sources.journal_entry:
Antwerp situation is stabilizing. We found a replacement client, not as big but enough to keep the operation running while we diversify the pipeline. I spent three days in Antwerp this week working on-site with the team and it reminded me that I actually enjoy the problem-solving part of this work more than the deal-making part.

There is something specific about walking into a warehouse that is half-empty and figuring out how to fill it. Not the adrenaline of a new deal but the satisfaction of fixing what is broken. Maybe that is the version of this work that does not require me to keep jumping off cliffs.

Had a long phone call with Ingrid tonight and told her about the replacement client. She sounded relieved, which I noticed because she had been careful not to sound worried all week. She said she is glad I was there in person rather than just sending emails. She is right. The founder needed to see someone calm in the room. I think I needed to be that person for my own reasons too.

One of our portfolio companies, the cold storage outfit in Antwerp, just lost their anchor client. Found out this morning from a panicked call from the founder who I could barely understand because he was speaking so fast. This is the company where we parked the biggest chunk of operational capital.

I spent the entire day on calls, restructuring scenarios, talking to our lawyer about contract terms. By evening I had a workable plan but the whole time there was this tight feeling in my chest. Not about the money exactly, we can absorb the hit if we need to. It is more that I had just gotten comfortable with the idea of things being stable and now the ground shifted.

What irritates me is that I know this is part of the game. I have been through worse. The first company almost went under twice before we found our footing. But back then the instability felt like fuel. Now it just feels like a threat to something I have built up carefully. I do not know when that switch happened.

sources.journal_entry: Did the Kinderdijk trip. Walked for hours, barely talked, ate pannenkoeken at that place near the windmills. It was exactly what I needed and I managed to leave my phone in the car for most of it.

Got an email from the Lisbon founder today. She closed the round without us, brought in a Madrid-based firm instead. Good for her. But I would be lying if I said it did not sting. Not because we lost the deal, I walked away from it deliberately. It stings because reading her update about the progress they have made in the last three weeks made me feel like I am standing still.

I know that is irrational. The studio is doing fine, the Antwerp crisis proved the model works, we are in good shape. But "good shape" feels like treading water sometimes. Like I am maintaining rather than building. And maintaining is not something I have ever been good at sitting with.

Ingrid would say this is exactly the pattern she warned me about. I get things to a good place, feel restless, then go looking for the next thing to keep myself occupied. She is probably right. But knowing it is a pattern does not make the restlessness go away. I keep checking the inbox for something that will make tomorrow feel different from today.
sources.nudge_response: Nothing changed. I just had a slow day and read an email at the wrong time. It is fine. The Antwerp thing took a lot out of me and I probably just need a proper weekend off. Ingrid suggested we drive out to Kinderdijk, maybe I will take her up on that.

sources.journal_entry:
Antwerp situation is stabilizing. We found a replacement client, not as big but enough to keep the operation running while we diversify the pipeline. I spent three days in Antwerp this week working on-site with the team and it reminded me that I actually enjoy the problem-solving part of this work more than the deal-making part.

There is something specific about walking into a warehouse that is half-empty and figuring out how to fill it. Not the adrenaline of a new deal but the satisfaction of fixing what is broken. Maybe that is the version of this work that does not require me to keep jumping off cliffs.

Had a long phone call with Ingrid tonight and told her about the replacement client. She sounded relieved, which I noticed because she had been careful not to sound worried all week. She said she is glad I was there in person rather than just sending emails. She is right. The founder needed to see someone calm in the room. I think I needed to be that person for my own reasons too.

One of our portfolio companies, the cold storage outfit in Antwerp, just lost their anchor client. Found out this morning from a panicked call from the founder who I could barely understand because he was speaking so fast. This is the company where we parked the biggest chunk of operational capital.

I spent the entire day on calls, restructuring scenarios, talking to our lawyer about contract terms. By evening I had a workable plan but the whole time there was this tight feeling in my chest. Not about the money exactly, we can absorb the hit if we need to. It is more that I had just gotten comfortable with the idea of things being stable and now the ground shifted.

What irritates me is that I know this is part of the game. I have been through worse. The first company almost went under twice before we found our footing. But back then the instability felt like fuel. Now it just feels like a threat to something I have built up carefully. I do not know when that switch happened.

Saturday morning, sitting with coffee in the kitchen. The house is quiet. Ingrid went to the market early which means she is buying too much cheese again and I will pretend to be surprised when she gets back.

I made a decision last night. I am going to pass on the Lisbon deal. Not because the numbers are wrong or because the founder is not impressive but because I realized I was looking for a feeling, not a business case. The feeling of the leap. That rush of committing to something uncertain and then having to make it work. I know that feeling well and it has served me, but I do not think chasing it right now is the responsible move.

We have the reserves in a good place. The studio has three portfolio companies that need attention. Ingrid and I are in a solid rhythm. I do not need to blow that up to feel alive. At least that is what I am telling myself this morning. Ask me again next week when I am bored.

Valentine's dinner last night, the Italian place near Erasmusbrug. We had a good time, actually managed to not talk about business for most of it. Ingrid brought up taking a trip to Gotland this summer to visit her mother, maybe staying a few weeks. I said yes immediately, genuinely meant it.

But then on the walk home I caught myself thinking about the Lisbon timeline and whether a few weeks in Sweden would slow down onboarding if we signed the deal. I did not say that out loud. I wonder when I started splitting like this, one half of me wanting to just be present and the other half always running the next scenario.
sources.nudge_response: That is the problem, they both do. The planning half is not some unwanted intruder, it is the part that built everything we have. But the part that wanted to just walk along the water with Ingrid without calculating anything, that felt real too. I think they used to be the same thing but somewhere along the way they started pulling in different directions.

sources.journal_entry:

sources.journal_entry:
My advisor asked today why I chose the topic of hospitality rituals in Levantine households when there are "more contemporary angles" I could take. I told her it was methodologically sound and left it at that. I don't owe anyone an explanation for why this subject matters to me. She's Swedish. She studies migration patterns. The way my grandmother set a table is not something she would understand, and I'm not interested in making it legible to her.

Came home and made musakhan from scratch, the whole process — rolling the dough, roasting the sumac onions until they were dark and sweet. Ate it alone at the kitchen table while my mother watched her show in the other room. The apartment smelled right. That was enough of an answer for one day.
sources.nudge_response: I like cooking. It's not that deep. The musakhan was good and I hadn't made it in a while. Sometimes dinner is just dinner.

I told her it was methodologically sound and left it at that. I don't owe anyone an explanation for why this subject matters to me. She's Swedish. She studies migration patterns. The way my grandmother set a table is not something she would understand, and I'm not interested in making it legible to her.

Came home and made musakhan from scratch, the whole process — rolling the dough, roasting the sumac onions until they were dark and sweet. Ate it alone at the kitchen table while my mother watched her show in the other room. The apartment smelled right. That was enough of an answer for one day.
sources.nudge_response: I like cooking. It's not that deep. The musakhan was good and I hadn't made it in a while. Sometimes dinner is just dinner.

sources.journal_entry:
My cohort went out for dinner last night at a rooftop restaurant in Jabal Amman. I almost didn't go. I had reading to finish and my mother had made lentil soup, and leaving her eating alone feels wrong even when she tells me to go. But I went, and I'm glad I did.

There were eight of us, all at different stages. Layla is twenty-seven and finishing her masters. Khaled is thirty-three and already published twice. And then there's me, the oldest by a decade and a half, ordering an extra plate of mezze because the lamb was extraordinary and the arak was cold and the evening air on that rooftop was exactly right. Layla asked me once why I came back to school so late, and I told her the truth — I wanted to, and I finally could, and life is too short to keep postponing the things that interest you.

She looked at me like I'd said something profound. I don't think it was. I think it was just unusual for someone my age in our context to say out loud that wanting something was reason enough to pursue it. Most of the men my brother's age would find that embarrassing. A man approaching fifty should have his affairs settled, not be starting over in a seminar room. But I'm not sure I care about what those men think anymore. The lamb was perfect. The conversation was good. I walked home through the old streets and felt awake in a way that the library doesn't give me.

Had a strange afternoon. After seminar I went to the old souk downtown instead of going home to write. I just walked. Bought a bag of roasted pistachios from the same vendor my father used to take me to when I was a boy. The man running it now is probably the vendor's grandson, same spot, same brass scale. I sat on a bench near the mosque and ate them slowly, one by one, listening to the call to prayer echo off the stone.

I haven't prayed regularly in years. My mother doesn't know this. She assumes I go to the mosque near campus on Fridays, and I don't correct her. The truth is I stopped feeling anything during prayer around the time I turned forty. The motions are still in my body — I could do them in my sleep — but the connection isn't there. And yet sitting there today, hearing the adhan bounce off those old walls while I cracked pistachios, I felt something close to what prayer used to give me. Stillness. Presence. The taste of salt and the sound of something ancient happening around me.

I don't know what to do with that. I can't tell my mother I've replaced prayer with pistachios and a bench. That would break her heart. But I also can't pretend the mosque still does for me what it used to. I'm stuck between what's honest and what's kind.
sources.nudge_response: I think I stopped believing that anyone was listening. Not God necessarily — I haven't worked that out — but the structure of it. The imam, the rows, the routine. It started to feel like I was performing for an audience that included my dead father and my living mother but not me. On the bench I wasn't performing for anyone. I was just a man eating pistachios in the late sun, and that was enough. Maybe what I lost wasn't faith. Maybe I lost the ability to feel things inside a frame someone else built, and I can only feel them when I stumble into them on my own. That's a lonely thought. But it felt true sitting there.

sources.journal_entry: Can't stop thinking about what Faisal said. Opened a bottle of that Jordanian red wine I've been saving and I'm sitting on the balcony. My mother would not approve of the wine but she went to bed early and what she doesn't see doesn't trouble her.

My brother Faisal made a comment at Friday lunch about how I'm "still playing student" while his sons are already building careers. His eldest is twenty-six and works at a bank. I smiled and passed the hummus. What I wanted to say was that I spent twenty years running hotel operations so our family name meant something in the hospitality industry, and now I'm doing something for myself, and that should be allowed.

But it wouldn't have been the right moment. My mother was sitting right there, and she gets anxious when Faisal and I disagree. So I stayed quiet, helped clear the plates, and drove home listening to Fairuz with the windows down. The breeze off the hills felt good. I don't need Faisal's approval. I know what I'm doing and why.
sources.nudge_response: My mother would have gone quiet. Faisal would have gotten louder. His wife Rania would have changed the subject to the children, which she always does. And on the drive home I would have felt worse, not better, because I'd have disrupted the one gathering that keeps us together. The lunch matters more than being right. That's something Faisal wouldn't understand because he's never had to choose.

sources.journal_entry:
Got an email from my advisor asking me to justify why my fieldwork methodology is "sufficiently distanced" from my own background. She phrased it politely but the implication is clear — studying my own culture's domestic practices introduces bias. As if the Swedish anthropologists who study Swedish folk customs don't exist. As if proximity is only a problem when you're from the region being studied.

I wrote a professional reply explaining my positionality framework and reflexive methodology. It was measured and appropriate. But sitting here now, I want to throw something. I left a career. I'm spending my savings. My mother eats dinner alone three nights a week because I'm at the library. And someone who has never set foot in a Jordanian kitchen is telling me I'm too close to the food. I need her approval to move forward with this chapter. But some nights the cost of fitting myself into their frame feels like it's eating the thing that brought me here.
sources.nudge_response: The feeling. That's what I'm afraid of losing. The reason I walked into a classroom at forty-nine wasn't the degree or the title. It was because something about the way my mother cooks, the way that woman in Irbid folds bread, the way my father used to pour coffee for guests with both hands — those things mean something, and I wanted to understand why they move me the way they do. But the more I translate that into academic language, the further I get from the feeling that started it. I'm terrified that by the time I finish this dissertation, I'll have a perfect theoretical framework for something I can no longer feel. And then what was the point? I'll have turned something alive into something correct. My advisor would say that's the job. But I don't want that to be my job. I want to hold both — the rigor and the warmth. I just don't know if the institution lets you do that.

sources.journal_entry: Sat down to write after the Dead Sea trip. Got four hundred words down, all of them bad. My mother asked if I'd been to campus today and I said yes. First time I've lied to her about something this small. Too tired to think about what that means.

Canceled my library session today and drove to the Dead Sea. Told myself it was for thinking but really I just wanted to float. Paid for one of the resort day passes, the expensive one with the private beach and the buffet lunch. My fellowship stipend doesn't really cover that kind of thing but I did it anyway. Lay in the water for an hour, completely weightless, staring at the sky.

The buffet was ridiculous. Grilled prawns, tabbouleh, four kinds of baklava. I ate slowly and deliberately and didn't check my phone once. Drove home in the early evening with the salt drying on my skin and this lightness I haven't felt in weeks. I know I should have been writing. The chapter is overdue. But I can't bring myself to feel guilty about it.
sources.nudge_response: Not really. I've always been someone who needs a good meal and a change of scenery to function. The Dead Sea was beautiful and now I'm recharged. I'll write tomorrow. It's fine.

sources.journal_entry:
My mother made knafeh today. She does this maybe twice a year, always unannounced, and when I came home from campus the whole apartment smelled like orange blossom and melted cheese. She was standing at the stove watching it with that focused expression she gets, and I sat at the kitchen table pretending to read but really just watching her.

She's seventy-six. Her hands shake a little now but she still moves through the kitchen with this sureness that I don't have anywhere in my life. She poured the syrup in one smooth motion, tilted the pan, pressed the edges with a spoon. Every step inherited from her mother, who learned from her mother before that.

I ate two pieces standing at the counter before she'd even plated it properly and she swatted my hand and called me greedy. I am greedy. I wanted a third piece and I took it. The sweetness was so intense it almost hurt, that good kind of too-much where your whole mouth is alive. My mother watched me eat and looked satisfied in a way that goes deeper than food. She was feeding her son. That's a complete sentence in her world.

Later I sat with my laptop open and thought about how this is exactly what my dissertation is about, but I can't write about my own mother. It would feel like a betrayal. Like turning something sacred into data. But she's the reason I'm writing about any of this in the first place.
sources.nudge_response: It would mean she becomes a subject. A case study. Her knafeh becomes "an example of embodied intergenerational knowledge transfer" and the orange blossom becomes a footnote. I'd be taking something that belongs to our kitchen and putting it in a seminar room for people who have never tasted it to analyze. My advisor would call that rigorous. I'd call it taking something warm and making it cold. I know that's not a rational objection. I just feel it in my chest when I think about writing her name in an academic paper. She deserves better than being theorized.

One of my subjects, a woman in her seventies from Irbid, described how she prepares mansaf for her family exactly the way her mother taught her, down to the specific way she folds the bread under the rice. She said she doesn't think about why she does it that way. She just does. Her hands know.

That's the thing I'm trying to capture in this dissertation and I keep circling around it without landing. The knowledge that lives in practice, not in explanation. My advisor wants me to theorize it and I understand why, but there's something that gets lost when you turn a grandmother's hands into a framework. I don't have a solution yet. I just know the gap is there and it bothers me.

I'll have turned something alive into something correct. My advisor would say that's the job. But I don't want that to be my job. I want to hold both — the rigor and the warmth. I just don't know if the institution lets you do that.

sources.journal_entry: Sat down to write after the Dead Sea trip. Got four hundred words down, all of them bad. My mother asked if I'd been to campus today and I said yes. First time I've lied to her about something this small. Too tired to think about what that means.

Canceled my library session today and drove to the Dead Sea. Told myself it was for thinking but really I just wanted to float. Paid for one of the resort day passes, the expensive one with the private beach and the buffet lunch. My fellowship stipend doesn't really cover that kind of thing but I did it anyway. Lay in the water for an hour, completely weightless, staring at the sky.

The buffet was ridiculous. Grilled prawns, tabbouleh, four kinds of baklava. I ate slowly and deliberately and didn't check my phone once. Drove home in the early evening with the salt drying on my skin and this lightness I haven't felt in weeks. I know I should have been writing. The chapter is overdue. But I can't bring myself to feel guilty about it.
sources.nudge_response: Not really. I've always been someone who needs a good meal and a change of scenery to function. The Dead Sea was beautiful and now I'm recharged. I'll write tomorrow. It's fine.

sources.journal_entry:
My mother made knafeh today. She does this maybe twice a year, always unannounced, and when I came home from campus the whole apartment smelled like orange blossom and melted cheese. She was standing at the stove watching it with that focused expression she gets, and I sat at the kitchen table pretending to read but really just watching her.

She's seventy-six. Her hands shake a little now but she still moves through the kitchen with this sureness that I don't have anywhere in my life. She poured the syrup in one smooth motion, tilted the pan, pressed the edges with a spoon. Every step inherited from her mother, who learned from her mother before that.

I ate two pieces standing at the counter before she'd even plated it properly and she swatted my hand and called me greedy. I am greedy. I wanted a third piece and I took it. The sweetness was so intense it almost hurt, that good kind of too-much where your whole mouth is alive. My mother watched me eat and looked satisfied in a way that goes deeper than food. She was feeding her son. That's a complete sentence in her world.

Later I sat with my laptop open and thought about how this is exactly what my dissertation is about, but I can't write about my own mother. It would feel like a betrayal. Like turning something sacred into data. But she's the reason I'm writing about any of this in the first place.
sources.nudge_response: It would mean she becomes a subject. A case study. Her knafeh becomes "an example of embodied intergenerational knowledge transfer" and the orange blossom becomes a footnote. I'd be taking something that belongs to our kitchen and putting it in a seminar room for people who have never tasted it to analyze. My advisor would call that rigorous. I'd call it taking something warm and making it cold. I know that's not a rational objection. I just feel it in my chest when I think about writing her name in an academic paper. She deserves better than being theorized.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent the morning transcribing interviews for my fieldwork chapter. One of my subjects, a woman in her seventies from Irbid, described how she prepares mansaf for her family exactly the way her mother taught her, down to the specific way she folds the bread under the rice. She said she doesn't think about why she does it that way. She just does. Her hands know.

That's the thing I'm trying to capture in this dissertation and I keep circling around it without landing. The knowledge that lives in practice, not in explanation. My advisor wants me to theorize it and I understand why, but there's something that gets lost when you turn a grandmother's hands into a framework. I don't have a solution yet. I just know the gap is there and it bothers me.

My cohort went out for dinner last night at a rooftop restaurant in Jabal Amman. I almost didn't go. I had reading to finish and my mother had made lentil soup, and leaving her eating alone feels wrong even when she tells me to go. But I went, and I'm glad I did.

There were eight of us, all at different stages. Layla is twenty-seven and finishing her masters. Khaled is thirty-three and already published twice. And then there's me, the oldest by a decade and a half, ordering an extra plate of mezze because the lamb was extraordinary and the arak was cold and the evening air on that rooftop was exactly right. Layla asked me once why I came back to school so late, and I told her the truth — I wanted to, and I finally could, and life is too short to keep postponing the things that interest you.

She looked at me like I'd said something profound. I don't think it was. I think it was just unusual for someone my age in our context to say out loud that wanting something was reason enough to pursue it. Most of the men my brother's age would find that embarrassing. A man approaching fifty should have his affairs settled, not be starting over in a seminar room. But I'm not sure I care about what those men think anymore. The lamb was perfect. The conversation was good. I walked home through the old streets and felt awake in a way that the library doesn't give me.

Had a strange afternoon. After seminar I went to the old souk downtown instead of going home to write. I just walked. Bought a bag of roasted pistachios from the same vendor my father used to take me to when I was a boy. The man running it now is probably the vendor's grandson, same spot, same brass scale. I sat on a bench near the mosque and ate them slowly, one by one, listening to the call to prayer echo off the stone.

I haven't prayed regularly in years. My mother doesn't know this. She assumes I go to the mosque near campus on Fridays, and I don't correct her. The truth is I stopped feeling anything during prayer around the time I turned forty. The motions are still in my body — I could do them in my sleep — but the connection isn't there. And yet sitting there today, hearing the adhan bounce off those old walls while I cracked pistachios, I felt something close to what prayer used to give me. Stillness. Presence. The taste of salt and the sound of something ancient happening around me.

I don't know what to do with that. I can't tell my mother I've replaced prayer with pistachios and a bench. That would break her heart. But I also can't pretend the mosque still does for me what it used to. I'm stuck between what's honest and what's kind.
sources.nudge_response: I think I stopped believing that anyone was listening. Not God necessarily — I haven't worked that out — but the structure of it. The imam, the rows, the routine. It started to feel like I was performing for an audience that included my dead father and my living mother but not me. On the bench I wasn't performing for anyone. I was just a man eating pistachios in the late sun, and that was enough. Maybe what I lost wasn't faith. Maybe I lost the ability to feel things inside a frame someone else built, and I can only feel them when I stumble into them on my own. That's a lonely thought. But it felt true sitting there.

sources.journal_entry: Can't stop thinking about what Faisal said. Opened a bottle of that Jordanian red wine I've been saving and I'm sitting on the balcony. My mother would not approve of the wine but she went to bed early and what she doesn't see doesn't trouble her.

My brother Faisal made a comment at Friday lunch about how I'm "still playing student" while his sons are already building careers. His eldest is twenty-six and works at a bank. I smiled and passed the hummus. What I wanted to say was that I spent twenty years running hotel operations so our family name meant something in the hospitality industry, and now I'm doing something for myself, and that should be allowed.

But it wouldn't have been the right moment. My mother was sitting right there, and she gets anxious when Faisal and I disagree. So I stayed quiet, helped clear the plates, and drove home listening to Fairuz with the windows down. The breeze off the hills felt good. I don't need Faisal's approval. I know what I'm doing and why.
sources.nudge_response: My mother would have gone quiet. Faisal would have gotten louder. His wife Rania would have changed the subject to the children, which she always does. And on the drive home I would have felt worse, not better, because I'd have disrupted the one gathering that keeps us together. The lunch matters more than being right. That's something Faisal wouldn't understand because he's never had to choose.

sources.journal_entry: Spent twelve hours in the library and barely got through two chapters of my lit review. My back hurts, my eyes hurt, and I keep wondering what possessed me to do this at forty-nine. Going to bed.

My advisor asked today why I chose the topic of hospitality rituals in Levantine households when there are "more contemporary angles" I could take. I told her it was methodologically sound and left it at that. I don't owe anyone an explanation for why this subject matters to me. She's Swedish. She studies migration patterns. The way my grandmother set a table is not something she would understand, and I'm not interested in making it legible to her.

Came home and made musakhan from scratch, the whole process — rolling the dough, roasting the sumac onions until they were dark and sweet. Ate it alone at the kitchen table while my mother watched her show in the other room. The apartment smelled right. That was enough of an answer for one day.
sources.nudge_response: I like cooking. It's not that deep. The musakhan was good and I hadn't made it in a while. Sometimes dinner is just dinner.

sources.journal_entry:
My direct report Andrés came in excited about some new automation software he wants to pilot on the production line. He showed me a demo and honestly it looked impressive — would probably cut processing time by fifteen percent. But the implementation would mean shutting down Line 2 for three weeks and retraining half the floor staff. Three weeks of lost output during our busiest quarter.

I told him to write up a proposal and I would review it, but the truth is I already know I am going to push it to next fiscal year. Maybe the quarter after that. I could hear how flat my voice sounded when I said it and I think he noticed too.
sources.nudge_response: Because I know I am probably being the bottleneck. Andrés is sharp, the software looked solid, and fifteen percent is not nothing. But shutting down a line for three weeks when corporate is already talking about restructuring — that is the kind of disruption that puts a target on your department. I would rather deliver predictable numbers and keep everyone employed than chase an improvement that could backfire at the worst possible time. I just wish I could explain that to Andrés without sounding like I have given up.

sources.journal_entry:
Corporate sent an email Friday about "restructuring opportunities" in the operations departments across all three plants. The language was carefully neutral, all about efficiency and modernization, but I have been doing this long enough to recognize what that kind of memo actually means. Somebody is going to lose headcount.

I spent part of Sunday looking through my employment contract — the termination clauses, the severance calculations, the notice periods. Lucía noticed me reading it at the kitchen table instead of doing our usual budget review and asked if something was wrong. I told her I was just being thorough, which is true but also not the whole picture.

The thing that bothers me is not the restructuring itself. Companies do this. What bothers me is that I had filed my contract in the closet three years ago and forgot exactly where. It took me twenty minutes to find it. That should not have happened. I need a better system for keeping important documents where I can reach them quickly.
sources.nudge_response: The severance is decent — four months for my tenure — but decent is not the same as comfortable. We could cover things for ten months total if I combined severance with savings, but that assumes nothing else breaks. The car is twelve years old, the roof needs work eventually. Ten months sounds like a lot until you start listing what eats into it.
