Lucía's mother called this morning to say she wants to sell the family house in Morelia and move into one of those assisted living places. Lucía was quiet for a long time after hanging up. Her mother has lived in that house for forty years — it is where Lucía grew up, where we had our wedding reception in the backyard.

The practical side of it is complicated. Lucía's sister wants to buy the house but does not have enough for a down payment and asked if we could co-sign a loan. I have never co-signed anything in my life. My father told me when I was nineteen: never put your name on someone else's debt, no matter who they are. But this is Lucía's family, and the look on her face when her sister called tonight was not something I can just calculate my way around.

I told them both I needed a few days to think. Lucía did not argue, which means she understands my hesitation even if she hopes I land somewhere different than where I am leaning.
sources.nudge_response: Toward no. I know how that sounds, and I know what it might cost with Lucía's family. But co-signing means if her sister cannot pay, we pay. And if we pay, that is the emergency fund, that is the roof repair, that is everything I have built to make sure we never end up like Lucía's cuñado in León. I would rather help them find another way — maybe lend a smaller amount directly, something we could absorb if it disappeared. But putting our name on a bank loan is a different thing entirely.

sources.journal_entry:
Plumber came, turned out it was just a faulty meter reading — no actual leak. Lucía laughed about me turning the water off every night for five days. I told her better cautious than flooded, and she kissed my forehead and said "sí, mi amor, así eres tú."

The restructuring memo turned into a town hall meeting this week. They are consolidating some administrative roles at the Querétaro plant but operations at our site stays as-is for now. My boss Carlos pulled me aside afterward and said my numbers were part of the reason they kept Guadalajara intact. Sixteen years of consistent output apparently counts for something.

I reorganized the filing cabinet this weekend. Employment contracts, insurance policies, property deed, car title — all in labeled folders now, easy to grab. Lucía thinks I am being excessive but she also put her own documents in the system without me asking, so I think she sees the point even if she would not say it directly.
sources.nudge_response: Relieved, obviously, but also something I did not expect — vindicated, maybe. I have spent years being the manager who says no to flashy ideas, who keeps the same routines, who does not chase promotions. Sometimes I wonder if people think that means I lack ambition. But steady output is what saved those jobs. Not innovation, not bold moves. Just showing up and delivering the same thing every quarter. It is not exciting but it held.

sources.journal_entry: Got the water bill and it was almost double the usual amount. Probably a leak somewhere. Called a plumber but the earliest appointment is next Thursday, so I have been turning the main valve off at night just in case.

My direct report Andrés came in excited about some new automation software he wants to pilot on the production line. He showed me a demo and honestly it looked impressive — would probably cut processing time by fifteen percent. But the implementation would mean shutting down Line 2 for three weeks and retraining half the floor staff. Three weeks of lost output during our busiest quarter.

I told him to write up a proposal and I would review it, but the truth is I already know I am going to push it to next fiscal year. Maybe the quarter after that. I could hear how flat my voice sounded when I said it and I think he noticed too.
sources.nudge_response: Because I know I am probably being the bottleneck. Andrés is sharp, the software looked solid, and fifteen percent is not nothing. But shutting down a line for three weeks when corporate is already talking about restructuring — that is the kind of disruption that puts a target on your department. I would rather deliver predictable numbers and keep everyone employed than chase an improvement that could backfire at the worst possible time. I just wish I could explain that to Andrés without sounding like I have given up.

sources.journal_entry:
Corporate sent an email Friday about "restructuring opportunities" in the operations departments across all three plants. The language was carefully neutral, all about efficiency and modernization, but I have been doing this long enough to recognize what that kind of memo actually means. Somebody is going to lose headcount.

I spent part of Sunday looking through my employment contract — the termination clauses, the severance calculations, the notice periods. Lucía noticed me reading it at the kitchen table instead of doing our usual budget review and asked if something was wrong. I told her I was just being thorough, which is true but also not the whole picture.

The thing that bothers me is not the restructuring itself. Companies do this. What bothers me is that I had filed my contract in the closet three years ago and forgot exactly where. It took me twenty minutes to find it. That should not have happened. I need a better system for keeping important documents where I can reach them quickly.
sources.nudge_response: The severance is decent — four months for my tenure — but decent is not the same as comfortable. We could cover things for ten months total if I combined severance with savings, but that assumes nothing else breaks. The car is twelve years old, the roof needs work eventually. Ten months sounds like a lot until you start listing what eats into it.

sources.journal_entry: Spent Saturday morning fixing the back fence with my compadre Tomás. Felt good to work with my hands for once instead of staring at spreadsheets. Lucía brought us agua de jamaica and we sat in the yard afterward just talking about nothing important.

Lucía mentioned her sister's husband lost his job at the autoparts factory in León. Just like that — twenty-two years and they called a meeting on a Friday afternoon. I checked our savings account twice after dinner, which is not something I normally do on a weekday.

People at the plant keep asking why I don't apply for the regional director position now that Héctor is retiring. I know exactly why — the travel, the relocating, none of that sits right with me. My team runs well, my commute is twenty minutes, and I sleep fine at night.
sources.nudge_response: Not really. Maybe five years ago I would have thought about it differently, but I watched Héctor miss his daughter's quinceañera because he was in Monterrey for a plant inspection. That told me everything I needed to know.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent New Year's Eve at Lucia's apartment with a few people from the office. Nothing big -- arepas, aguardiente, the countdown on the TV. I didn't check my phone once the whole night, which felt strange at first but I stopped noticing after a while. Lucia made fun of me for not knowing any of the songs on the playlist.

On January first I went for a run along the ciclovia and came back with an idea for restructuring the southern corridor drops. Not the full routing plan Diego shut down -- something smaller, a pilot with just the Cali deliveries. If I can show a cost reduction on one leg, the rest of the argument builds itself. Nobody has to approve a pilot. I can just run it with the three drivers who already told me the current route doesn't make sense.

I drafted the pilot scope on my laptop sitting on Lucia's couch while everyone was watching a movie. Felt good to have something concrete again instead of waiting for permission. I want to own how this unfolds, start to finish.

Still at the office. Everyone else left at six but I'm going through the client satisfaction numbers from Q4 because nobody else is going to do it. Found three accounts where response times slipped below target because the team was running the old dispatch sequence I already flagged two months ago. Two months.

My mom called while I was pulling the spreadsheets. I let it go to voicemail. She'll ask why I'm still at work, then she'll ask when I'm coming home for New Year's, and I don't have answers to either one right now.
sources.nudge_response: Probably not. There's too much to clean up here before January. She'll understand. She usually does.

sources.journal_entry:
The meeting with Diego didn't go how I planned. He sat there scrolling through my routing proposal on his laptop, barely looking up, and when he finally said something it was about the formatting. The formatting. Three months of pulling delivery data, testing alternate corridors, calling warehouse contacts in Medellin -- and he wants to talk about fonts.

I should have pushed back harder. Instead I just nodded and said I'd revise it. The whole walk back to my desk I was already rewriting my argument in my head, all the things I should have said. The numbers speak for themselves. Our current route through Bucaramanga adds two days and the clients in the southern corridor keep complaining.

Part of me wonders if I backed down because he's been here fifteen years and I've been here eleven months. That shouldn't matter when the data is right there. But I sat quiet like it did matter, and now I'm stuck doing cosmetic edits on something that should already be approved.

sources.journal_entry:
Call with the VP happened. Forty-five minutes. She asked detailed questions about methodology, cost projections, scalability to other corridors. She knew what she was talking about, which made it feel real -- not like presenting to someone who just wants to check a box.

At the end she said she wants me to present to the regional leadership group in February. A full presentation, not a one-pager. My stomach dropped when she said it, not because I'm scared but because I've never had that kind of stage before and I want it to go perfectly. I already know I'm going to over-prepare.

Called my mom after to tell her. She said "mija, eat something, you sound wired." She's not wrong. I had an empanada for lunch and nothing since. But this is the thing I've been pushing for since I got here and it's actually happening. Not because someone handed it to me -- because I built it and put it out there myself.
sources.nudge_response: Numbers that nobody can argue with, questions I already have answers for, and walking out knowing they couldn't have gotten that analysis from anyone else on the team.

sources.journal_entry:
Lucia told me today that some people on the team think I'm "trying to skip levels." She said it like she was doing me a favor by telling me, and maybe she was, but it stung. I've been busting myself on this project and the fact that doing good work gets read as political maneuvering makes me want to throw my laptop into the Magdalena.

I asked her who said it and she wouldn't tell me. Fine. But now I'm sitting here wondering if I should tone it down for the February presentation or just go harder. Toning it down feels like giving up ground I earned. Going harder might prove their point. I don't know.

Stayed up until three working on the deck. Caught myself copying Diego's formatting from an old presentation because I thought it would make the leadership group take it more seriously. Closed the file and went to bed feeling off about it.

Call with the VP happened. Forty-five minutes. She asked detailed questions about methodology, cost projections, scalability to other corridors. She knew what she was talking about, which made it feel real -- not like presenting to someone who just wants to check a box.

At the end she said she wants me to present to the regional leadership group in February. A full presentation, not a one-pager. My stomach dropped when she said it, not because I'm scared but because I've never had that kind of stage before and I want it to go perfectly. I already know I'm going to over-prepare.

Called my mom after to tell her. She said "mija, eat something, you sound wired." She's not wrong. I had an empanada for lunch and nothing since. But this is the thing I've been pushing for since I got here and it's actually happening. Not because someone handed it to me -- because I built it and put it out there myself.
sources.nudge_response: Numbers that nobody can argue with, questions I already have answers for, and walking out knowing they couldn't have gotten that analysis from anyone else on the team.

sources.journal_entry:
Diego pulled me into his office yesterday and I thought he was going to tear into me about the pilot but he just asked for the full data set. No commentary, no lecture, just "send me the spreadsheet." I sent it within the hour. He forwarded it to the VP of ops in Mexico City. I know because the VP emailed me directly asking for a call next week.

That call could be anything. Could be a reprimand, could be an expansion. Either way the work is out there now and it's mine. I keep refreshing my email like that's going to make the calendar invite appear faster. Need to stop doing that.
sources.nudge_response: I don't know. Something that makes the last three months feel like they counted.

sources.journal_entry:
The Cali pilot is running. Three drivers, rerouted through Palmira instead of the standard loop. I didn't tell Diego. I told the drivers it was a test week and tracked the first four deliveries myself from the dashboard. Average time dropped by six hours per run. Six hours. That's not a font issue.

I built a one-page summary with the numbers and sent it to the full operations chat, not just Diego. Maybe that was aggressive. Lucia said I should have gone through him first, and she's probably right in terms of politics. But if I go through him it sits in his inbox for two weeks and nothing changes. I've watched that happen before.

He hasn't responded yet. Part of me is nervous but mostly I feel like I did the thing I actually wanted to do instead of waiting around editing slide decks. If the numbers hold through Friday, the argument is over. I want this to stand on the work, not on who approved it.

Spent New Year's Eve at Lucia's apartment with a few people from the office. Nothing big -- arepas, aguardiente, the countdown on the TV. I didn't check my phone once the whole night, which felt strange at first but I stopped noticing after a while. Lucia made fun of me for not knowing any of the songs on the playlist.

On January first I went for a run along the ciclovia and came back with an idea for restructuring the southern corridor drops. Not the full routing plan Diego shut down -- something smaller, a pilot with just the Cali deliveries. If I can show a cost reduction on one leg, the rest of the argument builds itself. Nobody has to approve a pilot. I can just run it with the three drivers who already told me the current route doesn't make sense.

I drafted the pilot scope on my laptop sitting on Lucia's couch while everyone was watching a movie. Felt good to have something concrete again instead of waiting for permission. I want to own how this unfolds, start to finish.

Still at the office. Everyone else left at six but I'm going through the client satisfaction numbers from Q4 because nobody else is going to do it. Found three accounts where response times slipped below target because the team was running the old dispatch sequence I already flagged two months ago. Two months.

My mom called while I was pulling the spreadsheets. I let it go to voicemail. She'll ask why I'm still at work, then she'll ask when I'm coming home for New Year's, and I don't have answers to either one right now.
sources.nudge_response: Probably not. There's too much to clean up here before January. She'll understand. She usually does.

sources.journal_entry:
The meeting with Diego didn't go how I planned. He sat there scrolling through my routing proposal on his laptop, barely looking up, and when he finally said something it was about the formatting. The formatting. Three months of pulling delivery data, testing alternate corridors, calling warehouse contacts in Medellin -- and he wants to talk about fonts.

I should have pushed back harder. Instead I just nodded and said I'd revise it. The whole walk back to my desk I was already rewriting my argument in my head, all the things I should have said. The numbers speak for themselves. Our current route through Bucaramanga adds two days and the clients in the southern corridor keep complaining.

Part of me wonders if I backed down because he's been here fifteen years and I've been here eleven months. That shouldn't matter when the data is right there. But I sat quiet like it did matter, and now I'm stuck doing cosmetic edits on something that should already be approved.

sources.journal_entry:
Diego sent me "feedback" on the presentation draft. Half of it is adding his name to the second slide as a co-contributor. He didn't contribute. He sat on my original proposal for weeks and only engaged after I went around him. Now he wants credit on the version that works.

I know the smart move is probably to add his name and keep the peace. Everyone keeps telling me to "play the game." But I didn't build this by playing the game. I built it by ignoring the game and doing the actual work. If I put his name on it, what am I even presenting? Someone else's stamp on my project. I'm going to push back. Maybe that's stupid. I don't care.

Finished the presentation draft this morning. Fourteen slides, every number sourced, three scenario projections. I ran through it out loud twice in my apartment and timed it at eighteen minutes, which leaves room for questions. My neighbor probably thinks I'm losing it.

Went to my abuela's for almuerzo after. She made sancocho and didn't ask about work at all, just told me about her friend Doris who's fighting with her landlord. Sat there eating soup and listening and realized I hadn't thought about the presentation for almost two hours. That's probably the longest I've gone without thinking about it in weeks.
sources.nudge_response: Good. Like my brain got to stop running for a bit. I forgot what that was like.

No commentary, no lecture, just "send me the spreadsheet." I sent it within the hour. He forwarded it to the VP of ops in Mexico City. I know because the VP emailed me directly asking for a call next week.

That call could be anything. Could be a reprimand, could be an expansion. Either way the work is out there now and it's mine. I keep refreshing my email like that's going to make the calendar invite appear faster. Need to stop doing that.
sources.nudge_response: I don't know. Something that makes the last three months feel like they counted.

sources.journal_entry:
The Cali pilot is running. Three drivers, rerouted through Palmira instead of the standard loop. I didn't tell Diego. I told the drivers it was a test week and tracked the first four deliveries myself from the dashboard. Average time dropped by six hours per run. Six hours. That's not a font issue.

I built a one-page summary with the numbers and sent it to the full operations chat, not just Diego. Maybe that was aggressive. Lucia said I should have gone through him first, and she's probably right in terms of politics. But if I go through him it sits in his inbox for two weeks and nothing changes. I've watched that happen before.

He hasn't responded yet. Part of me is nervous but mostly I feel like I did the thing I actually wanted to do instead of waiting around editing slide decks. If the numbers hold through Friday, the argument is over. I want this to stand on the work, not on who approved it.

Spent New Year's Eve at Lucia's apartment with a few people from the office. Nothing big -- arepas, aguardiente, the countdown on the TV. I didn't check my phone once the whole night, which felt strange at first but I stopped noticing after a while. Lucia made fun of me for not knowing any of the songs on the playlist.

On January first I went for a run along the ciclovia and came back with an idea for restructuring the southern corridor drops. Not the full routing plan Diego shut down -- something smaller, a pilot with just the Cali deliveries. If I can show a cost reduction on one leg, the rest of the argument builds itself. Nobody has to approve a pilot. I can just run it with the three drivers who already told me the current route doesn't make sense.

I drafted the pilot scope on my laptop sitting on Lucia's couch while everyone was watching a movie. Felt good to have something concrete again instead of waiting for permission. I want to own how this unfolds, start to finish.

Still at the office. Everyone else left at six but I'm going through the client satisfaction numbers from Q4 because nobody else is going to do it. Found three accounts where response times slipped below target because the team was running the old dispatch sequence I already flagged two months ago. Two months.

My mom called while I was pulling the spreadsheets. I let it go to voicemail. She'll ask why I'm still at work, then she'll ask when I'm coming home for New Year's, and I don't have answers to either one right now.
sources.nudge_response: Probably not. There's too much to clean up here before January. She'll understand. She usually does.

sources.journal_entry:
The meeting with Diego didn't go how I planned. He sat there scrolling through my routing proposal on his laptop, barely looking up, and when he finally said something it was about the formatting. The formatting. Three months of pulling delivery data, testing alternate corridors, calling warehouse contacts in Medellin -- and he wants to talk about fonts.

I should have pushed back harder. Instead I just nodded and said I'd revise it. The whole walk back to my desk I was already rewriting my argument in my head, all the things I should have said. The numbers speak for themselves. Our current route through Bucaramanga adds two days and the clients in the southern corridor keep complaining.

Part of me wonders if I backed down because he's been here fifteen years and I've been here eleven months. That shouldn't matter when the data is right there. But I sat quiet like it did matter, and now I'm stuck doing cosmetic edits on something that should already be approved.

sources.journal_entry:
Committee meeting today. Dr. Khalil brought up timeline again, asked when I would have my methodology chapter finalized. I told him the fieldwork is taking longer because I am doing it properly, not rushing through interviews like they are survey forms. He gave me that look, the one he gives when he thinks I am being difficult. Said something about how at my stage of career I should know how to work within constraints.

At my stage. Meaning old. Meaning I should be grateful they let me in at all, should play by the rules without questioning. He does not say this directly but I hear it. The younger students in my cohort, they nod along, they revise when told to revise. Maybe that is smarter. Maybe I am wasting everyone's time insisting my approach matters. But every time I sit down to write the chapter his way, my hands just stop. Something in me refuses.
sources.nudge_response: He wants me to treat the farmers as data points. Sample size, response rates, coding categories. I understand the logic, I am not stupid about methodology. But when I sit down to write it that way, I keep seeing Abu Mahmoud's face. He trusted me with his story. Reducing it to a variable in a regression feels like betraying that trust. Like I am doing the same thing I did as an engineer, just with different paperwork.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent the whole afternoon with Abu Mahmoud at his farm outside Karameh. Three hours sitting on plastic chairs drinking tea while he showed me where the irrigation canal used to run before the allocation changed. His hands, the way he traced the old waterline in the dirt like drawing a map from memory. Forty years he worked that land. Now his grandson is driving trucks in Amman because there is nothing left to grow.

I recorded everything but the recording will not capture how quiet he got when I asked about the cooperative's petition. How he looked past me toward the orchards, half of them dried stumps now. Dr. Khalil wants regression models and policy impact matrices. What I have is Abu Mahmoud saying "we wrote letters until we ran out of paper." This is what I came here for. Not the degree, not the credentials. This.
sources.nudge_response: Thirty years I designed systems to move water from where it was to where it was needed. Good work. Useful work. But always I was working for someone else's priorities, someone else's calculations about who matters. The last project, we diverted a whole tributary for a development that displaced six villages. I signed my name to those drawings. Came home and could not sleep for a week. Told my husband I needed to understand the other side of my own blueprints.

Spent Saturday morning reorganizing my lesson plan binder for October. Color-coded tabs, printed calendar, all the supplementary worksheets hole-punched and filed. Took almost three hours and I didn't need to do it until next week but it felt good having everything lined up.

Close to school, close to them. I bookmarked them. I'll probably go to a few open houses next month, when the semester pace slows down a bit.
sources.nudge_response: Probably yes. My dad will ask about it and I'll feel guilty if I haven't. And honestly the practical reasons are real, the commute would be easy and I could still do Sunday dinners without driving. It just feels like I'm filling in a template someone else drew.

sources.journal_entry:
Checked my savings account this morning before work, just out of habit. The number is fine, it's growing the way it should. Emergency fund fully topped up, separate account for the apartment deposit whenever I decide to actually buy. But standing in the bathroom brushing my teeth and staring at the banking app, I thought, what am I saving toward exactly? A place that looks like my parents' apartment ten minutes away?

One of my students drew a picture of an airplane today and told me she's going to be a pilot. I said that's wonderful. I meant it. But I kept thinking about it through afternoon classes, the certainty she had, like there was no question the world would let her do it.

One of the newer teachers, Miss Shin, asked me at lunch why I didn't apply for the curriculum coordinator position that opened up. She said it like it was obvious I should want it. I told her I'm happy in the classroom, which is true. I like knowing exactly what my day looks like. I know my students, I know the parents, I know which copy machine jams less. There's something to be said for that.

But she kept pushing, saying I'd be "great at leadership" and how it's a step up. A step up from what? I'm not stuck. I chose to stay in this role. The coordinator position means late meetings, district politics, and honestly a barely noticeable pay bump that isn't worth the headache. My contract is stable, my pension is on track, I know what I'm doing here.

I mentioned it to my mom on the phone later and she agreed, said there's no reason to fix what isn't broken. She reminded me that my uncle switched careers three times and now he's borrowing money from grandma. I laughed but it landed differently than she probably intended.
sources.nudge_response: Because mom used him as a cautionary tale, someone who took risks and failed. And I'm supposed to feel reassured that I'm not him. But part of me wondered if at least he tried something. That's an ugly thought. He's struggling. I don't actually want that. I think I just don't want my only proof that I made the right choice to be someone else's failure.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a long call with my brother Faisal today. He has been at the same bank for twenty-two years now and just got promoted to department head. The whole family is celebrating. My mother called separately to tell me how proud she is of him, which — fine. He earned it. I am not bitter about that.

What got under my skin was when Faisal said, near the end of the call, something like "you should think about going back to a real company, you know, before it is too late." He did not mean it cruelly. He genuinely thinks he is helping. But the assumption underneath it — that what I do is somehow less real because I do not sit in an office with a title on my door — that has been following me around since I left the telecom job.

The thing is, I make roughly the same money he does. I pick my own projects. I took three weeks off last November without asking anyone for permission. I built a small open-source tool last year that people in four countries actually use. None of that registers as success in his framework, and honestly, it does not need to. I just wish the conversations did not always circle back to the same place.
sources.nudge_response: Probably nothing they could do. I think the honest answer is that some part of me still measures myself by their yardstick even though I walked away from it. If I were fully settled about the path I chose, Faisal's comment would roll off. It mostly does. But "mostly" is not "completely" and that gap shows up at 11pm when I am lying in bed running the conversation back.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent most of today going back and forth with the logistics client about the on-site requirement. Their project manager, a guy named Khaled, kept framing it as a "collaboration opportunity." I told him I have been collaborating fine over Zoom for six months. He said upper management wants to "see bodies in the building." That phrase — bodies in the building — is exactly why I left corporate work in the first place.

I offered a compromise: one day a week on-site, the rest remote. Khaled said he would take it up the chain but his tone suggested it was not going to fly. Part of me is already drafting a mental exit plan. I have two other clients and a lead on a new project through my old colleague Rami. The money would be tighter for a couple months but manageable.

Nadia thinks I am being rigid. She might be right. But there is a difference between being rigid and knowing what makes you actually function well. Every time I have forced myself into someone else's structure for long enough, the work gets worse, not better. I tried explaining that over dinner and she nodded but I could tell she was thinking about the school fees.

The logistics client wants me to come on-site three days a week starting next month. Three days. In an office, at a desk they pick, on their schedule. Nadia says I should consider it because the contract is good but I feel like my chest is tightening just reading the email.

It is just a stupid way to work.

Sitting in their office from 9 to 5 means pretending to be productive during the two hours after lunch when I am basically useless, and then having to leave at five when I am finally hitting a good rhythm. It is just a stupid way to work.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a long call with my brother Faisal today. He has been at the same bank for twenty-two years now and just got promoted to department head. The whole family is celebrating. My mother called separately to tell me how proud she is of him, which — fine. He earned it. I am not bitter about that.

What got under my skin was when Faisal said, near the end of the call, something like "you should think about going back to a real company, you know, before it is too late." He did not mean it cruelly. He genuinely thinks he is helping. But the assumption underneath it — that what I do is somehow less real because I do not sit in an office with a title on my door — that has been following me around since I left the telecom job.

The thing is, I make roughly the same money he does. I pick my own projects. I took three weeks off last November without asking anyone for permission. I built a small open-source tool last year that people in four countries actually use. None of that registers as success in his framework, and honestly, it does not need to. I just wish the conversations did not always circle back to the same place.
sources.nudge_response: Probably nothing they could do. I think the honest answer is that some part of me still measures myself by their yardstick even though I walked away from it. If I were fully settled about the path I chose, Faisal's comment would roll off. It mostly does. But "mostly" is not "completely" and that gap shows up at 11pm when I am lying in bed running the conversation back.

My dad asked me over dinner last night if I was taking my job seriously. I told him I just got a satisfactory rating on my performance review, and he said that was not the point. He meant whether I was staying late, whether I was sacrificing for the company the way he did at my age. I did not know how to explain to him that I work differently. I finished my projects ahead of deadline, I cover for my team when it matters, and I still make time for things I care about. That should count for something.

I spent today a bit distracted, replaying that conversation. Part of me wonders if he has a point, if I am missing something by not grinding harder. But then I think about my uncle, who worked sixty-hour weeks for thirty years and retired bitter and exhausted. I do not want that. I want to be good at my job and still have energy left for everything else.
sources.nudge_response: I guess I would need to keep proving myself over time. If I can keep getting promoted and still leave at reasonable hours, that should speak for itself eventually. We will see.

sources.journal_entry:

My manager gave me this look when I submitted the leave request, like I was abandoning ship during a crisis. We are not even that busy right now. I completed everything on my plate before noon.

The meal was worth it. Twelve courses, and each one was like a small surprise. Jun and I barely talked during the first half because we were so focused on the food. By dessert, we were laughing about how serious we had been. Walking out, I felt genuinely recharged. My manager will survive. I needed that afternoon more than the company needed me at my desk pretending to look occupied.

But I do not want to spend ten years proving myself by sitting around after my work is done. I would rather prove it by actually delivering, then having a life outside.

sources.journal_entry:
After that breakdown earlier I decided to actually be productive. Finished the attachment theory chapter and three of the discussion questions. Emailed my practicum site to confirm January hours. Called Mom's memory care coordinator to check in on the transition plan for when she needs more support, which might be sooner than we thought based on what Lisa's been describing.

The coordinator said they have a spot opening up in the assisted living wing in February. Lisa and I need to talk about it. It would take the daily pressure off Lisa but Mom would hate it. She still has enough awareness to know she's being moved, and I think that would devastate her. But Lisa can't keep doing this alone and I can't move back to Duluth right now, not with one semester left.

Made a list of things to handle this week: Tyler's FAFSA, my spring course registration, groceries for New Year's, and calling the insurance company about Mom's coverage changes. Also need to pick up Lisa's Christmas gift, which I completely forgot to order. She wanted that weighted blanket. I'll find one at Target tomorrow.

I noticed I feel calmer after making the list. That's the pattern again, isn't it. Anxiety happens and I make a list of ways to help other people and suddenly I can breathe. At least I can see it now even if I can't stop it.

Weird thing happened today. I was reading for my human development course, this chapter about attachment theory and caregiving patterns, and I just started crying at the kitchen table. Tyler walked in and asked what was wrong and I said nothing, just allergies, which is such a mom thing to say and we both knew it was a lie.

The chapter was about how some people develop their identity almost entirely around being needed by others. How it starts in childhood, usually with a parent who needed caretaking themselves, and it becomes this pattern where you feel most yourself when you're giving to someone else. And I'm sitting there with a highlighter in my hand thinking, this is literally my biography.

I called Lisa after Tyler went to bed. Told her about the chapter and she laughed and said yeah, no kidding, you've been like that since you were ten. She reminded me how I used to make lunches for both of us when Mom was going through her rough patches. I was in fourth grade. I don't remember it as a burden though. I remember feeling useful. Important, even.

I guess what's getting to me is wondering whether I chose social work because I genuinely want to help people or because I literally don't know how to exist without someone to take care of. That's a scary thought to put on paper. But my practicum supervisor keeps saying self-awareness is the first tool, so here it is. I'm aware. Now what.
sources.nudge_response: Maybe not. Lisa said something similar, that both things can be true. That I can genuinely care about this work and also recognize the pattern. I just don't want to end up burning out because I never learned how to sit still without a to-do list for someone else. I watched that happen with Mom before she got sick. She ran herself ragged for everyone and then there was nobody left to run for her.

sources.journal_entry:

I keep wanting to fix it for him. Check his portal, email admissions, do something. But he's seventeen and he needs to learn to sit with uncertainty. A classmate in my cohort made a comment during seminar about how people who go into social work are usually "working out their own stuff." She said it like it was a joke but half the room went quiet. I wanted to say something but I just sat there. She's twenty-six and has never had to take care of anyone but herself.

That's not fair, I don't know her story. But it bothered me more than it should have. Maybe because I know she's not wrong, at least in my case. But there's a difference between understanding your own patterns and having some kid with no life experience reduce your entire motivation to a punchline. I'm here because I've lived this. That counts for something.
sources.nudge_response: The part about working out your own stuff, obviously. But everyone does that. Every doctor who lost a parent to cancer, every teacher who had a bad one growing up. That's not a weakness, that's fuel. I just didn't appreciate the delivery.

sources.journal_entry:

sources.journal_entry: Spring semester started. First class back and I actually felt ready. Not fixed, not finished figuring anything out. Just present. Lisa texted me good luck this morning with a heart emoji. I saved it.

Drove up to Duluth Saturday morning. Tyler came with me. He sat with Mom for an hour while Lisa and I toured the assisted living wing. It's clean, the staff seemed attentive, there's a garden area for warmer months. Mom would have a private room.

Lisa and I agreed we'll bring it up with Mom's doctor at the next appointment. Neither of us said it out loud but we both know this is probably happening in the next few months. On the drive home Tyler was quiet. Then he said, "She remembered my name today." I just reached over and squeezed his hand.

Made it home by eight. Did laundry, packed Tyler's lunch for Monday, prepped my notes for practicum. Ordinary things that felt good to do.

A classmate in my cohort made a comment during seminar about how people who go into social work are usually "working out their own stuff." She said it like it was a joke but half the room went quiet. I wanted to say something but I just sat there. She's twenty-six and has never had to take care of anyone but herself.

That's not fair, I don't know her story. But it bothered me more than it should have. Maybe because I know she's not wrong, at least in my case. But there's a difference between understanding your own patterns and having some kid with no life experience reduce your entire motivation to a punchline. I'm here because I've lived this. That counts for something.
sources.nudge_response: The part about working out your own stuff, obviously. But everyone does that. Every doctor who lost a parent to cancer, every teacher who had a bad one growing up. That's not a weakness, that's fuel. I just didn't appreciate the delivery.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a long phone call with Lisa last night. We talked for almost two hours, which we haven't done in months because usually our calls are logistics. Where's the insurance card, did you call the pharmacy, can you come up this weekend. But this time we actually talked.

She told me she doesn't resent me for going back to school. I didn't realize how much I needed to hear that until she said it and I couldn't talk for a minute. She said she's proud of me, which made me feel about six years old in the best way. Then she said she's also exhausted and scared and doesn't know how long she can keep doing the day-to-day with Mom by herself.

We made a plan. I'll come up every other weekend starting this month, and we're going to look into the assisted living option together. Not making any decisions yet, just touring the place and talking to Mom's doctor. Lisa also said she wants me to stop apologizing every time we talk. She said, "You're doing what you need to do. Stop acting like you're abandoning us." I wrote that on a sticky note and put it on my laptop.

Tyler overheard part of the conversation and came in after to ask if Grandma was okay. I told him the truth, that she's not getting better but we're figuring it out as a family. He said he'd come with me to Duluth next time. He didn't have to offer that. Moments like that make me think I must have done something right with him.

Lisa just told me she's thinking about taking a leave from her job to handle Mom full-time. She can't afford that. I should be the one doing this but I'm stuck here finishing a degree that doesn't pay anyone's bills yet.

After that breakdown earlier I decided to actually be productive. Finished the attachment theory chapter and three of the discussion questions. Emailed my practicum site to confirm January hours. Called Mom's memory care coordinator to check in on the transition plan for when she needs more support, which might be sooner than we thought based on what Lisa's been describing.

The coordinator said they have a spot opening up in the assisted living wing in February. Lisa and I need to talk about it. It would take the daily pressure off Lisa but Mom would hate it. She still has enough awareness to know she's being moved, and I think that would devastate her. But Lisa can't keep doing this alone and I can't move back to Duluth right now, not with one semester left.

Made a list of things to handle this week: Tyler's FAFSA, my spring course registration, groceries for New Year's, and calling the insurance company about Mom's coverage changes. Also need to pick up Lisa's Christmas gift, which I completely forgot to order. She wanted that weighted blanket. I'll find one at Target tomorrow.

I noticed I feel calmer after making the list. That's the pattern again, isn't it. Anxiety happens and I make a list of ways to help other people and suddenly I can breathe. At least I can see it now even if I can't stop it.

Weird thing happened today. I was reading for my human development course, this chapter about attachment theory and caregiving patterns, and I just started crying at the kitchen table. Tyler walked in and asked what was wrong and I said nothing, just allergies, which is such a mom thing to say and we both knew it was a lie.

The chapter was about how some people develop their identity almost entirely around being needed by others. How it starts in childhood, usually with a parent who needed caretaking themselves, and it becomes this pattern where you feel most yourself when you're giving to someone else. And I'm sitting there with a highlighter in my hand thinking, this is literally my biography.

I called Lisa after Tyler went to bed. Told her about the chapter and she laughed and said yeah, no kidding, you've been like that since you were ten. She reminded me how I used to make lunches for both of us when Mom was going through her rough patches. I was in fourth grade. I don't remember it as a burden though. I remember feeling useful. Important, even.

I guess what's getting to me is wondering whether I chose social work because I genuinely want to help people or because I literally don't know how to exist without someone to take care of. That's a scary thought to put on paper. But my practicum supervisor keeps saying self-awareness is the first tool, so here it is. I'm aware. Now what.
sources.nudge_response: Maybe not. Lisa said something similar, that both things can be true. That I can genuinely care about this work and also recognize the pattern. I just don't want to end up burning out because I never learned how to sit still without a to-do list for someone else. I watched that happen with Mom before she got sick. She ran herself ragged for everyone and then there was nobody left to run for her.

sources.journal_entry:
Christmas Eve and I'm wrapping presents at the kitchen table while Tyler's on the couch watching something on his phone. He's been quiet lately. I asked him if he was okay and he said yeah, just stressed about early decision. He applied to UW-Madison and won't hear back until February.

I keep wanting to fix it for him. Check his portal, email admissions, do something. But he's seventeen and he needs to learn to sit with uncertainty. That's the hardest part of caring about someone, I think. Knowing when to step back. I'm not very good at it. I'd rather stay up all night worrying on someone's behalf than let them worry alone. I don't know if that's love or just a habit I can't break.

My cohort advisor emailed about missing a group meeting last Friday. I was in Duluth taking care of my mother. Some things are more important than a Zoom call. I'll make it up but I'm not going to apologize for being there.
sources.nudge_response: It's fine, I manage. People do harder things. The advisor is understanding, I'm probably overreacting because I'm tired from the drive.

sources.journal_entry:
Got an email today from a former colleague, Deepa, about a senior position opening at the water authority back in Chennai. Permanent role, government pension, the whole thing. She said she thought of me immediately. My mother would cry with happiness if I took it. Appa would finally stop asking pointed questions about "what the plan is." Arjun's parents would stop whispering about how their son married a woman who can't settle down.

I sat with the email open for maybe twenty minutes. I could picture the whole life — the flat in Adyar, Meera going to the same school I went to, weekend lunches at my parents' house. Predictable. Comfortable. Everything mapped out for the next thirty years. And I felt this thing in my chest, not panic exactly but something close. Like the walls of that life were already closing in even though I haven't said yes to anything. I know the stipend is barely enough. I know Arjun is tired of being the only one earning properly. I know my savings are basically gone. I know all of this.

But I closed the email and went back to my data. I'll probably tell Deepa thanks but not now, maybe later, which is what I always say. The part I can't explain to anyone is that the uncertainty here feels more honest than the certainty there. That sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud but there it is.
sources.nudge_response: About what I actually want, I think. The Chennai job would be fine. Good, even. But it would be someone else's version of my life. The one everyone expected me to have. Here I'm struggling but at least the struggle is mine.

sources.journal_entry: My friend Valentina says I'm "too attached to the past." She means it gently but it still stings. She left Guadalajara for Monterrey and barely comes back for holidays now. Good for her. I'm not running from anything by staying. This is where I'm needed. My grandmother is eighty-three. My students know me. The roots here are mine.

The new principal at school announced we're "modernizing" the curriculum. Tablets for third graders. Interactive lessons instead of textbooks. She presented it like everyone should be excited but I sat in that meeting thinking about Sister Magdalena who taught at this school for forty years and how her chalkboard handwriting was so beautiful my mother still talks about it. I'm not against technology — I use my phone constantly, I'm not a dinosaur — but something about the way the principal said "we need to move past old methods" made me want to dig my heels in.

After the meeting Roberto from fifth grade asked what I thought and I said it sounded fine. I don't know why I didn't say what I was really thinking. Maybe because I didn't want to be the young teacher defending old ways. Maybe because I don't even know if I'm right. The kids might love the tablets. Sister Magdalena isn't here to ask.

I keep thinking about how my mother taught me to read with a book of saints' stories, turning actual pages, her finger tracing the words. What gets lost when everything becomes a screen? Or am I just afraid of change and calling it something nicer?
sources.nudge_response: That maybe we should pilot it in one classroom first instead of rolling it out everywhere at once. That the older teachers who've been here for decades deserve to have their methods respected, not treated like problems to be solved. That learning isn't just information transfer — it's also ritual, routine, the physical feeling of a pencil in your hand. But standing up in a staff meeting to say "I think ritual matters" sounds ridiculous. So I stayed quiet and now I'm typing it into my phone at 11pm instead.

sources.journal_entry:
Brought Carlos to Sunday lunch at my parents' house. My hands were shaking when we walked through the door. My mother had set an extra place — she knew I wouldn't come alone after our last conversation. She's always known more than she lets on.

It wasn't easy. There were silences that stretched too long and my father asked pointed questions about where Carlos sees himself in five years. But my grandmother held his hand when he talked about his daughter from his first marriage, and said children are always a blessing no matter the circumstances. That's not the same as approval but it's not rejection either.

After dessert, while Carlos helped my father clear plates, my mother pulled me aside and said "I don't understand all of it but I can see he's good to you." That's enough for now. Maybe that's what Father Miguel meant — bringing my life to the tradition honestly doesn't mean it fits perfectly. It just means I stop hiding the pieces that don't.

I told my mother about Carlos. Not everything — not the divorce — but that I've been seeing someone. She asked when she could meet him and I panicked and said "soon" which is what I always say. She knows me too well. She could hear the hesitation and asked what I wasn't telling her.

I almost said it. The words were right there. But then my abuela came into the room asking about dinner and the moment passed and I felt relief and shame in equal measure. Relief because I got more time. Shame because I'm a grown woman hiding in the kitchen of my childhood home, still arranging my life around moments that are safe.

Carlos deserves better than being my secret. I deserve better than feeling like a coward. Something has to break.
sources.nudge_response: Telling the full truth and accepting whatever comes after. Not performing okay-ness at the next family gathering. Letting my mother feel her feelings without me trying to manage them. Maybe it looks like a difficult Sunday dinner where Carlos sits across from my father and answers questions about his first marriage. Maybe it looks like my grandmother going quiet in that way she does when she disapproves. I can survive that. I've survived other hard things. What I can't survive is another six months of living in two separate worlds that never touch.

sources.journal_entry: School starts back next week. Spent the afternoon organizing my classroom. Put up the same San Francisco de Asis poster my mother gave me my first year teaching. The corners are getting worn. Considered replacing it but decided against it. Some things are allowed to show their age.

Went to confession today for the first time in months. Didn't plan to — I was walking past the church after buying bread and the door was open. Father Miguel has known me since my first communion so there was no hiding behind anonymity. I told him I've been lying to my mother about something important. He didn't ask what. Just waited.

I ended up talking for twenty minutes about Carlos, about feeling stuck, about how the rules I grew up with don't seem to have instructions for this situation. He said something I keep turning over: "The tradition doesn't ask you to stop living. It asks you to bring your life to it honestly." I don't know exactly what that means yet but it felt like permission to stop pretending there's a perfect answer.

After confession I sat in the pew where my grandmother always sits and just breathed. The church smelled the same way it did when I was seven. Some things don't change and today that felt like comfort instead of a cage.

Carlos and I had a real fight. Not yelling — we don't do that — but the cold kind where you both know something broke. He asked if I was ashamed of him and I didn't answer fast enough. I'm not ashamed. I'm scared. There's a difference but I couldn't find the words to explain it while he was standing there looking at me like he'd already made up his mind about what my silence meant.

My parents have been married for thirty-two years. They met at church, got engaged with my grandfather's blessing, had the wedding everyone still talks about. That's the script. I don't know how to write a different one and still feel like myself. Carlos doesn't fit the script but neither does walking away from him. I lay awake until three trying to figure out which betrayal I could live with.
sources.nudge_response: I want to say yes. The optimistic answer is that my family loves me and they'll accept whoever makes me happy. My cousin got pushback about her civil ceremony and now everyone's fine at Christmas dinner. But I know my mother. She carries things quietly for years. She'd show up to the wedding and smile and then I'd catch her crying in the kitchen when she thinks no one's looking. I don't know if I can build a life on top of that image. Maybe that's my problem — I'm not choosing between Carlos and my family. I'm choosing between the version of me who disappoints people and the version who disappears herself to keep everyone comfortable.

sources.journal_entry: My friend Valentina says I'm "too attached to the past." She means it gently but it still stings. She left Guadalajara for Monterrey and barely comes back for holidays now. Good for her. I'm not running from anything by staying. This is where I'm needed. My grandmother is eighty-three. My students know me. The roots here are mine.

The new principal at school announced we're "modernizing" the curriculum. Tablets for third graders. Interactive lessons instead of textbooks. She presented it like everyone should be excited but I sat in that meeting thinking about Sister Magdalena who taught at this school for forty years and how her chalkboard handwriting was so beautiful my mother still talks about it. I'm not against technology — I use my phone constantly, I'm not a dinosaur — but something about the way the principal said "we need to move past old methods" made me want to dig my heels in.

After the meeting Roberto from fifth grade asked what I thought and I said it sounded fine. I don't know why I didn't say what I was really thinking. Maybe because I didn't want to be the young teacher defending old ways. Maybe because I don't even know if I'm right. The kids might love the tablets. Sister Magdalena isn't here to ask.

I keep thinking about how my mother taught me to read with a book of saints' stories, turning actual pages, her finger tracing the words. What gets lost when everything becomes a screen? Or am I just afraid of change and calling it something nicer?
sources.nudge_response: That maybe we should pilot it in one classroom first instead of rolling it out everywhere at once. That the older teachers who've been here for decades deserve to have their methods respected, not treated like problems to be solved. That learning isn't just information transfer — it's also ritual, routine, the physical feeling of a pencil in your hand. But standing up in a staff meeting to say "I think ritual matters" sounds ridiculous. So I stayed quiet and now I'm typing it into my phone at 11pm instead.

sources.journal_entry: Spent the evening at Abuela's preparing food for tomorrow's final night of the novena. Chopped onions until my eyes burned. My cousin Daniela brought her new baby and everyone passed him around the kitchen like a small warm blessing. The prayers start at seven. I'll be there early to set up chairs like I have been every year since I was fourteen.

Carlos asked to meet my family this weekend. I made up something about it being a busy week with the novena. He looked hurt. I feel like I'm lying to two worlds at once — telling him we just need more time, telling my mother I'm too focused on work to date. Neither story is true. The true story is that I don't know how to bring a divorced man into a family that still whispers about my cousin's civil ceremony.
sources.nudge_response: She wouldn't yell. That's not how she operates. She'd get quiet and then start asking gentle questions that feel like tiny knives — How long has this been going on? Has he been to confession? What does his family think about all this? And I'd have no good answers. I don't even know if I want to marry him. I just want space to figure that out without the weight of everyone's expectations pressing down on me before I've made up my own mind.

sources.journal_entry:
My mother called to remind me about the novena for Tía Carmen's anniversary next week. Didn't need the reminder — it's been circled on my calendar since January. When I was small I used to think these gatherings were just adults talking over coffee, but now I understand them differently. Nine nights of prayer, nine nights of family filling up the house. There's something steady about it.

I taught my third graders how to fold paper flowers today for the altar at school. One little boy asked why we do it every year and I told him the same thing my grandmother told me: because the dead don't really leave if we keep making space for them. He seemed satisfied with that. Sometimes children accept what adults forget — that repetition isn't emptiness, it's a choice to keep something alive.

sources.journal_entry:
Came back to write more because I could not sleep after that last entry. Nikhil also mentioned that his old manager from the gaming company reached out to me apparently. Said they are looking for someone to lead backend on an accessibility project, adaptive interfaces for visually impaired users. The pay would be significantly better than what I make now and the work would not feel empty the way pure fintech might.

But here is the thing. If I leave the startup, the offline-sync project does not have a clear owner. Karthik could take it over eventually but he joined four months ago and the codebase is, frankly, held together with duct tape and my institutional memory. The Hubli pilot is supposed to expand to three more districts by January. If that rollout stumbles because of a handoff gap, actual kids lose access.

I know I am not irreplaceable in some cosmic sense. People leave jobs and the world continues. But the timing feels like it matters. Priya's placement means I could take a risk on staying. Or it means I finally have the breathing room to go somewhere that pays properly. Same fact, two completely different stories depending on which direction I face. Lying here staring at the ceiling fan trying to figure out which story I actually believe.

Had coffee with Nikhil today. He moved to a fintech company six months ago, says the work is mostly CRUD but the pay let him put his parents in a nicer flat. He was not bragging. He looked tired actually. I kept nodding and thinking about Amma's knee and the 2G kids in Hubli at the same time.
sources.nudge_response: I think the honest answer is I don't know yet and that scares me more than either option. If I leave for more money I know I'll resent sitting in standups about payment conversion funnels. But if Amma needs that surgery and I am still making idealistic-startup money, then what was all of it for? I keep framing it like a binary but maybe the part I can't say out loud is that I'm afraid whichever I pick I'll feel like I failed someone.

sources.journal_entry:
Coming back to this because something has been sitting with me since the afternoon. When Priya showed me the offer letter I noticed the salary. It is nearly the same as mine, fresh out of college. I am not jealous of her, that is not it. She earned it completely. But it made me do the math I keep avoiding.

I have been at this startup for three years and the increments have been modest. The work is the most fulfilling thing I have done but I also know Amma's knees are getting worse and the consultation she needs is not cheap. Priya's new salary helps but she will have her own rent and expenses. I keep circling back to the same question without finishing the thought.

Priya got her campus placement offer today. It is a decent product company in Hyderabad with good benefits. Amma cried at lunch, the happy kind, and then immediately started worrying about Priya living alone. I told her Priya would be fine. Honestly I am just relieved one less thing is on the table financially.

Could not sleep last night. Kept turning over the rebranding conversation. Went down to the kitchen at two in the morning and found Baba's old notebooks in the drawer where Mama keeps the good tablecloths. He used to write down every buyer's name, where they were from, what they ordered. Pages of it in his careful handwriting.

I sat there reading for an hour. He wrote about a French buyer in 1991 who wanted to change the oil blend and he refused. Lost the account. Got it back three years later when the buyer admitted the original was better. I do not know if that story is supposed to comfort me or scare me. The market is different now.

The thing that unsettles me is not the Italian distributor. It is that part of me can see his point. The rational part. And I do not know what it means that I can see it and still feel like acting on it would be a kind of betrayal. Like I would be the one who finally broke the thread.

sources.journal_entry:
The new Italian distributor wants us to rebrand. Sleeker labels, English-only packaging, drop the family crest. He said the current look feels "regional." I almost hung up on him. Regional. My father designed that label with a calligrapher from Salt in 1982. It has been on every bottle we have ever shipped.

I brought it up with Samir, my operations manager, and he shrugged and said maybe the Italian has a point. That the European market responds to minimalism. sources.journal_entry: Told Nadia she can apply to London. She cried. I cried. Rania stood in the doorway pretending she was not crying. The house felt lighter after, like we had been holding our breath for weeks.
sources.nudge_response: Nothing changed, really. I just stopped waiting for the feeling to go away and made the decision with it still there. Maybe that is what my father did too. Carried the weight and moved anyway.

sources.journal_entry:
The Italian distributor sent a revised proposal. They will keep the family crest but want to modernize the typography and add English and Italian text below the Arabic. Samir thinks it is a fair middle ground. I stared at the mockup for twenty minutes.

It looks fine. Objectively, it looks fine. The crest is there, the Arabic is there, just smaller. And I keep telling myself that Baba adapted too, that the company looked different in 1995 than it did in 1978. But he was the one making those changes. He earned the right to decide what stayed and what evolved. I inherited the decision and it does not sit the same way.

Rania asked me tonight if I have thought more about Nadia and London. I told her not now. She said there will never be a right time and she is probably correct. The June deadline I set is almost here and I do not have an answer. I do not even have a framework for the answer. Just this weight in my chest every time I think about the company ten years from now with no family in it.

Nadia came back from the documentary shoot glowing. She talked through dinner about camera angles and interview techniques. I listened and felt two things at once: pride and something heavier I cannot name.

Took the kids to Friday prayers at the old mosque near Jabal Amman instead of our usual one. The imam there knew my father. Afterward he told my youngest, Omar, a story about how Baba once donated an entire shipment to a refugee camp in the eighties. Omar's eyes went wide. He had never heard that one.

Drove home with all three kids in the back seat arguing about whether Jiddo was a hero or just generous. Nadia said both. I did not correct anyone. It was a good morning.
sources.nudge_response: That he was not being generous. He was being obligated. In our family, in our community, you give because that is what you do. It is not heroism, it is just the way things work. But watching Omar hear it as something extraordinary made me realize maybe that way of doing things is not as obvious to them as it was to us. And that worries me.

sources.journal_entry:
Quarterly numbers came in and they are flat. Not terrible, but flat in a market that is growing means we are losing ground. Samir put together a presentation about expanding into the Gulf retail market. New packaging, smaller bottles, gift sets for Ramadan. I told him to go ahead with the proposal.

I did not fight it this time. Maybe because I am tired, maybe because the port delays last week reminded me how fragile our European pipeline really is. Diversifying makes sense. I told myself the Gulf packaging can look different from the European line without touching the original label. A compromise. Baba would have called it something else.

Nadia asked me at dinner if she could shadow a documentary crew in Amman next week. Some university project. I said fine without really thinking about it. Rania gave me a look, like she was surprised I did not put up a fight. I did not have one in me tonight.

Actually, the mansaf was good even cold. Rania uses Mama's recipe, the one with the dried yogurt from the women's co-op in Ajloun. Small thing but it reminded me that some things do carry forward without anyone forcing them.

Long week. Two shipments delayed because of port congestion in Aqaba, had to personally call four buyers to explain. Spent most of Thursday driving to Irbid because Mama's water heater broke and my brother the Dubai expert could not exactly fix it from there.

Came home to Rania and the kids eating mansaf without me. They saved me a plate. Ate it cold at ten o'clock watching the news. Just one of those weeks where everything takes twice as long and nothing feels finished.

Nadia brought home a prospectus from the London film school. Left it on the kitchen table like it was a magazine. Rania pretended not to notice. I noticed.

She has been building her case quietly. Showing us short films she made on her phone, mentioning alumni who work at Al Jazeera and BBC Arabic. She is smart about it. She knows a direct argument will not work with me so she is laying evidence like a lawyer. I would admire it if it were not aimed at dismantling the one plan I had for this family's future.

My brother Kamal called and said I should let her go, that holding her back will only push her further away. Easy for him to say. He moved to Dubai fifteen years ago and calls on holidays. He has no idea what it takes to keep things together here. To sit at Mama's table every Friday and hold the center while everyone else drifts toward their own orbits. Someone has to be the anchor and apparently that someone is always me.
sources.nudge_response: Both, I think. It happened because I was the eldest and stayed. But I also chose it every single time I could have left. The problem is I chose it so many times it stopped feeling like a choice and started feeling like who I am. I do not know how to separate the two anymore.

sources.journal_entry:
Could not sleep last night. Kept turning over the rebranding conversation. Went down to the kitchen at two in the morning and found Baba's old notebooks in the drawer where Mama keeps the good tablecloths. He used to write down every buyer's name, where they were from, what they ordered. Pages of it in his careful handwriting.

I sat there reading for an hour. He wrote about a French buyer in 1991 who wanted to change the oil blend and he refused. Lost the account. Got it back three years later when the buyer admitted the original was better. I do not know if that story is supposed to comfort me or scare me. The market is different now.

The thing that unsettles me is not the Italian distributor. It is that part of me can see his point. The rational part. And I do not know what it means that I can see it and still feel like acting on it would be a kind of betrayal. Like I would be the one who finally broke the thread.
sources.nudge_response: Everything. The way we do business, yes, but also who I am in relation to my father. If I change the way he built things, I am saying his way was not good enough. And I am not ready to say that, even if the numbers eventually force me to.

sources.journal_entry:
The new Italian distributor wants us to rebrand. Sleeker labels, English-only packaging, drop the family crest. He said the current look feels "regional." I almost hung up on him. Regional. My father designed that label with a calligrapher from Salt in 1982. It has been on every bottle we have ever shipped.

I brought it up with Samir, my operations manager, and he shrugged and said maybe the Italian has a point. That the European market responds to minimalism. I asked him if he would strip his grandmother's embroidery off the wall because a decorator said it clashed with the furniture. He laughed. I was not joking.

Rania told me later I am letting sentiment run the business. Maybe. But if I strip away everything that connects this company to where it came from, what exactly am I running? A logistics operation with my name on it. That is not what Baba built and it is not what I agreed to carry.

My cousin Faisal called to say his son is taking over his construction firm this year. He did not say it to make a point, but it landed like one. His kid is twenty-three and already stepping in. Meanwhile I cannot even get Nadia to visit the warehouse.

People keep acting like I should just let her go do whatever she wants. Rania says I am being stubborn. But nobody asks what happens to this company in fifteen years. Nobody asks who carries it forward. I did not choose this either, but I showed up.
sources.nudge_response: That was a different time. There was no question to ask.

sources.journal_entry: Told Nadia she could take the summer to think about London but that we would discuss it seriously in June. She looked relieved but I felt nothing. I keep wondering if I am just delaying because I do not know how to say no to her face.
sources.nudge_response: More than the argument itself. I think it would mean admitting the business is not enough to hold the family together the way it held us when Baba was running it.

sources.journal_entry:
Second entry today because something's been sitting with me since this morning. Baba asked if I could help in the shop tomorrow because his back is bad again. I said fine but inside I was annoyed. It's his shop, his thing—he never asks my opinion on how to run it, never treats me like I might actually know something about business.

But then I thought about it more and realized part of the annoyance is that when I'm in his shop I'm just his son moving boxes. Not the guy managing a fleet. I shrink in that space and I hate it. I don't think he does it on purpose. He just doesn't see me the way I need to be seen.

Good day actually. Had all three scooters running, no breakdowns, deliveries going smooth. Sami and Yousef both hit their targets and I told them I'd add a small bonus this week. Felt good telling them that, like I'm actually running something real. Standing in the kitchen tracking the routes on my phone and for a second it felt like I had a grip on things.

My friend Khaled called to see if I wanted to come play football but I told him I had to stay on the routes. Truth is the routes were fine, I just didn't want to step away. When things are going well I want to be right there watching it happen. Maybe that's weird but I don't trust good days to last if I'm not paying attention.

Met with the owner of Shawarma House on Mecca Street about getting their lunch deliveries. He kept talking to his manager instead of me, asking him questions like I was some intern. I'm the one who handles the logistics, I'm the one signing the agreement, but apparently I don't look old enough to be taken seriously.

Got the deal in the end because my prices were better than the other guy's. But the whole meeting left a bad taste. I keep replaying the moments where he looked past me. I should be used to it by now—people always underestimate the young one in the room—but it still gets under my skin every time.
sources.nudge_response: If he'd looked me in the eye and talked to me directly. If he'd treated the meeting like I was the one making decisions, not some errand boy. The money is good but I need people to understand who they're dealing with.

sources.journal_entry:
Can't sleep so I'm writing again. Today wore me out but it's not just the deliveries. I keep thinking about this pattern where I put myself at the center of everything and then get angry when people don't orbit around me the way I want. Yousef left because the warehouse was better for him. Nader didn't show because he had his own reasons. Neither of them owed me anything beyond the work.

But it doesn't feel that way. It feels like when people leave or let me down, they're saying what I'm building doesn't matter. And if what I'm building doesn't matter then what am I? Just some guy with three scooters and a spreadsheet. My mother keeps telling me I work too hard and I should find a girl and settle down like my cousin Ahmad. Ahmad works at a bank. Ahmad has a car. But Ahmad also asks his father permission before he goes anywhere and I'd rather eat glass than live like that.

I think the reason I can't let go of anything—the routes, the negotiations, even the small stuff—is because the moment I'm not in charge of something, I feel like I'm nobody. That's not a comfortable thing to write down. I don't know what to do with it. But Yousef quitting and Nader ghosting in the same week made something crack open and I'm just sitting here looking at it.
sources.nudge_response: That maybe I've been so focused on people respecting me that I forgot to ask if I respect myself without all of this. Like if the scooters disappeared tomorrow and I was just Tariq, not Tariq who runs a fleet—would that be enough? I don't think I know the answer yet.

sources.journal_entry: Nader didn't show up for his trial. Didn't call, didn't text. I covered his entire route myself, thirteen deliveries in the rain. My hands are still shaking from the cold.
sources.nudge_response: Yeah. And I was wrong. Or maybe he's exactly like me and decided he didn't want to answer to someone else. I don't know which is worse.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent the morning interviewing two guys to replace Yousef. One of them, Issa, seemed okay but kept asking about hours and breaks before even asking what the job was. The other one, Nader, was hungrier—reminded me of myself when I started. I told him he could do a trial run tomorrow. Already planning his routes in my head.

I notice I always pick the one who reminds me of me. The one who wants it. Khaled says I should pick the reliable one but reliable is boring. I want someone who's going to hustle because they want to prove something, not just clock in and clock out. Maybe that's a mistake. Yousef was reliable and he still left. At least with the hungry ones you know what drives them.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly, it's fifty-fifty. Some of them burn bright and then flame out. But the ones who stay—they get it, they understand what we're building. Sami was like that. He's still here. I'd rather have one Sami than three guys who don't care.

sources.journal_entry: Yousef quit today. Said he got a warehouse job that pays steady. I told him good luck but when he left I punched the wall in my room. Losing a rider means losing a route means losing income.
sources.nudge_response: Both. He was my first hire. I trained him, gave him a shot when nobody else would. And he just walks away like it meant nothing. Like what I built wasn't worth staying for.

Hired Issa after all—the "reliable" one Khaled told me about. He did his first full week and showed up every day on time. Not flashy, doesn't try to impress me, just does the work. I'm not used to that being enough but I'm trying to let it be.

Had dinner at home tonight and baba asked about the business for the first time without me bringing it up. He asked how many restaurants I work with now and when I said eleven he went quiet for a second and then said "ya'ni, that's more than I thought." It wasn't a celebration or anything. But he looked at me differently, even for a moment, and I carried that home with me like it was something fragile.

I keep coming back to what I wrote last week about needing to be in charge to feel like somebody. I don't think that feeling goes away overnight. Neither of them was about me being in control. Both of them felt good in a way I wasn't expecting. I'm not saying I've figured anything out. But maybe not everything has to go through me for it to count.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent the whole morning at Leopold's working on sketches for the cafe mural commission. There's something about sitting in a busy space that helps ideas flow — all that ambient noise and people-watching. I ordered three cups of chai and didn't feel guilty about it. The sketches are coming together. Abstract florals with these hidden eyes peeking through petals. The cafe owner wanted "something colorful" which honestly gives me so much room to play.

I keep thinking about what Neha said last week, how she can't understand spending money on experiences when we're always behind on rent. But like... what's the point of hustling if you never actually enjoy anything? I'm not being irresponsible. I finished the commission brief. I just also let myself have a nice morning. Both things can be true.
