sources.journal_entry:
Ma called again. The usual script. "Beta, you're 22 now. Meera aunty's daughter just got placed at Infosys. When are you going to think about your future?" I tried to explain that I AM thinking about my future, that the mural commission could lead to more work with the cafe chain, that I've been approached about teaching at an actual studio. But she doesn't hear any of that. She only hears "no salary, no benefits, no husband."

I hung up crying. Not because I doubt myself — I KNOW this is what I'm meant to do. But it's exhausting to constantly defend my choices to people who refuse to see them as valid. Papa at least stays quiet now. But Ma... she makes it sound like I'm throwing my life away for finger painting.

Rohan came over with biriyani and let me rant for an hour. He gets it — his family was the same way until he started making decent money from photography. He said something that stuck with me: "They'll come around when they see you're serious. You just have to outlast their doubt." But how long is that supposed to take? And why should I have to prove myself to people who should just... believe in me?

I painted until 3am. Angry brushstrokes that somehow turned into something beautiful. Maybe that's the only way I know how to process this.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly? I don't know if I can feel at peace with it. Part of me still wants her approval even though I hate admitting that.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a rare quiet day. Slept in until noon, made myself a proper breakfast instead of grabbing biscuits, then just... existed. Watered all the plants. Put on a Norah Jones record. Sat by the window with my sketchbook and didn't force anything. Some days the best thing I can do is nothing at all.

I've been thinking about what success means to me. Society has this very narrow definition — salary, title, marriage, house. But when I imagine my ideal life, it's this: a studio of my own, enough commissions to stay comfortable, mornings where I can drink chai without rushing, the freedom to say no to projects that don't excite me. That's it. That's the whole dream.

People act like wanting to enjoy your life is lazy or lacking drive. But I think it takes more courage to opt out of the rat race than to join it. Anyone can chase money. Not everyone can figure out what actually makes them happy and then structure their life around it.

The mural money came through. I'm putting half toward rent and supplies, and the other half toward that weekend trip to Goa with Rohan and Meera. Non-negotiable. We need this.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly it doesn't feel that far off. A few more consistent clients, maybe. Right now I'm just focused on the Goa trip.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a rare quiet day. Slept in until noon, made myself a proper breakfast instead of grabbing biscuits, then just... existed. Watered all the plants. Put on a Norah Jones record. Sat by the window with my sketchbook and didn't force anything. Some days the best thing I can do is nothing at all.

I've been thinking about what success means to me. Society has this very narrow definition — salary, title, marriage, house. But when I imagine my ideal life, it's this: a studio of my own, enough commissions to stay comfortable, mornings where I can drink chai without rushing, the freedom to say no to projects that don't excite me. That's it. That's the whole dream.

People act like wanting to enjoy your life is lazy or lacking drive. But I think it takes more courage to opt out of the rat race than to join it. Anyone can chase money. Not everyone can figure out what actually makes them happy and then structure their life around it.

The mural money came through. I'm putting half toward rent and supplies, and the other half toward that weekend trip to Goa with Rohan and Meera. Non-negotiable. We need this.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly it doesn't feel that far off. A few more consistent clients, maybe. Right now I'm just focused on the Goa trip.

I know people mean well. I know they're just parroting the same fears their parents parroted to them. But I'm so tired of being treated like I haven't thought this through. sources.journal_entry:
Teaching day. Seven kids between ages 8-12, all hyped up on whatever sugar their parents gave them before drop-off. We did texture collages — fabric scraps, sandpaper, dried leaves. One kid, Advait, made this incredible piece with torn newspaper headlines layered under tissue paper. He said it was "all the boring words adults say, trapped under clouds." Eight years old. I was floored.

Sometimes I think about what I would've been like if someone had let me make weird art at that age instead of drilling multiplication tables into my skull. Maybe I'd be further along now. Maybe not. Hard to know. Anyway the studio paid me in cash and I bought myself fancy dark chocolate on the way home because why not, the day was good.

Ma called again. The usual script. "Beta, you're 22 now. Meera aunty's daughter just got placed at Infosys. When are you going to think about your future?" I tried to explain that I AM thinking about my future, that the mural commission could lead to more work with the cafe chain, that I've been approached about teaching at an actual studio. But she doesn't hear any of that. She only hears "no salary, no benefits, no husband."

I hung up crying. Not because I doubt myself — I KNOW this is what I'm meant to do. But it's exhausting to constantly defend my choices to people who refuse to see them as valid. Papa at least stays quiet now. But Ma... she makes it sound like I'm throwing my life away for finger painting.

Rohan came over with biriyani and let me rant for an hour. He gets it — his family was the same way until he started making decent money from photography. He said something that stuck with me: "They'll come around when they see you're serious. You just have to outlast their doubt." But how long is that supposed to take? And why should I have to prove myself to people who should just... believe in me?

I painted until 3am. Angry brushstrokes that somehow turned into something beautiful. Maybe that's the only way I know how to process this.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly? I don't know if I can feel at peace with it. Part of me still wants her approval even though I hate admitting that.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent the whole morning at Leopold's working on sketches for the cafe mural commission. There's something about sitting in a busy space that helps ideas flow — all that ambient noise and people-watching. I ordered three cups of chai and didn't feel guilty about it. The sketches are coming together. Abstract florals with these hidden eyes peeking through petals. The cafe owner wanted "something colorful" which honestly gives me so much room to play.

I keep thinking about what Neha said last week, how she can't understand spending money on experiences when we're always behind on rent. But like... what's the point of hustling if you never actually enjoy anything? I'm not being irresponsible. I finished the commission brief. I just also let myself have a nice morning. Both things can be true.

sources.journal_entry: Spoke too soon this morning. Investor call this evening, and Vikram — my own co-founder — cut me off mid-pitch to "clarify" my revenue projections. The investor looked at him, not me, for the rest of the call. I didn't say anything.

Good morning for once. Walked into the all-hands and the team actually went quiet when I started talking. Not in a forced way — more like they were waiting for what I'd say because it mattered. I laid out the Q3 roadmap, handled the questions without anyone second-guessing the direction, and wrapped it in thirty minutes flat. Even Priya, who always has a follow-up objection, just nodded.

After the meeting, Arjun from engineering came up and said he liked the framing on the enterprise pivot. Didn't ask for it, didn't fish for it. He just said it. Small thing, but I've been pushing this pivot for two months against a lot of internal skepticism, and hearing someone voluntarily say it made sense — that hit differently.

I know some people think I care too much about being the one steering the ship, and maybe I do. But days like today remind me why I left a comfortable desk to do this. I didn't want to execute someone else's vision forever. I wanted the room to look at me and know that I'm the one making the call. Today they did, and it felt right.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a strategy disagreement with Vikram again, this time about pricing. I wanted to go aggressive — undercut the market, lock in the enterprise accounts, worry about margins later once we have the install base. He wanted a premium positioning play, said undercutting makes us look desperate. We went back and forth for an hour in the conference room and I could tell the team outside could hear us through the glass.

The thing is, I still think I'm right. I've done the competitor analysis, I know what Freshworks did in their early days, I know how this market works. But Vikram had the numbers laid out differently and the team started leaning his way. Nisha from sales said "I think the premium angle is easier to pitch," and once she said that, it was over. I agreed to his approach because fighting it further would have made me look like I was digging in out of ego rather than strategy.

But sitting here now, what sticks with me isn't even the pricing decision. It's the moment I saw the room shift. It's the feeling of having built this company, having recruited every person in that room, and watching them choose someone else's direction over mine. My father ran his garment business for twenty-five years and nobody in his shop would have contradicted him publicly like that. Different era, I know. But I keep thinking about it.

Spent half the week waiting on this one decision. We need approval from the enterprise client's procurement team to move forward with the pilot, and they keep saying "by end of week" and then nothing. I've sent three follow-up emails, each one a little more carefully worded than the last because you can't sound desperate, you can't sound pushy, you just have to sound like you're casually checking in even though the entire Q3 plan hinges on this one green light from someone I've never met.

My Amma called yesterday and asked how business is going. I told her great, growing fast. Didn't mention that I'm sitting here refreshing my inbox like an intern waiting for a response from a mid-level procurement officer named Suresh who probably doesn't even know what our product does. I'm the CEO of this company and I can't move my own roadmap forward because some guy in a cubicle in Pune hasn't gotten around to clicking approve.

The worst part is Vikram doesn't seem bothered. He said "these things take time" like that's an acceptable answer. Maybe for him it is. He's the CTO, he can go write code while we wait. I'm the one who has to explain to the board why the pilot hasn't started yet. I'm the one who looks like he can't close.

Didn't mention that I'm sitting here refreshing my inbox like an intern waiting for a response from a mid-level procurement officer named Suresh who probably doesn't even know what our product does. I'm the CEO of this company and I can't move my own roadmap forward because some guy in a cubicle in Pune hasn't gotten around to clicking approve.

The worst part is Vikram doesn't seem bothered. He said "these things take time" like that's an acceptable answer. Maybe for him it is. He's the CTO, he can go write code while we wait. I'm the one who has to explain to the board why the pilot hasn't started yet. I'm the one who looks like he can't close.

Spoke too soon this morning. Investor call this evening, and Vikram — my own co-founder — cut me off mid-pitch to "clarify" my revenue projections. The investor looked at him, not me, for the rest of the call. I didn't say anything.

Good morning for once. Walked into the all-hands and the team actually went quiet when I started talking. Not in a forced way — more like they were waiting for what I'd say because it mattered. I laid out the Q3 roadmap, handled the questions without anyone second-guessing the direction, and wrapped it in thirty minutes flat. Even Priya, who always has a follow-up objection, just nodded.

After the meeting, Arjun from engineering came up and said he liked the framing on the enterprise pivot. Didn't ask for it, didn't fish for it. He just said it. Small thing, but I've been pushing this pivot for two months against a lot of internal skepticism, and hearing someone voluntarily say it made sense — that hit differently.

I know some people think I care too much about being the one steering the ship, and maybe I do. But days like today remind me why I left a comfortable desk to do this. I didn't want to execute someone else's vision forever. I wanted the room to look at me and know that I'm the one making the call. Today they did, and it felt right.
Long day. Back-to-back calls with the ops team, then a vendor demo that went nowhere. Ordered biryani from that place near Koramangala and ate it standing at my desk between Slack messages.

sources.journal_entry:
Went to the literacy camp in Sultanpur today and I keep thinking about this one girl, maybe seven or eight, who was holding the pencil like she'd never held one before. And honestly she probably hadn't. She was gripping it so tight her knuckles were white and she kept looking at me like she was asking permission to write her own name.

I sat with her for almost an hour. The other volunteers were doing group activities but I just couldn't move on from this kid. Her name is Fatima. She got the first two letters right and then she looked at me and smiled and it was like, okay, this is why I wake up early on Saturdays and take that awful bus that takes ninety minutes one way.

I know this sounds naive or whatever. Didi would say I'm romanticizing things. But I was there today and she wasn't. There's something about being in the room with someone who just learned they can write their own name that makes all the other noise—the salary complaints, Baba asking when I'll "move up," the crumbling school building—feel small. Not irrelevant, just not the point.
Parent-teacher meeting ran late. Most parents didn't show up, same as last month. Spent the rest of the evening marking notebooks and helping Amma sort the kitchen.

sources.journal_entry:
Week went by fast. Exams are coming so the classroom mood has shifted—less exploration, more revision. I don't love exam season but it's part of the deal. Spent most of the week drilling multiplication tables and grammar rules, which is fine, just not what I find interesting about teaching.

Saturday camp was cancelled because of some local election rally blocking the roads to Sultanpur. So I had the whole day free, which almost never happens. Used it to reorganize my lesson plans for after the exams. Want to do a unit on water and sanitation since the Ravi thing showed me the kids actually carry these conversations home.

Baba asked over dinner if I'd thought about the B.Ed entrance coaching that Didi offered to pay for. He thinks a higher qualification will help me "move to a better school." I told him I like my school. He said he knows, but he worries. I think he genuinely does. It's not like Didi's thing where she's comparing our lives—Baba just wants to know I'll be okay. Told him I'm okay right now and that has to count for something. He nodded and changed the subject to cricket, which is his way of accepting things he doesn't fully understand. I'll take it.

Still thinking about yesterday but also something from today that's bothering me more. Went to the market after school to buy supplies for next week's art project. The stationery shop I usually go to was closed so I went to the bigger one near Hazratganj. More expensive but they had everything I needed.

Here's the thing. There's a local self-help group run by women from the basti near school—they make paper products, notebooks, craft materials. I know about them because one of my students' mothers is involved. They sell at lower prices and the money goes directly back to the community. I've bought from them before. But today I was tired and the Hazratganj shop was right there and I just wanted to get it done fast. So I spent probably twice as much at a chain store when I could have waited one more day and supported the women's group instead.

It's not a huge deal in isolation. Nobody's tracking my purchases. But it's the kind of thing that nags at me because I talk a lot, in my own head at least, about wanting things to be more fair, about wanting the system to work differently. And then when I have an actual tiny concrete chance to put money where my mouth is, I go for the convenient option. Feels hypocritical. The women's group doesn't need my patronage to survive but it's the principle of it. Or maybe I'm overthinking a stationery run, I don't know. I just don't like who I was at that checkout counter today.

sources.journal_entry:
Three doubles in a row. I can barely keep my eyes open to write this. My feet feel like they're on fire. The new duty roster came out and I got moved to the night shift rotation for February. After five years of day shifts. Five years of building my life around that schedule.

The worst part is I only found out through the WhatsApp group. No one told me directly. HR just posted the new roster like it was nothing.

I had booked a trip to Goa for the first weekend of February. Non-refundable Airbnb. I was going to sit on the beach and eat fish curry and do absolutely nothing productive for three days. Now I have to figure out if I can get someone to swap with me. If not, I lose the booking.

I'm too tired to be angry right now. That will come tomorrow.

Another Monday, another twelve-hour shift. We had two code blues today. One patient made it, one didn't. The family of the one who passed was inconsolable. I stayed an extra forty-five minutes helping them with paperwork because nobody else was available.

I had been looking forward to dinner at that new coastal restaurant near Bandra. Had to cancel my reservation. Texted Anita that I couldn't make it and she understood, but I could tell she was disappointed. I was disappointed too. I had been thinking about their prawns all week.

The hospital cafeteria food was stale as usual. Ate a vada pav from the cart outside instead. At least that was fresh.

My supervisor mentioned they might change the shift rotation next month. Nothing confirmed. I don't like the uncertainty. The current schedule works for me.
sources.nudge_response:
The family was alone. The wife kept asking the same questions over and over, like her mind couldn't accept what had happened. Nobody else was there to help them. My replacement nurse was already swamped with her own patients.

Was it hard to stay? Yes and no. I was exhausted and hungry. But leaving felt wrong. You don't just walk away from people in that state. My mother always said that when someone is drowning in grief, you throw them a rope, even if your arms are tired.

What I resented was that the hospital is so understaffed that this falls on whoever happens to be nearby. That's not a system, that's luck. Bad luck for me today, but worse luck for that family if I hadn't been there.

Spoke to the nursing supervisor today about the shift change. She said "everyone has to be flexible" and "you've had the good shifts for a long time." As if the good shifts were a favor rather than something I earned through seniority. As if flexibility is only something that flows one direction.

I didn't raise my voice but I wanted to. I explained about the Goa booking, about how night shifts affect my health, about how I specifically took this hospital because they promised schedule stability during my interview. She just nodded and said she would "see what she could do" which means nothing.

My cousin called me dramatic when I told her. She works in IT from home and doesn't understand what it means to have your whole life rearranged by someone else's spreadsheet. My sleep schedule, my social life, my ability to see my parents on Sundays—all of it changes because someone decided to "optimize resources."

I found someone who might swap one week with me, so I can still do Goa. But it cost me. She wanted me to take her Diwali shift in October. October! That's nine months away and I've already traded away a holiday.

I just want some predictability. Is that too much to ask? I work hard. I show up. I don't complain about the difficult patients or the long hours. But I need to know that my life outside these walls is mine to plan.

My cousin called me dramatic when I told her. She works in IT from home and doesn't understand what it means to have your whole life rearranged by someone else's spreadsheet. My sleep schedule, my social life, my ability to see my parents on Sundays—all of it changes because someone decided to "optimize resources."

I found someone who might swap one week with me, so I can still do Goa. But it cost me. She wanted me to take her Diwali shift in October. October! That's nine months away and I've already traded away a holiday.

I just want some predictability. Is that too much to ask? I work hard. I show up. I don't complain about the difficult patients or the long hours. But I need to know that my life outside these walls is mine to plan.

Three doubles in a row. I can barely keep my eyes open to write this. My feet feel like they're on fire. The new duty roster came out and I got moved to the night shift rotation for February. After five years of day shifts. Five years of building my life around that schedule.

The worst part is I only found out through the WhatsApp group. No one told me directly. HR just posted the new roster like it was nothing.

I had booked a trip to Goa for the first weekend of February. Non-refundable Airbnb. I was going to sit on the beach and eat fish curry and do absolutely nothing productive for three days. Now I have to figure out if I can get someone to swap with me. If not, I lose the booking.

I'm too tired to be angry right now. That will come tomorrow.

Another Monday, another twelve-hour shift. We had two code blues today. One patient made it, one didn't. The family of the one who passed was inconsolable. I stayed an extra forty-five minutes helping them with paperwork because nobody else was available.

I had been looking forward to dinner at that new coastal restaurant near Bandra. Had to cancel my reservation. Texted Anita that I couldn't make it and she understood, but I could tell she was disappointed. I was disappointed too. I had been thinking about their prawns all week.

The hospital cafeteria food was stale as usual. Ate a vada pav from the cart outside instead. At least that was fresh.

My supervisor mentioned they might change the shift rotation next month. Nothing confirmed. I don't like the uncertainty. The current schedule works for me.

Took myself to brunch alone today. First time in months I didn't organize it for a group or invite anyone. Just me, a table by the pool at Sofitel, unlimited sparkling and eggs royale. It felt strange at first — I kept checking my phone like I was waiting for someone. But by the third glass I was actually relaxed in a way I haven't been in weeks.

I've been thinking about why I always need an audience. Even good things feel less real if no one sees them. Like, if I have a nice meal alone, did it even happen? That's probably not healthy. My grandfather used to take long walks by himself every evening and he seemed at peace. I can't imagine doing that. The thought of unwitnessed time makes me uncomfortable.

But today was good. The food was good. The sun was good. Maybe I don't need everyone to know I was there. Maybe the experience is enough. I'm not convinced yet but I'm thinking about it.

I've been chasing this ladder since I was 19 and I've never actually pictured what's at the top. A corner office? More money? More people asking for my approval?

He looked... relaxed. Happy maybe. We talked for ten minutes and he didn't mention his job once except to laugh about how his commute is now a five-minute walk to the beach.

I thought I'd feel sorry for him. Instead I felt something closer to envy and I don't know what to do with that. His life is small by every metric I care about. No status, no visibility, probably makes less than my car payment. But he's not performing anything. He's just there, doing what he wants, and it seems like enough for him.

I can't imagine that being enough for me. And yet the fact that it bothers me is bothering me more.

sources.journal_entry:
Got up at six like I said. Sat at the kitchen table with coffee and opened the statement document. Wrote two paragraphs, deleted one, rewrote it. What I have now is decent but there's a line in it that says "my work interrogates the boundary between observation and belonging" and I don't know if that's true or if it's just the kind of thing you're supposed to write. It sounds like everyone else's statement.

My father texted asking if I could come to Sunday lunch. I said yes immediately even though I was planning to photograph canvases this afternoon. Because you don't say no to Sunday lunch. You just don't. But now I've lost four hours I needed and I'm sitting here resenting something I actually want to do, which feels wrong.

Third time opening this today. It's late and I should sleep but my mind won't stop cycling. I printed Oriane's statement and mine side by side -- well, hers and the half-page of notes I have. Hers reads like someone who knows exactly who she is as an artist. Mine reads like a studio coordinator who also paints.

I'm going to set the alarm for six and work on the statement before anyone else gets to the studio. That's the plan. Whether I actually get up is another question but writing it down makes it feel slightly more real.

Still thinking about the Prix Dauphine thing. Went back through my portfolio folder after dinner and actually it's not as scattered as I thought. The river paintings connect. The printwork connects to the paintings if you read them as studies. I could frame it. But then I keep imagining the selection panel looking at it and seeing someone who doesn't know what she is yet. Which is worse than being rejected outright honestly.

The deadline is October 15th. That's less than three weeks. If I'm going to do it I need to start the statement this weekend, pick the images, and get decent photographs of the two canvases that are only on my phone right now. Sylvain has a good camera. I could ask him but then he'd know I'm applying and if I don't get it that's a conversation I don't want.

Oriane texted to say thanks for the edits. I said bonne chance and meant it but also felt something hard in my chest when I typed it. Not jealousy exactly. More like watching someone do the thing you keep postponing and knowing it's your own fault.

Oriane told me she submitted to the Prix Dauphine. Same one I've been thinking about for two months. She asked if I'd look over her artist statement and I said yes because what else do you say. Spent twenty minutes editing her paragraphs and they were good, really good, and I haven't even started mine.
sources.nudge_response: Time, mostly. Or that's what I tell myself. The application needs ten images and a statement and I keep thinking my recent work isn't cohesive enough. Oriane's is. She has a clear thread. Mine is all over the place.

sources.journal_entry:
Good day actually. Spent the morning in the studio alone before anyone else arrived. Got the underpainting done on the large canvas I've been circling around for weeks. It's a night scene, the Saone from the Passerelle footbridge, and I think I finally found the right temperature for the water. Cool greens, not the blue I kept defaulting to.

My mother called at lunch. She asked about the heating bill dispute and I gave her the short version. She said I was sensible to handle it and that managing people is a real skill. Coming from her that means something because she manages twelve employees at the firm. She doesn't say things like that lightly.

Then the afternoon was admin. Filed the collective's quarterly report for the Mairie, updated the shared calendar, responded to three emails about the open studio weekend in November. Tedious but I got through it fast. There's a rhythm to it when I'm in a decent mood. The trick is not letting it eat into the morning. Mornings are mine.

Had the quarterly meeting with the collective this evening. Usual stuff -- dividing the heating bill, scheduling who gets the large press for October. I ended up mediating between Sylvain and Oriane again because they both wanted the same two-week block and neither would yield. I proposed a split arrangement, alternating days, and they both agreed. Took about forty minutes to get there.

Afterward Sylvain thanked me and said the collective would fall apart without me. Meant it as a compliment, I think. But it felt like being told my role is to hold other people's work together. Not sure when I became the person who manages everyone's access instead of using the press myself. My own print series hasn't moved since July.

Walking home I passed the new gallery on Rue de la Republique. They had a group show opening, all artists around my age. I recognised one name from school. Stood outside for a minute but didn't go in. Wasn't dressed for it, and I didn't want to make small talk about what I've been working on because the honest answer is administrative emails.

sources.journal_entry: Finished the artist statement. Photographed all ten pieces with Sylvain's camera -- told him it was for the collective website, which is technically true since two of them are on there. Application is drafted. Just need to press send.

Just got off the phone with Maman. She mentioned that my cousin Emilie got a promotion at her firm. Regional manager now, at thirty-one. Maman didn't compare us directly but she said "she's done so well" in that particular tone. Then she asked how the open studio planning was going, not how my painting was going. Because the planning is the part she can understand.

I'm tired of being the one in the family who chose the impractical path and then compensates by being responsible about everything else. I iron my clothes, I pay bills on time, I coordinate a collective of four adults who can't share a printing press without a mediator. And somehow it still doesn't add up to enough in certain conversations.

Sunday lunch was actually good. Papa made his dauphinois and we talked about the collective's funding application. He doesn't understand art but he understands budgets, so he went through the numbers with me and caught two errors in our projected costs. I felt useful sitting next to him with the laptop out, the two of us going line by line.

On the drive home I realised something. The reason I keep taking on the coordination work isn't just that nobody else will do it. It's that when I'm managing things, I'm in charge. People ask me. People defer to my schedule, my decisions about the shared space. If I step back and just become one of five artists in the collective, I lose that. I'm just another painter hoping for a gallery spot.

That's an ugly thought and I almost didn't write it. But it's true. When Sylvain says the collective would fall apart without me, part of me likes hearing it. Not because I want to do admin forever but because it means I matter in a way that doesn't depend on whether my paintings are good enough. Which is the one question I keep avoiding.
sources.nudge_response: I don't know. Maybe getting into something like the Prix Dauphine. Maybe selling a painting to someone who isn't a friend of my parents. Honestly I'm not sure that's the right question because the bar keeps moving.

My mother called at lunch. She asked about the heating bill dispute and I gave her the short version. She said I was sensible to handle it and that managing people is a real skill. Coming from her that means something because she manages twelve employees at the firm. She doesn't say things like that lightly.

Then the afternoon was admin. Filed the collective's quarterly report for the Mairie, updated the shared calendar, responded to three emails about the open studio weekend in November. Tedious but I got through it fast. There's a rhythm to it when I'm in a decent mood. The trick is not letting it eat into the morning. Mornings are mine.

Had the quarterly meeting with the collective this evening. Usual stuff -- dividing the heating bill, scheduling who gets the large press for October. I ended up mediating between Sylvain and Oriane again because they both wanted the same two-week block and neither would yield. I proposed a split arrangement, alternating days, and they both agreed. Took about forty minutes to get there.

Afterward Sylvain thanked me and said the collective would fall apart without me. Meant it as a compliment, I think. But it felt like being told my role is to hold other people's work together. Not sure when I became the person who manages everyone's access instead of using the press myself. My own print series hasn't moved since July.

Stood outside for a minute but didn't go in. Wasn't dressed for it, and I didn't want to make small talk about what I've been working on because the honest answer is administrative emails.

sources.journal_entry:
Submitted the Prix Dauphine application six days ago. Haven't told anyone except writing it here. Results aren't until December so there's a long stretch of not-knowing ahead. I've been filling it by throwing myself back into the collective stuff -- finalised the open studio weekend schedule, ordered new ink for the press, had a long call with the Mairie about our lease renewal.

Part of me knows I'm using the admin to avoid sitting with the fact that I put my work out there and it might not be enough. But another part thinks this is just what I do: I keep things running while I wait. It's not avoidance if the work genuinely needs doing. Or maybe I'm making excuses. Hard to tell from the inside.

Oriane asked at the studio yesterday if I'd ever considered applying for anything. I said "maybe at some point" and changed the subject to the November schedule. She nodded and moved on. I could have told her. I chose not to. It felt safer to be the person who organises things than the person who wants things. There's less to lose that way, or at least that's what I keep telling myself.

Finished the artist statement. Photographed all ten pieces with Sylvain's camera -- told him it was for the collective website, which is technically true since two of them are on there. Application is drafted. Just need to press send.

Just got off the phone with Maman. She mentioned that my cousin Emilie got a promotion at her firm. Regional manager now, at thirty-one. Maman didn't compare us directly but she said "she's done so well" in that particular tone. Then she asked how the open studio planning was going, not how my painting was going. Because the planning is the part she can understand.

I'm tired of being the one in the family who chose the impractical path and then compensates by being responsible about everything else. I iron my clothes, I pay bills on time, I coordinate a collective of four adults who can't share a printing press without a mediator. And somehow it still doesn't add up to enough in certain conversations.

Sunday lunch was actually good. Papa made his dauphinois and we talked about the collective's funding application. He doesn't understand art but he understands budgets, so he went through the numbers with me and caught two errors in our projected costs. I felt useful sitting next to him with the laptop out, the two of us going line by line.

On the drive home I realised something. The reason I keep taking on the coordination work isn't just that nobody else will do it. It's that when I'm managing things, I'm in charge. People ask me. People defer to my schedule, my decisions about the shared space. If I step back and just become one of five artists in the collective, I lose that. I'm just another painter hoping for a gallery spot.

That's an ugly thought and I almost didn't write it. But it's true. When Sylvain says the collective would fall apart without me, part of me likes hearing it. Not because I want to do admin forever but because it means I matter in a way that doesn't depend on whether my paintings are good enough. Which is the one question I keep avoiding.
sources.nudge_response: I don't know. Maybe getting into something like the Prix Dauphine. Maybe selling a painting to someone who isn't a friend of my parents. Honestly I'm not sure that's the right question because the bar keeps moving.

sources.journal_entry:
People keep telling me I need to set boundaries, like it's so easy. My friend Ana was saying how I should stop lending money to Diego because he never pays me back. But she doesn't understand—he's family. His girls needed new shoes for school and what was I supposed to do, just say no? He's trying his best with that construction job but the hours aren't steady.

I know I can't save everyone. I know that. But when someone in my life needs help and I have even a little bit to give, how do I look them in the eye and say sorry, I'm saving for myself? Maybe I'm the fool here but I'd rather be broke and know I showed up for people than comfortable and wondering if I did enough.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly? I don't know if I'd recognize myself. Like, the version of me who doesn't pick up the phone when Diego calls, who doesn't drive 40 minutes to help tia Elena with her groceries... that person feels like a stranger. Sometimes I wonder if I help because I want to or because I'm scared of who I'd be if I stopped. My mom was the same way. She gave and gave until there was nothing left. I don't want to end up like that but I also don't know any other way to be.

sources.journal_entry:
New Year's Eve was nice, actually. Ana came over with some of the other girls from the building and we did the grape thing at midnight—you know, eating twelve grapes for twelve wishes. Tia Elena made it too, even with her hip still sore. Diego's kids were running around screaming happy new year and setting off these little firecrackers in the parking lot.

I caught myself just standing in the kitchen at one point, watching everyone eat my food and laugh, and I felt... full. Not from the pernil, though that was good too. But like, okay, this is why I do everything. These people, this noise, this mess. Ana asked me what my resolution was and I said to take better care of myself but honestly I don't even know what that means. I've never been good at that part. Taking care of other people is easy—there's always a clear next thing to do. But taking care of myself feels selfish, or maybe I just don't know how.

My cousin said something that stuck with me though. She said you can't pour from an empty cup. I've heard that before but this time it hit different. Maybe because I've been running on empty for months and it's starting to show. Snapping at people in traffic, too tired to cook some nights, just ordering delivery even though I can't afford it. I want to do better this year but I don't know where to start.
sources.nudge_response: I keep thinking about Sunday mornings. When I was little, before my mom got sick, she used to make herself coffee and sit on the porch alone for like an hour. She called it her "moment." I never understood it then—I thought she was just being lazy. Now I get it. I don't have a porch but I could... I don't know, maybe just sit with my coffee before I start driving. Not check my phone, not worry about who needs what. Just ten minutes of quiet. It sounds so small but I honestly can't remember the last time I did nothing without feeling guilty about it.

But like, okay, this is why I do everything. These people, this noise, this mess. Ana asked me what my resolution was and I said to take better care of myself but honestly I don't even know what that means. I've never been good at that part. Taking care of other people is easy—there's always a clear next thing to do. But taking care of myself feels selfish, or maybe I just don't know how.

My cousin said something that stuck with me though. She said you can't pour from an empty cup. I've heard that before but this time it hit different. Maybe because I've been running on empty for months and it's starting to show. Snapping at people in traffic, too tired to cook some nights, just ordering delivery even though I can't afford it. I want to do better this year but I don't know where to start.
sources.nudge_response: I keep thinking about Sunday mornings. When I was little, before my mom got sick, she used to make herself coffee and sit on the porch alone for like an hour. She called it her "moment." I never understood it then—I thought she was just being lazy. Now I get it. I don't have a porch but I could... I don't know, maybe just sit with my coffee before I start driving. Not check my phone, not worry about who needs what. Just ten minutes of quiet. It sounds so small but I honestly can't remember the last time I did nothing without feeling guilty about it.

sources.journal_entry: Tia Elena fell yesterday. She's okay, just bruised, but I wasn't there. I was doing a delivery across town and didn't see her call until an hour later. I should have been there.
sources.nudge_response: I know, I know. But she lives alone. What if next time it's worse? I've been thinking about asking her to move in with me but my place is so small and she's proud, she wouldn't want to feel like a burden. I don't know.

sources.journal_entry: My brother called from Bogota—he's struggling with rent again. I already sent what I could last month but I'll figure something out. He's my little brother; that's just what you do.
sources.nudge_response: It means I pick up extra shifts, maybe skip the new tires for another month. It's fine, I've done it before. My brother didn't ask to be born into this situation, you know?

sources.journal_entry: Made tamales with tia Elena for the holidays. She taught me her mother's recipe, the one with the olives. Spent the whole afternoon together, just us and the masa.

sources.nudge_response: I don't know, it was just sweet. Kids being kids. Anyway, it was a good day—better than most this week.

sources.journal_entry: Twelve hours of driving today. Picked up tia Elena's medication on my break because the pharmacy was on my route anyway. Just want to sleep.

Monday coffee again. This time I told the three of them I'd need to scale back for the next two weeks because of the paper deadline. Katja immediately said of course, Leon nodded, Simone looked a bit lost but said she understood. Nobody collapsed. Nobody resented it, at least not visibly.

sources.nudge_response: My father, probably. He was a teacher too, and his door was always open. Students, colleagues, neighbours. I grew up believing that being good at what you do means being available to everyone who needs you. The problem is you can spend a whole career being available and still feel like you haven't done the thing you were actually capable of. I don't want to retire with a drawer full of other people's thank-you cards and an empty shelf where my own work should have been.

sources.journal_entry:

Brigitte said something last night that I keep turning over. We were in the kitchen and she mentioned, casually, that she'd stopped inviting the Fischers for dinner because I always cancel or sit there half-present checking my phone for student emails. I started to argue but she cut me off and said she wasn't angry, just adjusting. That word, adjusting, hit harder than any argument.

I've been telling myself the work matters, and it does. The department results prove it, the younger teachers tell me constantly how much the Monday sessions help. But Brigitte adjusting means she's already factored in my absence as the default. My sister noticed the same thing on the phone last week. I don't think I'm neglecting them on purpose. It's more that every time I choose between something with a measurable outcome and something that just asks me to be present, I pick the one I can point to later and say, see, this counted.

I don't know when being present stopped counting for me. Or if it ever did count and I just never built the habit of valuing it properly. The conference paper is going well now and I should feel satisfied. But Brigitte adjusting is sitting in my chest like a stone and I can't spreadsheet my way out of it.

Monday coffee again. This time I told the three of them I'd need to scale back for the next two weeks because of the paper deadline. Katja immediately said of course, Leon nodded, Simone looked a bit lost but said she understood. Nobody collapsed. Nobody resented it, at least not visibly.

Walking home I felt lighter than I have in weeks but also oddly guilty, as though I'd broken an unspoken contract. Brigitte would say that contract only exists in my head. She'd probably be right. I sat down with the draft again after dinner and got another page done. The structure is taking shape.
sources.nudge_response: My father, probably. He was a teacher too, and his door was always open. Students, colleagues, neighbours. I grew up believing that being good at what you do means being available to everyone who needs you. The problem is you can spend a whole career being available and still feel like you haven't done the thing you were actually capable of. I don't want to retire with a drawer full of other people's thank-you cards and an empty shelf where my own work should have been.

Sat through the entire biostatistics review session without asking about the regression exercise even though I got a completely different answer from everyone at my table. Dr. Pham went around the room and each group shared their approach and all of them had the same output, the same neat little table, and mine was off by enough that it wasn't rounding. I kept waiting for someone else to flag something but nobody did so I just nodded along.

After class I went to the TA's office hours and she helped me find the mistake — I'd misread the variable coding in the dataset. A small thing. Ten-minute fix. But the whole two hours in that classroom I was turning it over and over, wondering if I should raise my hand, wondering what Dr. Pham would say, what the twenty-three-year-olds at my table would think about the oldest person in the room not being able to read a codebook properly.

Came home and made lentil soup, the one my mother used to make with cumin and a whole lime squeezed in at the end. Ate it standing at the counter reading next week's assignment. The apartment was quiet, which was fine. Called Patricia and she said the kids have a stomach bug so Sunday dinner might just be the two of us. That's okay too.
sources.nudge_response: Probably nothing bad. Dr. Pham is patient, he wouldn't have made a scene. I think part of it is that at the clinic I spent thirty years making sure everything ran without friction — no surprises, no awkward moments for the doctors or the patients. Asking a question that might slow everyone down or reveal I'm behind, it feels like making a mess someone else has to clean up. Even when I know that's not how a classroom works.

Sunday dinner went long. Patricia, the kids, Miguel and his wife Estela. I made the arroz con pollo and Estela brought a tres leches. The kids chased each other through the apartment and knocked over the little cactus by the window but nobody minded. It was loud and full in the way I miss sometimes during the week when it's just me and the textbooks.

I've been thinking about what it means to be a student again at this point in my life. Not the academics — I can handle the reading, the exams. It's more the social part, figuring out where I fit with people half my age and whether fitting in even matters or if I'm looking for something else entirely. At the clinic I knew my place, I knew the rhythms. Here I'm still learning them. But tonight, scooping rice onto plates while Estela told a story about her neighbor's dog, I thought maybe the rhythms I already know are enough. They just show up in different rooms now.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly I don't know. Maybe I'll figure it out when I stop asking.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent the afternoon in the library finishing the epidemiology reading. Three chapters on study design — cohort, case-control, cross-sectional. Made notes in the margins the way I always do, small stars next to things I want to revisit. The reading itself was straightforward. I've been working through the textbook slowly, one section at a time, and it helps to have that rhythm.

Ran into Miguel from the parish at the coffee shop on Guadalupe. He asked about classes and I gave the usual answer — busy but managing. He's been here longer than I have, twelve years now, and he said the first couple of years in any new system are the hardest. He wasn't talking about school specifically but it landed anyway.

Walked home through campus when the light was going gold. Students everywhere on the lawn, studying, throwing a frisbee. I bought a pan dulce from the bakery on the corner and ate it on the bench outside my building. Patricia texted that the kids are better and they want abuela's arroz con pollo this Sunday. That settled something in me I didn't know was unsettled.
sources.nudge_response: I think he meant that anywhere you go, there's a way things are done, and it takes time to figure out the unwritten parts. The rules nobody tells you. He was talking about immigration but it applies to school too — figuring out when to speak, how to disagree, what's expected versus what's just tolerated.

I don't know why the group project is still eating at me. It's done. We submitted. The restructured version was fine, probably even better than what I had. So what's the problem. Kayla even texted afterward and said she appreciated how flexible I was, and I think she meant it genuinely.

The thing is, everyone keeps talking about how grad school is supposed to push you and make you uncomfortable and I don't think they mean this kind of uncomfortable. They mean presenting at conferences or learning R. Not sitting in a meeting biting the inside of your cheek because you disagree but saying it out loud would make everything tense. That's a different kind of hard and nobody gives you credit for it because from the outside it looks like you just went along.

My daughter would say I'm overthinking. She's probably right. She's lived here since she was nineteen and she learned fast that Americans speak up, they push back, they call it being assertive and they admire it. I learned different things. In the clinic we kept things running by reading the room, by knowing when to let something go. That wasn't weakness. But lately it feels like the skills I spent a lifetime building don't translate. Like I'm fluent in a language nobody here speaks.

Group project meeting went sideways. Kayla proposed we restructure the entire literature review two days before the draft is due and everyone just went along with it. I had already written my sections the way we agreed last week. I sat there while they talked about the new framework and I wanted to say this is not what we decided, we had a plan, but Kayla was so energized and the others were nodding and I didn't want to be the one who drags things backward.

sources.journal_entry:
The studio smells like turpentine again because I forgot to cap the jar before I left yesterday. Spent six hours on the commission piece for that hotel lobby in Abdoun. Massive canvas, three meters wide, and the client wants "something that feels Middle Eastern but modern." I've heard that phrase so many times it's lost all meaning. I painted geometric patterns, scraped them off, painted loose abstractions over them, scraped those off too. Ended up with something layered that looks like a wall that's been lived on for decades. It might work. I'm too tired to tell.

Drove to the center after to set up for tomorrow's session. The hallway light is still broken so I propped the door open for daylight while I organized supplies. The kids went through all the blue paint last week so I picked up more on the way, the cheap kind because the good acrylics cost too much for how fast they use them. Counted the brushes. We're down to fourteen. I keep forgetting to ask Huda if the center can budget for more or if that's coming out of my pocket again.

The drive home was quiet. Ramadan traffic has died down, the streets were almost empty. I ate leftover mujaddara standing at the kitchen counter and went straight to bed. My shoulders ache from reaching up at the canvas all day. I should stretch more. I never do.

sources.journal_entry:
Workshop today. One of the boys, Ahmad, who's maybe twelve, has been coming every week since January. He barely spoke for the first month, just painted the same image over and over, a grey building with no windows. Today he painted a garden. Green everywhere, flowers I don't think he's ever seen in real life, a yellow bird. He didn't say anything about it. He just held it up to dry and went to wash his brushes.

I didn't make a fuss. I just told him the yellow was a good choice and helped him find a spot on the drying rack. It was a small thing. But I drove home feeling like something had actually worked, not because of me specifically, just because the space existed for him to get there on his own. That felt right. I'm exhausted but it's the kind of tired I don't mind.

Something happened at a dinner at my uncle's house on Friday that I'm still thinking about. His neighbor was there, an older man, very confident in his opinions. He started talking about the Sudanese workers at a construction site near his building. Calling them lazy, saying they were "bringing problems," that the government should stop giving them permits. The usual garbage. My aunt was nodding along. My cousin was on his phone, not paying attention. My uncle said nothing, which for him is the same as agreeing.

I sat there with my fork in my hand and I didn't say a single thing. I knew exactly what I wanted to say. That these men left everything behind and are breaking their bodies on scaffolding in forty-degree heat for wages that wouldn't cover his grocery bill. That my grandmother was a refugee once too. That the least we owe people who have lost their homes is not talking about them like they're pests at a dinner table. I had all of it ready and I just kept eating.

Part of it was exhaustion, I'd been at the studio since seven that morning. Part of it was knowing it wouldn't change his mind. But mostly I think I just didn't want the tension. Supervisor meeting was actually good. She wasn't upset — she wanted to talk about narrowing my scope so the paper is submittable by July. She drew this diagram on the whiteboard, crossing off two whole sections I'd been agonizing over. Felt like someone opened a window.

Walked home through the park after and sat on the bench near the pond for a while. Called Mama from there. Told her about the meeting and she said "habibi, you always worry too much." She's right, probably. Noor texted later that she found a cheaper repair guy through a friend at the souk. Small thing but I felt my shoulders drop reading it.

Three nights of maybe four hours' sleep each and I still didn't finish the conference paper draft on time. I emailed my supervisor asking for two more days and she replied with a single line: "Let's discuss priorities in our next meeting." I've read that sentence fifteen times. It could mean nothing. It could mean she thinks I'm falling behind. Both feel equally possible and I can't stop cycling through it.

Noor called tonight about the shop — the main printer broke down again and the repair estimate is more than what I usually send in a month. I told her I'd figure it out. Didn't tell her I've been eating rice and lentils for two weeks straight to keep my own rent covered. She doesn't need that. She's handling the shop and Papa's physiotherapy appointments and I'm over here unable to finish a twenty-page paper.

The worst part is I know people in my cohort half my age are publishing faster. Ahmed from the lab already has two journal submissions this year. I'm not jealous of him specifically, it's more that I keep measuring myself against a timeline that was never mine to begin with. I chose to come here late. I keep forgetting that.

sources.journal_entry:
End-of-term presentations today. I went third. My slides were clean, my data was organized, I rehearsed four times this morning. And then during Q&A, Professor Chen asked a question about my sampling methodology that I couldn't answer clearly. I fumbled through something about stratified approaches and he just nodded politely. That polite nod — I know what it means. It means the answer wasn't good enough.

The frustrating thing is I knew the answer. I'd written about it in section four of my draft. But standing there with twelve faces staring at me, half of them twenty-six years old and already sharper on their feet, my mind just locked. I sat down after and my hands were shaking slightly. Nobody noticed, I think.

Came home and couldn't eat dinner. Opened the spreadsheet where I track my targets — publication by August, comprehensive exam in October, teaching assistantship application due next week. Every single line has a yellow or red flag next to it. I used to run project teams of forty people. I built a bridge overpass in Zarqa. And now I can't get through a fifteen-minute Q&A without my voice going thin. I keep telling myself this is worth it, that the degree changes everything, but tonight I'm not sure what "everything" even refers to anymore.
sources.nudge_response: I think I pictured myself walking across a stage and my mother watching from the front row. Papa too, before the stroke. The degree was supposed to prove that leaving the career and the salary wasn't reckless — that I could build something bigger than a bridge. But now most days it just feels like I traded one kind of pressure for another, except this one pays nothing and nobody at home understands what a comprehensive exam is.

sources.journal_entry:
Ahmed asked me at lunch if I'd thought about switching to a more "applied" research track since I have industry experience. He meant it helpfully, I'm sure. But the way he said it — like the theoretical work is too much for someone who came in mid-career — sat with me all afternoon. I told him I didn't leave a perfectly good job to do a watered-down version of what I already know. He looked surprised. Maybe I was too sharp.

But I'm tired of the assumption that because I'm older and came from practice, I should be doing something "practical." I'm here because I wanted the harder version. I wanted to understand the theory underneath the things I built for twenty years. That's not a consolation prize, it's a deliberate choice. People keep framing it like I'm catching up when I'm actually trying to go deeper.

The thing I didn't say to Ahmed is that his question hit exactly where I'm already uncertain. The comprehensive exam reading list is dense and some of the mathematical modeling chapters make me read the same page four times. I am keeping pace, but barely. And when someone who's been in academia since undergrad casually suggests I take the easier route, it confirms the thing I'm afraid of — that maybe the gap between where I started and where I need to be is wider than effort alone can close. I don't actually believe that. But I didn't need him planting the seed.

Quiet week for once. Submitted the revised paper draft, supervisor said it reads much better with the narrower scope. No major feedback, just a few citation formatting things. I spent Saturday catching up on the teaching assistantship application — recommendation letters are in, statement is drafted, just need to polish the research summary section.

Called home and for once it was a normal conversation. Mama talked about the neighbors' daughter's engagement party. Noor complained about a supplier who keeps shorting her on paper stock. Nobody asked me when I'm coming back. It felt different. Lighter.

I realized I've been here almost three semesters and I still eat dinner alone most nights. There's a departmental social on Thursday that I keep meaning to attend but I always find a reason not to. Last time it was the paper deadline. Before that it was needing to call home during the time slot. I'm not lonely exactly — I talk to my family every day and I see my labmates — but there's a gap between being around people and actually having someone here who knows me beyond my research topic. It's not urgent. It's just something I notice when the work quiets down enough to notice anything.

And when someone who's been in academia since undergrad casually suggests I take the easier route, it confirms the thing I'm afraid of — that maybe the gap between where I started and where I need to be is wider than effort alone can close. I don't actually believe that. But I didn't need him planting the seed.

One of them is building a fintech play in Vietnam, another is doing sustainable fashion in Seoul. Neither of them has stable jobs either. Nobody questioned each other's choices.

sources.journal_entry:
Got another call from my mom today. She forwarded me a LinkedIn post about my high school classmate Kenji who just made senior associate at McKinsey Tokyo. She didn't say it directly, but I could hear it in her voice—"See? He has stability. What do you have?"

I have three half-built companies and a carry-on bag. I have a network across four cities. I have ideas that keep me up at night. But sure, I don't have a business card with a respectable title or a steady paycheck.

The thing is, I'm not failing. The app has 2,000 beta users already. We're getting organic signups from word of mouth. But to her, none of that counts until there's a salary deposited every month. She doesn't understand that the salary is the trap. That's how they get you—comfortable enough that you stop looking for what else is out there.

The thing is, I'm not failing. The app has 2,000 beta users already. We're getting organic signups from word of mouth. But to her, none of that counts until there's a salary deposited every month. She doesn't understand that the salary is the trap. That's how they get you—comfortable enough that you stop looking for what else is out there.

I know she means well. I know she just wants me to be okay. But her version of "okay" feels like suffocation. Every time we talk, I have to defend choices that feel obvious to me. It's exhausting.

The investor meeting is in three days. If this round comes through, maybe that'll finally be proof enough. Or maybe it won't matter and she'll just find something else to worry about.
sources.nudge_response: Both, that's the problem. I know she loves me and that's exactly why it hurts. If she didn't care, I could just ignore her. But she does, and her caring looks like wanting me to be someone I'm not. The suffocation is heavier, if I'm being honest. Because at least if she were indifferent, I'd be free.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a meeting this morning with the developer team in Bangkok about the app. We went over the feature backlog and prioritized the location-based discovery algorithm for the next sprint. The flight over was uneventful—grabbed the red-eye from Taipei so I could hit the ground running.

Afterward, I walked around Thonglor for a few hours. Found this basement bar that only opens after 11pm and doesn't show up on any maps. The owner is a former DJ from Berlin who moved here three years ago. We talked about how Bangkok's nightlife scene is evolving faster than Tokyo's right now. He introduced me to his network of venue owners. Could be useful for partnerships.

Spent the evening updating the pitch deck for next week's investor meeting in Singapore. The current traction numbers look decent but not explosive. Need to figure out how to make the growth story more compelling. Booked a hostel near Clarke Quay for the trip—the one with the rooftop bar where you can network with other founders.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly, I just kept walking. I'd already been to the main spots everyone knows, and I was bored. Turned down some alley because I saw a guy carrying vinyl records disappear into a doorway. Followed him. Turns out the entrance is behind a laundromat. You have to know to knock twice. The owner said he doesn't want it on Google—says the moment a place gets discovered, it dies.

sources.journal_entry:
Called my mom today—not because she called me, but because I wanted to. Told her about the investor meeting, the co-founder leaving, the uncertainty. She listened more than she lectured, which was surprising. At the end, she just said: "You'll figure it out. You always do. Just don't forget to eat."

It wasn't the conversation I expected. Maybe I've been so busy defending myself that I forgot she's also capable of just being my mom. Not the version of her I argue against in my head, but the real one who's worried and proud in equal measure.

Still don't know what I'm going to tell the angel investor next month. But I'm less afraid of the question now. Maybe the answer doesn't have to be forever. Maybe it just has to be honest.

Had a call with a potential angel investor today. She's based in Hong Kong, built and exited two companies before she was 35, now advises early-stage founders in the region. She listened to my pitch, asked sharp questions, and then said something that's been echoing in my head since.

She said: "You clearly have energy. But energy without focus is just noise. What's the one thing you're willing to be boring about for the next five years?"

Five years. That's longer than any relationship I've had—with a person or a project. The question isn't whether I can handle it. It's whether I even want to. Part of me thinks that's the whole point: find the thing worth being boring for. Another part of me thinks that's just conformity dressed up in startup language.

I don't know. I told her I'd think about it. She said that's fine, but the market won't wait forever for me to figure myself out. She's probably right. She also said she'd check in next month to see where my head's at.

The runway isn't just money. It's time. And I'm spending both whether I have a plan or not.

Spent the day wandering Shibuya without any plan. Haven't done that in months—usually I'm running between meetings or on a call with someone in a different timezone. But today I just walked. Watched people. Sat in a coffee shop for three hours. Read a book I've been meaning to finish since January.

There's this weird guilt that comes with unproductive time. Like I should be building or networking or optimizing something. But also... I felt more present than I have in weeks. Noticed things I usually miss. The way the light hits the buildings around 4pm. The sound of trains overhead mixed with street musicians.

I used to do this all the time in university—before I decided that was boring and left. Maybe the problem isn't that I need more novelty. Maybe I've just been looking for it in the wrong places. Or maybe I'm just tired and romanticizing a slow day because it's different from my usual pace.

Either way, it was good. I think I needed to remember that standing still isn't the same as being stuck.
sources.nudge_response: I chose it. That's the difference. When I'm stuck, it feels like the walls are closing in and I can't move. Today I could've moved—I just decided not to. There's freedom in that. The stillness was on my terms.

sources.journal_entry: Couldn't sleep last night. Kept thinking about the runway—four months left, maybe five if I cut costs. The app is growing but not fast enough. Wondering if I should take on contract work to extend the timeline or if that would just distract me from the main thing.
sources.nudge_response: The money is the easy answer. But honestly, it's more like... what if I'm running out of runway on me? Like, what if I've been chasing this feeling of building something new for so long that I've forgotten how to actually finish anything? That thought hit me around 3am and I haven't been able to shake it.

sources.journal_entry:
Why does everyone act like pivoting is failure? I've done it three times now and people look at me like I'm lost. I'm not lost—I'm searching. There's a difference. Lost means you don't know where you're going. Searching means you know the destination exists, you just haven't found the right path yet.

My aunt asked when I'm going to "settle down" with one business. Settle down. Like I'm supposed to marry a startup. Maybe the right one hasn't appeared yet. Maybe the point is to keep exploring until something feels like it can hold my attention for more than a year. Is that so wrong?
sources.nudge_response: That's the million-dollar question, isn't it? I'll let you know when I figure it out. For now, I'm just trusting the process.

sources.journal_entry: Co-founder officially left. Can't say I'm surprised. Starting over again with a smaller team and lower runway, but weirdly I feel lighter. At least now every decision is mine.

Investor meeting didn't go the way I hoped. They liked the concept but wanted to see "more traction" before committing. Classic. They want to fund things that are already working, not things that could work. Where's the vision in that?

I tried explaining that nightlife discovery is a category that doesn't exist yet—you can't show hockey stick growth for something people don't know they need until they have it. But they kept asking about retention metrics and monthly active users. Numbers I don't have because we're still in beta. It felt like being graded on a test I wasn't given.

My co-founder suggested we pivot to something safer. Maybe restaurant recommendations or travel itineraries—stuff with proven demand. I told him if I wanted to build something boring, I would've just stayed in university. That conversation didn't end well.
sources.nudge_response: He said I care more about the idea being interesting than the idea being successful. Like those are mutually exclusive. We're still talking, but there's this distance now. I think he wants out but doesn't want to say it directly. Maybe I should just ask. Or maybe I don't want to hear the answer.

sources.journal_entry:
Still thinking about that call. Went out tonight to clear my head—hit up three different rooftop bars with some founders I met last week. One of them is building a fintech play in Vietnam, another is doing sustainable fashion in Seoul. Neither of them has stable jobs either. Nobody questioned each other's choices.

Maybe that's why I surround myself with people like this. Not because I need validation, but because I need to be around people who get that the risk is the point. You don't build something new by playing it safe. And yeah, maybe some of us will fail—statistically, most of us will. But at least we'll know we tried something different.
sources.nudge_response: Ha, family is a strong word. We're more like... fellow travelers, I guess. People passing through the same checkpoint at the same time. Some of them I'll probably never see again after this month. That's fine though. I'm not looking for permanence.

Can't stop replaying dinner. Camila brought up the director thing again, not even an hour after I told her I said no. She had that voice, the one where she's being very calm and very patient like she's talking to one of her students instead of her husband. She asked what my "plan" was. sources.journal_entry:
Sunday and I'm wiped. Camila's parents came down from Zacatecas for the weekend and I spent two days doing the good son-in-law routine. Don Aurelio wanted to sit in the living room and watch fútbol all afternoon and I sat there with him because that's what you do. Four hours of commentary about the ref and the state of Mexican soccer and me nodding along while my brain was climbing the walls. I kept thinking about the Sayulita forecast, perfect swell all weekend and I'm on the couch watching a replay of a game I already know the score of.

Camila noticed I was restless. She told me to relax and be present. I wanted to say that sitting still and watching something I've already seen is the opposite of present for me, but I didn't. I just went to the kitchen and made everyone coffee and let it go. By tonight I felt like I'd been holding my breath for 48 hours and only just exhaled.
sources.nudge_response: She would have said I was being selfish in front of her parents. And honestly, maybe she'd be right. They drove five hours to visit. I just can't fake enjoying something I'm not enjoying, and pretending drains me more than anything else.

sources.journal_entry: Budget meeting ran long. Signed up for a weekend mezcal tasting in Oaxaca next month. Tomás asked if I was "collecting hobbies" and I told him I was collecting experiences, which shut him up.
sources.nudge_response: Saw it online somewhere. Looked fun, just booked it.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent the whole day at the distribution center running damage control on a shipment mix-up with the Monterrey warehouse. Five hours of calls and spreadsheets and a very annoyed client who kept asking to speak to "someone higher up." Normally this kind of chaos makes me want to throw my phone off the roof, but today I sort of got into it. There was a rhythm to it. I called in a favor from Beto at the trucking company, rerouted three pallets through Aguascalientes, and had the corrected order confirmed by four o'clock. The client's tone shifted completely once he realized I'd actually fixed it same-day.

Drove home with the windows down, cumbia loud, and stopped at the fish market in Chapala on the way back. Picked up red snapper and a bag of limes. Made a zarandeado on the grill while the sun went down. Camila came out and sat with me while I cooked and we didn't talk about the director thing or plans or any of it. She just ate and said it was the best fish I'd made all year. That was the whole evening and it was perfect.

I think the good days look like this. Something that gets my blood going during the hours I'm working, and then the reward after. The snapper, the lime, the smoke off the grill, my wife telling me I got the char exactly right. I don't need a bigger title for that. I just need the space to keep having days like this one.

Took the day off Friday and drove out to Sayulita alone. The waves were clean, offshore wind, barely anyone out. I caught a left that held up for maybe six seconds and when I came off the board I was laughing out loud with nobody around to hear it. Ate ceviche at that stand near the plaza where the guy recognizes me now and gives me extra tostadas.

On the drive home I called my brother Ernesto in Puebla. He's been grinding sixty-hour weeks at his plant and sounded terrible. I told him to come visit, we'd go out on the boat, eat well, do nothing useful for three days. He said he couldn't, too many deadlines. He sounded exactly like the version of me I've spent five years trying not to become. But surfing alone on a Friday while he sat in a fluorescent office tells me I'm doing the right thing, even when Camila and Tomás think I'm wasting my potential. I'm not wasting anything. I'm spending it.

Five hours of calls and spreadsheets and a very annoyed client who kept asking to speak to "someone higher up." Normally this kind of chaos makes me want to throw my phone off the roof, but today I sort of got into it. There was a rhythm to it. I called in a favor from Beto at the trucking company, rerouted three pallets through Aguascalientes, and had the corrected order confirmed by four o'clock. The client's tone shifted completely once he realized I'd actually fixed it same-day.

Drove home with the windows down, cumbia loud, and stopped at the fish market in Chapala on the way back. Picked up red snapper and a bag of limes. Made a zarandeado on the grill while the sun went down. Camila came out and sat with me while I cooked and we didn't talk about the director thing or plans or any of it. She just ate and said it was the best fish I'd made all year. That was the whole evening and it was perfect.

I think the good days look like this. Something that gets my blood going during the hours I'm working, and then the reward after. The snapper, the lime, the smoke off the grill, my wife telling me I got the char exactly right. I don't need a bigger title for that. I just need the space to keep having days like this one.

Can't stop replaying dinner. Camila brought up the director thing again, not even an hour after I told her I said no. She had that voice, the one where she's being very calm and very patient like she's talking to one of her students instead of her husband. She asked what my "plan" was. I said the plan is the same plan it's always been, I do good work, I enjoy my life, and I don't let some title turn me into someone who eats sad lunches at a desk in a city I don't even like.

She didn't say anything for a while. Then she said maybe the problem isn't the job, maybe the problem is that I always need something new and nothing is ever enough. That sat weird. Because I don't think wanting to feel alive is the same as nothing being enough. But I also couldn't explain why she's wrong without sounding like I'm the one who doesn't get it.
sources.nudge_response: Maybe a small one. I don't get bored with her. But I get bored with everything around us if it stays the same too long, and I think she takes that personally even when it's not about her.

sources.journal_entry: Turned down the director thing. Everyone at the office looked at me like I'd lost my mind, including Tomás who's been pushing me toward it for two years. I don't owe anyone an explanation for wanting to keep my Fridays.
