values.user_phrase: Having the freedom to choose my own path
values.approved_definition: Independent thought and action — choosing, creating, exploring. Derives from organismic needs for control and mastery (e.g., Bandura, 1977; Deci, 1975) and interactional requirements of autonomy and independence (e.g., Kluckhohn, 1951; Kohn & Schooler, 1983).

sources.journal_entry:
Had a meeting with Dr. Villanueva about the dissertation chapter on extractive policy in Peru. For once he actually engaged with the argument instead of just redirecting me toward his framework. He pushed back on my case selection, which was fair, but he did it by asking questions rather than just telling me to change it. That felt different. I left his office thinking clearly for the first time in weeks.

Walked to the mercado afterward and sat with a coffee going through my notes. The chapter outline is solid. The theoretical framing is mine -- not his, not borrowed from the lab's usual line. I've been circling this argument for months and it finally has shape. There's a version of this that could become a standalone article, which matters because I need publications that aren't just appendages to his projects.

I forget sometimes that I came here with a decade of professional experience. I wasn't some kid who wandered into a program. I chose this. I left a salary and a title because the work I was doing in Bogota hit a ceiling I couldn't break through without the credential. Days like today remind me the trade-off has a point.

sources.journal_entry:
Lab meeting today was three hours of performative agreement. Villanueva presented his new grant proposal and everyone nodded along like it was revelation. Half the methodology section is recycled from a paper we all know didn't replicate well. I sat there biting my tongue because the last time I raised a concern in front of the group he reframed it as me "not understanding the nuance yet." In front of the first-years. That was six months ago and I still feel it.

Marina, the other senior student, caught my eye during his presentation. She sees it too but she's smarter about it than I am -- she just stays quiet, publishes on the side, and keeps her head down. I can't do that. Something in me won't let me just sit there when the reasoning is sloppy. But speaking up costs more than staying silent, at least in this lab.

Came home and opened the Peru chapter again. The contrast is sharp. In Villanueva's lab I'm a student who should listen. In my own work I'm building something that could actually matter for how these countries manage their mining conflicts. The gap between those two versions of me is getting harder to hold.

sources.journal_entry: Got a call from Don Alfredo across the street — he needs his whole kitchen faucet replaced plus some tile work. That's a good-sized job, probably two days of work. Felt like I could breathe again for the first time all week.

Bad week. The delivery app lowered the per-trip rate again, no warning, no explanation. Just opened the app Monday morning and the numbers were different. I did the same twelve deliveries I always do on a weekday and came home with almost twenty percent less. Twenty percent. That's not nothing. That's a week of groceries, that's Negrita's vet visit I've been putting off.

The handyman side is slower too because people are tightening up. I had three jobs lined up this week and two of them canceled last minute — one lady said she'd "wait until next month" to fix her bathroom faucet and the other one just stopped responding. So now I'm sitting here Thursday night with the calculator app open, moving numbers around like I'm playing some kind of sad puzzle game, trying to figure out where the motorcycle payment comes from.

The thing that really gets to me is the feeling. It's not just about the money, it's the not knowing. Every month is a guess. Every week I wake up and I don't know what I'm going to make. I used to think that was the trade-off for not having a boss breathing down my neck. Lately I'm not so sure the trade-off is worth it. But what am I supposed to do, crawl back and prove Graciela right? No. I'll figure it out. I always figure it out.

My sister Graciela keeps calling to tell me I should go back to a regular job. She doesn't get it. I'm not going to sit in some warehouse again answering to a guy ten years younger than me who treats people like furniture.
sources.nudge_response: It's not impossible, I just don't want to. There's a difference. Look, I know what I'm doing. I've been managing fine for five years this way. Graciela worries because she's Graciela. She married an accountant, everything in her life has a line item. Not everyone lives like that.

sources.journal_entry: Don Alfredo recommended me to his daughter for some painting work at her new apartment. Three rooms, good rate, she even offered to pay half upfront. I bought Negrita the fancy wet food she likes to celebrate.

Picked up the motorcycle from Raul this morning. It rides clean now, brakes feel solid. That's something. But I'm running on maybe four hours of sleep from the last few days and I can feel it in my eyes, in the way I'm slow to react at intersections. Almost clipped a bus mirror on Corrientes.

Saturday is coming and Cacho already texted about the parrilla. Part of me wants to skip it this week, save the money. But another part of me — the louder part — says that's the one thing that keeps me sane. You take away the asado with friends and what do I have left? A cat, a calculator, and a leaking faucet in my own bathroom that I haven't even bothered to fix.
sources.nudge_response: It's the only time during the week where I'm not counting anything. Not counting deliveries, not counting pesos, not counting hours. I sit down, the meat comes, somebody pours the wine, and for a few hours I'm just Roberto having a good time with his friends. Nobody's asking me to fix something or deliver something or be somewhere in fifteen minutes. It's the closest thing I have to feeling like my life is actually mine.

sources.journal_entry: Couldn't sleep. Opened the app at 1am to see if there were any late-night delivery runs. There were two. I took them both, rode the bicycle I borrowed from my neighbor. Came home at 3am with barely enough to cover tomorrow's gas.

Motorcycle started making a noise yesterday. A grinding thing when I brake. I took it to Raul's shop and he looked at it and said the brake pads are gone and the disc is warped, it needs replacing. He quoted me a number that wiped out everything I'd saved from the Alfredo job. Every peso.

I stood there in Raul's shop and felt my stomach just drop. Because it's not optional — the motorcycle is how I make deliveries. Without it I'm on foot or taking the subte, which means fewer trips, which means less money, which means next month's rent gets tight. It's like this chain where one thing breaks and everything behind it starts wobbling. I told Raul to do it, because what choice do I have. But I walked home and I couldn't even eat dinner.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly, I was thinking about my old man. He worked at the same factory for thirty-two years. Hated it, but every month the check came in. He never had to wonder if the floor was going to fall out from under him. I used to think that was a sad way to live. Now I'm not so sure. He always had a little envelope in the dresser drawer with cash for emergencies. I don't have that envelope. I don't have anything between me and the next bad surprise. And that thought — that I'm one broken motorcycle or one bad month away from not being able to pay rent — that sat on my chest the whole walk home.

sources.journal_entry:
Painting job at Don Alfredo's daughter's place is done. She was happy with it, paid the balance, even tipped me a little extra. So the money situation is stable for the moment. Rent is covered, motorcycle payment is covered, Raul is paid. There's a small cushion again, not much, but it's there.

Went to the parrilla Saturday like always. Pocho brought his nephew, a kid of about twenty-five who does the same delivery app I do but also drives for a rideshare service on the side. He was telling me about his "strategy" — how he works the surge hours, how he tracks which neighborhoods tip best, how he's saving for a down payment on his own place. The whole table was impressed. I just sat there eating my chorizo and feeling old.

It's not jealousy exactly. The kid has energy and optimism and a plan, and good for him. But I was that kid once. I had the energy to work sixteen-hour days and still go dancing with my ex-wife on Saturday night. Now I do eight hours of deliveries and my back locks up. sources.journal_entry: Couldn't sleep. Opened the app at 1am to see if there were any late-night delivery runs. There were two. I took them both, rode the bicycle I borrowed from my neighbor. Came home at 3am with barely enough to cover tomorrow's gas.

sources.journal_entry: Got a call from Don Alfredo across the street — he needs his whole kitchen faucet replaced plus some tile work. That's a good-sized job, probably two days of work. Felt like I could breathe again for the first time all week.

Bad week. The delivery app lowered the per-trip rate again, no warning, no explanation. Just opened the app Monday morning and the numbers were different. I did the same twelve deliveries I always do on a weekday and came home with almost twenty percent less. Twenty percent. That's not nothing. That's a week of groceries, that's Negrita's vet visit I've been putting off.

The handyman side is slower too because people are tightening up. I had three jobs lined up this week and two of them canceled last minute — one lady said she'd "wait until next month" to fix her bathroom faucet and the other one just stopped responding. So now I'm sitting here Thursday night with the calculator app open, moving numbers around like I'm playing some kind of sad puzzle game, trying to figure out where the motorcycle payment comes from.

The thing that really gets to me is the feeling. It's not just about the money, it's the not knowing. Every month is a guess. Every week I wake up and I don't know what I'm going to make. I used to think that was the trade-off for not having a boss breathing down my neck. Lately I'm not so sure the trade-off is worth it. But what am I supposed to do, crawl back and prove Graciela right? No. I'll figure it out. I always figure it out.

sources.nudge_response: It's not impossible, I just don't want to. There's a difference. Look, I know what I'm doing. I've been managing fine for five years this way. sources.journal_entry:

sources.journal_entry:
Second time writing today, which I never do. But I sat down to draft the self-assessment after dinner and something shifted.

Started listing my projects and realized I've been carrying more than I thought. The payment gateway wasn't just a migration—it was six months of reverse-engineering undocumented legacy code while keeping the live system running. The mentoring wasn't casual either. I had weekly one-on-ones with Daniela and Esteban, reviewed their PRs line by line, talked them through architectural decisions. That's not a line item. That's shaping how two engineers think.

Maybe the problem isn't that I can't write about my work. Maybe it's that where I grew up, talking about yourself like that was considered feo—ugly, tasteless. You let your elders praise you. You didn't praise yourself. My mother would have given me a look if I'd walked around listing my accomplishments.

But I'm not in Medellín anymore. And the rules here are different. Not better or worse, just different. Fernando isn't going to guess what I've done. He has thirty direct reports. If I don't tell him, he genuinely won't know.

I wrote four paragraphs. Strong verbs and all. Read it back and it sounded like someone else, but maybe that's okay. Maybe learning a new professional language isn't the same as losing the old one.

Performance review cycle opened today. I hate this time of year. You have to write a self-assessment that's basically a sales pitch for yourself, and I've never been good at selling. Camila says I undersell. My manager Fernando says I need to "make my impact more visible." Everyone has advice.

The thing is, I know what I've done. Seventeen production releases this year. Zero rollbacks. Mentored two junior engineers who both got promoted. Reduced our CI pipeline time by forty percent. But writing it all out in first person with action verbs and metrics feels like performing. "I spearheaded." "I drove." Those aren't words real people use.

My colleague Ana has the opposite problem—she writes these self-assessments that read like award acceptance speeches. And it works for her. She got promoted last year. I've been at the same level for four years. So maybe the system rewards the performance, not the work.

I'll write the self-assessment this weekend. I'll use the strong verbs. I'll quantify everything. It just feels like wearing a costume that doesn't fit. My papá was a carpenter in Medellín. He didn't have to write paragraphs about how well he built a cabinet. The cabinet spoke for itself.

Monday standup, same routine. Gave my update, kept it short. Marcos asked if anyone had concerns about the new API rate-limiting approach and I almost said something. Almost. Because I think the threshold they picked is going to choke under real load. I ran the numbers over the weekend, actually. But Diego already endorsed the approach and Diego is the architect, so.

Funny how that works. You have the data, you have the experience, but you also have a sense of when speaking up will just make things awkward. Diego doesn't take pushback well. Everyone knows it. Nobody says it.

Went to the gym after work. Deadlifts. There's something honest about weight on a bar. Either you lift it or you don't. No politics in iron.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly, probably nothing dramatic. Diego would have nodded, said "good point, let's take it offline," and then nothing would change. That's the pattern. I've seen it enough times. It's not worth the energy to test it again. Better to document my concerns in the ticket comments so there's a paper trail when it breaks. That way I'm covered without making it a thing.

Had the meeting with Fernando. It was... better than expected. He said the director position is opening again in Q2, and this time he's putting me forward as the internal candidate. Not a guarantee, but a real recommendation. He said my self-assessment was "the strongest you've written" and that the team's reliability metrics speak for themselves.

I thanked him. Shook his hand. Walked back to my desk and just sat there for a while.

The strange part is I expected to feel more. Elated, relieved, something big. Instead it was quiet. Like I'd been holding my breath for a long time and finally let it out, but the exhale was so slow I barely noticed. Maybe that's what it feels like when something you've wanted actually moves closer—not fireworks, just a slight loosening in the chest.

Camila was happy when I told her. She said "finally they're seeing what I've always seen." I almost corrected her—they're not seeing me, they're seeing a version of me that learned to write in their language. But I didn't say that because it would've turned a good moment into a philosophy seminar. And she deserved to just be happy for me.

Took the girls out for helado to celebrate. Lucía got three scoops. Sometimes that's enough.
sources.nudge_response:
I've been thinking about that since I wrote it. And honestly... yes. I think it is. It's not the whole me. It's not the me who eats tamales on the balcony or argues about fútbol with my brother-in-law. But it's not fake either. It's the part of me that learned to operate in a system that wasn't built for people like me. A Colombian who came here with an accent and a degree nobody recognized at first.

Maybe I resented it for a long time because it felt like the system was asking me to become someone else. But writing that self-assessment—I wasn't lying. I was translating. And translation isn't betrayal. My papá spoke three regional dialects. He didn't lose himself switching between them.

sources.journal_entry: Fernando scheduled a "career path conversation" for Monday. I don't know what that means. Could be good—could be the director track opening up. Could also be them telling me to lateral into some platform team nobody wants to join. I've seen both versions. People keep saying I should be hopeful but I don't want to get set up for another no.

Second time writing today, which I never do. But I sat down to draft the self-assessment after dinner and something shifted.

Started listing my projects and realized I've been carrying more than I thought. The payment gateway wasn't just a migration—it was six months of reverse-engineering undocumented legacy code while keeping the live system running. The mentoring wasn't casual either. I had weekly one-on-ones with Daniela and Esteban, reviewed their PRs line by line, talked them through architectural decisions. That's not a line item. That's shaping how two engineers think.

Maybe the problem isn't that I can't write about my work. Maybe it's that where I grew up, talking about yourself like that was considered feo—ugly, tasteless. You let your elders praise you. You didn't praise yourself. My mother would have given me a look if I'd walked around listing my accomplishments.

But I'm not in Medellín anymore. And the rules here are different. Not better or worse, just different. Fernando isn't going to guess what I've done. He has thirty direct reports. If I don't tell him, he genuinely won't know.

I wrote four paragraphs. Strong verbs and all. Read it back and it sounded like someone else, but maybe that's okay. Maybe learning a new professional language isn't the same as losing the old one.

Performance review cycle opened today. I hate this time of year. You have to write a self-assessment that's basically a sales pitch for yourself, and I've never been good at selling. Camila says I undersell. My manager Fernando says I need to "make my impact more visible." Everyone has advice.

The thing is, I know what I've done. Seventeen production releases this year. Zero rollbacks. Mentored two junior engineers who both got promoted. Reduced our CI pipeline time by forty percent. But writing it all out in first person with action verbs and metrics feels like performing. "I spearheaded." "I drove." Those aren't words real people use.

My colleague Ana has the opposite problem—she writes these self-assessments that read like award acceptance speeches. And it works for her. She got promoted last year. I've been at the same level for four years. So maybe the system rewards the performance, not the work.

I'll write the self-assessment this weekend. I'll use the strong verbs. I'll quantify everything. It just feels like wearing a costume that doesn't fit. My papá was a carpenter in Medellín. He didn't have to write paragraphs about how well he built a cabinet. The cabinet spoke for itself.

Monday standup, same routine. Gave my update, kept it short. Marcos asked if anyone had concerns about the new API rate-limiting approach and I almost said something. Almost. Because I think the threshold they picked is going to choke under real load. I ran the numbers over the weekend, actually. But Diego already endorsed the approach and Diego is the architect, so.

Funny how that works. You have the data, you have the experience, but you also have a sense of when speaking up will just make things awkward. Diego doesn't take pushback well. Everyone knows it. Nobody says it.

Went to the gym after work. Deadlifts. There's something honest about weight on a bar. Either you lift it or you don't. No politics in iron.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly, probably nothing dramatic. Diego would have nodded, said "good point, let's take it offline," and then nothing would change. That's the pattern. I've seen it enough times. It's not worth the energy to test it again. Better to document my concerns in the ticket comments so there's a paper trail when it breaks. That way I'm covered without making it a thing.

sources.journal_entry:
Long week. Delivered the payment gateway migration three days early and nobody said a word about it. Just got folded into the next sprint like it was expected. Meanwhile Tomás presented his dashboard prototype at the all-hands and got a round of applause. A prototype. Not even in production.

I'm not bitter about it. That's just how things work. You do the plumbing, someone else gets to show off the faucet. I knew that when I chose backend over product years ago.

Camila made tamales tonight. Sat on the balcony eating them while the girls did homework inside. The jalapeños she planted last month are actually coming up. Small green shoots pushing through the soil. That's the thing about growing something—it doesn't need anyone to clap for it. It just grows.

I wrote four paragraphs. Strong verbs and all. Read it back and it sounded like someone else, but maybe that's okay. Maybe learning a new professional language isn't the same as losing the old one.

sources.journal_entry:
Mum called from Leeuwarden. Wanted to "check in" which always means she has something to say. She asked how Lotte was doing and I gave her the update from the neurologist. Long pause. Then she said maybe I'm "doing too much" and that it's "not sustainable." She suggested Lotte look into professional home care. I told her that costs money Lotte doesn't have. She said maybe I should focus on my own life, find a partner, think about what I want.

Right. What I want. As if I haven't thought about that. As if I'm some martyr running around Utrecht with a spanner because I haven't considered the alternative. I do think about it. I think about it on every solo ride home. But thinking about what I want doesn't change what Lotte needs, and nobody else is stepping in, least of all Mum who calls once a fortnight from three hours away.

I know she means well. I do. But there's something in the way she says it -- "focus on your own life" -- as if helping Lotte is separate from my life. It IS my life. She's my sister. Her kids call me Oom Sansen because Mats couldn't say Sander when he was two and it stuck. I'm not doing this out of obligation. I'm doing it because I'd rather be tired than be the kind of person who steps away when things get hard. That's not something I need advice about from someone who sends a card on birthdays.
sources.nudge_response: The kind where you wake up already behind. Not sleepy tired. More like the tank is always half-empty and everything costs a bit more than it should. I manage. But some mornings I sit on the edge of the bed for a while before I stand up.

sources.journal_entry: Went to Jeroen's birthday. Stayed three hours. Drank too many Jupilers, talked rubbish, laughed until my stomach hurt. He gave me a hug when I left and said he's glad I came. Lotte had texted to say the kids were fine at their dad's for once. I cycled home through the quiet streets feeling lighter than I have all week. Small thing. Good thing.

Lotte had a hospital appointment today. New neurologist, younger guy, very direct. He told her the progression is slow but real and that she should "plan her support network" for the next few years. She looked at me when he said that. Not at Pieter, who wasn't there. Not at our parents, who live in Friesland and visit twice a year. At me.

I sat in the corridor afterwards while she got dressed and I stared at a poster about hand hygiene and thought about what "the next few years" means. More school runs. More leaking taps. More weekends. That sounds terrible written down. I don't mean it that way. I mean I'm trying to understand the shape of what I'm signing up for, and whether it's something I'm choosing or something that's choosing me.

Rode home the long way through Amelisweerd. The trees are turning and the light through the leaves was that specific October gold that makes you slow down even if you don't want to. Stopped on the bridge over the Kromme Rijn for a few minutes. A heron was standing in the shallows looking patient. I don't feel patient. I feel like I'm holding something that keeps getting heavier and everyone assumes I'm fine because I keep showing up with the wrench.
sources.nudge_response: I don't know. Lotte has nobody else who shows up consistently. If I step back even a little, the gap isn't filled by someone else, it just stays empty. So putting it down doesn't feel like an option. It feels like leaving a hole.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a full delivery day for once. Eight runs between nine and four, mostly parcels for that organic food box service. My legs are cooked but the earnings are decent -- sixty-two euros before the platform cut. One of the customers, an older woman near Griftpark, invited me in for coffee. I said no because I was behind schedule, then felt guilty about it for the next two hours. She looked lonely. I don't know why that stuck.

My mate Jeroen called and asked if I wanted to come to his birthday drinks on Friday. I said yes but I'm already calculating whether Lotte will need me with the kids that evening. Haven't asked her yet. I should just go. Jeroen always shows up for me. I just need to show up back. That should be simple but somehow it never is.
sources.nudge_response: It's not complicated. I'll go. Just need to sort out the logistics first.

sources.journal_entry:
Later. Went back inside and Lotte had made coffee, which felt like her way of saying it was fine. We didn't talk about it. Played a board game with the kids -- Mats cheats spectacularly and Eva keeps a running tally of his crimes in a little notebook, which is both hilarious and slightly concerning. Normal afternoon. Good one, actually.

On the ride home I kept replaying the kitchen thing. She said "I feel like I'm ruining your weekends" and the truth is some weekends do feel like they disappear into errands for her. But I can't say that because it would confirm exactly what she's afraid of. So I carry it. It's not heavy most days. Today it's a bit heavy. Poes was waiting by the door when I got in, which helps more than a cat should.

Sunday and I thought I'd have the morning to myself but Lotte rang at half seven because the downstairs tap was leaking and Pieter -- her ex -- isn't answering his phone as usual. Cycled over with a wrench and some thread tape. The washer was gone, ten-minute fix, but then she started crying at the kitchen table and I didn't know what to do so I just sat there. She said she's tired of asking me for things. That she feels like she's ruining my weekends. I told her that's stupid, she's not, but the word "stupid" came out too fast and she flinched.

I'm sitting on her front step now writing this. The kids are inside watching cartoons. I can hear Mats laughing. I want to go back in and say something better but I don't know what that would be. Sometimes being there isn't enough and you can't fix it with a wrench.

Picked up Lotte's kids from school again because she had a bad flare. Mats had a meltdown about his shoelaces in the car park and I spent ten minutes crouched on the tarmac retying them while Eva sat in the back seat reading like nothing was happening. That girl is ice. Bought them both stroopwafels from the bakker on Voorstraat and dropped them home. Lotte was on the sofa looking grey. I made her tea and put a load of washing on before she could say she'd do it herself.

Then I had to sprint across town for a delivery window I'd nearly forgotten about. Some law firm on the Maliebaan wanted documents by five and I made it with three minutes to spare, sweating through my jacket. The receptionist didn't look up. Forty minutes of cycling for eight euros fifty. That's the maths of it.

Got home, fed Poes, sat down, and realised I hadn't eaten since a cheese sandwich at eleven. My knee is doing that clicking thing again. I should stretch more. I should do a lot of things. The fern on the windowsill is browning at the tips, which probably means I've been overwatering. Even the plants aren't getting my best these days. Not complaining, just noticing how the day went.

The course is fascinating. We are learning about designing for users with limited internet, older phones, and varying literacy levels. It reminded me of my grandmother who never learned to read but could recognize patterns in kolam designs that would challenge any algorithm I could write.

For Raghav, work is a transaction, skills exchanged for money. For me, at this stage in life, it feels like there should be more. Not everyone has thirty years of experience building systems. Maybe that expertise could serve people who actually need it, not just corporations looking to squeeze more margins. But then again, my daughter's tuition fees come from those same corporate margins. The math doesn't always work out cleanly.

sources.journal_entry: Same day, later. After the call I went for a walk and found myself outside the construction site again. This time the workers had finished for the night. Empty scaffolding and silence. Felt strangely peaceful.

Video call with Priya tonight. She's doing well in Toronto, enjoying her research on climate modeling. She asked about my work and I found myself describing it with more cynicism than usual. She paused and then said something that stuck: "Appa, you taught me that every small action matters. Why don't you believe that for yourself?"

She's right, of course. I've always told her and her generation that individual choices ripple outward, that systemic change starts with personal conviction. But somewhere along the way I started feeling like my own choices were too small to matter against the scale of suffering I see.

The conversation reminded me of why I became an engineer in the first place. Growing up, technology represented possibility, a way out of predetermined fates. I wanted to build things that would make life better. When did I lose that thread? Or maybe I haven't lost it, I've just buried it under spreadsheets and sprint cycles.

Sprint planning ran until 7 PM. We're building features no one asked for because some VP read an article about what competitors are doing. I sat there for four hours nodding along, contributing where required, while part of me was calculating how many village school teachers' salaries could be paid with the cost of this one unnecessary feature.

I know this kind of thinking isn't productive. You can't compare everything to some moral baseline or you'll go mad. But today I'm too tired to pretend the comparison doesn't exist in my head.
sources.nudge_response: Because I remember what it felt like to have nothing and know that luck was the only difference between me and so many others. Every rupee spent on nonsense feels like stolen opportunity for someone who could have used it better. I know that's not how economics works, but the feeling doesn't care about economics.

The fifth day I want to dedicate to teaching coding at a community center in Koramangala that serves domestic workers and their children. I reached out to them last week and they welcomed the offer. First session scheduled for next Friday.

Same day, later. After the call I went for a walk and found myself outside the construction site again. This time the workers had finished for the night. Empty scaffolding and silence. Felt strangely peaceful.

Video call with Priya tonight. She's doing well in Toronto, enjoying her research on climate modeling. She asked about my work and I found myself describing it with more cynicism than usual. She paused and then said something that stuck: "Appa, you taught me that every small action matters. Why don't you believe that for yourself?"

She's right, of course. I've always told her and her generation that individual choices ripple outward, that systemic change starts with personal conviction. But somewhere along the way I started feeling like my own choices were too small to matter against the scale of suffering I see.

The conversation reminded me of why I became an engineer in the first place. Growing up, technology represented possibility, a way out of predetermined fates. I wanted to build things that would make life better. When did I lose that thread? Or maybe I haven't lost it, I've just buried it under spreadsheets and sprint cycles.

Sprint planning ran until 7 PM. We're building features no one asked for because some VP read an article about what competitors are doing. I sat there for four hours nodding along, contributing where required, while part of me was calculating how many village school teachers' salaries could be paid with the cost of this one unnecessary feature.

I know this kind of thinking isn't productive. You can't compare everything to some moral baseline or you'll go mad. But today I'm too tired to pretend the comparison doesn't exist in my head.

First teaching session did not go as planned. I had prepared carefully, slides on basic programming concepts, examples I thought would be relatable. But the students struggled with the mouse and keyboard basics I had taken for granted. One woman, Kamala, works as a housekeeper in my neighborhood. I felt useless, like I had parachuted in with my fancy knowledge completely missing what they actually needed. By the end I had abandoned my lesson plan entirely and we spent the last hour just practicing how to open and close windows on the screen.

Walking home I felt deflated, then embarrassed for feeling deflated. Who did I think I was, expecting to transform lives in one session? This is going to be harder and slower than I imagined. The question is whether I have the patience and humility to stick with it.

sources.journal_entry: Spent the morning reorganizing the exam schedule for finals. Nobody asked me to — I just saw that the current draft from admin had conflicts that would affect my students. Fixed it, sent it to the vice-rector with my corrections marked in red, cc'd the relevant people. That is how you get things done around here. You do not wait for permission, you present the solution.

Faculty meeting this morning, the big monthly one with the coordinadora and all department heads. I had prepared a ten-minute summary of our curriculum adjustments for next semester. Detailed slides, enrollment data by section, everything organized the way I like — no fluff, just facts and a clear recommendation.

I got three minutes in before the coordinadora cut me off. Said she wanted to "open the floor" for a more collaborative discussion. Then Profesor Ríos from the science department started talking about interdisciplinary projects and somehow my curriculum adjustments became a footnote to his pitch. He used my enrollment data — the numbers I had just shown — to support his own proposal. Nobody seemed to notice. Or maybe they noticed and did not care.

I sat there for the rest of the meeting contributing when asked but mostly just watching my work get absorbed into someone else's narrative. I wanted to say something. That those were my numbers, my analysis, my recommendation. But the coordinadora had already set the tone and pushing back would have looked petty. So I smiled. Nodded. Made a note in my planner to address it privately later.

Walking back to my classroom I could feel it in my jaw, the clenching. Fifteen years I have been building this department and Ríos, who has been here four years, gets to repurpose my work in real time while I sit there like I am attending someone else's meeting.

Still thinking about that meeting. The truth is Camila looked a little deflated when I moved past her. But if I let every junior teacher pitch their favorite material mid-agenda we would never get through anything. The department works because someone holds the line. That someone is me and it has been me for fifteen years.

sources.journal_entry: Third time writing today but Patricia's comment is still rattling around in my head. She is not wrong that I bring work home. But she married a man who takes charge of things. That is who I am at school and at the junta and at home. I do not know how to be half of that.

Coming back to this because something happened after classes. The vice-rector stopped me in the hallway and thanked me for the exam schedule corrections I sent last week. It reminded me of something my father used to say. He managed a textile warehouse in Medellín for twenty-something years and he always told me the man who controls the calendar controls the operation. I did not understand it when I was young. Now I live it. Every week I review the departmental calendar, the exam schedule, the committee meeting dates. I know what is happening before most people know it is happening. That is not obsession, that is just how you keep things from falling apart.

My wife Patricia says I should relax more at home, that I bring the school energy into the house. Maybe she has a point. But when I relax, things slip. I have seen it happen to other department heads. They let go of the reins and within a semester the curriculum is a mess, the exam dates are wrong, and everyone is scrambling. I will not be that person.

Regular Wednesday. Classes went fine. The eleventh graders are reviewing for their exam on Independence movements and most of them actually did the reading, which is a first this semester. Ate lunch at my desk grading quizzes while the other teachers chatted in the sala de profesores.

Had a team standup today and Ravi brought up that our payment processing pipeline is rejecting a disproportionate number of transactions from certain Southeast Asian corridors. The data was right there in the dashboard. Mostly remittance flows, the kind migrant workers use to send money home. Something about the fraud model flagging certain patterns that are just... normal behavior for people sending small amounts frequently.

I knew what I was looking at. I've sat across the table from guys at the worker center who tell me how hard it is to send money back to their families, the fees they pay, the delays. And here's our system making it worse. But when Ravi raised it, the lead just said we'd revisit the thresholds next quarter and moved on. I could have pushed. I had the context, the stories, the data to make a case. But I just nodded and typed something in the chat about checking the logs.

Part of me says it wasn't the right moment, that I need to build a proper case first. But honestly I think I was just worried about being the guy who derails standup with a soapbox moment. My parents always told me not to stick out, keep your head down and do good work. Maybe that advice served them well in a factory town in Fujian. I'm not sure it serves me well here, sitting on information that could change something.
sources.nudge_response: Probably something about how the people on the other end of those rejected transactions aren't abstractions. They're the same guys I see on Saturday mornings trying to figure out medical claims. But saying that out loud at work feels like crossing a line I can't uncross.

sources.journal_entry:
Went to the worker center this morning. There was a new guy, Suresh, from Tamil Nadu. Fell from scaffolding three weeks ago and his employer hasn't filed the injury report. He showed me the bruises on his back, purple-yellow, still swelling around his ribs. I helped him draft a letter to MOM. My Mandarin-accented English and his Tamil-accented English, both of us stumbling through legalese neither of us was built for.

But we got it done. He shook my hand with both of his and said thank you in a way that made me want to cry in the stairwell afterward. I held it together. Barely.
sources.nudge_response: It felt undeserved. All I did was help write a letter. He's the one living through it, sleeping on a bunk bed with broken ribs because he can't afford to stop working.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a team standup today and Ravi brought up that our payment processing pipeline is rejecting a disproportionate number of transactions from certain Southeast Asian corridors. The data was right there in the dashboard. Mostly remittance flows, the kind migrant workers use to send money home. Something about the fraud model flagging certain patterns that are just... normal behavior for people sending small amounts frequently.

I knew what I was looking at. I've sat across the table from guys at the worker center who tell me how hard it is to send money back to their families, the fees they pay, the delays. And here's our system making it worse. But when Ravi raised it, the lead just said we'd revisit the thresholds next quarter and moved on. I could have pushed. I had the context, the stories, the data to make a case. But I just nodded and typed something in the chat about checking the logs.

Part of me says it wasn't the right moment, that I need to build a proper case first. But honestly I think I was just worried about being the guy who derails standup with a soapbox moment. My parents always told me not to stick out, keep your head down and do good work. Maybe that advice served them well in a factory town in Fujian. I'm not sure it serves me well here, sitting on information that could change something.
sources.nudge_response: Probably something about how the people on the other end of those rejected transactions aren't abstractions. They're the same guys I see on Saturday mornings trying to figure out medical claims. But saying that out loud at work feels like crossing a line I can't uncross.

Team dinner tonight. Quarterly thing, company card. The conversation turned to hiring and someone made a comment about how candidates from certain countries need more "handholding." A few people laughed. I didn't laugh but I also didn't say anything. Just moved the ice around in my glass.

The thing is I know exactly what that comment means. I've been on the receiving end of it, the assumption that because you come from a certain place you're somehow less. And I've watched the guys at the center deal with far worse versions of the same attitude every day. But at the table I just sat there because it was a team dinner and I didn't want to make it awkward. I'm so tired of choosing comfort over what I actually think.
sources.nudge_response: I don't know. Probably both. It's easier to blame it on not wanting confrontation than to admit I'm scared of being seen differently by people I work with every day.

sources.journal_entry:
Sister texted asking if I'm coming to Christmas dinner at her place this year. I want to say yes but I'm looking at the schedule and Christmas Eve and Christmas Day are usually the best earning days because everyone else takes off. Last year I worked both and just stopped by Mom and Dad's for an hour between rides.

Part of me thinks I should just take the hit and be there for the whole dinner. Dad's been doing better but who knows how many of these we get, you know? But then another part of me is like, one good day of driving could cover half my car insurance payment. I don't know. I'll probably end up doing what I always do which is work until the last possible minute and then rush over stressed and half-present anyway.

Twelve-hour day yesterday and another one today. Holiday surge is good for earnings but my back is killing me from sitting in the car so long. At least I was able to drop off the pharmacy money to Mom on my way between zones. She tried to give me back half of it and I told her no, just keep it in case something else comes up.

Had a passenger tonight who was heading to the airport for some tropical vacation and I sat there thinking about how I haven't taken more than a day off in probably six months. Not complaining really, it is what it is. Just tired.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly? I'd probably sleep until noon. Maybe drive out to the mountains just to sit somewhere quiet without my phone buzzing. But then I'd probably spend the whole time calculating how much money I'm losing by not working, so maybe that defeats the purpose.

sources.journal_entry:
Pop-up at Koregaon Park went well. Sold eleven pieces including two of the bomber prototypes. One girl asked if we had an Instagram — we do, but it's barely set up. Diya handled the money stuff while I talked to people. That part I'm good at. Strangers telling me they like something I made with my hands, that's a specific kind of high.

Afterwards we went to this new rooftop bar Adi told me about. Spent way too much on cocktails but the music was perfect and the city looked ridiculous from up there. Diya said it was our "revenue celebration." We made maybe eight thousand rupees today and spent half of it on drinks and that felt exactly right.

Spent most of the afternoon sourcing fabric swatches with Diya at this tiny warehouse in Camp. The guy running the place kept talking about minimum order quantities and I could see her doing math in her head, getting stressed. I just wanted to touch everything, feel the weight of it. Found this insane indigo block-print that would be perfect for the bomber jackets we've been sketching.

On the rickshaw back I was thinking about how three months ago I was sitting in a lecture hall pretending to care about supply chain management and now I'm actually doing it, badly, in real life. The irony isn't lost on me. Mum called while I was out but I let it ring. Didn't feel like hearing about Priya's wedding venue shortlist again.

On the rickshaw back I was thinking about how three months ago I was sitting in a lecture hall pretending to care about supply chain management and now I'm actually doing it, badly, in real life. Can't sleep, brain won't stop. Thinking about the consignment thing and whether it's a step up or just giving our margins away for the ego of seeing our label in a shop. Diya ran the numbers and we'd need to sell through at least seventy percent to break even after materials. That's tight. Also still chewing on the Adi thing from the other night. It's not that I don't want to be with him, it's that the second you sign a lease with someone the whole shape of your days changes. You eat dinner at the same time, you watch the same shows, you wake up and there's no surprise about who's next to you. That sounds awful when I write it out but I don't mean it in a cruel way. I just like having space where I can decide at midnight to rework a pattern or go meet Diya for chai without explaining.

Maybe I'm overthinking this. He didn't bring it up again and maybe he won't. Part of me kind of wants him to, just so I know he actually means it instead of it being some lease-expiry convenience thing. I should probably eat something, I skipped dinner and my stomach is doing that acidic thing.

Went home for lunch yesterday because Dad's birthday. Mum cornered me in the kitchen to ask if I've "thought about what comes next" if the brand doesn't work out. Priya was right there smiling with her ring and her Infosys lanyard still around her neck like some kind of prop. I know Mum means well but I'm so tired of being the cautionary tale at family gatherings.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent the whole morning at the Diwali mela helping set up the community puja. I did the rangoli at the entrance the way my grandmother taught me, rice flour with turmeric borders, none of the acrylic paint shortcuts the younger crowd uses. Three women came up and asked me to show them how. Felt good.

Later, back home, I worked on a new indigo resist pattern. Nobody was around to comment on it. Ravi had taken Arjun and Vihaan to the cricket match. Two hours of silence and my hands doing what they wanted to do. I didn't even check my phone.

Made aloo paratha for breakfast the way Appa used to, with extra ajwain in the dough. The smell filled the whole kitchen and for a second I was back in our old house in Mysore, watching him roll them out, flour everywhere.

Arjun's parent-teacher meeting today. The class teacher mentioned he draws during free period instead of playing cricket with the other boys and asked if everything is okay at home. I wanted to say, yes, everything is fine, my son likes drawing, why is that a problem? But I smiled and nodded and said I'd encourage him to be more social.

Came home and told Ravi about it and he said maybe Arjun should join a sport, that it would be good for him. And I thought, here we go. Everyone has an opinion about what the boy should be doing except the boy himself.
sources.nudge_response: I don't know. You just don't, do you? Not in that setting.

sources.journal_entry:
Mummyji made a comment at lunch about the indigo stains on my fingernails. She didn't say anything directly, just that thing she does where she looks at my hands and then looks at the dal and raises her eyebrows. Ravi was right there and said nothing. I know he thinks the dyeing thing is fine, he's told me so, but he won't say it in front of her. So I'm the one who looks like I'm neglecting things.

The thing is, the kitchen was spotless. Lunch was on time. Arjun's tiffin was packed before school. I don't know what more she wants from me. Or maybe I do know and I just don't want to give it, which is this complete surrender of any time that's mine. Like the house should swallow me whole and I should be grateful for it.

I scrubbed the indigo off after lunch. Took ten minutes with lemon and baking soda. I shouldn't have had to do that. But I did it anyway and I'm not sure what that says about me.
sources.nudge_response: Because it was easier than sitting through another silent dinner with her staring at my hands. I pick my fights and that one wasn't worth it. But it felt like erasing something.

Sat down this morning to teach Vihaan the first twenty verses. He's quicker than I expected. He kept asking what the words meant and I found myself explaining them properly, not just the rote way I was taught but actually talking about what each name describes. He asked why Vishnu has so many names and I said because one name is never enough for something that big. He seemed satisfied with that.

It reminded me of sitting with Appa in the puja room, early mornings, the smell of camphor and sandalwood paste. He was patient. He never rushed me or made it feel like a chore. I want to give Vihaan that same feeling, not the pressure of getting it right, but the warmth of sitting together with something that matters. The sense that this is ours, this thread that connects us backward through generations, something nobody can take away or schedule over.

Mummyji passed by the room and listened for a while and actually smiled. She didn't say anything, didn't correct his pronunciation or mine. She just stood there and smiled. That was enough for today.

Mummyji wants me to start teaching Vihaan the Vishnu Sahasranama. He's seven. She says she learned it by six. I said I'd start next week, which I will, because it's important, Appa made sure I knew it by heart and I'm glad he did. But there's this edge to the way she asks, like she's testing whether I'm doing enough.

Ravi's cousin Priya called in the evening. She started a small catering business last year and wanted to know if I'd be interested in supplying hand-dyed table linens. I said I'd think about it. Didn't mention it to anyone at home yet.

I did the rangoli at the entrance the way my grandmother taught me, rice flour with turmeric borders, none of the acrylic paint shortcuts the younger crowd uses. Later, back home, I worked on a new indigo resist pattern. Nobody was around to comment on it. Ravi had taken Arjun and Vihaan to the cricket match. Two hours of silence and my hands doing what they wanted to do. I didn't even check my phone.

Arjun's parent-teacher meeting today. The class teacher mentioned he draws during free period instead of playing cricket with the other boys and asked if everything is okay at home. Came home and told Ravi about it and he said maybe Arjun should join a sport, that it would be good for him. And I thought, here we go. Everyone has an opinion about what the boy should be doing except the boy himself.

sources.journal_entry:
Can't sleep. Ravi's parents left after dinner and everyone is being normal now but I keep replaying the table conversation. The worst part isn't what Mummyji said, it's that nobody asked me a real question about it. Nobody said, what kind of fabric, what's the process, how did you learn. They only wanted to know if it would interfere with anything.

I keep thinking about Appa's workshop in Mysore. He repaired watches. Tiny, patient, precise work. Nobody ever questioned whether he should be doing it. It was just what he did. I want that. Not the permission, not the approval. Just the quiet assumption that of course I do this, it's mine.

Mummyji brought up the store room idea at dinner, in front of Ravi's parents who were visiting. She said something like, "Meera is thinking of opening a factory in the house." She was smiling but it was the wrong kind of smile. Ravi's father asked what she was talking about and I had to explain the dyeing and the linen idea in front of everyone while trying not to sound like I was defending myself.

Ravi stepped in eventually and said it was just a small project. The word "small" stuck. I know he was trying to help but it felt like he was shrinking it to make it palatable. I didn't say anything after that. Finished dinner. Cleared the plates. Went upstairs.

Told Ravi about Priya's proposal over chai after the boys went to bed. He was more supportive than I expected. He said if I wanted to try it, he'd help me figure out the money side. He even suggested converting part of the back store room into a workspace. I hadn't thought about that.

What surprised me was my own hesitation. He was offering exactly what I thought I wanted, backing, space, permission. But when it was right there in front of me I felt this pull backward, like, who am I to run a business? My mother didn't. Mummyji didn't. All the women I grew up watching ran homes, not enterprises. And I love running this home. That's the part that gets lost when people hear I want to do something else. I don't want to leave, I want to also.
sources.nudge_response: Mornings with the boys, school drop-off, puja, cooking. Afternoons when they're in school or doing homework, that's my window. Three, maybe four hours. It's not a lot but it's mine. I just need people to stop treating those hours like leftover time that belongs to the house.

sources.journal_entry:
Called Priya back tonight and said yes to the February order. Twelve runners, twenty napkins, indigo with a kalamkari-inspired border block I've been working on. She sounded happy. I felt terrified and then calm, in that order, like jumping into cold water.

Haven't told Mummyji yet. Told Ravi, who said congratulations and then asked if I needed help setting up the store room this weekend. I said yes. Vihaan overheard and asked if he could help with the blue. I said yes to that too. I don't know if I'm doing the right thing. But I know I'm doing my thing, and right now that has to be enough.

Took the boys to the Ganesh temple this morning for the monthly abhishekam. Vihaan recited the first twenty verses of the Sahasranama on the auto ride there, unprompted. I didn't even know he'd been practising on his own. The priest noticed and said something to me about keeping these things alive. I felt proud but also this strange defensiveness, like I needed to prove I wasn't only about the dyeing, that I still carry all of this too.

Why do I feel like I have to choose? Like every hour I spend with the indigo is an hour stolen from something else. Nobody told Ravi he has to choose between his consulting work and being a father. It's just assumed he can be both.

Can't sleep. Ravi's parents left after dinner and everyone is being normal now but I keep replaying the table conversation. The worst part isn't what Mummyji said, it's that nobody asked me a real question about it. Nobody said, what kind of fabric, what's the process, how did you learn. They only wanted to know if it would interfere with anything.

I keep thinking about Appa's workshop in Mysore. He repaired watches. Tiny, patient, precise work. Nobody ever questioned whether he should be doing it. It was just what he did. I want that. Not the permission, not the approval. Just the quiet assumption that of course I do this, it's mine.

Mummyji brought up the store room idea at dinner, in front of Ravi's parents who were visiting. She said something like, "Meera is thinking of opening a factory in the house." She was smiling but it was the wrong kind of smile. Ravi's father asked what she was talking about and I had to explain the dyeing and the linen idea in front of everyone while trying not to sound like I was defending myself.

Ravi stepped in eventually and said it was just a small project. The word "small" stuck. I know he was trying to help but it felt like he was shrinking it to make it palatable. I didn't say anything after that. Finished dinner. Cleared the plates. Went upstairs.

Told Ravi about Priya's proposal over chai after the boys went to bed. He was more supportive than I expected. He said if I wanted to try it, he'd help me figure out the money side. He even suggested converting part of the back store room into a workspace. I hadn't thought about that.

What surprised me was my own hesitation. He was offering exactly what I thought I wanted, backing, space, permission. But when it was right there in front of me I felt this pull backward, like, who am I to run a business? My mother didn't. Mummyji didn't. All the women I grew up watching ran homes, not enterprises. And I love running this home. That's the part that gets lost when people hear I want to do something else. I don't want to leave, I want to also.
sources.nudge_response: Mornings with the boys, school drop-off, puja, cooking. Afternoons when they're in school or doing homework, that's my window. Three, maybe four hours. It's not a lot but it's mine. I just need people to stop treating those hours like leftover time that belongs to the house.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent the afternoon cataloguing my dye samples. I have fourteen shades of indigo now, ranging from almost-grey to a deep navy that I got by double-dipping with a fermentation vat I built from a recipe in an old Kalamkari manual. Labelled each one with the mordant used, the dip count, the fabric type. Cotton takes differently than silk, and I'm getting more consistent results with the cotton muslin I sourced from a weaver in Solapur.

Priya messaged again about the linens. She has a wedding order for February. Twelve table runners, twenty napkins. The money would be decent. I told her I need to think about scale. My terrace setup can handle maybe four meters of fabric at a time. I'd need to figure out drying space and timing around the kids' schedules.

Vihaan came up to the terrace after his homework and asked if he could dip his hand in the vat. I let him. His palm came out blue and he ran downstairs to show everyone. Mummyji was not pleased.

sources.journal_entry:
Sat down this morning to teach Vihaan the first twenty verses. He's quicker than I expected. He kept asking what the words meant and I found myself explaining them properly, not just the rote way I was taught but actually talking about what each name describes. He asked why Vishnu has so many names and I said because one name is never enough for something that big. He seemed satisfied with that.

It reminded me of sitting with Appa in the puja room, early mornings, the smell of camphor and sandalwood paste. He was patient. He never rushed me or made it feel like a chore. I want to give Vihaan that same feeling, not the pressure of getting it right, but the warmth of sitting together with something that matters. The sense that this is ours, this thread that connects us backward through generations, something nobody can take away or schedule over.

Mummyji passed by the room and listened for a while and actually smiled. She didn't say anything, didn't correct his pronunciation or mine. She just stood there and smiled. That was enough for today.

Mummyji wants me to start teaching Vihaan the Vishnu Sahasranama. He's seven. She says she learned it by six. I said I'd start next week, which I will, because it's important, Appa made sure I knew it by heart and I'm glad he did. But there's this edge to the way she asks, like she's testing whether I'm doing enough.

Ravi's cousin Priya called in the evening. She started a small catering business last year and wanted to know if I'd be interested in supplying hand-dyed table linens. I said I'd think about it. Didn't mention it to anyone at home yet.

Spent the whole morning at the Diwali mela helping set up the community puja. I did the rangoli at the entrance the way my grandmother taught me, rice flour with turmeric borders, none of the acrylic paint shortcuts the younger crowd uses. Three women came up and asked me to show them how. Felt good.

Later, back home, I worked on a new indigo resist pattern. Nobody was around to comment on it. Ravi had taken Arjun and Vihaan to the cricket match. Two hours of silence and my hands doing what they wanted to do. I didn't even check my phone.

Made aloo paratha for breakfast the way Appa used to, with extra ajwain in the dough. The smell filled the whole kitchen and for a second I was back in our old house in Mysore, watching him roll them out, flour everywhere.

Arjun's parent-teacher meeting today. The class teacher mentioned he draws during free period instead of playing cricket with the other boys and asked if everything is okay at home. I wanted to say, yes, everything is fine, my son likes drawing, why is that a problem? But I smiled and nodded and said I'd encourage him to be more social.

Came home and told Ravi about it and he said maybe Arjun should join a sport, that it would be good for him. And I thought, here we go. Everyone has an opinion about what the boy should be doing except the boy himself.
sources.nudge_response: I don't know. You just don't, do you? Not in that setting.

sources.journal_entry:
Mummyji made a comment at lunch about the indigo stains on my fingernails. She didn't say anything directly, just that thing she does where she looks at my hands and then looks at the dal and raises her eyebrows. Ravi was right there and said nothing. I know he thinks the dyeing thing is fine, he's told me so, but he won't say it in front of her. So I'm the one who looks like I'm neglecting things.

The thing is, the kitchen was spotless. Lunch was on time. Arjun's tiffin was packed before school. I don't know what more she wants from me. Or maybe I do know and I just don't want to give it, which is this complete surrender of any time that's mine. Like the house should swallow me whole and I should be grateful for it.

I scrubbed the indigo off after lunch. Took ten minutes with lemon and baking soda. I shouldn't have had to do that. But I did it anyway and I'm not sure what that says about me.
sources.nudge_response: Because it was easier than sitting through another silent dinner with her staring at my hands. I pick my fights and that one wasn't worth it. But it felt like erasing something.

Needed sign-off from Legal on the new supplier contract. Straightforward, or so I thought. Sent it Thursday, followed up Friday morning, got told Anke was "reviewing priorities" and would get to it when she could. Meanwhile the supplier's deadline is Tuesday and I'm the one who'll look like I dropped the ball.

I run a forty-three person division and I can't move a standard supplier agreement through because someone in a different department decides the timeline. I almost went to the CEO directly but thought better of it. Probably should have.

Ran the quarterly review myself today, no slides from anyone else, just my numbers, my narrative. The room was quiet in that good way where people are actually listening. Felt like the division is finally mine in the way I wanted it to be.

Quiet Sunday, Lotte took the girls to her mother's in Leiden. House to myself. Made coffee the slow way, French press, sat in the kitchen looking at the garden. The hedge needs cutting again. Thought about calling my brother but didn't, we'd just end up talking about the house in Zeeland that neither of us wants to deal with.

Spent an hour going through old emails, not for work reasons, just sorting. Found some from when I first got promoted to division head. I was so careful in those early messages, checking every word. Now I fire things off without thinking. Not sure if that's confidence or just not caring as much.
Pieter did it again in the client call. Spoke over me, redirected the conversation to his numbers. I corrected him this time but it came out sharper than I meant and the client noticed.

Sunday but I can't stop thinking about Friday. New hire, Jeroen, fresh from his MBA, has been here eight weeks. In the project kickoff he interrupted me to "build on" my point, then spent five minutes explaining container throughput metrics to me like I haven't been running this operation for a decade. The room just let it happen. Nobody stepped in.

What gets me is that I know this kid's type. He's positioning. He's already had coffee with the CEO twice, which I only know because I saw it in the calendar. And I just sat there and let him reframe my own analysis back to me. I should have shut it down. I should have said, "Jeroen, I've been doing this since before you started your bachelor's." But I didn't. I smiled and nodded like it was a collaborative discussion.

I keep thinking about what my father would say. He ran his own business for thirty years and nobody ever talked over him because he made sure of it from day one. I don't know when I started letting people do this to me. Maybe it's the restructure, maybe I'm spread too thin to fight every battle. But it feels like something I'm losing and I can't quite name what it is.

Had a clear plan for the fleet optimization rollout. Presented it in the ops meeting. Sandra pushed back hard, said we should phase it differently, go region by region instead of all at once. Others started nodding along with her, and I could feel the room shifting.

sources.journal_entry:
Monday. Staff meeting went long because Thomas wanted to discuss the new reporting structure again. I'd already decided on it two weeks ago and communicated it clearly, but apparently some people need to re-litigate everything. Let them talk for ten minutes, then moved on.

Lotte asked how work was over dinner. I said fine. She gave me that look, the one that means she knows I'm not actually answering. I wasn't trying to be evasive, I just genuinely didn't have the energy to translate the day into something she'd find interesting. Watched the football afterward, fell asleep on the couch again.
Routine day. Back-to-back calls, budget reconciliation, nothing unusual. Grabbed a broodje kroket from the canteen and ate it at my desk between meetings.

Needed sign-off from Legal on the new supplier contract. Straightforward, or so I thought. Sent it Thursday, followed up Friday morning, got told Anke was "reviewing priorities" and would get to it when she could. Meanwhile the supplier's deadline is Tuesday and I'm the one who'll look like I dropped the ball.

It's not even about the contract, really. It's that I had to sit there refreshing my inbox like some junior waiting for permission. I run a forty-three person division and I can't move a standard supplier agreement through because someone in a different department decides the timeline. I almost went to the CEO directly but thought better of it. Probably should have.

Ran the quarterly review myself today, no slides from anyone else, just my numbers, my narrative. The room was quiet in that good way where people are actually listening. Felt like the division is finally mine in the way I wanted it to be.

Pieter talked right over me in the steering committee today, mid-sentence, and presented the container routing proposal like it was his. I just sat there. Too tired to fight it, too angry to let it go, and now it's midnight and I'm still turning it over.

Board prep meeting today. The CFO asked me to "walk him through" my division's numbers as if I hadn't already submitted a forty-page deck last week. He does this to me every quarter. He doesn't do it to Pieter, doesn't do it to Sandra. Just me. Like I need to audition for the right to present my own results.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a one-on-one with Lisa from my team today. She's been struggling with the new reporting system and came in looking like she expected to be reprimanded. I didn't do that. Just walked through it with her, showed her the shortcuts I use, told her it took me three months to stop hating the interface too. She actually laughed.

Small thing, but it reminded me of something. When people come to me for direction and I give it clearly, no games, no politics, just here's how we do this — that's when I feel most like myself. Not the boardroom stuff, not the jockeying. Just someone who knows what they're doing, passing it on. Drove home in a decent mood for once.

Quiet Sunday, Lotte took the girls to her mother's in Leiden. House to myself. Made coffee the slow way, French press, sat in the kitchen looking at the garden. The hedge needs cutting again. Thought about calling my brother but didn't, we'd just end up talking about the house in Zeeland that neither of us wants to deal with.

Spent an hour going through old emails, not for work reasons, just sorting. Found some from when I first got promoted to division head. I was so careful in those early messages, checking every word. Now I fire things off without thinking. Not sure if that's confidence or just not caring as much.
Pieter did it again in the client call. Spoke over me, redirected the conversation to his numbers. I corrected him this time but it came out sharper than I meant and the client noticed.

Sunday but I can't stop thinking about Friday. New hire, Jeroen, fresh from his MBA, has been here eight weeks. In the project kickoff he interrupted me to "build on" my point, then spent five minutes explaining container throughput metrics to me like I haven't been running this operation for a decade. The room just let it happen. Nobody stepped in.

What gets me is that I know this kid's type. He's positioning. He's already had coffee with the CEO twice, which I only know because I saw it in the calendar. And I just sat there and let him reframe my own analysis back to me. I should have shut it down. I should have said, "Jeroen, I've been doing this since before you started your bachelor's." But I didn't. I smiled and nodded like it was a collaborative discussion.

I keep thinking about what my father would say. He ran his own business for thirty years and nobody ever talked over him because he made sure of it from day one. I don't know when I started letting people do this to me. Maybe it's the restructure, maybe I'm spread too thin to fight every battle. But it feels like something I'm losing and I can't quite name what it is.
sources.nudge_response: The room's assumption that I'm the one who decides.

sources.journal_entry:
Second time writing today, which I almost never do. After the tea with Mei-ling I went back to my study to look over the Q3 projections and ended up just sitting there. Not anxious, not relieved — more like noticing the room. The desk lamp I have had since the company's first year. The filing cabinet that still has paper copies of our original business registration. Mei-ling keeps telling me to digitize everything but there is something about opening a drawer and seeing the actual stamps on the actual paper.

I called my younger brother Weijun in Kaohsiung. He asked about the Formosa deal and I told him it went through. He said congratulations and then started talking about his daughter's wedding plans. Normal conversation. But I realized I had called him specifically so someone outside the company would know the ground is solid. Like I needed a witness. Not sure what that is about. Maybe just habit — our father always reported good news to the family first, bad news never.

The neighborhood was quiet tonight. Mrs. Lin across the alley had her laundry out late again. I can see it from my study window. Small things like that — the rhythm of the block staying the same — I notice them more than I used to.

Got the renewal confirmation from Formosa Plastics this afternoon. Three-year contract extension, same volume, small price adjustment we can absorb. I sat with the letter for a while before telling anyone. Twenty-three years of this company and these moments still feel like exhaling after holding your breath. The terms are not exciting. No growth clause, no expanded scope. But when I walked through the warehouse floor afterward, I counted the stations — forty-two people whose paychecks run through what I decide. That number has not changed in four years and I am fine with that.

My son Jia-hao asked why I did not push for a bigger increase in the unit price. He pulled up competitor rates and showed me a spreadsheet. He is sharp, I will give him that. But he has not sat across from a procurement manager who controls a quarter of your annual revenue and watched them consider whether you are worth the trouble. You do not squeeze someone who keeps coming back. You make it easy for them to stay.

Mei-ling and I had tea after dinner and she said I looked lighter than I have in weeks. She is right. A locked-in contract means the next three years have a floor under them, and that matters more to me than a ceiling I might not reach.

sources.journal_entry:
Had lunch with old colleague Lao Zhang today. We worked together at the engineering firm before I left to start the company. He retired last year from the same desk he sat at for thirty-one years. Full pension, government health coverage, the works. We ate at the beef noodle place on Zhongxiao East Road that has not changed its menu since we were in our thirties.

He told me he is bored. Gets up, reads the paper, watches his grandchildren on video calls, goes to bed. Said he envies me for still having something to wake up for. I told him I envy his pension. We both laughed but I think we both meant it. The difference is I chose the path where nothing is guaranteed month to month, and some part of me has never fully forgiven myself for that, even though the company has been stable for over a decade. I still check the accounts receivable every Monday morning before anyone else arrives.

I suppose that lunch reminded me why I keep the reserve fund where it is, even when Jia-hao argues we should reinvest. Lao Zhang's safety net was built into his employment. Mine I had to build by hand, brick by brick, and if I pull bricks out to build something taller, the foundation gets thinner.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly, I do not think I can. The choice was right — the company employs forty-two families. But the version of me that wanted a predictable life, that version does not care about being right. He just wanted to stop worrying. And I still have not given him that.

Spent the weekend with Jia-hao's proposal spread across my desk. Read it three times. The margins are tighter than he presented — I found some cost assumptions that do not account for certification delays in biodegradable materials, which can take six to eight months in Taiwan. But the core idea is sound. The food service sector is moving that direction whether we participate or not.

I kept thinking about what Mei-ling said, about him starting his own thing. My father ran a hardware store in Tainan for forty years. Same location, same inventory categories, same suppliers. When I told him I was leaving the engineering firm to start my own company, he did not speak to me for two weeks. Not out of anger — he genuinely could not understand why anyone would walk away from a monthly salary. I swore I would never do that to my children. And here I am, not refusing to speak, but maybe doing something worse — keeping him inside a structure that is shaped entirely around how I see the world.

I circled three sections of his proposal where the numbers need work and left it on his desk with a note that said "Let's talk Monday." That is further than I wanted to go. But the alternative — watching him leave the way I left my father's orbit — I cannot do that either. I keep turning it over. I agreed to look, not to leap. But I am not sure the distinction matters to anyone but me.

Mei-ling brought it up after dinner. She thinks I was too quick to shut Jia-hao down this morning. She did not say it that way — she said maybe I should look at the proposal more carefully before deciding. But I know what she means. She has been the translator between me and the children for decades.

She also mentioned that Jia-hao talked to her about possibly starting his own company if there is no room for his ideas here. She said it casually, while washing dishes. I do not think it was casual. I told her I would read the proposal again this weekend. Then I went to my study and closed the door.

Jia-hao came to me with a proposal to take on a new product line — biodegradable packaging for the food service sector. He had the whole pitch: market research, supplier contacts, projected margins. I told him we would revisit it after the Formosa contract settles in. He did not argue but I could see the frustration. I am not going to let that happen to ours.

sources.journal_entry:
I had a proper meltdown today, and I'm not even sorry about it. My mother-in-law came over for what was supposed to be a "quick visit" and ended up rearranging half my kitchen because apparently I was storing the spices wrong. Wrong! As if there's a universally correct way to store paprika. I didn't say anything at first, just watched her shuffle things around with that satisfied look on her face, and then something snapped. I told her, very calmly, that I'd prefer she asks before moving things in my home. She looked at me like I'd slapped her.

Erik called later and said she was upset, that I'd embarrassed her. Maybe I did. But this is my space. I've set it up the way that works for me, for Astrid, for our little morning routine where she "helps" me make breakfast by pointing at ingredients. It's taken me months to figure out a system that doesn't make me feel like I'm drowning in domestic chaos. And someone just walked in and decided she knew better.

I know she meant well. I know that. But meaning well isn't the same as respecting that I've built something here on purpose. Not by accident. On purpose.
