sources.journal_entry: Sold three prints today from my original collection, not commissions. Actual things I made because I wanted to make them. It's not life-changing money but it's proof that what I create on my own terms has value to someone else too.

Later the same day now, after Erik and I talked again. Astrid's finally asleep. I'm on the couch with a glass of wine that I'm too tired to actually drink.

We didn't fight, exactly. He backed off the daycare thing, said he just wanted to help. And I believe him. But I still feel weird. Like I have to defend choices I make in my own home. Like staying home with my daughter and running my shop is something that requires justification.

My mother worked full-time, same as my dad. They split everything 50/50, very modern, very practical. When I told them I was going to stay home after Astrid was born, they didn't say it was wrong, but they didn't say it was right either. Just... nothing. And Erik's family has a stay-at-home mom who followed rules and schedules I can't even fathom. Neither model fits me. I'm not building my life based on their blueprints.

I'm so tired of feeling like I'm doing this wrong no matter which direction I lean. I'm doing it my way. That's supposed to be enough.
sources.nudge_response: Tomorrow I'll wake up at 5:30 before Astrid, make coffee, and spend an hour on the frozen lake piece before she's up. Then we'll do breakfast together—she helps me pick which fruit to cut. After lunch when she naps, I'll work on shop orders or answer emails, depending on what feels right in that moment. Maybe I'll take a walk with her in the late afternoon to the park she likes. Erik comes home, I hand off, and the evening is mine. That's it. That's my way. Flexible but intentional.

sources.journal_entry:
Erik brought up the idea of Astrid starting daycare two days a week. He framed it as giving me more time for the shop, which sounds supportive, but I could hear the subtext loud and clear: he thinks I'm not managing well. Or that I'm wasting time. Or both.

And maybe I am struggling some days. Maybe there are afternoons where Astrid naps and I just sit on the couch scrolling instead of working on prints. But that's my choice to make. I'm the one here every day. I know what I need. Some days I need to create. Some days I need to rest. And I don't need someone who's at an office until 7pm deciding what my schedule should look like.

I know daycare isn't a punishment. Plenty of parents do it, and their kids are fine, great even. It's not about whether daycare is good or bad. It's about this being my decision, about my time, about my daughter—and it wasn't offered as an option. It was presented as a solution to a problem I didn't say I had.

I told him I'd think about it. But I'm not sure what I'm supposed to be thinking about. Whether to accept having my days restructured for me?
Astrid started saying "no" to everything today and honestly, same. I get it kid. Sometimes every option feels like the wrong one.
sources.nudge_response: Oh, nothing specific really. Just one of those days where even deciding what to make for dinner feels like too much. Probably just tired.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent the whole morning on a commission that I probably should have turned down. A client wanted a custom piece—a mountain landscape in my style—but then kept sending "small suggestions" that were basically a different style entirely. Softer edges, she said. More realistic trees. At some point I had to ask myself: is this even my work anymore, or am I just a hand executing someone else's vision?

I did finish it, and she loved it. Paid extra, even. But sitting here now, looking at the file, I feel hollow about it. It's not bad. It's just not mine. And that distinction matters to me more than I sometimes admit.

There's a practical voice in my head that says income is income, especially since the shop has been slow this month. But there's another voice—louder, if I'm honest—that asks what the point is if I'm not making the things I actually want to make. I could have spent those hours on my own collection instead. I chose not to. For money. And now I'm sitting with that choice.

I don't regret it exactly. I just notice how it sits differently than the pieces I create for myself.
sources.nudge_response: I've had this image in my head for weeks—a single figure standing at the edge of a frozen lake, back to the viewer, and the ice is cracking but in a pattern that looks almost like tree roots spreading. It's about choosing to step forward even when the ground feels unstable. I've sketched it twice but haven't committed to the full piece yet. That's what I would have worked on.

sources.journal_entry:
I got an email today from my old agency in Amsterdam. They're doing a freelance project and apparently thought of me. Just a small illustration job, a few days of work, good pay. The catch is I'd need to come into the office for meetings, which means finding childcare for Astrid those days.

I've been staring at the email for three hours. Part of me wants to jump at it—prove that I'm still a real designer, that staying home hasn't erased my skills. Another part feels sick at the thought of slotting back into someone else's schedule, their briefs, their revisions cycle. And then there's the practical part doing math on whether the pay is even worth the hassle of arranging care.

What's strange is how guilty I feel about even considering it. Like wanting something outside of motherhood and my little shop is some kind of betrayal. But also guilty about not wanting it enough. Because shouldn't I be excited? Shouldn't a part of me miss that world?

I don't know what I want. That's the honest answer. I don't know what I want and I hate not knowing.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly? I lean toward saying no. Not because I'm scared or because it's too hard, but because the thought of sitting in their office making small talk about clients and deadlines makes me feel heavy. I left that for a reason. I don't miss it. I just sometimes miss being seen as competent by people who aren't related to me.

sources.journal_entry: Astrid poured yogurt on the cat today. I should have been faster but honestly I was sketching in my head and didn't notice she'd climbed onto the counter. We're all learning I guess.

sources.journal_entry:
Listed the frozen lake piece on the shop this morning. Set the price higher than usual because it took more out of me and I want that reflected. Someone already messaged asking if I do bulk orders for offices. I said no.

Also enrolled Astrid in a parent-toddler art class on Thursday mornings. It was my idea, on my timeline. That distinction matters. She'll get to smash paint around with other kids and I'll get to see if I can stand being around other parents for two hours.

I said no to the Amsterdam job. Wrote the email this morning, polite but clear. And then I finished the frozen lake piece. Both in the same hour, which feels meaningful somehow.

Looking at the finished illustration, I'm struck by how much of me is in it. The figure on the ice—that's not some generic person, it's me, the version of me that's still learning to trust her own footing. The cracks spreading like roots—that's about how breaking apart can also be growing. I don't think anyone buying it will see all that. But I know, and that's what makes it feel real.

I've been thinking about what makes work meaningful to me. It's not the money, though money is necessary. It's not even external recognition, though that's nice. It's whether I can look at something and see my own choices reflected back. When I was at the agency, every project was filtered through client needs, brand guidelines, stakeholder feedback. The work was often beautiful. But it wasn't mine. And that matters to me in a way I've stopped apologizing for.

Astrid pointed at the print today and said "lady cold." Accurate assessment, kid.
sources.nudge_response: I think it would look like not second-guessing myself when Erik or my parents or anyone else offers an alternative path. Not because their ideas are bad, but because I'd be so secure in mine that I could hear them out without feeling threatened. Right now I still get defensive. Fully trusting would mean being curious instead—hearing what they suggest and knowing I can take it or leave it without my whole sense of direction wobbling.

The work was often beautiful. But it wasn't mine. And that matters to me in a way I've stopped apologizing for.

Astrid pointed at the print today and said "lady cold." Accurate assessment, kid.
sources.nudge_response: I think it would look like not second-guessing myself when Erik or my parents or anyone else offers an alternative path. Not because their ideas are bad, but because I'd be so secure in mine that I could hear them out without feeling threatened. Right now I still get defensive. Fully trusting would mean being curious instead—hearing what they suggest and knowing I can take it or leave it without my whole sense of direction wobbling.

sources.journal_entry:
I got an email today from my old agency in Amsterdam. They're doing a freelance project and apparently thought of me. Just a small illustration job, a few days of work, good pay. The catch is I'd need to come into the office for meetings, which means finding childcare for Astrid those days.

I've been staring at the email for three hours. Part of me wants to jump at it—prove that I'm still a real designer, that staying home hasn't erased my skills. Another part feels sick at the thought of slotting back into someone else's schedule, their briefs, their revisions cycle. And then there's the practical part doing math on whether the pay is even worth the hassle of arranging care.

What's strange is how guilty I feel about even considering it. Like wanting something outside of motherhood and my little shop is some kind of betrayal. But also guilty about not wanting it enough. Because shouldn't I be excited? Shouldn't a part of me miss that world?

I don't know what I want. That's the honest answer. I don't know what I want and I hate not knowing.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly? I lean toward saying no. Not because I'm scared or because it's too hard, but because the thought of sitting in their office making small talk about clients and deadlines makes me feel heavy. I left that for a reason. I don't miss it. I just sometimes miss being seen as competent by people who aren't related to me.

sources.journal_entry: Astrid poured yogurt on the cat today. I should have been faster but honestly I was sketching in my head and didn't notice she'd climbed onto the counter. We're all learning I guess.
sources.nudge_response: That I can't always be in two places at once. That some moments require my full presence and others can bend a little. That the cat will forgive us. That my brain doesn't shut off just because I'm watching a toddler, and maybe that's okay—maybe even necessary for my sanity.

sources.journal_entry: Sold three prints today from my original collection, not commissions. Actual things I made because I wanted to make them. It's not life-changing money but it's proof that what I create on my own terms has value to someone else too.

Later the same day now, after Erik and I talked again. Astrid's finally asleep. I'm on the couch with a glass of wine that I'm too tired to actually drink.

We didn't fight, exactly. He backed off the daycare thing, said he just wanted to help. And I believe him. But I still feel weird. Like I have to defend choices I make in my own home. Like staying home with my daughter and running my shop is something that requires justification.

My mother worked full-time, same as my dad. They split everything 50/50, very modern, very practical. When I told them I was going to stay home after Astrid was born, they didn't say it was wrong, but they didn't say it was right either. Just... nothing. And Erik's family has a stay-at-home mom who followed rules and schedules I can't even fathom. Neither model fits me. I'm not building my life based on their blueprints.

I'm so tired of feeling like I'm doing this wrong no matter which direction I lean. I'm doing it my way. That's supposed to be enough.
sources.nudge_response: Tomorrow I'll wake up at 5:30 before Astrid, make coffee, and spend an hour on the frozen lake piece before she's up. Then we'll do breakfast together—she helps me pick which fruit to cut. After lunch when she naps, I'll work on shop orders or answer emails, depending on what feels right in that moment. Maybe I'll take a walk with her in the late afternoon to the park she likes. Erik comes home, I hand off, and the evening is mine. That's it. That's my way. Flexible but intentional.

sources.journal_entry:
Erik brought up the idea of Astrid starting daycare two days a week. He framed it as giving me more time for the shop, which sounds supportive, but I could hear the subtext loud and clear: he thinks I'm not managing well. Or that I'm wasting time. Or both.

And maybe I am struggling some days. Maybe there are afternoons where Astrid naps and I just sit on the couch scrolling instead of working on prints. But that's my choice to make. I'm the one here every day. I know what I need. Some days I need to create. Some days I need to rest. And I don't need someone who's at an office until 7pm deciding what my schedule should look like.

I know daycare isn't a punishment. Plenty of parents do it, and their kids are fine, great even. It's not about whether daycare is good or bad. It's about this being my decision, about my time, about my daughter—and it wasn't offered as an option. It was presented as a solution to a problem I didn't say I had.

I told him I'd think about it. But I'm not sure what I'm supposed to be thinking about. Whether to accept having my days restructured for me?
Astrid started saying "no" to everything today and honestly, same. I get it kid. Sometimes every option feels like the wrong one.
sources.nudge_response: Oh, nothing specific really. Just one of those days where even deciding what to make for dinner feels like too much. Probably just tired.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent the whole morning on a commission that I probably should have turned down. A client wanted a custom piece—a mountain landscape in my style—but then kept sending "small suggestions" that were basically a different style entirely. Softer edges, she said. More realistic trees. At some point I had to ask myself: is this even my work anymore, or am I just a hand executing someone else's vision?

I did finish it, and she loved it. Paid extra, even. But sitting here now, looking at the file, I feel hollow about it. It's not bad. It's just not mine. And that distinction matters to me more than I sometimes admit.

There's a practical voice in my head that says income is income, especially since the shop has been slow this month. But there's another voice—louder, if I'm honest—that asks what the point is if I'm not making the things I actually want to make. I could have spent those hours on my own collection instead. I chose not to. For money. And now I'm sitting with that choice.

I don't regret it exactly. I just notice how it sits differently than the pieces I create for myself.
sources.nudge_response: I've had this image in my head for weeks—a single figure standing at the edge of a frozen lake, back to the viewer, and the ice is cracking but in a pattern that looks almost like tree roots spreading. It's about choosing to step forward even when the ground feels unstable. I've sketched it twice but haven't committed to the full piece yet. That's what I would have worked on.

sources.journal_entry:
I had a proper meltdown today, and I'm not even sorry about it. My mother-in-law came over for what was supposed to be a "quick visit" and ended up rearranging half my kitchen because apparently I was storing the spices wrong. Wrong! As if there's a universally correct way to store paprika. I didn't say anything at first, just watched her shuffle things around with that satisfied look on her face, and then something snapped. I told her, very calmly, that I'd prefer she asks before moving things in my home. She looked at me like I'd slapped her.

Erik called later and said she was upset, that I'd embarrassed her. Maybe I did. But this is my space. I've set it up the way that works for me, for Astrid, for our little morning routine where she "helps" me make breakfast by pointing at ingredients. It's taken me months to figure out a system that doesn't make me feel like I'm drowning in domestic chaos. And someone just walked in and decided she knew better.

I know she meant well. I know that. But meaning well isn't the same as respecting that I've built something here on purpose. Not by accident. On purpose.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a good run at the RC meeting tonight. The lobby renovation proposal has been stalling for months because of Uncle Tan and his little coalition of holdouts, but I came prepared this time. Pulled together three contractor quotes, a cost-per-household breakdown, a maintenance projection over ten years. Laid it all out on the whiteboard. Even Mrs. Lim, who has been sitting on the fence, nodded along when I showed the depreciation numbers.

The thing is, nobody else would have done this homework. They would have kept going back and forth at every meeting, complaining about the cracked tiles and the peeling paint, never actually resolving anything. I spent two weekends on those quotes. Called in a favor from a guy I know at a building management firm. That is how things get done — you do the legwork, you control the information, you set the direction.

When the vote came, it was seven to two. Uncle Tan and his friend held out but it did not matter. I kept my voice level, thanked everyone for attending, wrapped up in under ninety minutes. Walked home feeling like myself. Like the version of me that knows how to move a room. It has been a while since I felt that at the office.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a disagreement with the GM over the warehouse staffing model. I have been running the weekend shift allocation the same way for eight years. It works. Attrition is low, the supervisors know the rotation, the overtime costs are predictable. Then Priscilla from HR comes in with a "flexible rostering" proposal that basically throws the whole structure out and lets staff bid on shifts through an app.

I told the GM this would cause chaos. You cannot run a warehouse floor on preferences. People need structure. You need to know who is where and when, and someone needs to own that decision. He listened, then said let us pilot Priscilla's model for one quarter and review. Just like that. Not even a counter — just "let's try it."

I could have pushed harder. I had the data, the history, the operational knowledge. But Priscilla had a slide deck with engagement scores and a Harvard Business Review citation, and I could feel the room tilting her way. So I said fine. I will support the pilot. Shook her hand after. My supervisor Michelle asked me later if I was okay with it. I told her it is what the GM wants, so we execute. That is the job. But I keep running the numbers in my head and I know this is going to cost us. When it does, I will be the one cleaning it up, not Priscilla.

sources.journal_entry:
Quiet weekend. Mei Ling had a catering job Saturday so I was home alone most of the day. Made myself kaya toast and coffee for breakfast, read the Straits Times cover to cover. The downstairs coffeeshop uncle gave me an extra egg when I bought lunch, said I looked tired. I probably do.

Watched the F1 qualifying in the evening. Spent too long on a WhatsApp group chat with my army mates arguing about whether the new Tampines hawker centre is better than the old one. It is not, but Raymond insists. Fell asleep on the couch before the replay finished. Nothing remarkable. Just a day that passed the way days pass when nobody needs anything from you.

Sat through a two-hour leadership development workshop today. Mandatory for all senior managers. The facilitator — could not have been older than thirty-five — spent forty minutes explaining stakeholder mapping as if half the room had not been managing stakeholders since before she graduated. She asked me to share "a time when I had to earn buy-in from a resistant stakeholder." I gave a polished answer about the Suzhou warehouse relocation in 2019. She smiled and said "great example of vulnerability."

That is not what it was. It was an example of knowing when to push and when to wait, and reading a room of Chinese factory managers who were not going to respond to some consultant's empathy framework. I did not say that. I just nodded. I am too tired to fight these battles anymore. Every year there is a new person who thinks they can teach me how to do what I have been doing for two decades. And every year I sit in the chair and nod.

What does she know about what I need from this job. She runs a catering business out of our kitchen. This is a forty-five person operation across three countries.

But I did not say that. Because somewhere underneath the anger I know she might have a point. This used to be the place where I mattered. Where my decisions moved things. Now I sit in meetings and nod and watch younger people present my ideas and get called innovative. I am not sure what I am holding onto anymore. The title still says Senior Operations Manager. But it is starting to feel like a frame around an empty picture.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a disagreement with the GM over the warehouse staffing model. I have been running the weekend shift allocation the same way for eight years. It works. Attrition is low, the supervisors know the rotation, the overtime costs are predictable. Then Priscilla from HR comes in with a "flexible rostering" proposal that basically throws the whole structure out and lets staff bid on shifts through an app.

I told the GM this would cause chaos. You cannot run a warehouse floor on preferences. People need structure. You need to know who is where and when, and someone needs to own that decision. He listened, then said let us pilot Priscilla's model for one quarter and review. Just like that. Not even a counter — just "let's try it."

I could have pushed harder. I had the data, the history, the operational knowledge. But Priscilla had a slide deck with engagement scores and a Harvard Business Review citation, and I could feel the room tilting her way. So I said fine. I will support the pilot. Shook her hand after. My supervisor Michelle asked me later if I was okay with it. I told her it is what the GM wants, so we execute. That is the job. But I keep running the numbers in my head and I know this is going to cost us. When it does, I will be the one cleaning it up, not Priscilla.

The new procurement system rollout requires sign-off from Group IT before we can configure anything for our department. I submitted the request form nine days ago. Called James in IT twice, emailed once, even copied his manager. Got a reply today saying it is "in the queue" and they will "circle back next week."

Meanwhile my team is stuck running parallel processes on the old system, burning hours on manual reconciliation that should have been automated a month ago. I have done everything I can do. The bottleneck is not mine. But when the GM asks why we are behind on the migration timeline, it will be my name on the status report, not James's. Twenty-three years and I still have to sit and wait for a thirty-year-old IT coordinator to decide when my department gets to function properly.

Daniel presented my regional consolidation idea at the leadership sync this morning. Same structure, same three-phase approach I pitched to him informally two weeks ago over coffee. He did not credit me. I sat there, mouth half open, and just let it happen.
sources.nudge_response: Everyone was already nodding. If I spoke up it would have looked petty. Like the older guy clinging to credit. I know how that plays. So I sat there and smiled.

sources.journal_entry: Managed to restructure the KPI reporting template my department uses before the quarterly review — simplified it, made the data speak for itself instead of burying it in twelve different tabs the way Daniel's team does. sources.nudge_response: It meant he still sees the difference between someone who knows how to run operations and someone who hides behind frameworks and buzzwords. That is all.

The thing is, nobody else would have done this homework. Staff meeting today went sideways. The principal announced they're changing the Class III syllabus mid-term and everyone just nodded along like this was normal. I sat there wanting to say something because I've already prepped my unit plans through June and this throws everything off. But Mrs. Kulkarni was agreeing, and she's been teaching twenty-three years, so what do I know. I just kept quiet and wrote notes.

After the meeting Neha—she joined the same year as me—asked if I thought the change made sense. I said it was fine, it'll be fine. She looked at me like she knew I was lying. I probably was. The thing is, even if I did speak up, what would I say? "Excuse me, ma'am, I disagree"? That's not how it works here. You're new, you keep your head down, you follow the lead of people who've been around longer. That's what Amma always says.

But walking home I kept replaying it and feeling this tight, hot thing in my chest. Not anger exactly. More like frustration at myself for not even trying. I had a valid point and I swallowed it whole. I do this constantly. In meetings, at family dinners, everywhere. I just smile and go along with things and then come home and feel this restless itch like I've betrayed something. I don't even know what.
sources.nudge_response: Maybe my own opinion? Like the fact that I even had one. Everyone assumes I'm just agreeable by nature but sometimes I have things I want to say and I just... don't. And then it's like those thoughts don't count because I never let them out. It's exhausting pretending you don't have a voice.

Parent-teacher meetings ran until seven tonight. I'm so tired I can barely think straight. Had a difficult conversation with one father who was upset about his son's handwriting marks. He kept raising his voice and I kept saying "I understand, uncle" over and over like a broken toy. But another part of me wanted to tell that man his son's handwriting isn't poor because of me, it's because the boy doesn't practise at home. I had the words right there. I didn't say them. I never do. Came home, ate dinner in silence, helped Bhabhi clear the dishes. Now I'm lying in bed typing this and I can still hear his raised voice in my head. I wish it didn't stick.

Which I know is ridiculous because he was being unreasonable. But my whole body just goes into this mode where I have to fix it, calm it down, make it okay. I've been like this since I was small. Loud voices in the house meant someone was unhappy and it was everyone's job to make it stop.

Writing again because I can't sleep. I keep thinking about Arjun and the note I'm supposed to send. I haven't written it yet. Part of me wants to just talk to his mother directly, gently, without framing it as a disciplinary thing. I could say something like "I've noticed he seems distracted, is everything okay at home." I smiled at him and quietly gave him a spare. Nobody noticed. That felt right. The note home doesn't feel right. But doing what feels right and doing what you're told are two different things and I don't know when I got so afraid of the gap between them.

Something happened at lunch today. A group of the senior teachers were discussing a student in my class—Arjun, the one who's been acting out. They were saying he needs stricter discipline, maybe a note home to his parents. I know Arjun. His parents are going through a separation and he's been coming to school with unwashed uniforms. He doesn't need punishment, he needs someone to be patient with him.

I almost said something. I opened my mouth and Mrs. Deshpande looked at me and I just said "yes ma'am, I'll send the note." I felt sick walking back to my classroom. Still do.
sources.nudge_response: Because I know I'm right about Arjun and I still didn't say it. It's one thing to stay quiet about syllabus changes or meeting agendas—that's just politics. sources.journal_entry:
Friday and I'm sitting on the balcony while everyone watches that serial on TV. Bhabhi asked if I wanted to join and I said in a minute but I just want to sit here with the noise from the street and not talk to anyone for a bit.

This week has been strange. The Arjun thing—I keep turning it over. I did something different. I didn't just follow orders. I found a way to do what I thought was right without directly confronting anyone. Maybe that's the only way I can operate. Not rebellion, not silence, something in between. Like, I bent the expectation without breaking it. And nothing bad happened. Mrs. Deshpande didn't yell at me, Arjun's mother was grateful, the world didn't end.

I think I've been telling myself a story that any deviation from what's expected will result in disaster. Like if I push back even slightly, everything will collapse—my reputation, my relationships, my family's opinion of me. But today I'm sitting here and nothing collapsed. The serial is still playing, Bhabhi is still laughing, Amma just brought me chai without asking. Everything is the same except I feel a tiny bit less compressed. Like there's a millimeter more room inside my chest.

Spoke to Arjun's mother after school today, just casually near the gate. Kept it light, asked how things were going. She got teary and said it's been a hard few months. I told her I'd keep an eye on him and she held my hand and thanked me. I didn't mention the note.

Mrs. Deshpande asked if I'd sent it. I said I spoke with the mother directly and she seemed satisfied. Mrs. Deshpande paused, then said "fine." It wasn't warm but it wasn't a reprimand either. I survived it. My heart was pounding the entire time though.

Writing again because I can't sleep. I keep thinking about Arjun and the note I'm supposed to send. I haven't written it yet. Part of me wants to just talk to his mother directly, gently, without framing it as a disciplinary thing. I could say something like "I've noticed he seems distracted, is everything okay at home." That's not disobeying anyone. That's just being a teacher.

But then I imagine Mrs. Deshpande finding out I went around her suggestion and the thought makes my stomach drop. She's the one who writes my probation review. She's been teaching since before I was born. Who am I to decide my approach is better?

I smiled at him and quietly gave him a spare. Nobody noticed. That felt right. The note home doesn't feel right. sources.journal_entry:
Report cards went home yesterday and a parent emailed the principal to say I graded her daughter too harshly in Hindi. The principal called me in and asked me to "reconsider." Not directly, not as an order—just that little tilt of the head and "maybe you could take another look." I know what that means. It means change the grade.

The grade is accurate. I checked three times. The girl is struggling with grammar and I wrote detailed comments about how to improve. But the parent is on the school trust and the principal doesn't want problems. So now I'm sitting here trying to decide whether to bump a B+ to an A- to keep everyone comfortable.

I hate this. This is exactly the kind of thing I got into teaching to fight against—marking a child on who her parents are instead of what she's learned. But if I refuse, the principal remembers. My probation review is in August. Is one grade worth the trouble?

I already know what I'm going to do. I'm going to change it and tell myself it doesn't matter in the long run, and feel this same sick feeling I felt about Arjun, and go to bed and wake up tomorrow the same person who keeps the peace at any cost. And one day I'll wonder when I stopped trusting my own judgment. Or maybe I'll just stop noticing. That's the scarier thought.
sources.nudge_response: Someone to tell me it's okay to hold my ground. Which is pathetic because I shouldn't need permission. But I've spent my whole life being told that keeping things smooth is the right thing to do, and when every single person around you believes that, it's hard to trust the one voice saying otherwise—especially when that voice is just mine.

sources.journal_entry: Quiet week at school. Adjusted the unit plans to fit the new syllabus. Amma said she was proud of me for not making a fuss.

Staff meeting today went sideways. The principal announced they're changing the Class III syllabus mid-term and everyone just nodded along like this was normal. I sat there wanting to say something because I've already prepped my unit plans through June and this throws everything off. But Mrs. Kulkarni was agreeing, and she's been teaching twenty-three years, so what do I know. I just kept quiet and wrote notes.

After the meeting Neha—she joined the same year as me—asked if I thought the change made sense. I said it was fine, it'll be fine. She looked at me like she knew I was lying. I probably was. The thing is, even if I did speak up, what would I say? "Excuse me, ma'am, I disagree"? That's not how it works here. You're new, you keep your head down, you follow the lead of people who've been around longer. That's what Amma always says.

But walking home I kept replaying it and feeling this tight, hot thing in my chest. Not anger exactly. More like frustration at myself for not even trying. I had a valid point and I swallowed it whole. I do this constantly. In meetings, at family dinners, everywhere. I just smile and go along with things and then come home and feel this restless itch like I've betrayed something. I don't even know what.

sources.journal_entry:
Went to the refugee resettlement office for my translation shift. They had a backlog of about forty documents — medical intake forms, mostly. One was for a family from Myanmar with three kids under ten. The mother had written additional notes in the margins in Burmese that I couldn't read, so I flagged them for the Burmese translator. Just small handwritten lines. Probably questions she was too afraid to ask out loud. That kind of thing breaks something in me every time.

Came home and Eun-bi had drawn a picture of our family at school. She drew me holding a big stack of papers. Hyun-woo laughed and said "even she knows." I laughed too but it landed weird. Like even my six-year-old sees me as the woman with the papers instead of — I don't know. I don't know what I expected her to draw. I am the woman with the papers. I just wish that didn't feel like it needed defending.

Can't sleep. Kept thinking about the river cleanup people. Found their group online — they meet every Saturday, which is the one morning Hyun-woo is reliably home with the kids. I could go. But then I'd be giving up the only morning I have for grocery shopping, meal prep, and the laundry pile that's been staring at me all week.

My friend Ji-yeon texted asking if I wanted to join her yoga class on Saturday mornings. Everyone keeps offering me ways to spend my time that are about me. Yoga, self-care, "you need a break." But I don't want a break. I want to be useful beyond these walls. That probably sounds ungrateful. I have a warm apartment and two healthy children and a husband who comes home every night. But I keep reading the news about the factory fire in Gimpo where those migrant workers were locked in because the exits were blocked and I can't just — I can't just do yoga about it.

Took the kids to the park near the river this morning. Eun-bi wanted to feed the ducks and Jun-ho wanted to throw rocks, so we compromised — ducks first, then rocks at a different spot. Standard negotiation. It was actually nice until I noticed a group of volunteers doing a river cleanup downstream. They had those grabber tools and black trash bags and matching vests from some environmental group I didn't recognize.

I stood there watching them for probably five minutes while the kids played. Part of me wanted to walk over and ask how to join. I used to do cleanups like that every month before Jun-ho was born. Our old NGO partnered with a river conservation group in Mapo-gu and I'd spend whole Saturdays hauling plastic out of the Cheonggyecheon tributaries. Felt like I was doing something tangible, something I could point at and say today this stretch of water is cleaner because I was here.

Now I watch from the playground. I'm not complaining about my life — the kids are wonderful and I chose this. But there's this gap between what I used to be able to do and what my days look like now. I don't know what to do with that gap except notice it and move on. Jun-ho threw a rock into the water and it made a perfect splash and he was so proud. I clapped and said "good one" and we went home for lunch.

sources.journal_entry: Sent the letter. Also emailed the river cleanup group about joining their Saturday rotation starting August. Hyun-woo agreed to handle Saturday mornings. Feels like a small step but at least it's forward.

Kids are better. Jun-ho's fever broke around noon and Eun-bi was already bouncing off the walls by breakfast. There's a piece about a proposed bill that would make it harder for undocumented workers to access emergency medical care. I read it twice. Then I started drafting a letter to our local representative, citing cases I'd seen at the resettlement office — anonymized, of course. I wrote about the Myanmar family's intake forms and the gap between what the system promises and what reaches people. It took me two hours and I don't even know if anyone will read it.

The sky is not the problem.

Both kids had fevers last night so I was up every two hours with wet towels and children's Tylenol. Jun-ho finally slept at 4am. I skipped the recycling committee meeting and I feel guilty about it even though I know that's absurd.

sources.journal_entry:
First full week done at Birch Lane. The kids are sweet. One boy, Mateo, already told me he wants to read "chapter books like his sister." That kind of thing is why I'm here. The building is old and the supply closet is basically empty, but I spent the weekend printing worksheets at the library and laminating them myself. Cost me about forty dollars out of pocket, which I noticed when I checked my account this morning.

I set up a reading corner with pillows I found at a thrift store. It looks decent. The other second-grade teacher, Mrs. Okada, lent me a box of leveled readers she wasn't using. I mapped out the first unit already and I feel like I actually know what I'm doing for Monday. Haven't felt that way in a while. Small thing, but it matters. The commute is long and the parking lot has potholes, but I walked into that classroom and the kids were waiting and it just felt like where I was supposed to be.
sources.nudge_response: Because if I don't set this up right from the start, the kids lose momentum and I lose the year. I've seen it happen during student teaching. You can't get that first month back.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a normal day for once. Taught the short vowel unit, kids did okay on the pre-assessment. Ate lunch in the staff room instead of my classroom, which I almost never do. Talked to the PE teacher about the fall festival coming up. She asked if I wanted to run a booth and I said sure without even thinking about it. That felt easy for once.

After school I graded papers and reorganized the reading corner. Mateo finished his first leveled reader and asked if he could take the next one home. I said yes. His mom came to pick him up and thanked me for sending books home. She said he reads to his little brother at night now. That's the kind of thing that doesn't show up on any evaluation form but it's the whole point.

Drove home, made pasta, watched half a movie. Nothing remarkable. Just a day that went the way it was supposed to. Even the drive home felt calm. No knot in my stomach, no replaying conversations. Just a Tuesday.

Birch Lane sent around a memo about possible mid-year budget cuts. Nothing confirmed, but the newer hires would be first to go. That's me. Mrs. Okada told me not to worry, that they say this every fall, but she's been here eleven years so of course she's not worried.

Meanwhile my mom keeps forwarding me job postings from the county school district back home. Steady pay, pension, close to family. Every time she sends one I feel my chest tighten. She's not wrong — those jobs are real and they'd solve a lot of problems. But I keep picturing myself in a fluorescent classroom running a curriculum someone else wrote, and something in me just won't do it. I deleted the emails.
sources.nudge_response: Like I said, it's just stress. Everybody's stressed in September.

sources.journal_entry: Barely slept. Kept going over that phone call. The Edina salary would have covered my student loans and left room to breathe. I know exactly what I'm giving up and I still can't make myself call her back.

My old cooperating teacher from Edina called today to tell me they still have a position open. Full benefits, union contract, thirty kids max per class. She said she put in a word for me and they'd probably take me without a second interview.

I told her I'd think about it and then I sat in the parking lot for twenty minutes. Birch Lane doesn't even have a functioning copier half the time. But the literacy program here is the whole reason I came. I keep thinking about Mateo and the other kids who just started trusting me. I said no. I think I said no. I told her I'd call back Monday but I already know I'm not going to.
sources.nudge_response: Whether I'm being stupid. Whether six months from now I'll wish I'd just taken the safe thing.

values.approved_definition: Understanding, appreciation, tolerance, and protection for the welfare of all people and for nature. sources.journal_entry:
Board meeting for the trade association today. One of the newer members, a woman from a Cambodian labour rights group, raised concerns about working conditions at several member factories — specifically about informal workers who sort e-waste without proper protective gear. She had photos. She had data from a university study. She asked the board to issue a formal statement and require audits before renewing factory memberships.

I didn't say anything. I just sat there. A few other board members started pushing back immediately — talking about how the data was old, how conditions had improved, how public statements would hurt investment confidence in the sector. The usual deflections. And I know they're partly right, some of those factories have made genuine improvements. But the photos were recent. The data wasn't old. I could see the timestamps.

The thing is, two of those factories are long-standing clients of mine. We process their scrap. If I backed the statement, it would put those relationships at risk. Not just financially — personally. I've known these owners for over a decade. We've eaten at each other's homes. It's not as simple as just raising your hand and saying yes, we should hold them accountable. There are layers to this. But I keep replaying her face when nobody supported her motion. She looked like she expected it. That's worse somehow — that she wasn't even surprised.
sources.nudge_response: The relationships. Twenty years of built trust. You don't blow that up in a board meeting.

sources.nudge_response: Not just income. The ability to actually do something about the problems I see. Money is leverage.

sources.journal_entry:
Flew back from a factory visit in Penang. The new processing line looks good, efficiency is way up, costs are down. Everyone was pleased. On the drive to the airport the plant manager mentioned casually that they'd switched to a cheaper chemical solvent for circuit board stripping. Cheaper and, I suspect, not properly rated for ventilation in that building. I could smell it from the parking lot.

I didn't ask about it. I could have. I had forty minutes in the car and I know enough about chemical handling to ask the right questions. But I was tired and the deal was done and bringing it up would have meant delaying the whole partnership review. I chose convenience. The flight home felt longer than usual.

My son called from Jakarta. His NGO just secured funding to expand their mangrove restoration project into two new provinces. I could hear it in his voice — the energy, the belief that what he's doing actually matters. I told him I was proud. I meant it completely.

After we hung up I transferred some money to the foundation account. Not a huge amount, but enough to cover the clean-water pump installation we've been delaying in Siem Reap because the supplier raised prices. My wife asked why I didn't just wait until next quarter when cash flow is better. I told her some things shouldn't wait. She gave me that look she gives when she thinks I'm being impulsive, but she processed the transfer anyway.
sources.nudge_response: Hearing him talk about the mangroves reminded me why I started the foundation. Sometimes you forget.

sources.journal_entry:
Board meeting for the trade association today. One of the newer members, a woman from a Cambodian labour rights group, raised concerns about working conditions at several member factories — specifically about informal workers who sort e-waste without proper protective gear. She had photos. She had data from a university study. She asked the board to issue a formal statement and require audits before renewing factory memberships.

I didn't say anything. I just sat there. A few other board members started pushing back immediately — talking about how the data was old, how conditions had improved, how public statements would hurt investment confidence in the sector. The usual deflections. And I know they're partly right, some of those factories have made genuine improvements. But the photos were recent. The data wasn't old. I could see the timestamps.

The thing is, two of those factories are long-standing clients of mine. We process their scrap. If I backed the statement, it would put those relationships at risk. Not just financially — personally. I've known these owners for over a decade. We've eaten at each other's homes. It's not as simple as just raising your hand and saying yes, we should hold them accountable. There are layers to this. But I keep replaying her face when nobody supported her motion. She looked like she expected it. That's worse somehow — that she wasn't even surprised.
sources.nudge_response: The relationships. Twenty years of built trust. You don't blow that up in a board meeting.

sources.journal_entry:
Saturday morning, went to the hawker centre near our old Toa Payoh flat. The uncle who runs the wonton noodle stall has been there since my kids were small, must be almost thirty years now. We talked for a while. He's worried about his lease renewal, says the rents keep going up and the younger hawkers can't make it work anymore. Whole stretch of stalls might close.

I started thinking about whether the trade association could do something — not directly but maybe model something. We talk a lot about industry sustainability but it's always about supply chains and compliance frameworks. Nobody talks about what happens to the communities around these supply chains. The hawker uncle isn't e-waste, obviously, but it's the same pattern. Small people squeezed by systems that don't see them. I should bring this up at the next meeting. Or maybe I'll just sit there again. Don't know.
sources.nudge_response: Probably nothing. The agenda is always packed and nobody wants to hear philosophy from the recycling guy.

sources.journal_entry: People keep asking why I don't just retire and run the foundation full-time. As if it's that simple. The business funds everything — the foundation, my children's projects, the scholarships. Without it there's nothing to give.
sources.nudge_response: Not just income. The ability to actually do something about the problems I see. Money is leverage.

sources.journal_entry:
Flew back from a factory visit in Penang. The new processing line looks good, efficiency is way up, costs are down. Everyone was pleased. On the drive to the airport the plant manager mentioned casually that they'd switched to a cheaper chemical solvent for circuit board stripping. Cheaper and, I suspect, not properly rated for ventilation in that building. I could smell it from the parking lot.

I didn't ask about it. I could have. I had forty minutes in the car and I know enough about chemical handling to ask the right questions. But I was tired and the deal was done and bringing it up would have meant delaying the whole partnership review. I chose convenience. The flight home felt longer than usual.

My son called from Jakarta. His NGO just secured funding to expand their mangrove restoration project into two new provinces. I could hear it in his voice — the energy, the belief that what he's doing actually matters. I told him I was proud. I meant it completely.

After we hung up I transferred some money to the foundation account. Not a huge amount, but enough to cover the clean-water pump installation we've been delaying in Siem Reap because the supplier raised prices. My wife asked why I didn't just wait until next quarter when cash flow is better. I told her some things shouldn't wait. She gave me that look she gives when she thinks I'm being impulsive, but she processed the transfer anyway.
sources.nudge_response: Hearing him talk about the mangroves reminded me why I started the foundation. Sometimes you forget.

I found out today that Ahmad—who joined the company six months after me—is also being considered for the senior manager position. We have the same title. Same level. But he's been here less time, has less experience, and somehow we're competing for the same promotion.

I know I shouldn't compare. I know the advice is "focus on your own race." But how can I not? We sit in the same open office. I see his calendar, his meetings, how he operates. He's good at being visible. Always volunteering for the high-profile projects that get executive attention, while I'm handling the operations that actually keep this company running.

Maybe that's the game. Maybe I've been playing it wrong. I thought doing excellent work would speak for itself. But excellent work that nobody sees might as well not exist.

I couldn't focus on anything else today. Kept replaying the conversation with HR, analyzing every word. They said "both strong candidates." What does that mean? Is it 50-50? Or are they just being diplomatic?

My stomach has been in knots since morning. I hate that this affects me this much.
sources.nudge_response: Frustrated. It feels unfair. But I need to adapt.

New year. Everyone's posting about fresh starts and intentions. I don't know what mine are yet. Get the promotion, obviously. But what else?

I went for a walk along the Marina last night at midnight. All these people celebrating, fireworks going off over the water. I stood there alone and felt... nothing? Not sad, not happy. Just watching. Like I was outside of my own life looking in.

I keep thinking about what Tariq said. "Dubai changed you." Maybe it did. Or maybe this is just who I become when I'm in survival mode. Head down, eyes on the goal, don't look around too much because the periphery is full of things that will slow you down.

Is that bad? Or is that just what it takes?

sources.journal_entry:
I video-called into the engagement party. It was awkward—the connection kept dropping, everyone was loud and happy and I was sitting alone in my apartment with my laptop. Layla smiled when she saw me but I could tell she'd wanted me there in person. Mama barely looked at the camera.

My cousin Tariq asked why I couldn't "just take a few days off." I said I had responsibilities. He laughed and said "Dubai changed you."

He doesn't understand. None of them do. They have stable government jobs back home, houses their families helped them buy. I'm building from nothing in a place where your visa is tied to your employment. If I lose this job, I have 30 days to find another or leave. That's not paranoia, that's reality.

But sitting here tonight, in the quiet after the call ended, I wonder if I'm using that reality as an excuse to avoid other fears.

End of year push. Everyone wants everything done before the holidays. I've been in the office until 9pm every day this week. My flatmate asked if I still live here—I've barely seen him.

The promotion decision got pushed to January. "Too much going on, we'll revisit in the new year." I don't know if that's good or bad. More time to prove myself, or more time to overthink everything?

Mama called asking about my holiday plans. I told her I'm staying in Dubai—too much work, flights are expensive. She was quiet for a long time. I could tell she was disappointed. My sister's engagement party is on the 27th. I should be there. But the thought of being away while Ahmad is here, possibly making moves... I can't.

I don't even know if staying will make a difference. But leaving feels like a risk I can't take.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a one-on-one with my director today. She was more candid than usual. Said she appreciates my "operational excellence" but that senior leadership roles require "strategic visibility." She suggested I present at the next all-hands meeting.

Part of me bristled at the feedback. I've been doing critical work, keeping the machine running while others polish their personal brands. But another part of me heard what she was actually saying: the game has rules, and I've been refusing to play by some of them.

I've always thought self-promotion was distasteful. Where I come from, you don't brag about your work—you let it speak. Boasting is seen as shallow. But I'm not where I come from anymore. I'm in a place where speaking up isn't bragging; it's survival.

I signed up for the presentation slot. It felt uncomfortable, almost wrong. But I did it.

I also booked a flight home for Mama's birthday in February. Non-refundable. I need to stop letting work consume everything. The promotion matters, but it can't be the only thing that matters.

My cousin Tariq asked why I couldn't "just take a few days off." I said I had responsibilities. He laughed and said "Dubai changed you."

He doesn't understand. None of them do. They have stable government jobs back home, houses their families helped them buy. I'm building from nothing in a place where your visa is tied to your employment. If I lose this job, I have 30 days to find another or leave. That's not paranoia, that's reality.

But sitting here tonight, in the quiet after the call ended, I wonder if I'm using that reality as an excuse to avoid other fears.

End of year push. Everyone wants everything done before the holidays. I've been in the office until 9pm every day this week. My flatmate asked if I still live here—I've barely seen him.

The promotion decision got pushed to January. "Too much going on, we'll revisit in the new year." I don't know if that's good or bad. More time to prove myself, or more time to overthink everything?

Mama called asking about my holiday plans. I told her I'm staying in Dubai—too much work, flights are expensive. She was quiet for a long time. I could tell she was disappointed. My sister's engagement party is on the 27th. I should be there. But the thought of being away while Ahmad is here, possibly making moves... I can't.

I don't even know if staying will make a difference. But leaving feels like a risk I can't take.
sources.nudge_response: It's just one event. I'll make it up to her later.

sources.journal_entry:
I found out today that Ahmad—who joined the company six months after me—is also being considered for the senior manager position. We have the same title. Same level. But he's been here less time, has less experience, and somehow we're competing for the same promotion.

I know I shouldn't compare. I know the advice is "focus on your own race." But how can I not? We sit in the same open office. I see his calendar, his meetings, how he operates. He's good at being visible. Always volunteering for the high-profile projects that get executive attention, while I'm handling the operations that actually keep this company running.

Maybe that's the game. Maybe I've been playing it wrong. I thought doing excellent work would speak for itself. But excellent work that nobody sees might as well not exist.

I couldn't focus on anything else today. Kept replaying the conversation with HR, analyzing every word. They said "both strong candidates." What does that mean? Is it 50-50? Or are they just being diplomatic?

My stomach has been in knots since morning. I hate that this affects me this much.
sources.nudge_response: Frustrated. It feels unfair. But I need to adapt.

sources.journal_entry:
I got the promotion.

The email came this afternoon. Senior Operations Manager, effective February 1st. A 15% salary increase and a team of twelve direct reports instead of five.

I sat in the conference room alone for ten minutes after reading it, just letting it settle. Two years of work. All those late nights, the stress, the sacrifices. It paid off.

I called Baba first. He said "This is good. Keep going." Classic Baba. Then I called Mama and she cried, which made me tear up too even though I tried not to. "I'm so proud of you, habibi. When are you coming home?" I told her February, for her birthday, and she made me promise three times.

Tonight I'm going to dinner with colleagues to celebrate. I picked a nice place, not the most expensive because I'm still me, but nice enough to mark the occasion.

Sitting here now, I'm thinking about what I wrote a few weeks ago—about not knowing what the final goalpost looks like, about whether there even is one. I still don't know the answer. Maybe there isn't one. Maybe that's okay.

What I do know is that I can't let the pursuit of the next thing erase the moment when I actually get something I worked for. Tonight, I'm going to let myself feel this. Tomorrow the new worries will start: proving myself in the senior role, saving for the apartment, thinking about what's next. But tonight, just tonight, I made it.

Did the all-hands presentation. Nervous beforehand but it went well. Several people came up after to compliment the insights. Ahmad was one of them—said he learned things about the operations he didn't know.

Strange to think of him as just a colleague now, not a threat. The competition hasn't changed. But my relationship to it has, slightly.

Had a one-on-one with my director today. She was more candid than usual. Said she appreciates my "operational excellence" but that senior leadership roles require "strategic visibility." She suggested I present at the next all-hands meeting.

Part of me bristled at the feedback. I've been doing critical work, keeping the machine running while others polish their personal brands. But another part of me heard what she was actually saying: the game has rules, and I've been refusing to play by some of them.

I've always thought self-promotion was distasteful. Where I come from, you don't brag about your work—you let it speak. Boasting is seen as shallow. But I'm not where I come from anymore. I'm in a place where speaking up isn't bragging; it's survival.

I signed up for the presentation slot. It felt uncomfortable, almost wrong. But I did it.

I also booked a flight home for Mama's birthday in February. Non-refundable. I need to stop letting work consume everything. The promotion matters, but it can't be the only thing that matters.
sources.nudge_response: I realized I was building a life I wouldn't want to live.

New year. Everyone's posting about fresh starts and intentions. I don't know what mine are yet. Get the promotion, obviously. But what else?

I went for a walk along the Marina last night at midnight. All these people celebrating, fireworks going off over the water. I stood there alone and felt... nothing? Not sad, not happy. Just watching. Like I was outside of my own life looking in.

I keep thinking about what Tariq said. "Dubai changed you." Maybe it did. Or maybe this is just who I become when I'm in survival mode. Head down, eyes on the goal, don't look around too much because the periphery is full of things that will slow you down.

Is that bad? Or is that just what it takes?

Spent most of the day doing Deliveroo runs in the rain. The app kept sending me to Kralingen and back, which eats petrol. Made about seventy euros after costs. Not terrible, not good.

Drove past the old Fenix warehouse on the way home. They've turned it into some kind of food hall now. Mam and I used to go there when I was small — it was still a working warehouse then, real dockworkers loading ships. She'd bring me along when she visited Tante Lien. Strange seeing the same walls but everything inside different. The bones are there but the life has changed.

Called Mam tonight. She asked when I'm coming for Sunday. Told her this week looks difficult because of a booking in Dordrecht. She didn't say anything but the silence was louder than words.

sources.journal_entry:
Can't sleep so writing again. Mind is jumping around. Listened to a recording of the Zeeland dialect my cousin Jaap posted in the family WhatsApp group — some old farmer telling a story about the flood of '53. My grandfather survived that flood. He never talked about it directly but it shaped everything about how he lived afterward. Every decision was about making sure the family had solid ground.

That's what I keep coming back to. Solid ground. My grandfather rebuilt after the water took the house. My father kept the shop going for four decades in the same spot. And here I am checking an app to see if someone in Rotterdam-Zuid wants their Pad Thai delivered before it gets cold.

But tonight something small happened that felt right. One of my regular delivery customers — an old woman on Nieuwe Binnenweg — she recognised me and asked me to come in for a moment. She'd made a pot of coffee and had nobody to drink it with. I said I had five minutes. We talked about the weather and she showed me a photo of her late husband. I was fifteen minutes late on my next delivery and got a warning from the app. Don't care.

Sitting with her felt like the most honest thing I'd done all week. Like something my father would have done without even thinking about it.

Long day. Did a furniture assembly job in Capelle through Werkspot, then four hours of deliveries in the evening. My back is killing me. Should probably see someone about it but I don't have the coverage for a physiotherapist right now. The basic insurance only goes so far.

Had a strange moment at the assembly job. The couple who hired me — young, maybe early thirties — they were hanging family photos on the wall of their new flat. Grandparents, wedding photos, kids at christenings. The man said something about wanting the living room to feel like his grandmother's house. I understood that completely. But then he also had this app controlling all the lights and the thermostat and I thought, you can't have your oma's living room run by a computer. It doesn't work like that.

Too tired to think about it more. Eating leftover stamppot and going to bed.
sources.nudge_response: Maybe. It's not about the smart lights, really. It's that everyone wants the feeling of the old way without actually living it. They want the photos on the wall and the gezelligheid but they also want the algorithm to set the temperature. You can't curate warmth. My grandmother's house was warm because she was there all day, baking, mending, talking to the neighbours. It wasn't a setting you could select. I think what bothers me is that I understand the impulse — I want it too — but I can see it slipping into something hollow. And I'm not sure I'm doing any better. I drive around all day for an app. My father would not have understood this life at all.

My father at fifty-one had the shop, the house, the family under one roof, the church council seat. He knew where he'd be every day for the next ten years. I don't know where I'll be next Tuesday.

Went to church this morning. Not my usual one in Rotterdam — I drove to Zeeland for the service at the old church in Goes. Sat in the same pew where my family has sat for as long as anyone remembers. Third row, left side, near the pillar.

Pastor de Vries preached about the parable of the sower. Seeds on rocky ground, seeds among thorns, seeds in good soil. I've heard it a hundred times. But this time I thought about it differently. The rocky ground isn't always a place — sometimes it's a season. Sometimes the soil is fine but the weather is wrong. You still plant.

After the service, old Meneer Bakker shook my hand and asked about my mother. Said he remembered my father fondly. "A man who kept his word and kept his shop clean." That's two things, but they capture Dad pretty well.

Drove back to Rotterdam in the afternoon. The highway was busy, everyone returning from the weekend. I had a delivery booking at four but I took the long route through the country roads instead, past the fields and the old dykes. Got to Rotterdam ten minutes late. Didn't rush.

I don't have the life my father had. I might never have it. But I can still sit in that pew and drive those roads and remember that the ground under all of this is the same ground. It doesn't move, even when I do.
sources.nudge_response: Family. The language. The church. The way Mam still sets the table the same way every Sunday. The fact that Bram asked me to say grace, which means something got passed along even through the mess of the divorce and the years I wasn't fully present. The ground is whatever doesn't change based on what app I open or what rate I get paid. It's the part of me that existed before any of this and will still be there after. I can't always stand on it — sometimes I'm too far away, too busy, too caught up in the week. But knowing it's there is what keeps me from feeling completely adrift.

Parent-teacher conferences ran until 7pm tonight. Twenty-three families, twenty-three variations of the same careful dance — praising where possible, suggesting improvements without offending, never saying anything that might prompt a complaint to Principal Wu. Mrs. Huang brought her mother-in-law, which meant I had two generations asking why her son wasn't top of the class. I said all the right things about Wei's potential and his need for more practice. I didn't mention that he spends most of class drawing in his notebook.

Walking home, I felt that familiar tiredness that comes from holding my face in the right expression all day. But also something like satisfaction. Nobody left upset. No difficult calls tomorrow. My colleague Teacher Lin had three parents demand meetings with administration after his conferences last month — he told one mother her daughter was "mediocre at best." He's not wrong, technically. But there are ways to say things, and there are other ways. I'd rather be tired than cause that kind of mess.

sources.journal_entry:
Saturday afternoon and I'm sitting in my apartment with a cup of cold tea I forgot to drink, thinking about the faculty dinner next Friday. Vice Principal Chang wants me to give a toast because I'm the "voice of the department" according to her, which means I'm the one who doesn't argue in meetings and makes everyone feel comfortable.

I've already written three drafts. The first was too long. The second used a metaphor about bamboo that sounded pretentious when I read it aloud. The third is fine, probably, but Teacher Lin will definitely make some comment afterward about how I'm "always so proper" and I can already feel myself smiling politely at him and saying something like "just doing my part."

There's a ceramics class starting at the community center next month. I saw the flyer at the grocery store. Every Saturday afternoon, two hours of making things with your hands. I keep thinking about it. I haven't signed up because it conflicts with my parents' usual visiting time. They would understand if I explained. They would say "of course, go to your class." But my mother's face would do that thing it does when she's disappointed but trying not to show it. And my father would eat dinner in silence the way he does when something's bothering him.

Is it ridiculous that I can't take a ceramics class because of a look on my mother's face? It sounds ridiculous when I write it out. Plenty of people would just go, would say "I'm an adult, I can spend my Saturdays how I want." But that's not... I don't know. That's not how my family works. We show up for each other. That's the deal.

I'll probably end up watching YouTube videos about ceramics instead. It's not the same, but it's something.
sources.nudge_response:
I think it's because nothing I do in a day has any shape to it. Teaching is important, but at the end of a class, what do I have? Lesson plans for tomorrow. Grades to record. The students leave and the room is empty. Even calligraphy — I've been doing it for years and the scrolls just go in a drawer.

With ceramics, you'd have something. A bowl. A cup. Something you made that exists outside of obligation. Something nobody asked you to make, that nobody needs you to make, that doesn't have any purpose except that you wanted to make it. I don't have much of that in my life. Things that are just mine, just because I wanted them. Most things I do are because someone is expecting me to do them, and if I'm honest, I've started to forget what I want when no one's watching.

sources.journal_entry: Long day. Department meeting after classes, then dinner at my parents' place, then home to grade thirty-eight exams. My mother asked again about "that nice man from church" and I said I'd think about it, same as last time, same as I will next time.
sources.nudge_response: It's not a big thing, really. My mother has been suggesting potential matches since I was thirty. It's just what mothers do. She means well. I told her I'm focused on work right now, which is true. The exam period is always exhausting and I don't have the energy to think about anything else.

sources.journal_entry:
My hands are still shaking a little. I had to report a student today — Jia-Hui, one of my brightest — for cheating on the midterm exam. She copied answers from the student beside her. I saw it clearly, and worse, she saw me see it.

The look on her face. Like I'd betrayed her somehow, when she was the one breaking the rules. I followed protocol exactly: documented the incident, submitted the report to the academic integrity office, informed her homeroom teacher. Everything by the book. But she's been crying in the bathroom all afternoon, and three of her friends gave me cold looks in the hallway.

The thing that keeps running through my head is what Principal Wu said when he reviewed my report: "Good catch, Teacher Chen. We appreciate your vigilance." Vigilance. Like I'm some kind of guard. I don't want to be the person students are afraid of. I want them to trust me. But if I'd looked away, if I'd pretended not to notice — wouldn't that be worse? Wouldn't that be telling Jia-Hui that rules don't matter, that integrity is flexible?

My mother would say I did right. "A teacher who ignores cheating isn't a teacher," she'd say. She taught chemistry for thirty years and never once let a student slide. I'm trying to believe that following the proper procedure was the correct choice. I just wish it didn't feel so much like I've lost something.
sources.nudge_response: Her trust, I suppose. Or maybe the version of myself that I prefer — the approachable teacher, the one students come to with their problems. Now I'm the one who reported Jia-Hui to administration. There's no taking that back. She'll always remember me as the teacher who got her in trouble, not the one who stayed after school to help her understand quadratic equations. I know I did what was expected of me. I just wonder sometimes if being the person everyone expects me to be means giving up other things I want to be.

But my mother's face would do that thing it does when she's disappointed but trying not to show it. And my father would eat dinner in silence the way he does when something's bothering him.

Is it ridiculous that I can't take a ceramics class because of a look on my mother's face? It sounds ridiculous when I write it out. Plenty of people would just go, would say "I'm an adult, I can spend my Saturdays how I want." But that's not... I don't know. That's not how my family works. We show up for each other. I followed protocol exactly: documented the incident, submitted the report to the academic integrity office, informed her homeroom teacher. Everything by the book. Marcus called today. My old business partner, from the agency days. He's still there—made partner eventually, corner office, the whole thing. Wanted to know if I'd consider coming back. Not as an employee, as a "strategic partner." They'd acquire the consultancy, I'd run a division, get their resources, their clients, their benefits package.

I said I'd think about it, which is what you say when you don't want to say no immediately.

But I already know.

The thing is, Marcus sounds tired. He sounds like someone who traded the thing that matters for the thing that lasts. Stability. Predictability. A clear path to retirement with a good pension. And I don't judge him for it—we're different people, wanted different things.

What I can't stop thinking about is whether I'm fooling myself. The consultancy had a rough year. We lost the Bergqvist account in March, spent too much on that software project that went nowhere. I'm fine, we're fine, but it's not the growth trajectory I imagined when I started.

Maybe Marcus is right and I'm just stubborn. Maybe there's a version of partnership that would give me what I need without taking what I can't give up.

Or maybe I just can't stomach the idea of someone else making decisions about my work again.

Went for a run after the call. Didn't help as much as I wanted it to.

sources.journal_entry:
Cannot sleep. Went back to my laptop after everyone was in bed and found a message from Youssef, my old university friend who still works at the consultancy I left. He forwarded a job listing -- senior engineering director, Dubai office, salary that would cover both girls' tuition in one year. He wrote "just in case" with a smiley face. I know he means well.

The thing that got me was not the money. It was the simplicity. Show up, solve technical problems, go home. Nobody asking me to justify why clean water matters more than a lower unit cost. Nobody expecting me to write another grant narrative about "impact metrics" while families in Azraq are drinking from storage tanks that have not been serviced in months. I sat there staring at the listing for maybe twenty minutes.

Then I closed the tab. But I did not delete the email, and I am not sure what that means. Rania would not pressure me either way, but she would be relieved, and I can picture exactly how her shoulders would drop. That image keeps coming back. I feel like I chose this path and I keep choosing it, but tonight the choosing feels heavier than usual.
sources.nudge_response: Because part of me wanted to keep the option visible. Not to take it, probably. But to know it exists. Like proof that I could still walk away if this gets too hard. That sounds pathetic written down.

sources.journal_entry:
Got an email from the procurement office in Mafraq saying they want to switch to a cheaper Chinese filter unit. Half the cost, sure, but the failure rate data I have seen from field tests in East Africa is not good. I started drafting a reply with the test results attached, then stopped. Because what if they just need to save money this quarter and I am the one being difficult.

Rania said at dinner that Noor needs new textbooks and the car registration is due. She did not say it as a complaint, just facts, and that somehow made it worse. I kept thinking about those filters in Mafraq and whether I am fighting the right fight or just being stubborn about something that is not mine to decide.
sources.nudge_response: When it is the right call I feel steady about it. This time I keep second-guessing, which probably means I know the cheaper option might actually work fine and I just hate the idea of cutting corners on something that goes to people who cannot complain if it breaks.

Third time opening this today. Just realized I never actually finished the tea. Found it cold on the railing. Going to bed.

Still up, can't really settle. After that last entry I went and made tea and sat back on the balcony, properly this time, no phone. And it was good for a few minutes, the air was cool and I could hear the mosque down the street and I was just sitting there with my tea. But then this thing started where I'm thinking about how I approved Fadi's leave for December which means I'll need to cover his shifts myself or find someone, and suddenly the tea doesn't taste like anything anymore.

It's stupid. I literally just wanted to sit and drink tea. That's all I was doing. And I couldn't let myself have it for more than five minutes before my head started making it into a problem that I wasn't being productive. I don't even know who I'm performing for at eleven at night on my own balcony.

sources.journal_entry:
Took the morning to deal with the new shift scheduling. HR wants us to finalize the December roster by Thursday which means I had to pull two supervisors into a room and sort through everyone's leave requests. Nothing dramatic, just the usual back and forth about who covers what. One of the guys asked for the entire last week of December off and I approved it because he hasn't taken time in months. Didn't think much of it at the time.

Lunch was at my desk again. Brought lentil soup from home but it had gone lukewarm by the time I got to it. I keep telling myself I'll start eating in the break room like a normal person but there's always one more email. After lunch I had the monthly safety review call with the Zarqa site, which went fine, nothing flagged. Then spent the rest of the afternoon updating inventory projections.

Drove home the long way because traffic on the highway was backed up near the Seventh Circle. Put on some Fairuz which was nice. Got home, heated up what was left of last night's mansaf, and sat on the balcony for maybe ten minutes before I started going through tomorrow's agenda on my phone.
sources.nudge_response: Nothing dramatic. I just remembered I hadn't confirmed the forklift maintenance slot for Thursday. Once I picked up the phone it was over.
