sources.journal_entry:
Everyone at work acts like I don't know how to take a break. My sister called on Friday and said Mama told her I looked tired at dinner, and then today Rami, one of my supervisors, made some comment about how I should use my own leave balance before telling everyone else to use theirs. And I get it, fine, they have a point on paper. But it's not like I'm some robot who doesn't want to rest. I do. I just can't flip a switch and turn off the part of my brain that keeps running through what needs to get done.

I was genuinely tired today, like the kind of tired where you sit down and your whole body feels heavy. And I thought about going home early, it was a quiet afternoon, nothing urgent. But then I started thinking about how that would look, leaving at three when my team is there until five. Even though nobody would care. Even though I tell my own people to go home early when it's slow. I couldn't give myself the same thing I'd give anyone else without it feeling like I was getting away with something.

So I stayed. Answered emails that could have waited. Drove home in the dark. Made rice and ate it standing in the kitchen. I know this is a pattern. I just don't know what I'm supposed to do differently when the guilt is louder than the tiredness.
sources.nudge_response: Because if I rest and something goes wrong, it's my fault. If they rest, I'm the one who covered. That's the deal I made with myself somewhere.

sources.journal_entry:
Took the morning to deal with the new shift scheduling. HR wants us to finalize the December roster by Thursday which means I had to pull two supervisors into a room and sort through everyone's leave requests. Nothing dramatic, just the usual back and forth about who covers what. One of the guys asked for the entire last week of December off and I approved it because he hasn't taken time in months. Didn't think much of it at the time.

Lunch was at my desk again. Brought lentil soup from home but it had gone lukewarm by the time I got to it. I keep telling myself I'll start eating in the break room like a normal person but there's always one more email. After lunch I had the monthly safety review call with the Zarqa site, which went fine, nothing flagged. Then spent the rest of the afternoon updating inventory projections.

Drove home the long way because traffic on the highway was backed up near the Seventh Circle. Put on some Fairuz which was nice. Got home, heated up what was left of last night's mansaf, and sat on the balcony for maybe ten minutes before I started going through tomorrow's agenda on my phone.

sources.journal_entry:
Got back from the studio late and Baba was already asleep but Mama was waiting up. She didn't say anything about me being late, she just set out the leftover kibbeh and sat across from me while I ate. The whole time I could feel her watching me and I knew she wanted to ask about the commission meeting. I told her it went fine, which it did, mostly. The client wants something for his hotel lobby, large scale, blues and golds, very safe. I said I'd do it.

But the thing is I'd spent the whole morning working on something else entirely, this series I've been sketching for months. Faces in crowds, people looking away from each other. Disconnection in tight spaces. It's the most honest work I've done in years and I can't show it to anyone. Not because it's bad but because every time I imagine hanging it somewhere or putting it in a show I can already hear my uncle asking why I'm painting something so depressing, or my cousin making that face she makes when she doesn't understand something but doesn't want to say so. So instead I took the hotel lobby job and told myself the other work can wait. It can always wait.

I keep doing this. The safe thing first, then the real thing never.
sources.nudge_response: I'd need to stop caring what people think, which is basically asking me to be a different person. Or I'd need someone to tell me it's okay, which is pathetic at my age.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a conversation with Rami at the studio today that's been sitting with me all evening. He got accepted into a group show in Beirut, contemporary stuff, political, boundary-pushing. They asked if I wanted to submit something too. I told him I'd think about it, which we both knew meant no.

He didn't push, which I appreciated, but later he said something offhand while cleaning his brushes. He said, "You're the most talented person I know who makes the least interesting work." He wasn't being cruel. He actually looked sad when he said it. I didn't know how to respond so I just laughed it off and changed the subject.

The thing is he's right. The hotel lobby commission is technically proficient and completely forgettable. The faces series sitting under the tarp in the corner of my studio is the best work I've ever done and no one has seen it. I keep telling myself I'm being strategic, building a reputation with the commercial work first, earning credibility. But at some point strategy becomes avoidance and I think I passed that line a while ago. I just don't know what to do about it because every option I can think of involves disappointing someone or drawing attention I'm not ready for.

Friday lunch was the usual production. My aunt brought her friend who has a daughter studying dentistry and somehow the conversation kept circling back to me and whether I'm seeing anyone. Mama smiled the whole time and said nothing, which is her way of agreeing without being the one to push. I just sat there eating and deflecting. "I'm focused on work right now." "Inshallah, when the time is right." All the correct answers.

My sister pulled me aside after and said I handled it well, which felt more like pity than praise. She knows I've been seeing someone casually, someone who isn't from the community, and she knows I'll never bring it up at Friday lunch. Not because I'm ashamed but because I can already map out the exact sequence of reactions and it's exhausting to even think about. My father asking quiet questions. My mother suddenly having a headache. My uncle making a joke that isn't a joke.

People think I'm easygoing because I never push back. The truth is I've just gotten very efficient at predicting which battles aren't worth starting. That's not the same thing as being at peace with it.
sources.nudge_response: Like holding your breath in a room full of people who think you're breathing normally. It's fine until it isn't.

sources.journal_entry:
Engagement party was fine. Loud. Lots of people I hadn't seen in months asking the usual things. How's the art going, meaning are you making money. Are you eating enough, meaning you look tired. When are you next, meaning why haven't you settled down. I smiled through all of it because that's what you do.

Danced with my mother at one point, which was actually nice. She was happy, genuinely, and I like seeing her like that. My father sat in the corner with the other men drinking coffee and nodding. He looked proud of my cousin. I wonder if he looks at me and feels something different, not disappointment exactly but maybe confusion. His son the painter. He's never said a negative word about it but he's also never asked to see my work. That silence says more than any criticism would.

After everyone left I helped stack chairs and my aunt squeezed my arm and told me I was such a good boy for always helping. I'm thirty-nine years old and I'm still being called a good boy. The worst part is I felt relieved by it. Like that's still the thing I'm chasing, the approval, the confirmation that I'm doing it right. Whatever "it" is.

sources.journal_entry:
Something shifted today, or maybe it's been shifting for a while and I only noticed now. I was working on the hotel commission, painting this massive blue gradient that's supposed to evoke the sea, and I caught myself adding tiny figures along the bottom edge. Almost invisible unless you're close. Faces turned away from each other, like my other series. I painted over them before anyone could see but for a few minutes they were there and the piece was better for it.

My sister came by the studio to drop off food Mama had made. She lingered, looking at canvases against the wall. She pointed at one of the commercial pieces and said, "This is pretty." Then she pointed at the corner where the faces series was partially visible under the tarp and said, "What's that one?" I told her it was nothing, just experiments. She said it looked interesting and I should show her sometime.

That's the thing about my sister. She asks without pushing. If I ever show the real work to anyone in my family, it'll start with her. Not because she'll necessarily understand it but because she won't make me feel wrong for having made it. That counts for more than most people realize.

I drove home feeling lighter than I have in weeks. Nothing has actually changed. I still didn't submit to Beirut. But someone in my family expressing even mild curiosity about the work I actually care about made me feel less like I'm carrying this alone.

Can't sleep. Spent the last two hours looking at Rami's work online, the pieces he's submitting to Beirut. They're raw and unfinished-looking on purpose and there's this energy in them that I used to have. I pulled out the faces series from under the tarp and laid them out on the studio floor and just stood there staring at them. They're good. I know they're good. That's not ego, that's honest assessment after twenty years of doing this.

I took a photo of the pieces laid out and almost posted it. My thumb was literally on the button. Then I imagined my mother scrolling past it and asking why the faces look so lonely, or my uncle forwarding it with a comment about how art these days has no beauty. So I put my phone down and covered everything back up.

I keep thinking about what Rami said. The most talented person he knows who makes the least interesting work. It's like a splinter I can't get out. If I showed the real work and people responded to it, everything would change. But if people in my life reacted badly, that would also change everything. I don't trust myself to handle that without losing something I need. The approval, the ease, the feeling of fitting in. People act like fitting in is small but when you've built your entire life around it, it becomes the foundation. I'm terrified of what happens if I pull a brick out.
sources.nudge_response: Submitting to a show, probably. Or just leaving the tarp off the canvases when my family visits the studio. Small things. Anyway, I need to sleep.

He looked proud of my cousin. I wonder if he looks at me and feels something different, not disappointment exactly but maybe confusion. His son the painter. He's never said a negative word about it but he's also never asked to see my work. That silence says more than any criticism would.

After everyone left I helped stack chairs and my aunt squeezed my arm and told me I was such a good boy for always helping. I'm thirty-nine years old and I'm still being called a good boy. The worst part is I felt relieved by it. Like that's still the thing I'm chasing, the approval, the confirmation that I'm doing it right. Whatever "it" is.

Long day finishing preliminary sketches for the hotel commission. The client wants revisions already, more warmth, more welcoming. I nodded through the whole meeting and made notes. On the drive home I realized I'd been clenching my jaw for hours and my neck is completely locked up.

Mama called to remind me about my cousin's engagement party this weekend. I said I'd be there. Of course I'll be there. Everyone will be there. I'll wear the right shirt, say the right things, congratulate the right people. I'm good at this part.

Had a conversation with Rami at the studio today that's been sitting with me all evening. He got accepted into a group show in Beirut, contemporary stuff, political, boundary-pushing. They asked if I wanted to submit something too. I told him I'd think about it, which we both knew meant no.

He didn't push, which I appreciated, but later he said something offhand while cleaning his brushes. He said, "You're the most talented person I know who makes the least interesting work." He wasn't being cruel. He actually looked sad when he said it. I didn't know how to respond so I just laughed it off and changed the subject.

The thing is he's right. The hotel lobby commission is technically proficient and completely forgettable. The faces series sitting under the tarp in the corner of my studio is the best work I've ever done and no one has seen it. I keep telling myself I'm being strategic, building a reputation with the commercial work first, earning credibility. But at some point strategy becomes avoidance and I think I passed that line a while ago. I just don't know what to do about it because every option I can think of involves disappointing someone or drawing attention I'm not ready for.

Friday lunch was the usual production. My aunt brought her friend who has a daughter studying dentistry and somehow the conversation kept circling back to me and whether I'm seeing anyone. Mama smiled the whole time and said nothing, which is her way of agreeing without being the one to push. I just sat there eating and deflecting. "I'm focused on work right now." "Inshallah, when the time is right." All the correct answers.

My sister pulled me aside after and said I handled it well, which felt more like pity than praise. She knows I've been seeing someone casually, someone who isn't from the community, and she knows I'll never bring it up at Friday lunch. Not because I'm ashamed but because I can already map out the exact sequence of reactions and it's exhausting to even think about. My father asking quiet questions. My mother suddenly having a headache. My uncle making a joke that isn't a joke.

People think I'm easygoing because I never push back. The truth is I've just gotten very efficient at predicting which battles aren't worth starting. That's not the same thing as being at peace with it.

sources.journal_entry:
Got back from the studio late and Baba was already asleep but Mama was waiting up. She didn't say anything about me being late, she just set out the leftover kibbeh and sat across from me while I ate. The whole time I could feel her watching me and I knew she wanted to ask about the commission meeting. I told her it went fine, which it did, mostly. The client wants something for his hotel lobby, large scale, blues and golds, very safe. I said I'd do it.

But the thing is I'd spent the whole morning working on something else entirely, this series I've been sketching for months. Faces in crowds, people looking away from each other. Disconnection in tight spaces. It's the most honest work I've done in years and I can't show it to anyone. Not because it's bad but because every time I imagine hanging it somewhere or putting it in a show I can already hear my uncle asking why I'm painting something so depressing, or my cousin making that face she makes when she doesn't understand something but doesn't want to say so. So instead I took the hotel lobby job and told myself the other work can wait. It can always wait.

I keep doing this. The safe thing first, then the real thing never.

sources.journal_entry:
Took my sister up on her offer. Showed her three of the faces pieces at the studio today. She looked at them for a long time without saying anything. Then she said, "These are different." I waited for the follow-up, the concern, the suggestion to maybe not show Baba. Instead she said, "You should make more of these."

I didn't know what to do with that so I made us tea and we sat on the studio floor talking about other things. But the pieces stayed uncovered the whole time. I didn't put the tarp back until after she left. Small thing. But I noticed it.
sources.nudge_response: Maybe I'm getting tired of hiding the work. Or maybe I just needed one person to see it and not flinch. Either way the tarp felt heavier putting it back on than it used to.

sources.journal_entry: Delivered the hotel commission today. Client was thrilled. Shook my hand and said it was exactly what he envisioned, which I think is the most depressing compliment I've ever received.

Something shifted today, or maybe it's been shifting for a while and I only noticed now. I was working on the hotel commission, painting this massive blue gradient that's supposed to evoke the sea, and I caught myself adding tiny figures along the bottom edge. Almost invisible unless you're close. Faces turned away from each other, like my other series. I painted over them before anyone could see but for a few minutes they were there and the piece was better for it.

My sister came by the studio to drop off food Mama had made. She lingered, looking at canvases against the wall. She pointed at one of the commercial pieces and said, "This is pretty." Then she pointed at the corner where the faces series was partially visible under the tarp and said, "What's that one?" I told her it was nothing, just experiments. She said it looked interesting and I should show her sometime.

That's the thing about my sister. She asks without pushing. If I ever show the real work to anyone in my family, it'll start with her. Not because she'll necessarily understand it but because she won't make me feel wrong for having made it. That counts for more than most people realize.

I drove home feeling lighter than I have in weeks. Nothing has actually changed. I still didn't submit to Beirut. But someone in my family expressing even mild curiosity about the work I actually care about made me feel less like I'm carrying this alone.

Can't sleep. Spent the last two hours looking at Rami's work online, the pieces he's submitting to Beirut. They're raw and unfinished-looking on purpose and there's this energy in them that I used to have. I pulled out the faces series from under the tarp and laid them out on the studio floor and just stood there staring at them. They're good. I know they're good. That's not ego, that's honest assessment after twenty years of doing this.

I took a photo of the pieces laid out and almost posted it. My thumb was literally on the button. Then I imagined my mother scrolling past it and asking why the faces look so lonely, or my uncle forwarding it with a comment about how art these days has no beauty. So I put my phone down and covered everything back up.

I keep thinking about what Rami said. The most talented person he knows who makes the least interesting work. It's like a splinter I can't get out. If I showed the real work and people responded to it, everything would change. But if people in my life reacted badly, that would also change everything. I don't trust myself to handle that without losing something I need. The approval, the ease, the feeling of fitting in. People act like fitting in is small but when you've built your entire life around it, it becomes the foundation. I'm terrified of what happens if I pull a brick out.
sources.nudge_response: Submitting to a show, probably. Or just leaving the tarp off the canvases when my family visits the studio. Small things. Anyway, I need to sleep.

sources.journal_entry:

Dropped the third app. Deleted it this morning, not worth the mental load. Back to the two I know. Lost the deposit but whatever, lesson paid for.

Regular Thursday route. Picked up from the arepas place on Carrera 7, three runs to Chapinero, one long one out to Usaquén that paid decent. Stopped at the tienda on the way home and Lina had saved me a plate of arroz con pollo from lunch. She'd had a slow afternoon — said the distributor raised prices on cooking oil again, which means she either eats the cost or marks up and risks losing her regulars. We talked about it for a bit. Not much to do about it.

Logged my earnings in the notebook. Slightly above average for a Thursday. Bike needs new brake pads soon, I can hear them starting to grind. Priced them out at the shop near the house — forty-five mil, which is fine. I'll do it Saturday when I'm off.

Stupid decision. Signed up for a third delivery platform because somebody at the parqueadero told me it pays well on weekends. Had to put down a deposit for their branded thermal bag — ninety mil — and now I'm juggling three apps on my phone at the same time and I can't keep track of which order belongs to which one.

Picked up a Rappi order thinking it was the new app and drove twenty minutes in the wrong direction before I realized. Lost the time and the gas. Lina asked how my day was and I just said fine because I didn't want to explain why I'm now paying for a third bag I might not even use past this week.

The thing is, I already have a routine that works. Two apps, I know the zones, I know which restaurants are slow, I know where to park. I broke my own system trying to grab a little more and now I'm scattered. Should have just stayed with what I had. The ninety mil bothers me more than it should — it's not huge, but it's money out the door for something I didn't need.

Week's been rough on the bike. The brake pads I was going to replace Saturday — didn't do it. Saturday got busy, Sunday Lina needed help at the tienda, Monday I forgot, and now it's Thursday and they're grinding metal on metal. I can feel the vibration through the handlebars when I stop.

But here's the thing — stopping for the repair means losing half a day of work, and this week the app has a streak bonus if I hit thirty deliveries by Friday. I'm at twenty-two. sources.journal_entry:
My cousin Andrés called, wants me to invest in a food truck he's putting together with some guys from his old job. Says I could put in two million and be a silent partner and make it back in three months. I told him I'd think about it but honestly I already know the answer.

People act like I'm afraid of opportunity. I'm not afraid. I just know what happens. Andrés has had three business ideas in two years and none of them lasted past the first quarter. Two million is two months of savings. It took me a year and a half to build what we have in that account and I'm not going to watch it disappear into a food truck that parks in a bad location and folds by August. Lina agrees with me but says I should at least hear him out so he doesn't feel dismissed. Fine, I'll have cafecito with him. But the money stays where it is.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly it's that he'll think I don't believe in him. Which — I mean, I don't, not with money. But he's family. I don't want him going around telling everyone I'm tacaño. I just can't be the one who funds his experiments.

sources.journal_entry: Fixed the brakes last Saturday, finally. Fifty-two mil with labor because I waited so long the rotor needed resurfacing. Could have been forty-five if I'd gone when I planned, but it's done and the bike stops clean now. Feel better on the road.

Week's been rough on the bike. The brake pads I was going to replace Saturday — didn't do it. Saturday got busy, Sunday Lina needed help at the tienda, Monday I forgot, and now it's Thursday and they're grinding metal on metal. I can feel the vibration through the handlebars when I stop.

I know it's not smart. Every day I ride with bad brakes is a day something could go wrong, and fixing a bent rotor costs ten times what pads cost. I've been through this before, years ago, ended up paying three hundred mil because I waited too long. You'd think I'd learn.

But here's the thing — stopping for the repair means losing half a day of work, and this week the app has a streak bonus if I hit thirty deliveries by Friday. I'm at twenty-two. If I stop tomorrow to fix the bike I lose the streak and probably two hundred mil in bonus. So I keep telling myself one more day, one more day. Lina doesn't know the brakes are this bad. She'd tell me to fix them immediately, and she'd be right.

Dropped the third app. Deleted it this morning, not worth the mental load. Back to the two I know. Lost the deposit but whatever, lesson paid for.

Regular Thursday route. Picked up from the arepas place on Carrera 7, three runs to Chapinero, one long one out to Usaquén that paid decent. Stopped at the tienda on the way home and Lina had saved me a plate of arroz con pollo from lunch. She'd had a slow afternoon — said the distributor raised prices on cooking oil again, which means she either eats the cost or marks up and risks losing her regulars. We talked about it for a bit. Not much to do about it.

Logged my earnings in the notebook. Slightly above average for a Thursday. Bike needs new brake pads soon, I can hear them starting to grind. Priced them out at the shop near the house — forty-five mil, which is fine. I'll do it Saturday when I'm off.

Stupid decision. Signed up for a third delivery platform because somebody at the parqueadero told me it pays well on weekends. Had to put down a deposit for their branded thermal bag — ninety mil — and now I'm juggling three apps on my phone at the same time and I can't keep track of which order belongs to which one.

Picked up a Rappi order thinking it was the new app and drove twenty minutes in the wrong direction before I realized. Lost the time and the gas. Lina asked how my day was and I just said fine because I didn't want to explain why I'm now paying for a third bag I might not even use past this week.

The thing is, I already have a routine that works. Two apps, I know the zones, I know which restaurants are slow, I know where to park. I broke my own system trying to grab a little more and now I'm scattered. Should have just stayed with what I had. The ninety mil bothers me more than it should — it's not huge, but it's money out the door for something I didn't need.
sources.nudge_response: Wasn't different really. Somebody just talked it up and I moved too fast. It happens.

sources.journal_entry:
Got a notification from the app that they're changing the pay structure again starting next month. Third time in a year. The base rate drops and they say the bonuses will make up for it, but last time they said that, my weekly take dropped by almost eighty mil. I wrote it down, I have the numbers.

Lina said don't worry about it yet, wait and see. But I can't just wait and see. I ran the numbers in my notebook during a break between deliveries and if it's like last time I'd need four extra hours a day to match what I'm making now. Four hours I don't have.

sources.journal_entry:
Wednesday. Steady day, nothing unusual. Eleven deliveries, which is about average for a midweek. The app paid out the streak bonus from last week, finally — showed up in my account this morning, a hundred and thirty mil. Transferred it to savings immediately before it sits in the checking account and turns into groceries.

Lina's tienda had a decent day too. She sold a bulk order of panela to a neighbor who's making natilla for a birthday party this weekend. She was happy about it, said it was the biggest single sale this month. We had dinner together for once — usually I'm still on the bike at eight but today I finished early.

Checked the notebook. Month is tracking slightly above April, which is good. If I keep this pace through the rest of May I can cover the bike insurance renewal in June without dipping into savings. That's the goal. One month at a time.

Took a shortcut through Suba today because Waze said it would save twelve minutes and I had back-to-back orders. Road was torn up, construction, no signs, just orange cones everywhere. Had to loop back and ended up twenty minutes late on the delivery. Customer gave me one star. One star because the city can't put up a proper detour sign.

Normally I stick to my routes. I have them memorized, I know which streets flood when it rains, I know where the potholes are. I don't need Waze. But I was behind and I got greedy with the time and now I have a one-star rating dragging down my average. If it drops below 4.7 they reduce your priority in the queue which means fewer orders which means less money.

That's what gets me — one bad rating from one shortcut I didn't need to take and now I'm spending the next two weeks being extra careful and extra polite trying to claw back points. All because I didn't just take the route I know. Lina says I obsess over the rating but she doesn't understand how the algorithm works. It's not just a number, it's whether I eat next month.
sources.nudge_response: Not yet. But I've seen it happen to guys at the parqueadero. One of them dropped to 4.5 and his orders went to nothing for a month. I'm not going to wait to find out firsthand.

Long day but the kind that feels right at the end. Fourteen deliveries, almost all in Chapinero which is my best zone — short distances, good tips, restaurants that have the food ready when I arrive. My rating came back up to 4.82. Took two weeks of clean runs but it's back where it should be.

Paid the bike insurance early. Lina looked at me funny because it's not due until June 15 but I told her I'd rather have it done. One less thing on the list. She gets it, she does the same thing with the tienda's distributor invoices — pays them the day they arrive even though she has thirty days. We're the same that way, both of us want the ledger clean.

Andrés never brought up the food truck again. I think he found someone else or maybe the whole thing fell apart. Either way I'm relieved. The savings account is at the highest it's been since December, and Lina and I are talking about maybe finally fixing the bathroom plumbing that's been leaking slow for months. Real things, things that last.

sources.journal_entry:
Made the kheer for Amma's birthday exactly how Nani used to make it. The cardamom from the Indian shop on Belgrave Road, not the supermarket stuff. Sat there stirring for forty-five minutes, watching the milk thicken, and it felt right. Like the kitchen back home, like Nani's hands guiding mine when I was eight years old and barely tall enough to reach the stove.

Called Amma after. She cried a little when I described the smell. Said she could almost taste it through the phone. She asked when I was coming next, and I told her maybe Diwali if I can get the time off. She said she will save her sari for me to help her drape it, like I always do.
sources.nudge_response: It is the only time I feel like her daughter again, not just someone who calls and sends money. She cannot do the pleats properly anymore, her hands shake. But she waits for me instead of asking the neighbour. It is our thing.

Brought leftover rotli from yesterday for lunch. Ate at my desk while filling in charts. Raj called to say he would be late picking up the groceries so I stopped at Tesco on the way home. Nothing interesting, just milk and bread and the biscuits Appa likes for when he visits next.

sources.journal_entry:
Had the conversation with Meera about Canada again. She has a job offer in Toronto, a good one, at a hospital that specializes in what she wants to do. I should be proud, and I am proud, but I also spent the whole dinner feeling like I was swallowing something sharp every time she talked about visa applications and apartment hunting.

She said I was being quiet and I said I was just tired. Which was not a lie, but it was not the whole truth either. The truth is I keep thinking about how I moved to England and left my parents behind and now my daughter wants to do the same to me. It is not fair to think that way. She has every right to build her life. I did the same thing.

But Amma stayed. My grandmother stayed. All the women in our family stayed close, within calling distance, within sari-draping distance, within "come over for chai" distance. And I broke that chain when I came here, and now Meera is breaking it further, and I cannot decide if this is progress or loss. Raj says I should be happy she is ambitious. I am happy. I am also something else that does not have a word.

Had a patient today who reminded me why I do this. Mrs. Okonkwo, eighty-three, recovering from a hip replacement. Her family is all in Nigeria and she kept asking when someone would come. I sat with her during my break, just talking about nothing—the food, the weather, whether the NHS would survive another winter. She held my hand and called me "daughter."

I know I cannot replace her actual children, but I can be there for the fifteen minutes between her medication rounds. Meera and I cooked together this evening. She asked me to teach her the dhokla recipe, the one from my mother's side that we only make for special occasions. Said she wanted to learn before she goes. We stood in the kitchen for two hours, me showing her how to test the batter, her writing everything down in that little notebook she keeps.

She asked about Nani, questions she has never asked before. What songs she used to sing, what her hands looked like, whether she was strict or soft. I found myself telling stories I had not thought about in years. The way Nani would wake before sunrise to pray. The way she saved the best pieces of mango for the grandchildren. Meera listened like she was memorising it all, and maybe she was. Maybe this is how it continues—not by staying in the same place, but by carrying the recipes and the stories wherever you go.
sources.nudge_response: Ask me again in a year when she is actually gone.

sources.journal_entry:
Still thinking about yesterday. Mentioned it to Abba over dinner and he said I should be grateful to have the position at all at my age, that most girls from our family are still finishing their degrees or married by now. He didn't mean it badly, I know that. He's proud of me in his way. But "grateful" is not the word I want to hear when someone erased my title in front of a client.

I wanted him to be angry for me. Instead he told me the story about how his boss at the textile mill passed him over for promotion three times before finally giving it to him. Like patience is the lesson. Like waiting is the same thing as earning. I've already earned this. I just need the people around me to see it the way I do.

Had a client visit today. The buyer from the UK account came for the factory walkthrough and the director introduced me as "one of our operations team." Not operations manager. Not the person who restructured the entire dispatch flow that got them their last three shipments on time. Just "one of our operations team."

I smiled and shook hands and walked them through the floor like nothing happened. The buyer asked good questions about our quality checks and I answered every single one without hesitating. By the end she was directing her questions to me, not the director. That felt like something. But the introduction stung. I'm not "one of" anything. I run that floor.

Bilal got the conference room booking system changed so department heads need to reserve through his assistant now. Used to be we could just block time directly on the calendar. He sent the email to all managers like it was a building-wide policy but I checked with procurement — it's just him adding a layer because someone double-booked the main boardroom last month.

It's a small thing. I know it's a small thing. But it means if I need the room for a client call at short notice, I have to go through his person first. I already sent a reply asking whether department heads with client-facing responsibilities could retain direct access. Kept it professional. He replied with a smiley face and "let's discuss offline." That means no.

I could go to the director about it but that feels like escalating a room booking dispute, which is exactly the kind of thing that makes a young manager look like she's overreacting. Ammi always says pick your fights carefully. She's right. But the small things add up and each one is a little bit of ground lost.
sources.nudge_response: The ability to move fast without asking permission. That's the whole reason the dispatch overhaul worked — I didn't wait for committees and approvals, I just did it. Every new process that adds a gatekeeper between me and getting things done slows me down. It's not about a room. It's about whether I can operate at my own pace or everyone else's.

sources.journal_entry:
Picked up a bubble tea order from Toa Payoh and the auntie at the shop asked if I ever get tired of riding around all day. Told her it beats sitting in an air-conditioned office watching my soul leak out through Excel spreadsheets. She laughed, said her son is trying to get her to hire a manager so she can rest. "Rest is for the dead," she said. I think about that sometimes—how some people need the motion, the doing, even when the body is telling them to stop.

Delivered to a condo in Newton. The guy who took the order was maybe mid-twenties, looked like he hadn't slept in days. Developer, probably. I remember that life—the midnight oil, the takeout containers stacking up. He tipped twenty bucks, which is rare. sources.journal_entry:

Priya finally said it out loud: she's scared. Not angry, not disappointed—scared. About what happens if I get injured, if the gig economy regulations change, if we never have enough for a real retirement. I wanted to argue, to list all the reasons this life is worth the risk. But looking at her face, I couldn't.

The thing is, I know she's not wrong. I've been telling myself that freedom is worth the instability, that I'm building something even if it doesn't look like what everyone else is building. But am I? Or am I just afraid of commitment dressed up as philosophy? The men at the shelter—they don't have the luxury of choosing instability. They're here because they have no choice. I'm here because I walked away from choices. There's a difference, and I'm not sure it's a flattering one.

Rode around Jurong West after we talked, just to clear my head. Ended up at a hawker center, eating prata and watching families come and go. A father helping his daughter with homework. An elderly couple sharing a plate of carrot cake. Ordinary scenes. The kind of life that requires showing up, day after day, even when it's boring. Especially when it's boring. Maybe that's its own kind of courage. Maybe I've been confusing restlessness with meaning.

Someone on a riders' Telegram group posted an article about gig workers "lacking ambition." Had to stop myself from typing a rant. Ambition isn't one-size-fits-all—some of us just refuse to let corporations define what success looks like.

New year. Priya wanted to watch the fireworks at Marina Bay but I couldn't face the crowds. We watched from the rooftop of our HDB instead, the view half-blocked by the neighboring tower. She fell asleep before midnight. I stayed up, counting the distant pops of light.

Made the usual resolutions in my head—save more, drink less, be more patient. But underneath all that, a different question kept surfacing: is this the life I want for another year? Not the delivery work specifically, but the uncertainty, the lack of a plan. I used to think planning was a trap. Now I'm wondering if having no plan is its own kind of trap. The kind where you wake up at fifty still "figuring things out."

One that doesn't feel like surrender.

sources.journal_entry:
Quiet week. Spent most of it in the library working through policy documents for chapter four. The snow has been heavy and cycling has been miserable but the bus is worse, so I keep at it. Had fika with Nils and our other housemate Sara on Wednesday. We talked about summer plans. Nils wants to do a hiking trip in Norway. Sara is going home to Malmö.

Cooked a big pot of lentil soup on Sunday that I've been eating all week. My mum called to check in, asked about the thesis timeline. I told her it's on track for June submission. She sounded relieved. Nothing eventful really. Just the steady rhythm of getting through January.

I told Lindqvist I'd pass on the Vattenfall liaison position. She took it well enough, said she understood, moved on to thesis feedback. I don't think she was surprised.

At the volunteer session on Saturday, one of the newer volunteers, a guy named Anders, made a comment about how some of the refugee families "don't even try to learn Swedish." He said it lightly, like it was just an observation. Two other volunteers nodded. I know for a fact that three of the families he's talking about attend SFI classes four mornings a week. One of the mothers, Amira, practices Swedish vocabulary with her kids at the kitchen table every evening. I've seen her notebook.

I didn't correct him. I thought about it. I opened my mouth and then just said something about how the language courses have long waiting lists, which is true but wasn't really the point. The point was that he was wrong and I sidestepped it instead of saying so directly. I keep doing this thing where I provide context instead of actually challenging what someone says. It feels diplomatic in the moment but afterward it just feels like cowardice dressed up as nuance.

Still thinking about the Vattenfall thing from this morning. Went for a walk along the river after dinner to try to sort it out and I'm not sure I managed. The thing is, I talk a lot about how corporations co-opt well-meaning people. I literally have a slide in my thesis presentation about it. "Institutional capture of reform narratives." That's my phrase. And now I'm being offered a small taste of exactly that.

Convenience is the word I keep coming back to. It would be convenient for my career. It would be convenient to tell myself I'm doing it for the right reasons. It would be convenient to let Professor Lindqvist handle the ethical questions while I just show up and take notes and put Vattenfall on my LinkedIn. That's what most people would do. That's what a practical person would do.

But I keep thinking about Fatima and her daughter from the refugee centre, and the Sámi reindeer herders whose grazing land got destroyed for a mine that Vattenfall then sold off when it became unprofitable. These are not abstract policy questions to me. Or at least they shouldn't be. If I take this liaison position, I become someone who files those things under "complicated" and moves on. And I've always told myself I wouldn't be that person. I just didn't expect the test to come from my own supervisor.

Had a supervision meeting with Professor Lindqvist today. She liked my chapter draft on enforcement gaps but said I need to address the "political feasibility" section more carefully. Fair enough. But then she casually mentioned that the department is being courted by Vattenfall for a research partnership and asked if I'd be interested in being a student liaison. Good for my CV, she said. Good connections.

Vattenfall is state-owned and technically pivoting toward renewables, but they also ran lignite mines in Germany for decades and their track record on indigenous Sámi land rights in the north is awful. I know this because I wrote a case study on it last year. Lindqvist knows I wrote it. She was my supervisor for that paper.

I should have said no on the spot. Instead I said I'd think about it. Because part of me is thinking about what it would look like on a job application. Part of me is doing the math on whether working with them from the inside might actually lead to something useful. And I hate that I'm even calculating like this, because I know that's how everyone justifies it. "Change from within." It's the oldest excuse in the book and I've heard it a hundred times from people I don't respect. But here I am, considering it for myself, because Professor Lindqvist smiled when she said my name and I liked being chosen.
sources.nudge_response: Both. But mostly the second one.

sources.journal_entry:
I'm so tired. Thesis crunch plus volunteering Saturdays plus a seminar on EU regulatory frameworks that runs three hours every Tuesday evening. I barely have energy to cook. Today I ordered Foodora twice. Both times it was from chains I know treat their delivery riders badly. I've seen the articles. I've shared the articles. And then I opened the app and ordered anyway because I couldn't face making pasta.

It's not that I forgot. I just didn't care enough in the moment. Or I cared but my tiredness won. I don't know which is worse. The riders are out there in January cold on bikes so I don't have to walk to my own kitchen. I can dress it up however I want but that's what happened.
Overheard Markus in the department kitchen making a joke about a Somali student's accent during a presentation. A couple of people laughed. I pretended I was busy with the coffee machine.

Spent the morning at Akademibokhandeln buying a new notebook for the semester and ended up at the Espresso House on Svartbäcksgatan after. I ordered a coffee and one of those wrapped sandwiches and then just stared at the packaging. Plastic wrap, plastic tray, a paper sleeve that probably isn't even recyclable. I've been reading about single-use packaging policy for my thesis for months. I know the numbers. I know what this stuff does. And I bought it anyway because I was hungry and didn't feel like walking home first.

It sounds ridiculous to feel bad about a sandwich wrapper. People would laugh. But it's the pattern that bugs me. I write about systemic failures in environmental policy and then I make the lazy choice when it's my own lunch. The gap between what I study and how I actually live keeps showing up in these small ways. I don't buy fast fashion anymore, I cycle, I eat less meat than I used to. But then there's this sandwich in a plastic coffin and I think, what's the point of any of it if I can't even get the small stuff right.

My housemate Nils would say I'm overthinking it. He'd say one sandwich wrapper doesn't matter. And he'd be technically correct. But I think the willingness to say "it doesn't matter" about any single thing is exactly how you end up not caring about anything.
sources.nudge_response: It's about whether I'm becoming someone who just talks.

sources.journal_entry:
New Year's Eve and I'm sitting at Erik's kitchen table while everyone else is in the living room watching some countdown special. His uncle was here earlier, going off about how the city council's new housing plan for asylum seekers is going to "ruin the neighbourhood." Nobody said anything. I didn't say anything. Had dinner with Lukas and Emma last night. They took me to some trendy place in Kreuzberg with exposed brick and cocktails that cost too much. We talked about the project, about their weekend plans, about nothing in particular.

At some point Emma asked how I ended up in Berlin. I told them the short version: got bored, saw a job posting, applied on a whim, got the offer, said yes. Lukas looked at me like I had told him I climbed Everest. "At 56?" he said. "My dad is 55 and he complains about learning new apps."

I did not know how to explain it to him. That staying in Amman felt like watching the same episode of a show I had already seen. That I needed to not know what was going to happen next. That the discomfort of being the oldest person in the room is better than the comfort of being exactly where everyone expected me to be.

I just shrugged and said, "Different people want different things."

sources.journal_entry:
Spent the morning going through invoices and realized we've burned through most of the Q1 budget already. The donation program is the biggest cost center and I know if I paused it for two quarters we'd actually be in the black for the first time since launch. My accountant has said this exact thing to me three times now. She's not wrong about the math.

Then I got an email from this woman in Flint — not even Flint proper, a small town forty minutes outside it — who got one of our units last spring. She said her daughter stopped getting rashes after they switched to our filter. Just a plain email, no dramatics. "I wanted you to know it's working. Thank you." That's it.

So no, I'm not pausing the donations. I'll figure out the money some other way. I always do, or I don't, and then I scramble and stress and eat takeout for a month. But I read that email and the spreadsheet argument just fell apart. I don't know how to explain that to my accountant. She'd probably say I'm being emotional. Maybe I am.

Last day of the year and I keep circling back to a decision I made this week. One of our suppliers offered me a deal on cheaper filter components — significantly cheaper, like enough to actually turn a real profit for once. The catch is they source from a factory in Guangzhou that I've seen flagged in two separate reports for dumping chemical waste into a river that feeds into local farmland. The reports aren't conclusive. There's plausible deniability. The factory passed its last audit.

I said yes. I placed the order Tuesday morning and I've felt off about it ever since. I keep telling myself it's pragmatic, that if the business goes under then nobody gets clean water from us, not the communities we donate to, nobody. You can't do good work if you can't keep the lights on. That's not wrong. But it also feels like exactly the kind of reasoning I used to hear from the guys at my old company when they were justifying selling marked-up devices to underfunded hospitals.

I don't know where the line is anymore. When I started this thing I thought I'd always know. Turns out running a mission-driven company doesn't protect you from making the same compromises as everyone else. It just makes you feel worse about them.
sources.nudge_response: Probably not entirely. But the fact that I even made the connection bothers me.

sources.journal_entry:
Went to the supplier meeting in Salem this morning about the spring distribution schedule. Drove past the reservation in Warm Springs on the way back — we installed twelve units there last October. Stopped in because I had time.

The community liaison, a guy named David, showed me around. The units are all still working. One family had rigged up an extra line to feed their greenhouse, which technically voids the warranty but honestly it was clever and I told him we'd look at a garden attachment for the next version. He laughed and said they'd already been thinking about that.

I left feeling steady. Not triumphant or anything close to it. Just like I was doing the thing I set out to do, in the specific place I set out to do it. The filters are filtering. The water is clean. David's family is using it to grow tomatoes in January. Sometimes the small evidence is enough to keep going. Drove home listening to the radio and didn't think about the budget once.
sources.nudge_response: Last week was numbers on a screen. Today was a guy growing tomatoes with clean water. Hard to argue with tomatoes.

Monday. Spent most of the day on logistics for the next batch of donation units. Coordinating shipping to three different sites in the Midwest and one in Appalachia. The Appalachia contact is a retired teacher who started a community health initiative out of her garage. She sends me handwritten letters, which I keep in a folder in my desk drawer. I should probably digitize them but there's something about the paper.

Had a call with my business partner, Lena, about the website redesign. She wants to add customer testimonials. I said fine but I don't want it to feel like we're using people's water problems as marketing copy. She said that's exactly what it is, and that's okay because it's also true. We went back and forth for twenty minutes and landed on letting people opt in to share their stories rather than us asking. Felt like the right call.

Ate leftover Thai food for dinner. Called my mom. She asked when I'm coming to visit and I said maybe February but I know I probably won't make it. Ordered new packing tape because we ran out. That's about it.

sources.journal_entry:
Meeting with Patricia from the environmental collective went better than expected. She's organizing a march next month about the deforestation in Guaviare and wants muralists to paint temporary pieces along the route. No committee, no brief, no polite rewrites — just paint what you see and feel. I said yes before I finished my coffee.

Spent the afternoon looking at satellite images of the cleared areas. It's staggering how fast the green disappears between one photo and the next. I started sketching a piece that layers the satellite view underneath a portrait of a family I met two years ago when I traveled there for a residency. They had this small farm at the edge of the forest. I keep wondering if that farm still exists.

The march is February 28. Patricia asked if I'd also speak at the rally beforehand. I told her I'd think about it. Speaking is different from painting — you can't hide behind brushstrokes. My mother would probably tell me to just do the mural and not draw attention to myself. She still worries about artists getting into trouble. But Patricia's right that the work means more when the person behind it shows up.

Good day at the workshop. One of the teenagers, David, showed up with a collage about his neighborhood flooding last year — garbage and river water mixed together. He made it beautiful without sanitizing it. I wish I had his nerve sometimes.
sources.nudge_response: He doesn't have a committee reviewing his work. He doesn't have a landlord or a mother who calls every Sunday asking if the grants are coming through. David just has cardboard and glue and something he needs to say. There's a freedom in that. I used to have it too, I think, before I learned all the reasons to hold back.

sources.journal_entry:
The Suba mural committee approved a revised design. I compromised — kept the river but softened the contamination imagery into something more abstract. Flowing blues and greens instead of the murky brown I originally wanted. They loved it. Said it was "inspiring." I nodded and thanked everyone and then sat in my car for ten minutes staring at the steering wheel.

I keep telling myself this is how it works. Public art is negotiation. You serve the community's vision, not just your own. And maybe the abstracted version will still land — maybe someone will look at those blues and sense that something is wrong underneath. That's the hope, anyway. But part of me keeps hearing David's collage in my head, all that directness, no translation required.

Called my cousin Marcela tonight. She's a lawyer in Medellin, very proper, always knows the right thing to say at family dinners. I told her about the march and she got quiet for a long time. Then she said, "Lu, you know how tia Rosa talks. Just be careful what you attach your name to." And I know she means it with love. I know the family worries. But careful has a cost too, and I'm starting to wonder how much it's adding up.
sources.nudge_response: Like a low hum. This background noise of things I chose not to say, images I softened, opinions I kept to dinner with close friends. None of it is dramatic on its own. But when I look at my portfolio from five years ago versus now, the work is technically better but quieter. The edges got filed down somewhere. I'm not sure when it happened exactly.

sources.journal_entry: Finished the base layer of the march mural today. It's honest work. Stood back and felt something I haven't felt in a while — that the paint is saying exactly what I mean.

Family group chat exploded today. My uncle Hernando posted a news article about the Guaviare deforestation — same issue the march is about — and wrote "sad but what can you do, these people need to eat." I started typing a response three times. Deleted all of them.

It's not that I disagree entirely — the economics of it are real and I've seen the poverty firsthand. But the framing drives me insane. "What can you do" as if there are no choices, no policies, no one responsible. I wanted to write about the logging companies, the lack of enforcement, the families who actually live there being displaced. But Hernando is my mother's brother and I can already picture the awkward silence at Easter dinner if I go off in the group chat.

So I sent a sad emoji and closed the app. Mature. Professional. Utterly hollow. Patricia would have posted a five-paragraph essay with citations. I admire that and also cannot imagine being that person in my own family. The mural for the march — that I can do. Words in the chat where my grandmother can see them — that's different somehow, and I hate that it's different.

The Suba mural committee approved a revised design. I compromised — kept the river but softened the contamination imagery into something more abstract. Flowing blues and greens instead of the murky brown I originally wanted. They loved it. Said it was "inspiring." I nodded and thanked everyone and then sat in my car for ten minutes staring at the steering wheel.

I keep telling myself this is how it works. Public art is negotiation. You serve the community's vision, not just your own. And maybe the abstracted version will still land — maybe someone will look at those blues and sense that something is wrong underneath. That's the hope, anyway. But part of me keeps hearing David's collage in my head, all that directness, no translation required.

Called my cousin Marcela tonight. She's a lawyer in Medellin, very proper, always knows the right thing to say at family dinners. I told her about the march and she got quiet for a long time. Then she said, "Lu, you know how tia Rosa talks. Just be careful what you attach your name to." And I know she means it with love. I know the family worries. But careful has a cost too, and I'm starting to wonder how much it's adding up.
sources.nudge_response: Like a low hum. This background noise of things I chose not to say, images I softened, opinions I kept to dinner with close friends. None of it is dramatic on its own. But when I look at my portfolio from five years ago versus now, the work is technically better but quieter. The edges got filed down somewhere. I'm not sure when it happened exactly.

sources.journal_entry:
Meeting with Patricia from the environmental collective went better than expected. She's organizing a march next month about the deforestation in Guaviare and wants muralists to paint temporary pieces along the route. No committee, no brief, no polite rewrites — just paint what you see and feel. I said yes before I finished my coffee.

Spent the afternoon looking at satellite images of the cleared areas. It's staggering how fast the green disappears between one photo and the next. I started sketching a piece that layers the satellite view underneath a portrait of a family I met two years ago when I traveled there for a residency. They had this small farm at the edge of the forest. I keep wondering if that farm still exists.

The march is February 28. Patricia asked if I'd also speak at the rally beforehand. I told her I'd think about it. Speaking is different from painting — you can't hide behind brushstrokes. My mother would probably tell me to just do the mural and not draw attention to myself. She still worries about artists getting into trouble. But Patricia's right that the work means more when the person behind it shows up.

Good day at the workshop. One of the teenagers, David, showed up with a collage about his neighborhood flooding last year — garbage and river water mixed together. He made it beautiful without sanitizing it. I wish I had his nerve sometimes.
sources.nudge_response: He doesn't have a committee reviewing his work. He doesn't have a landlord or a mother who calls every Sunday asking if the grants are coming through. David just has cardboard and glue and something he needs to say. There's a freedom in that. I used to have it too, I think, before I learned all the reasons to hold back.

sources.journal_entry: Can't sleep. Kept redoing the sketch for the Suba district mural because the committee wants something "uplifting" and every version I draw keeps drifting toward the river contamination. My hand knows what it wants to make but the brief says otherwise.
sources.nudge_response: They'd smile politely and tell me to try again. That's how these things work — you read the room, you adjust, you keep the project alive. It's not about my sketch.

But Patricia asked me specifically because she said artists need to be visible, not just their work. And she's not wrong. I just wish being visible didn't feel like standing in traffic.

sources.journal_entry:
Same day, later. The Suba committee emailed asking if I'd be interested in a second mural for a park renovation. They mentioned they saw "my recent public work" and want something with that "raw quality." I read the email four times.

On one hand — this is exactly what I wanted. Someone seeing the unfiltered version and asking for more of it. The kind of work where I don't have to translate myself into something palatable. But then I read the rest of the email and there are guidelines, approval stages, a heritage review board. The same machinery. And I started wondering whether they want the rawness or the idea of rawness, something that looks honest but still fits neatly into a park renovation plan.

I haven't replied yet. Part of me wants to say yes and fight for the real version from inside the process. Part of me wants to say no and keep doing the kind of work where I answer only to the paint. And there's a third part — the loudest one, honestly — that says: just be grateful someone asked, don't be difficult, say thank you and show up and do good work within the lines. That voice sounds a lot like my mother. I don't think she's wrong. I don't think she's entirely right either. Going to sleep on it.

The march was last Friday. I spoke. It was short — maybe three minutes — and my voice shook the entire time. I talked about how art can hold what policy reports can't, the texture of a place disappearing, the face of someone losing their home to a decision made in an office they'll never enter. Patricia squeezed my arm when I sat down. The crowd was bigger than I expected.

My mother hasn't mentioned it. Marcela sent a one-word text: "brave." I don't know if that's approval or a warning. Hernando liked a photo of the mural on Patricia's Instagram, which is confusing. The sky didn't fall. The family didn't fracture. I feel lighter than I have in weeks, and also a little raw, like a layer of skin is missing. Not sure if I'd do it again. But I'm glad I did it once.
sources.nudge_response: That nobody was angry. I'd built this whole catastrophe in my head — my mother crying, my uncle calling me irresponsible, the family closing ranks. None of it happened. The worst outcome was silence, and silence turned out to be bearable. The actual surprise was that the shaking in my voice didn't make me less credible. People came up to me afterward and said it made them listen harder. I don't know what to do with that yet.

sources.journal_entry: Finished the base layer of the march mural today. It's honest work. Stood back and felt something I haven't felt in a while — that the paint is saying exactly what I mean.

Family group chat exploded today. My uncle Hernando posted a news article about the Guaviare deforestation — same issue the march is about — and wrote "sad but what can you do, these people need to eat." I started typing a response three times. Deleted all of them.

It's not that I disagree entirely — the economics of it are real and I've seen the poverty firsthand. But the framing drives me insane. "What can you do" as if there are no choices, no policies, no one responsible. I wanted to write about the logging companies, the lack of enforcement, the families who actually live there being displaced. But Hernando is my mother's brother and I can already picture the awkward silence at Easter dinner if I go off in the group chat.

So I sent a sad emoji and closed the app. Mature. Professional. Utterly hollow. Patricia would have posted a five-paragraph essay with citations. I admire that and also cannot imagine being that person in my own family. The mural for the march — that I can do. Words in the chat where my grandmother can see them — that's different somehow, and I hate that it's different.

Called my cousin Marcela tonight. She's a lawyer in Medellin, very proper, always knows the right thing to say at family dinners. I told her about the march and she got quiet for a long time. Then she said, "Lu, you know how tia Rosa talks. Just be careful what you attach your name to." And I know she means it with love. I know the family worries. sources.nudge_response: Like a low hum. This background noise of things I chose not to say, images I softened, opinions I kept to dinner with close friends. None of it is dramatic on its own. sources.journal_entry:
Meeting with Patricia from the environmental collective went better than expected. She's organizing a march next month about the deforestation in Guaviare and wants muralists to paint temporary pieces along the route. No committee, no brief, no polite rewrites — just paint what you see and feel. I said yes before I finished my coffee.

Spent the afternoon looking at satellite images of the cleared areas. It's staggering how fast the green disappears between one photo and the next. I started sketching a piece that layers the satellite view underneath a portrait of a family I met two years ago when I traveled there for a residency. They had this small farm at the edge of the forest. I keep wondering if that farm still exists.

The march is February 28. Patricia asked if I'd also speak at the rally beforehand. I told her I'd think about it. Speaking is different from painting — you can't hide behind brushstrokes. My mother would probably tell me to just do the mural and not draw attention to myself. She still worries about artists getting into trouble. But Patricia's right that the work means more when the person behind it shows up.

sources.journal_entry:
Same day, later. The Suba committee emailed asking if I'd be interested in a second mural for a park renovation. They mentioned they saw "my recent public work" and want something with that "raw quality." I read the email four times.

On one hand — this is exactly what I wanted. Someone seeing the unfiltered version and asking for more of it. The kind of work where I don't have to translate myself into something palatable. But then I read the rest of the email and there are guidelines, approval stages, a heritage review board. The same machinery. And I started wondering whether they want the rawness or the idea of rawness, something that looks honest but still fits neatly into a park renovation plan.

I haven't replied yet. Part of me wants to say yes and fight for the real version from inside the process. Part of me wants to say no and keep doing the kind of work where I answer only to the paint. And there's a third part — the loudest one, honestly — that says: just be grateful someone asked, don't be difficult, say thank you and show up and do good work within the lines. That voice sounds a lot like my mother. I don't think she's wrong. I don't think she's entirely right either. Going to sleep on it.

The march was last Friday. I spoke. It was short — maybe three minutes — and my voice shook the entire time. I talked about how art can hold what policy reports can't, the texture of a place disappearing, the face of someone losing their home to a decision made in an office they'll never enter. Patricia squeezed my arm when I sat down. The crowd was bigger than I expected.

My mother hasn't mentioned it. Marcela sent a one-word text: "brave." I don't know if that's approval or a warning. Hernando liked a photo of the mural on Patricia's Instagram, which is confusing. The sky didn't fall. The family didn't fracture. I feel lighter than I have in weeks, and also a little raw, like a layer of skin is missing. Not sure if I'd do it again. But I'm glad I did it once.
sources.nudge_response: That nobody was angry. I'd built this whole catastrophe in my head — my mother crying, my uncle calling me irresponsible, the family closing ranks. None of it happened. The worst outcome was silence, and silence turned out to be bearable. The actual surprise was that the shaking in my voice didn't make me less credible. People came up to me afterward and said it made them listen harder. I don't know what to do with that yet.

sources.journal_entry:
Picked up two extra shifts this week. Covered for Anja on Tuesday and stayed late Thursday for the new grad's first code situation. She froze at the monitors and I had to talk her through it step by step while doing compressions. Afterwards she thanked me and I told her that's just how it goes the first time.

Thomas made a comment about never seeing me anymore. Fair. I've been home maybe four evenings this month. But the ward is short-staffed and I'm trying to show I can handle the load. Being reliable matters when you're trying to move up.

Got the feedback from Dr. Weiss today about the cardiac arrest protocol I revised. He actually read the whole thing. Said it was thorough, well-researched, that he'd pass it to the department head for review. I stood there nodding like it was no big deal but inside I was buzzing. This is the first time anyone senior has taken something I wrote seriously.

I've been working on that protocol for three months. Stayed after shifts, dug through research papers during lunch, ran the numbers on our ward's response times. Most of it I did on my own time because nobody asked me to. I just wanted to prove that I could contribute beyond bedside care. That I'm not just someone who checks vitals and changes IV bags.

After he left I went to the break room and just sat there for a minute. Didn't even get coffee. Just needed a second to let it land. It felt real. Like something I made mattered.

sources.journal_entry:
Finished the second panel for the Kungsbacka commission today. When I stepped back and looked at it hung up on the temporary rail, I actually liked it. Not in the way where you talk yourself into liking something because you spent forty hours on it. I genuinely liked the way the indigo section catches the light from the side window. I stood there for a while just looking.

Then I let myself leave the studio at four instead of pushing through to six. Walked down to the harbor and sat on the bench near the ferry terminal. Bought a cardamom bun from the kiosk. It was still warm. The whole walk home I felt good, and for once I didn't ruin it by calculating whether I'd done enough that day to justify leaving early. I just walked.

Ate the last of the good cheese after lunch today, the one from the market on Saturday. Just sat at the table with it and a coffee and some crackers. Then spent the rest of the afternoon annoyed at myself for not going straight back to the loom, as if ten minutes of sitting with cheese somehow cancelled out the six hours I'd already put in.

Writing again because something small happened after I put this down earlier. I was brushing my teeth before bed and noticed I'd left the studio light on, so I went in to switch it off. Ended up standing there in the dark with just the hallway light coming through the door, looking at the panels. They looked different at night. Quieter.

I almost went back to the loom. There was that pull, that voice that says you could get another hour in. But I didn't. I turned the light off and closed the door. It felt like a small right thing, choosing to stop. Going to bed now.

sources.journal_entry:
Long day but a strangely satisfying one. Woke up early because the light was doing that thing it does in November here, grey but somehow bright at the same time, and I wanted to see how it would fall across the third panel. So I was in the studio by seven, still in my wool socks, coffee going cold on the shelf behind me because I forgot about it.

Worked through until about one without stopping. Not because I was forcing myself but because the work was pulling me along. The warp tension on the new section was exactly right and the shuttle was moving the way I wanted. Those stretches don't happen every day and when they do you just stay in them.

After I stopped I heated up leftover soup and ate it standing at the kitchen counter, which I know isn't a proper lunch but it was warm and salty and I was hungry enough that it tasted better than it had any right to. Then I lay down on the sofa for twenty minutes. Just lay there with the radio on low. Didn't set a timer, didn't think about what I should be doing instead. I was tired enough that my body made the decision for me and I didn't argue with it. The afternoon I spent doing the boring parts, measuring and marking the next section, but even that felt okay because the morning had been so good.

Teaching day. The folk school wanted me to stay for the staff meeting after my afternoon class, so I did. It ran an hour longer than it needed to because people kept going in circles about the spring exhibition. I had opinions but didn't push them because I'm only there two days a week and it's not my place to take over other people's planning.

Someone asked what I'm working on in my own studio and I gave a short answer. I don't like talking about commissioned work with the folk school crowd because it always turns into a conversation about whether commercial work counts as real art. It does, for the record. The Kungsbacka library is going to have my panels on their walls for the next twenty years. But I don't feel like defending that every time.

sources.journal_entry:
Had the juniors present their oral history drafts today and it reminded me exactly why I do not want to hand this over to a shrink-wrapped curriculum. Daniela interviewed her grandmother about the Vanport flood. She brought in a photograph she had never seen before, one her grandmother kept in a shoebox for sixty years. The whole class went quiet.

You cannot buy that in a textbook package. You cannot script it. It comes from giving kids room to chase something that matters to them and getting out of the way. I told Daniela after class that her project was one of the best I have seen in nearly three decades, and she looked genuinely shocked, like no one had told her she was good at anything academic before.

Drove home with the windows down even though it was drizzling. Put on the Coltrane record Linda used to play on Friday evenings. Poured a glass of wine. Felt like myself for the first time all week. Whatever happens with the curriculum decision, today was proof that my way of teaching works. That has to count for something.

Could not sleep. Kept replaying the staff meeting from this afternoon. Reynolds stood up there with her slides about "instructional coherence" and basically told us the district is adopting a packaged curriculum for all social studies classes starting next fall. Everyone just nodded. I raised my hand and asked what happens to the electives I built. She said we would "discuss individual cases" later. That is code for no.

Twelve years of that program. I designed every unit, every field trip route, every community partner relationship. And some vendor's binder is supposed to replace it because test scores dipped two points in a grade level I do not even teach. I should have pushed harder in the meeting. Or maybe I should not have said anything at all. I do not know which one sits worse.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly, the room. Everyone had already accepted it. I looked around and realized I was the only one who cared enough to object, and that made me feel old and stubborn rather than right.

sources.journal_entry:
End of the year crunch is starting to show. Had three classes back to back this morning and by fourth period I was basically on autopilot. The juniors are doing their neighborhood oral history projects, which is the one part of the semester I still genuinely look forward to, but even that felt like pushing a boulder today.

Stayed late grading because I refuse to bring that stack home again. The custodian, Marco, stopped by and we talked for twenty minutes about his kid's Little League team. Probably the best conversation I had all day. Sometimes the building feels more like mine after everyone leaves. Quieter. No one asking me to fill out forms or attend alignment meetings.

Came home, heated up leftover chili, and sat in the garage for a while not really doing anything with the lathe. Just sitting. The dog parked herself at my feet. That was enough for tonight.

The 2016 kid, well she is twenty-five now, told me she works for the city planning office and still thinks about the neighborhood mapping project. I did not bring up the curriculum stuff. But it sat with me the whole drive home.

Graded the last round of oral history presentations tonight. Gave Daniela's project full marks and wrote her a recommendation letter she did not ask for. I figure if the program disappears next year, at least this cohort got the real version. The garage smelled like fresh-cut walnut when I came inside. The dog was asleep on the sawdust pile again. sources.journal_entry:
Farhan's abba made a comment at chai today. We were talking about schools — Zara is still over a year away from nursery but I've already been researching options, visiting campuses on my own, making a shortlist. I was explaining why I liked Beaconhouse over the closer option and he just looked at Farhan and said "let's not rush, she's still in diapers."

He wasn't even talking to me. I was mid-sentence and he redirected the conversation to his son like I wasn't sitting right there. Like the fact that I'd done the research was irrelevant because the decision will ultimately be made between the men.

And Farhan just nodded. Didn't say "actually Nadia's been looking into this" or "let's hear her out." Just nodded and changed the subject to cricket.

I went to the bedroom after and sat on the bed for a while. Zara was playing on the floor and babbling at me and I couldn't even engage with her properly because I was running the scene over and over. The look on his father's face. Not dismissive exactly — more like I simply didn't register as someone whose input counted.

I keep telling myself this is just how his generation is. But my generation is sitting right there too, not saying anything. That's the part that stings.

The dinner with Farhan's cousin happened. I'd planned the whole menu — mutton karahi, raita, kheer for dessert. Had the ingredients out by noon, started prep early so I could plate everything properly before they arrived.

Then Ammi came into the kitchen around four and just started making her own daal and a salad. Didn't ask. Didn't check with me. Just walked in and started chopping onions. When I said I had the menu handled, she said "it's not enough dishes for guests, they'll think we're not hospitable."

So we served her food too, and of course the cousin's wife complimented the daal specifically. Ammi smiled. I smiled. Nobody mentioned the karahi. I cleared the table afterward and Farhan told me "dinner was nice" like it was all one collective effort. It wasn't.

I know I should just let it go. I didn't. Still haven't.
sources.nudge_response: I think it's that nobody noticed the difference between what I did and what she added. Like my effort and her last-minute addition were equal. I planned for hours. She walked in and overrode me in twenty minutes. And the worst part is maybe she was right — maybe the table did look better with more dishes. But that doesn't change the fact that she didn't ask. And nobody saw that it mattered to me. I keep thinking about Ammi ji walking in and just starting to chop. Like the kitchen was hers. It still is, isn't it. That's the thing I can't let go of.
