It's his card linked to the account. I can't just do it myself. Sat there watching the clock feeling completely stuck.

sources.journal_entry:
Tuesday. Normal. Took Zara to the park in the morning. She's walking better now, holding onto my hand less. Talked to another mother there — her son is two months older than Zara. She asked where I got Zara's shoes. I told her. She asked about the brand review I posted last week. Turns out she follows my page. Didn't expect that.

Came home, gave Zara lunch, put her down. Ammi was watching a drama in the lounge. We had chai together. She asked if I'd heard from my mother, I said I'll call her this weekend. It was fine. Civil. Almost comfortable, which happens sometimes and I never know what to make of it.

Farhan brought home gulab jamun from the mithai shop near his office. Zara had a tiny piece and made a mess. I took a photo but decided not to post it — some things don't need to be content.

In the evening I went through my DMs and replied to questions about the stroller review. One woman said she bought the one I recommended and loves it. Wrote her a long reply. It's a strange feeling, being the person other people check with before spending their money. Not strange bad. Just new.
sources.nudge_response: It feels normal honestly. Like how it should be. If you put in the work to learn something properly, people should listen. That's not complicated. The weird part isn't that strangers ask my opinion — the weird part is that people in my own house don't.

sources.journal_entry:
Can't sleep, writing this in bed with the phone brightness way down so Farhan doesn't wake up. Still thinking about the reel. Three hundred views now. A parenting micro-influencer with eight thousand followers commented and said "great breakdown, following." That's real. That's someone who creates content full-time validating what I put together in my living room while Zara napped.

I think the reason it feels different from anything else is that nobody handed this to me. Nobody's mother-in-law set it up. Nobody's husband transferred money so I could do it. I used the free version of a video editing app, my phone camera, and my own knowledge. Start to finish, every choice was mine. What to review, what to say, how to frame it, when to post.

And the feedback loop is immediate and clear. If people like it, the numbers go up. If they don't, they don't. There's no ambiguity, no smiling politely while someone undoes your work.

I know it's just Instagram. I know it's not a career yet. But sitting here in the dark looking at three hundred strangers who chose to watch something I made — it's the first time in a long time I feel like I'm steering something. Not asking permission. Not waiting for someone to agree. Just doing it and seeing the results. I needed that tonight.

Zara learned to say "Ammi" properly today. Not the half-syllable thing she does — actually looked at me and said it clearly. Twice. The second time she was reaching for me while Ammi was holding her, which was honestly satisfying in a way I shouldn't probably admit.

Rest of the day was normal. Laundry, feeding schedule, cleaning up after lunch. Farhan came home around seven, ate, watched something on his phone, went to sleep. We barely talked. Not fighting or anything, just the usual weeknight nothing.

I posted a reel in the evening — unboxing a diaper bag a brand sent me for free. First time getting a free product. I didn't pitch them, they found my page and reached out. Two hundred views in the first hour. Comments from women I don't know. One said she'd been waiting for someone to review that exact bag. These are strangers treating my opinion like it matters.

Funny how that works. In this house I rearrange one drawer and it gets redone. Online I recommend a product and people actually listen. Maybe that says something about the house or maybe it says something about the internet. Either way, the reel got more engagement than anything I've posted before. I screenshot the analytics before bed.

Farhan's abba made a comment at chai today. We were talking about schools — Zara is still over a year away from nursery but I've already been researching options, visiting campuses on my own, making a shortlist. I was explaining why I liked Beaconhouse over the closer option and he just looked at Farhan and said "let's not rush, she's still in diapers."

He wasn't even talking to me. I was mid-sentence and he redirected the conversation to his son like I wasn't sitting right there. Like the fact that I'd done the research was irrelevant because the decision will ultimately be made between the men.

And Farhan just nodded. Didn't say "actually Nadia's been looking into this" or "let's hear her out." Just nodded and changed the subject to cricket.

I went to the bedroom after and sat on the bed for a while. Zara was playing on the floor and babbling at me and I couldn't even engage with her properly because I was running the scene over and over. The look on his father's face. Not dismissive exactly — more like I simply didn't register as someone whose input counted.

I keep telling myself this is just how his generation is. But my generation is sitting right there too, not saying anything. That's the part that stings.

The dinner with Farhan's cousin happened. I'd planned the whole menu — mutton karahi, raita, kheer for dessert. Had the ingredients out by noon, started prep early so I could plate everything properly before they arrived.

Then Ammi came into the kitchen around four and just started making her own daal and a salad. Didn't ask. Didn't check with me. Just walked in and started chopping onions. When I said I had the menu handled, she said "it's not enough dishes for guests, they'll think we're not hospitable."

So we served her food too, and of course the cousin's wife complimented the daal specifically. Ammi smiled. I smiled. Nobody mentioned the karahi. I cleared the table afterward and Farhan told me "dinner was nice" like it was all one collective effort. It wasn't.

I know I should just let it go. I didn't. Still haven't.
sources.nudge_response: I think it's that nobody noticed the difference between what I did and what she added. Like my effort and her last-minute addition were equal. I planned for hours. She walked in and overrode me in twenty minutes. And the worst part is maybe she was right — maybe the table did look better with more dishes. But that doesn't change the fact that she didn't ask. And nobody saw that it mattered to me. I keep thinking about Ammi ji walking in and just starting to chop. Like the kitchen was hers. It still is, isn't it. That's the thing I can't let go of.

sources.journal_entry:

Ammi asked what I was doing on my phone all afternoon. I said "work." She gave me that look but didn't push it. Farhan actually told her later that my page is "doing well" which is the most he's ever acknowledged it. Small win. But I'll take it because I built that page from nothing — every photo, every caption, every reply to every comment. That's mine.

Needed Farhan to transfer money for Zara's follow-up appointment. He said he'd do it after work. After work became after dinner. After dinner became "I'll do it in the morning." I asked three times. It's his card linked to the account. I can't just do it myself. Sat there watching the clock feeling completely stuck.
sources.nudge_response: Both. Neither. It's about the fact that something that matters to me — my daughter's appointment — depends on someone else remembering to press a button on their phone. And I just have to sit and hope they get around to it. That's the part that makes my jaw tight.

sources.journal_entry:
So apparently Ammi decided to rearrange Zara's entire wardrobe while I was out getting groceries this morning. When I came back, all the drawers were different. She'd sorted everything by fabric weight — cotton in one drawer, winter things in another — and thrown out two outfits she decided were "too tight." One of them I'd bought last week.

I didn't even know what to say. Farhan was at work. I just stood in the nursery holding the grocery bags and looking at it. She came up behind me and said "I organized it properly, it was a mess." Like she was doing me a favor. Like the way I had it was wrong and she was correcting it.

I wanted to say this is my daughter's room, these are her clothes, and I decide what goes where. But what actually came out was "okay, thank you." Because what happens if I push back? She tells Farhan. Farhan tells me to keep the peace. His father gives me that look at dinner. And then everyone acts like I'm the one creating problems in the house.

It's such a small thing. Drawers. Clothes. But it wasn't about the clothes. It was about the fact that she walked into that room and rearranged it without even asking me. Like my choices in my own daughter's room need her approval.
sources.nudge_response: It's not about what it would cost me. It's about the fact that I shouldn't have to fight for something this basic. Every house has a pecking order, that's just how joint family works. I know that. But knowing it and being fine with it are two different things.

sources.journal_entry:
Zara had her eighteen-month checkup today. Doctor said weight and height are both tracking well. I'd been worried because Ammi kept saying she looks thin, that I'm not feeding her enough roti, the usual. The doctor didn't say any of that. She said the diet plan I put together is fine.

Came home, made aloo paratha for lunch, put Zara down for her nap. Farhan called during his break. He wants his cousin's family to come for dinner on Friday. I told him fine but I'm deciding the menu, not his mother. He laughed like I was joking. I wasn't.

Spent the afternoon editing two product review posts. One got decent engagement — forty-seven likes, twelve comments. Not much by any standard but the comments were real questions from other mothers asking my opinion on the brand. That part felt good.

Spent most of the morning at the hospital with Mother again. Her blood pressure readings have been erratic and the doctors want to adjust her medication. I sat in that waiting room scrolling through my literature review notes, pretending I could focus on methodology while watching the clock. By the time we got home and I made sure she ate lunch and took her pills, half the day was gone.

I signed up for this PhD knowing it would be challenging. What I didn't account for was how often life would demand I put it aside. My advisor sent a gentle reminder about the chapter draft due next week. I haven't written a single new paragraph in twelve days.

Strange to be the oldest person in every seminar, still learning to say "I need more time" without feeling like a failure.
sources.nudge_response:
I suppose it looks like proving everyone right — my former colleagues who raised eyebrows when I resigned, my brother who thinks this degree is a vanity project. They expected me to enjoy retirement properly: travel with my husband, babysit grandchildren, maybe volunteer at the temple. Instead I'm chasing citations at fifty-eight.

But if I'm honest, the deeper fear is wasting whatever sharp years I have left. There's a clock now that wasn't there at thirty. Every delay feels heavier.

My daughter called crying at eleven last night. Her husband is traveling for work again and the baby has been colicky for three days straight. She asked if I could come stay for the weekend to help. I said yes before she finished the sentence, and then hung up and stared at my calendar.

The weekend is when I was supposed to finally sit down and write. I had blocked off Saturday and Sunday entirely — no hospital visits, no groceries, no family dinners. Just me, my laptop, and the quiet of an empty apartment. I was looking forward to it the way you look forward to a small holiday.

Now I'm packing a bag instead. And I feel terrible for resenting it, even a little. She's my daughter. She's exhausted and alone and I'm her mother. What kind of person calculates their writing time when their child needs them?

But another part of me is tired of always being the one who drops everything. My husband won't go — he says he's "not good with babies," as if that's a permanent condition and not something you can simply choose to do. So it falls to me. It always falls to me.

I'm bringing my laptop. I'm telling myself I'll write at night after the baby sleeps. We both know that's not going to happen.

The hot pot was wonderful. Crowded restaurant, too loud to hear anything, steam fogging my glasses every time I reached for the lamb slices. Xiao-Wei sat next to me and we discovered we both grew up eating the same brand of sesame paste that nobody makes anymore.

Funny how food carries so much. My mother used to mix that paste into noodles on cold days. Now I'm in a room full of people young enough to be my children, fishing mushrooms out of boiling broth, and for two hours I wasn't thinking about deadlines or hospital appointments or whether I'm falling behind.

I ordered a second round of the taro dumplings even though nobody asked. Sometimes you have to be the one who says "let's keep going." They didn't seem to mind.

Walked home through the night market after. Bought a bag of pineapple cakes I definitely don't need. Didn't feel guilty about it even once.
sources.nudge_response:
It is different. No one needed me to be anywhere else. No responsibility I was avoiding by being there. I was just having dinner because I wanted to, with people who expected nothing from me except to pass the chili oil.

Maybe that's the permission I've been missing — not from anyone else but from the situation itself. When there's no competing obligation, the enjoyment feels clean.

Called my brother back. Told him I'd handle the restaurant booking but the guest list and gifts are his responsibility this year. He sputtered but eventually agreed.

Then I made myself a proper cup of oolong and sat on the balcony watching the city lights come on. It's cold but I wrapped myself in the blanket my daughter gave me and stayed out there until the tea was gone.

Small rebellion. Small pleasure. Both felt earned.

Three hours later and I still haven't called him back. My husband thinks I'm overreacting. "He didn't mean it that way," he said. "You know how he is."

Yes. I know exactly how he is. I've known for fifty years. That's precisely the problem.

When I gave up my career advancement to take care of our father during his illness, my brother sent flowers. When I spent six months coordinating Mother's hip surgery and recovery while working full time, my brother called on weekends. When I finally, finally decided to do something entirely for myself — to pursue this degree I've wanted since I was thirty — he treats it like a hobby I can set aside.

I'm not even angry at him specifically anymore. I'm angry at the role I've been assigned in this family, the one I keep accepting because the alternative feels like abandoning people I love. The reliable one. The one who handles things. The one whose own aspirations come last because someone has to hold everything together.

My chest hurts. I should make tea and calm down but I don't want to calm down. I want to stay angry long enough to remember this feeling the next time I'm tempted to say yes to something I don't have room for.

sources.journal_entry:
Passed. The committee seemed genuinely interested in my research, asked questions I hadn't anticipated but could answer because I've been living inside this topic for two years. Dr. Huang said my clinical experience brought a perspective the literature lacks. Coming from him, that means something.

Called my mother first. She asked if this meant I was finally finished and I had to explain that no, there's still the dissertation, probably two more years. She sighed and said at least I'd be a doctor eventually and she could tell her mahjong friends. I'll take it.

My daughter sent flowers. Pink lilies and a card that said "So proud of you, Mom." I cried in my office for a solid five minutes.

Tonight my husband is taking me to the French restaurant we've been saying we'll try for a year. White tablecloths, a tasting menu, the whole indulgence. I bought a new dress — dark green, silk blend, probably too expensive. I'm going to enjoy every course without thinking about calories or cost or whether I should be home checking on Mother.

For once, I'm just going to let myself have the moment.

This degree might be a vanity project. It might be impractical at my age. It might mean missing things, disappointing people, constantly negotiating between who I want to be and who everyone needs me to be.

But today, sitting in that conference room, defending ideas I've been developing for two years — I felt like the version of myself I imagined when I was twenty-five and too afraid to try. She showed up after all. Just took her a few decades.

Comprehensive exams tomorrow. Studied at the library until closing, then walked the long way home through the park where the winter jasmine is blooming.

Stopped for beef noodle soup at my usual place. The owner remembered my order — extra green onion, light on the chili. There's something comforting about being known.

Feel as ready as I'll ever be.

Called my brother back. Told him I'd handle the restaurant booking but the guest list and gifts are his responsibility this year. He sputtered but eventually agreed.

Then I made myself a proper cup of oolong and sat on the balcony watching the city lights come on. It's cold but I wrapped myself in the blanket my daughter gave me and stayed out there until the tea was gone.

Small rebellion. Small pleasure. Both felt earned.

Three hours later and I still haven't called him back. My husband thinks I'm overreacting. "He didn't mean it that way," he said. "You know how he is."

Yes. I know exactly how he is. I've known for fifty years. That's precisely the problem.

When I gave up my career advancement to take care of our father during his illness, my brother sent flowers. When I spent six months coordinating Mother's hip surgery and recovery while working full time, my brother called on weekends. When I finally, finally decided to do something entirely for myself — to pursue this degree I've wanted since I was thirty — he treats it like a hobby I can set aside.

I'm not even angry at him specifically anymore. I'm angry at the role I've been assigned in this family, the one I keep accepting because the alternative feels like abandoning people I love. The reliable one. The one who handles things. The one whose own aspirations come last because someone has to hold everything together.

My chest hurts. I should make tea and calm down but I don't want to calm down. I want to stay angry long enough to remember this feeling the next time I'm tempted to say yes to something I don't have room for.
sources.nudge_response:
Terrifying. And also, maybe, free?

I think about my classmate Hui-Fang who went to Portugal last month just because she wanted to see the ocean. She didn't ask permission or coordinate schedules. She just booked a ticket and went.

I can't even imagine making a decision that clean. Every choice I make has to pass through a filter of who else it affects, who will be disappointed, who will need me to be somewhere else. I've been doing it so long I don't know if I'd recognize myself without it.

But there's something appealing about the idea of someone else handling Mother's birthday. Just this once. Just to see what happens.

My brother called this morning to remind me that Mother's 80th birthday is in three weeks and "everyone is expecting a proper celebration." By everyone he means himself and the cousins who haven't visited her in months. By proper celebration he means I'll be the one booking the restaurant, organizing the guest list, and making sure the gift is tasteful enough to photograph.

I told him I'm in the middle of my comprehensive exams and he laughed. Actually laughed. Said something about how I could take a break from "playing student" for one day.

I hung up on him. First time I've ever done that. My hands were shaking.

I know I should call back and smooth things over. That's what I always do. But I'm so tired of being the one who manages his feelings while he dismisses mine.

The hot pot was wonderful. Crowded restaurant, too loud to hear anything, steam fogging my glasses every time I reached for the lamb slices. Xiao-Wei sat next to me and we discovered we both grew up eating the same brand of sesame paste that nobody makes anymore.

Funny how food carries so much. My mother used to mix that paste into noodles on cold days. Now I'm in a room full of people young enough to be my children, fishing mushrooms out of boiling broth, and for two hours I wasn't thinking about deadlines or hospital appointments or whether I'm falling behind.

I ordered a second round of the taro dumplings even though nobody asked. Sometimes you have to be the one who says "let's keep going." They didn't seem to mind.

Walked home through the night market after. Bought a bag of pineapple cakes I definitely don't need. Didn't feel guilty about it even once.

Took Lucas fishing this morning. Marijke nearly fell over when I told her. I had no idea what I was doing — had to watch a YouTube video on how to bait a hook. Lucas thought that was hilarious. "Opa doesn't know everything!" He's right. I don't.

We sat on the dock for three hours and caught nothing. He told me about his school, his best friend who moved away, the video game he's trying to beat. I listened without trying to teach him anything or steer the conversation. Just listened. At one point he leaned against me and said this was fun. That was worth more than any contract I've ever closed.

On the drive home I thought about what I've been protecting all these years. The company, yes. But also this version of myself that only exists in boardrooms — the one who knows all the answers, who never looks foolish, who everyone defers to. That version doesn't know how to fish. Doesn't have time to learn. Doesn't get to sit with his grandson and be surprised by what a eight-year-old thinks about the world.

I'm not retiring. I'm not ready. But I'm starting to see that there might be more than one way to matter.

First day of Maarten handling the morning operations meeting without me. Sat in my office watching the clock. Didn't intervene. Reports came in normal. Nothing fell apart. Went home at 5 PM for the first time in months. Marijke asked if I was feeling alright. I told her I was trying something new.

Called Maarten this afternoon. Asked him if he'd be interested in taking on more strategic responsibility. Not as my replacement — as my partner in running the place. He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "I've been waiting ten years for you to ask." That stung. I thought I was being careful. Turns out I was being a bottleneck.

But you're right, if it's actually a leak and I wait, the damage gets expensive. I'll message the landlord tonight and tell him I want a proper plumber this time, not his cousin.

sources.journal_entry:
Still haven't looked at that vendor contract. It's been four days. Every morning I open my task list and it's there, highlighted yellow, and I just skip past it to whatever's on fire. Today it was a delivery routing issue that ate my entire afternoon.

The thing is, I know what I'd tell someone on my team — just block thirty minutes, pull the document, read the clauses, flag what needs flagging. It's not hard. But I keep not doing it and the longer I wait the more it feels like it's going to be a bigger problem than it actually is. Classic spiral.

Appa called tonight and asked about work. I said "all good, busy but managing." Which is mostly true. But I didn't mention the contract thing or the insurance bounce from last week, because then he'd worry, and then I'd have to manage his worry on top of everything else. I'm tired. Going to bed early and hoping tomorrow's lighter.

The warehouse team flagged a potential compliance issue with one of our vendor contracts — some clause about liability thresholds that might not match the new state guidelines. I should've pulled the contract and reviewed it today but I had back-to-back calls and a quarterly deck to finish.

Told myself I'd get to it tomorrow but I've said that before about smaller things and sometimes tomorrow just becomes next week. The vendor's been fine for three years so it's probably nothing. But "probably" isn't really how I like to operate.

Took an Uber instead of the bus to a client meeting because I woke up late. Spent four hundred rupees on a fifteen-minute ride I normally do for thirty. Doesn't sound like much but I'd just tightened my monthly transport budget last week.
sources.nudge_response: It's not about the money specifically. It's that I had a plan and I broke it on day two. If I let small stuff slide the bigger stuff starts sliding too, that's just how it works.

sources.journal_entry: Auto-debit for the health insurance premium bounced. Bank flagged insufficient funds because the salary credit was two days late this month. Sorted it manually but now I need to call the insurer to confirm coverage wasn't lapsed even briefly.
sources.nudge_response: It's not about feelings, it's about process. If payroll is going to shift dates without notice, I need a bigger buffer in that account. That's the fix.

sources.journal_entry:
Team review went well, Priya's onboarding tracker is actually working, the new hires are ramping faster than the last batch. I'd built the template she based it on, months ago, and watching it get adopted without anyone needing to ask me about it — that's the point, right? Systems that just run.

Renewed the apartment lease today, same terms, same landlord. He wanted to bump rent by two thousand but I showed him the market comparables I'd saved. He backed off. Walked home past the chai stall and the uncle remembered my order. Small thing but it's nice when the neighbourhood knows you.

Sat with Amma on the phone for almost forty minutes after dinner, which I don't usually do on weekdays. She was telling me about the new water heater she got installed and how the plumber tried to overcharge her. I walked her through how to cross-check rates online, sent her a few links. She kept saying "you sound like your father" which — I don't know, it hit different tonight.

After we hung up I checked my bank balance, not because I needed to, just habit. Everything's where it should be. The SIP went through on the 10th, the rent auto-debit cleared, the FD interest got credited. There's something about seeing those numbers line up that lets me breathe properly. I know people think it's boring, the spreadsheets, the tracking, but when I see it all working the way I set it up, it's like — okay, things are holding together.

Spent the rest of the evening ironing my shirts for the week. Put on an old Kishore Kumar playlist. Just felt settled. Not every night is like this but tonight was.

But watching Marcus Jr. (not named after me, just a coincidence) actually engage with something for the first time all year? sources.journal_entry:
Second entry today because I just need to get this out. Went to the grocery store after school, totally normal trip, and I just stood in the produce section for way too long looking at the plastic clamshells of strawberries. They're from Chile. In January. Wrapped in plastic that's going to exist for five hundred years so I can have strawberries in the middle of winter.

I bought them anyway. I bought the stupid strawberries because I was tired and I wanted something sweet and the farmer's market doesn't open until Saturday. And I know one person buying or not buying strawberries doesn't change the global supply chain but I still felt like a hypocrite putting them in my cart.

This is what I mean when I say it's exhausting to care about everything all the time. My students look at me like I have answers but I'm just as stuck as everyone else. I teach them about sustainability and then I buy Chilean strawberries in plastic. I tell them every choice matters and then I make choices that don't align with that. I don't know how to live in this world without constantly feeling like I'm failing at something.

The kids blew my mind today. We were talking about the water cycle and Jordan raised her hand and asked if the water we drink is the same water dinosaurs drank and I said yes, basically, and then she asked if that meant we were connected to dinosaurs and I said yes again and she got this look on her face like something clicked.

Then Carlos said if we're connected to dinosaurs through water we must be connected to each other too and to the fish and to the trees and I just stood there for a second because yes, exactly, that's exactly it. These ten-year-olds just figured out in five minutes what some adults never understand. We spent the rest of the period talking about interconnection and nobody complained and nobody looked at the clock.
sources.nudge_response: It reminded me why I do this job. Not for the test scores or the evaluations. For moments like that where kids discover something true about the world. That we're all connected, that what we do matters beyond ourselves. That's what I want them to carry with them.

sources.journal_entry:
Principal wants me to use the new standardized curriculum materials for social studies. They come from the district. They're fine, technically. Cover all the state requirements.

But they're so sanitized. The unit on immigration literally has two paragraphs on the Chinese Exclusion Act. Two paragraphs. My great-grandfather couldn't enter this country for decades because of that law. I told the principal I'd supplement with additional materials. She said to be careful about "going off curriculum." Said it in that way that means don't.
sources.nudge_response: I'm going to use the curriculum. But I'm also going to bring in my family photos and tell the real story during the personal narrative unit. They can't tell me I can't share my own family history. At least I don't think they can.

sources.journal_entry: Didn't call Grandma back again. She left another voicemail about the restaurant anniversary dinner planning and I just... let it go to voicemail. I'll call her tomorrow.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly, I know she's going to ask me to give a speech at the 60th anniversary dinner. In Cantonese. My Cantonese is terrible and I keep meaning to practice but I never do. It feels like I'm letting her down every time we talk and she hears how rusty I've gotten.

sources.journal_entry:
Made dumplings with Mom today for Lunar New Year prep. My hands remember the folding even when my brain forgets the right way to pleat them. She corrected me three times on the same fold and I wanted to be annoyed but honestly I was just grateful she's still here to correct me.

She told me stories about the restaurant again, the early days when Grandpa worked eighteen hour shifts and Grandma handled the front while raising Dad. Stories I've heard a hundred times but they never get old. There's something about flour on your hands and family around you that makes everything feel solid. Like no matter what else is happening in the world, this is real. This is what matters.

The diversity assembly actually worked! I've been pushing for this for two years and today we had speakers from five different community organizations talking to the whole school. Mrs. Okonkwo from the Nigerian cultural center, Mr. Patel from the Hindu temple, someone from the tribal council, and two others.

The kids were so engaged. They asked real questions. One of my students asked Mrs. Okonkwo what she missed most about Nigeria and she started crying a little and then laughed and said "the food, always the food" and everyone laughed and it was this beautiful human moment. This is what school should feel like. Not test prep and discipline charts. Actual humans connecting with each other, learning that the world is bigger than their own street.
sources.nudge_response: When I was a kid there was nobody who looked like me in the history books or the assemblies. I remember how alone that felt. I don't want any of my students to feel that way. I want them to see themselves in school, and I want them to see each other too.

values.user_phrase: Making the world a fairer, better place
values.approved_definition: Understanding, appreciation, tolerance, and protection for the welfare of all people and for nature. Derives from survival needs that become apparent when people recognize that failure to accept those who are different and treat them justly will lead to strife, and when people become aware of the scarcity of natural resources.

sources.journal_entry:
Made dumplings with Mom today for Lunar New Year prep. My hands remember the folding even when my brain forgets the right way to pleat them. She corrected me three times on the same fold and I wanted to be annoyed but honestly I was just grateful she's still here to correct me.

She told me stories about the restaurant again, the early days when Grandpa worked eighteen hour shifts and Grandma handled the front while raising Dad. Stories I've heard a hundred times but they never get old. There's something about flour on your hands and family around you that makes everything feel solid. Like no matter what else is happening in the world, this is real. This is what matters.

The diversity assembly actually worked! I've been pushing for this for two years and today we had speakers from five different community organizations talking to the whole school. Mrs. Okonkwo from the Nigerian cultural center, Mr. Patel from the Hindu temple, someone from the tribal council, and two others.

The kids were so engaged. They asked real questions. One of my students asked Mrs. Okonkwo what she missed most about Nigeria and she started crying a little and then laughed and said "the food, always the food" and everyone laughed and it was this beautiful human moment. This is what school should feel like. Not test prep and discipline charts. Actual humans connecting with each other, learning that the world is bigger than their own street.

sources.journal_entry: Called Grandma. We talked for forty minutes. I'm going to give the speech at the anniversary dinner. In Cantonese. She's going to help me practice.
sources.nudge_response: Nervous but good. It's important to her. The restaurant is important to the whole family, to the community really. Dad worked there every summer through high school. So did I. People need to hear what it means to us, in the language it's always been spoken in.

sources.journal_entry:
Second entry today because I just need to get this out. Went to the grocery store after school, totally normal trip, and I just stood in the produce section for way too long looking at the plastic clamshells of strawberries. They're from Chile. In January. Wrapped in plastic that's going to exist for five hundred years so I can have strawberries in the middle of winter.

I bought them anyway. I bought the stupid strawberries because I was tired and I wanted something sweet and the farmer's market doesn't open until Saturday. And I know one person buying or not buying strawberries doesn't change the global supply chain but I still felt like a hypocrite putting them in my cart.

This is what I mean when I say it's exhausting to care about everything all the time. My students look at me like I have answers but I'm just as stuck as everyone else. I teach them about sustainability and then I buy Chilean strawberries in plastic. I tell them every choice matters and then I make choices that don't align with that. I don't know how to live in this world without constantly feeling like I'm failing at something.

The kids blew my mind today. We were talking about the water cycle and Jordan raised her hand and asked if the water we drink is the same water dinosaurs drank and I said yes, basically, and then she asked if that meant we were connected to dinosaurs and I said yes again and she got this look on her face like something clicked.

Then Carlos said if we're connected to dinosaurs through water we must be connected to each other too and to the fish and to the trees and I just stood there for a second because yes, exactly, that's exactly it. These ten-year-olds just figured out in five minutes what some adults never understand. We spent the rest of the period talking about interconnection and nobody complained and nobody looked at the clock.

sources.journal_entry:

I bought them anyway. I bought the stupid strawberries because I was tired and I wanted something sweet and the farmer's market doesn't open until Saturday. I don't know how to live in this world without constantly feeling like I'm failing at something.

I wanted to take a long bath — the kind with the lavender salts my friend gave me for my birthday — but the bathroom still needed cleaning from the kids using it, and by the time I finished scrubbing I didn't feel like a bath anymore. I just showered and went to bed.

I know a massage would help. I know lying down with a heat pad for an hour would help. But I keep hearing my mother's voice in my head telling me not to be so pampered, that at her age she was carrying buckets of water uphill and still cooking for seven children. So I put Tiger Balm on it and kept going.

Went to Ma's nursing home today, usual Sunday visit. Brought her the dried tangerine peel she asked for and sat with her for two hours. She complained the aircon was too cold, same as always. I adjusted it, brought her an extra blanket, refilled her water thermos.

On the way home I stopped at the provision shop for dish soap and sponges. Cooked dinner. Washed up. Nothing unusual. I don't know why I'm even writing today, there's nothing to say really. Everything got done, nobody needed anything they didn't get. That should be enough.

Valentine's Day, not that it matters to us at this age, but husband brought home a box of those nice mooncake-style pastries from Bengawan Solo after work. The tau sar ones I like. He just left them on the counter and didn't make a big deal about it which is his way.

I wanted to sit down and have one with tea and just enjoy it, the way you see people do in those café videos online. But I was in the middle of folding the laundry and then I remembered I hadn't called Ma today and she gets anxious if I don't call by 7, so I called her first, then finished the laundry, and by then I was standing at the counter eating the pastry over the sink because I was also rinsing out the thermos.

And the whole time I was eating it I was thinking about how I should be enjoying this more, which is such a strange thing to think, because the act of thinking it already means you're not. Like the pastry was good. I know it was good. I could taste it. But my mind was already three tasks ahead. I don't know when eating something nice became just another thing I do between other things. I saved the rest of the box for the grandkids.
sources.nudge_response: Yes. I didn't even think about it until you asked. Of course you give the nice things to the children. That's just what you do.

Finished the grocery run this morning and treated myself to a bowl of laksa at the hawker centre after. I almost didn't — the queue was long and I had frozen things in the bag. But I thought, five more minutes won't matter, and I stood in line anyway.

The laksa was really good. Extra hum. I sat at one of those metal tables by myself and didn't look at my phone or think about what was next. Just ate. By the time I was done the ice cream in the grocery bag was starting to soften but honestly it was worth it.

sources.journal_entry:
Still tired from yesterday. Woke up with my neck stiff and couldn't really move it properly. Husband said I should go see the TCM doctor but I looked at the week ahead and there's grocery shopping tomorrow, Ma's checkup on Wednesday, and I told Mrs Tan I'd help with the community centre lunar new year cleanup on Thursday.

I know a massage would help. I know lying down with a heat pad for an hour would help. But I keep hearing my mother's voice in my head telling me not to be so pampered, that at her age she was carrying buckets of water uphill and still cooking for seven children. So I put Tiger Balm on it and kept going.

Spent the whole day with the grandkids as expected. They were fine, quite well behaved actually. But by 4pm I was so tired I could barely keep my eyes open. I sat down on the sofa for maybe ten minutes while they were watching cartoons and immediately felt guilty, like I should be doing something — cutting fruit, tidying up, checking if they needed water. So I got up.

Later after Wei Lin picked them up I heated some leftover soup and just stood in the kitchen eating it from the pot. Didn't even sit down. I wanted to take a long bath — the kind with the lavender salts my friend gave me for my birthday — but the bathroom still needed cleaning from the kids using it, and by the time I finished scrubbing I didn't feel like a bath anymore. I just showered and went to bed.

I keep thinking about the ten minutes on the sofa and how I couldn't even let myself have that. The children were fine. They were watching TV. Nothing was on fire. But something in me just wouldn't let it be okay to sit there.

Same day, writing again. Wei Lin called this afternoon and asked me to watch the grandkids next Saturday because she has a work event. I said yes obviously. But it means I'll miss the CNY market at Chinatown with Mei and Hwee Leng. We've been planning it for two weeks.

It's fine. The kids love coming over and I already told Wei Lin I would. Mei said they can go without me and bring me back some bak kwa. I told her to get the thick-cut one from Lim Chee Guan.

Mei and I talked the whole time about her daughter's wedding planning and it felt normal, like two friends just doing something together.

But on the MRT home I started thinking about the laundry I didn't hang up before leaving, and whether I'd left the rice cooker on, and I realised I'd chosen the useful thing to worry about instead of just sitting with the fact that I'd had a nice afternoon. The rice cooker was off. The laundry was fine. I just couldn't let the afternoon be what it was.

Mei asked me last week if I wanted to join her for a foot reflexology session — the new place near Bishan that has the herbal soak. I said I'd think about it and I've been thinking about it for five days now. It's $38 for an hour. That's not a lot of money. We can afford it easily.

But there's this thing where I feel like I need to justify it first. Like I need to have done enough to deserve an hour of someone rubbing my feet. Which is ridiculous when I say it out loud. My husband never thinks twice about buying fishing lures that cost more than that. But for me it feels different. It feels like something I have to earn, and I'm never quite sure I have.

Long day. The investor meeting got pushed to Thursday which should feel like breathing room but mostly just means I'll be anxious for two extra days. Had a working lunch with Priya going over the numbers. She brought biryani from that place near her flat which was good — proper Hyderabadi style with the rice done right. We ate while reviewing the P&L which felt wrong somehow, like the biryani deserved better attention than that.

After work I was too tired to cook so I ordered in and ate on the couch watching something forgettable. The flat was quiet. Not in a bad way, just quiet. I kept thinking about how my father used to come home from the office and sit in his chair for exactly fifteen minutes before dinner, not talking, not reading, just sitting. My mother never interrupted those fifteen minutes. I used to think it was strange but now I think I understand it — he needed a gap between the work version of himself and the home version.

I don't really have that gap. The work version and the home version blur into each other because I work from the same room I sleep in. Maybe that's part of it. Maybe if there were clearer edges I wouldn't feel so guilty about the in-between moments.

Third time writing today, which is unusual for me. I think the afternoon thing is still sitting with me. Had dinner — made egg curry, nothing special but the kitchen smelled good and I ate slowly for once instead of standing at the counter scrolling through Slack.

It occurs to me that the small things I actually enjoy — cooking, eating properly, having a pointless conversation about cricket — none of them take very long. It's not like I'm asking for a vacation. I just want to eat my food without feeling like I'm stealing time from something more important. That shouldn't be complicated.

Writing again because I left something out earlier. After the coffee and the cricket chat I actually felt good — like, weirdly good for a Tuesday. And I sat back down at my desk and instead of opening the spreadsheet I just sat there for a few minutes not doing anything. Not on my phone, not thinking about work. Just sort of enjoying the fact that the chai was good and the conversation was easy and the afternoon light through the window was warm.

Then I caught myself and opened the spreadsheet immediately, like I'd been caught doing something wrong. Nobody was watching. Nobody cares. But the instinct was there — that I was wasting time, that good feelings are a distraction, that if I'm not producing something then I'm falling behind. It's a stupid reflex and I know it's stupid but knowing doesn't seem to help.
sources.nudge_response: Nothing specific. That's the honest answer. It's not about an actual deadline — it's just this background hum that says I should always be doing more.

sources.journal_entry:
Normal morning. Replied to emails, had a standup call that went longer than necessary because Priya wanted to talk through the onboarding flow again. Grabbed idli from the canteen downstairs. The sambar was better than usual today.

Afternoon was mostly spreadsheet work. Nothing dramatic. Stepped out for a coffee around four and ran into the guy who runs the print shop next door. We talked about cricket for ten minutes. Came back and finished up.

Ravi invited me to this rooftop thing his friends were doing — live music, good food, casual. I actually wanted to go. But I had a pitch deck that needed reworking by Monday and I told myself it made more sense to stay in and finish it. Which it did, technically. The pitch is important. I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

But I sat at my desk all evening and the deck took twice as long as it should have because I kept checking Ravi's stories and seeing everyone having a good time. The tandoori looked incredible. Someone was playing guitar and people were just sitting around talking. Nothing fancy. The exact kind of night I would have loved.

I finished the deck around midnight and it's fine. It's solid. But the flat was so quiet and I just felt flat myself. Like I'd done the responsible thing and the reward for being responsible was sitting alone in a silent apartment eating cold chapati at midnight wondering what the point of all this work is if I never actually enjoy anything.

Couldn't sleep last night because I was so wound up from a client call that went badly. By 2 AM I was just lying there staring at the ceiling fan, and the obvious thing would have been to get up, make something warm, watch something stupid on my phone, let myself come down from it. But instead I just lay there telling myself I needed to sleep because tomorrow was going to be another long day and I couldn't afford to be foggy.

And the thing is, I know forcing sleep doesn't work. I know I would have been better off getting up and doing something comforting for twenty minutes. But some part of me kept translating "get up and do something nice for yourself" into "you're being weak, you can't even handle a bad call without needing to baby yourself."

So I just lay there for another hour and a half, exhausted but not sleeping, not resting, not doing anything useful either. The worst of all options. Woke up foggy anyway. Amma would have told me to drink warm milk and stop overthinking, and she would have been right.

Had dinner with old university friends last night. Lao Zhang just sold his logistics company, talking about retiring to Yunnan, painting landscapes. Everyone congratulated him. Someone turned to me and asked when I'd slow down too, said I looked tired. I told them I'm fine, business is growing, we're expanding into Southeast Asian markets.

On the drive home I kept replaying it. I don't look tired. Or maybe I do. But what am I supposed to do — Haojie needs tutoring fees paid, Ma's specialist appointments aren't cheap even with insurance, and Yuxin's Hong Kong rent went up again. Lao Zhang doesn't have parents to look after, his kids are already working. Easy to paint landscapes when nobody's depending on you.

It's not that I'm jealous. I chose this. When Ba died and Ma needed somewhere to go, I didn't hesitate. When Lifen suggested Yuxin should study locally to save money, I said no, let her go to Hong Kong, it's better for her career. These were my decisions and I'd make them again. I just wish people would stop looking at me like I'm some kind of cautionary tale when I'm doing exactly what I should be doing.
sources.nudge_response: Them. I know what I'm doing and why. The difference between me and Lao Zhang isn't that he's free and I'm stuck. He just doesn't have anyone who needs him the way my family needs me. That's not a burden, that's the whole point.

sources.journal_entry:
Look, the pivot makes sense. Everyone at the Thursday pitch night kept asking why we dropped the furniture line when we had traction, but traction is not the same thing as momentum. We had retailers interested, sure, but the margins were getting squeezed and the whole supply chain was becoming a nightmare with shipping costs out of Shenzhen. I am not going to sit there manufacturing the same shelving unit for the next ten years just because some shops in Eindhoven like them.

Pieter thinks I pulled the trigger too fast. He said that in the meeting, in front of Anouk and Daan, which I did not appreciate. He has been with me since the Philips days and sometimes he acts like that gives him permission to question every call I make publicly. Maybe it does. I do not know. But I also know that if I had listened to the cautious voices three years ago we would still be making Bluetooth speakers nobody asked for.

The urban farming kits — there is something there. I can feel it in the conversations I am having. The market is shifting, people want to grow things, they want control over food, they want something tangible. We just need six months to prove the concept. That is not reckless. That is reading the room.
sources.nudge_response: That he might be right. Not about the pivot being wrong, but about me not giving things enough time. I have heard it before from other people. It is a pattern I do not love seeing pointed out.

sources.journal_entry:
Weekend in Utrecht was hard. Matteo barely looked at me. Sven was fine, acted like nothing was wrong, which somehow felt worse. We went to get frites and walked along the canal and I kept trying to say something meaningful but everything came out flat.

On Sunday I took them to a climbing wall. Matteo actually engaged for the first time. Something about the challenge of it, figuring out the next hold, the height. He was grinning at the top. For about an hour he forgot he was angry with me.

Drove home and cried in the car. Not the dramatic kind, just the quiet leaking kind where you keep driving and wiping your face.
sources.nudge_response: Because it was not sitting across a table pretending everything is normal. It was doing something together that required focus and a bit of nerve. Maybe that is the only language I know how to speak. Maybe Matteo is the same way and I never noticed.

sources.journal_entry:
Katrien called. Not the boys, Katrien herself. She never does that unless something is wrong or she needs to tell me something I will not like.

Matteo has been acting out at school. Skipping classes, talking back to teachers. She thinks it started around the time I cancelled the last weekend because of the Lisbon trip. She did not say it is my fault, but she did not have to. The silence after she described what happened was louder than anything she could have said.

I sat in my car for twenty minutes after that call. Just sat there in the parking garage under the studio, engine off, staring at the concrete wall. I wanted to call Matteo but what would I say? Sorry I was looking at planters in Portugal instead of watching your football match? Sorry I keep choosing the next interesting thing over the predictable thing that happens to include you?

He is fourteen. He does not understand that I am trying to build something. Or maybe he understands perfectly and just does not think it is a good enough reason. Maybe he is right.

I am going to Utrecht this weekend. No excuses. I already told Pieter to handle the Friday call with Valencia.

Woke up at four again, brain already running. Kept thinking about whether the modular design should be stackable or side-by-side. Side-by-side takes more floor space but stackable has structural issues — the weight of wet soil plus the grow lights, it is not trivial. Sketched something on the back of an envelope before I even brushed my teeth.

Then my mind jumped to the lease. Studio lease is up in September. Pieter wants to renew for two years. Two years feels like a prison sentence. What if we need to move closer to a port? What if we need less space? What if we need more? I said let us do one year with an option to extend. He gave me that look. The one that says here we go again.

Had coffee with an old colleague from Philips, Joost. He is still there. Same building, same floor, different title. He seemed content but when I described what I was doing his eyes got wide and he said he could never do that. I used to find that flattering. Today it just made me feel alone.

Then back to the planters. Emailed three more suppliers. One in Valencia looks promising. Set up a video call for Friday. Kept going until my neck hurt and I realized it was already dark and I had not eaten. Ordered Thai food and ate it standing in the kitchen scrolling through competitor listings.
sources.nudge_response: The lease. Not because of the space, but because signing anything for a fixed term makes my chest tight. I know that is not rational. It is just how I am wired.

sources.journal_entry:
Two days of back-to-back calls with potential suppliers in Portugal and a prototype manufacturer in Ghent. My voice is shot. Ate a cheese sandwich at my desk around three and that was it until I got home and microwaved leftover stamppot that tasted like nothing.

The boys called. Sven wants to go to a music festival in Belgium and needs money. Matteo got a B+ on his physics exam and sounded genuinely proud, which made me proud too, even though I had nothing to do with it. Katrien is the one who sat with him while he studied. I was in Lisbon looking at terracotta planters.

I told Sven I would think about the festival money. What I actually thought was: I cannot keep saying yes to everything just because I feel guilty for not being there. But I will probably say yes anyway because that is what I do — throw money at the gap where my presence should be.

The Ghent manufacturer can do small runs. That is good. Keeps us lean. I should be more excited about that than I am right now. I think I am just tired.
sources.nudge_response: I do not know. Sitting in their kitchen helping with homework? Driving Sven to football practice? It sounds so ordinary but I have built my whole life to avoid ordinary, and now ordinary is the thing I cannot reach.

A whole week gone and I cannot tell you what I accomplished. Meetings, emails, a prototype review that raised more questions than it answered. The Valencia supplier fell through — their minimum order is ten times what we need. Back to square one on that front.

Pieter brought up the furniture line again. Casually, over lunch, like he was just thinking out loud. "We still have the moulds," he said. "The retailers would take us back." I did not respond. Just kept eating my soup.

I spent the evening reading about vertical farming startups in Copenhagen and Stockholm. Some of them are doing incredible things. Modular, scalable, beautiful design. Part of me got fired up. Part of me thought: they are already there. You are late. You are always starting things and by the time you get somewhere, someone else has already built it better.

Anouk sent me a link to a design competition in Milan. Entry deadline is August. I opened the page, looked at the brief, felt that old kick of energy. Then I closed the tab because I know what happens — I spend three weeks on it, neglect the actual business, and end up with a beautiful submission and no revenue.

I do not know what I am doing. I mean I know what I am doing day to day. I just do not know what it adds up to.

sources.journal_entry:
Pieter handed in his notice today. Twenty minutes before our morning standup, just walked into my office and put a printed letter on my desk. After eight years. Eight years of me dragging him through pivots and late nights and "trust me on this one."

He said he has taken a position at a consultancy in Amsterdam. Better pay, predictable hours, no more wondering whether the next quarter will exist. He was calm about it. Almost gentle. Said it was not personal, that he just needs stability, that he has a mortgage and a kid on the way.

I shook his hand and said I understood. And I do. I genuinely do. But the second he left my office I wanted to throw something. Not at him. At the wall, at the situation, at the fact that I am apparently the kind of person people eventually need a break from.

Anouk came in later and asked if I was okay. I said fine. She did not push it. I spent the rest of the day reorganizing the supplier spreadsheet, which did not need reorganizing, because I needed my hands to be doing something that did not require thinking about what happens next.

Katrien would say this is the cost. My mother would say this is the cost. Pieter leaving is just the latest version of someone choosing the stable path while I keep chasing whatever is around the next corner. But what is the alternative? Do what Joost does? Same floor, same desk, different title? I would rather fail at something new every two years than succeed at the same thing for twenty.

That sounds brave when I write it. It does not feel brave right now.
sources.nudge_response: Tired, mostly. I will figure it out. I always do. Just need a few days to regroup.

sources.journal_entry: Group meeting went sideways. The other three want to argue in the brief that the county should eliminate paper records entirely. I think that's reckless -- I've seen what happens when digital systems crash and there's no backup. But they all agreed so fast I just nodded. Sat in the parking ramp for twenty minutes after. Should have said something. Didn't.

Professor Vasquez handed back the first reading response today. I got a B-minus. Fine. I expected that. But the comment in the margin said "push beyond summary -- what's YOUR position?" and I've been turning that over since 2pm. I summarized the readings accurately. I cited everything properly. The formatting was correct. I don't understand what she wants that I didn't give.

The younger students all seem comfortable throwing out half-formed opinions in class. This one guy, Marcus, will say "I think the entire framework is wrong" and then Professor Vasquez nods and says "interesting, say more." If I said something like that I'd need to be sure it was right first. You don't just declare something wrong without evidence. That's how I was taught. You do the reading, you report what it says, you don't pretend you're smarter than the author.

My ex-wife Linda used to say I was allergic to having opinions. That's not fair. I have plenty of opinions. I just don't see the point of broadcasting them when nobody asked. The paper asked me to respond to the readings. I responded. If "push beyond summary" means I'm supposed to disagree with published experts for the sake of classroom performance, then I don't know what I'm doing here.

First full week of spring semester done. Managed to get through the group project meeting without making a fool of myself. The other three in my group are all in their mid-twenties. One of them, Priya, actually asked for my opinion on the policy brief outline. Small thing, but I didn't fumble the answer. Drove home to check on Mom after. She'd left the porch light on for me.

sources.journal_entry:
Mom had a fall this weekend. Nothing broken, thank God, but she bruised her hip badly and the visiting nurse said she needs to use a walker now. Spent all of Saturday rearranging her living room furniture so she has a clear path. She kept saying not to bother, that she was fine, that she'd been walking in that house for forty-three years without help. I moved the ottoman anyway.

My sister Karen called from Phoenix to "check in" which meant asking me if I'd looked into assisted living yet. I said no because Mom doesn't want that and I'm not going to force her. Karen said I was "enabling her stubbornness." I said okay and changed the subject. It's easy to have opinions about what Mom needs when you live two thousand miles away. I could have said that but I didn't. Not worth the phone call it would turn into.

Drove back to campus Sunday night. Missed the reading for Monday's class. I'll skim it before 9am and hope she doesn't cold-call me. I keep telling myself I can handle all of this -- school, Mom, the drive, the apartment -- but weeks like this I feel like I'm running on fumes. Not complaining, just noting it. Everybody has a lot going on.

Group meeting went sideways. The other three want to argue in the brief that the county should eliminate paper records entirely. I think that's reckless -- I've seen what happens when digital systems crash and there's no backup. But they all agreed so fast I just nodded. Sat in the parking ramp for twenty minutes after. Should have said something. Didn't.

Professor Vasquez handed back the first reading response today. I got a B-minus. Fine. I expected that. But the comment in the margin said "push beyond summary -- what's YOUR position?" and I've been turning that over since 2pm. I summarized the readings accurately. I cited everything properly. The formatting was correct. I don't understand what she wants that I didn't give.

The younger students all seem comfortable throwing out half-formed opinions in class. This one guy, Marcus, will say "I think the entire framework is wrong" and then Professor Vasquez nods and says "interesting, say more." If I said something like that I'd need to be sure it was right first. You don't just declare something wrong without evidence. That's how I was taught. You do the reading, you report what it says, you don't pretend you're smarter than the author.

My ex-wife Linda used to say I was allergic to having opinions. That's not fair. I have plenty of opinions. I just don't see the point of broadcasting them when nobody asked. The paper asked me to respond to the readings. I responded. If "push beyond summary" means I'm supposed to disagree with published experts for the sake of classroom performance, then I don't know what I'm doing here.

First full week of spring semester done. Managed to get through the group project meeting without making a fool of myself. The other three in my group are all in their mid-twenties. One of them, Priya, actually asked for my opinion on the policy brief outline. Small thing, but I didn't fumble the answer. Drove home to check on Mom after. She'd left the porch light on for me.

sources.journal_entry:
Group meeting again. We're finalizing the policy brief draft this week. Priya divided the sections and I got the implementation risks portion, which is fine because that's where my actual knowledge lives. Started writing it last night and it came out faster than anything I've written for this program so far. Three pages in two hours.

I included the thing about our county's failed digital archive migration. The one where the server crashed during a property tax audit and we had to pull paper backups from a warehouse in Proctor that hadn't been climate-controlled. Lost about six weeks of records. The kind of thing that doesn't show up in policy papers because the people who lived through it don't write policy papers.

Sent the draft to the group chat. Marcus replied with a thumbs-up emoji. Priya said "this is really good, Gerald." I stared at that message for longer than I should have. It shouldn't matter this much, a twenty-six-year-old telling me my writing is good. But the work I did at the county for three decades -- nobody ever said anything about it. You filed things right, nobody noticed. You filed things wrong, everybody noticed. Priya's two words did something the county never did.
sources.nudge_response: Because at the county, doing it right was just the minimum. Nobody thanks you for the minimum. Priya read what I wrote and responded to it like it mattered. Like what I thought was the point, not just whether the form was filled out correctly. I didn't know I needed that. Apparently I did.

Office hours today, first time I actually went. Sat outside Professor Vasquez's door for maybe ten minutes before I knocked. She was eating a sandwich, which made me feel bad for interrupting, but she waved me in. Asked about the reading response grade, what she meant by "your position." She said something about the difference between understanding an argument and engaging with it. That you can agree with a reading and still have something to add.

I nodded a lot. She asked me what I thought about the Ostrom reading specifically and I said I thought the commons framework made sense but I'd seen it fail in county-level resource sharing. She lit up at that, said that was exactly the kind of thing she wanted in my papers. Real-world pushback grounded in experience. I said I didn't think that counted as academic.

She laughed, not unkindly. Said "Gerald, your experience IS a source." I felt something shift, not sure what. Like being told a door I thought was locked was actually just stuck. sources.journal_entry: Valentines Day was yesterday and I thought about Linda for the first time in a while. Not missing her exactly. Just remembering how she'd get frustrated when I wouldn't pick the restaurant. She'd say "just choose something, Gerald." I never could. Felt like if I picked wrong she'd be disappointed. Easier to let her decide and go along. She left. So maybe going along wasn't working either.

Karen called again. She's been talking to Mom's neighbor, Barb, behind my back. Barb apparently told Karen that Mom left the stove burner on last Tuesday and didn't notice until the pot was dry. Karen said we need to "have a family conversation" about next steps. I said I'd handle it. She said I always say that and then nothing changes.

She's not wrong. But the way she frames it -- like I'm failing at this -- makes it impossible to hear. I know Mom needs more help. I've been the one driving back every other weekend, moving furniture, filling prescriptions, bringing groceries. Karen sends a check once a month and calls that "doing her part." I could say that. I won't. It would start something that can't be unsaid and then every holiday, every phone call would have that underneath it.

So I said I'd look into some options and we'd talk next weekend. I already know what will happen. She'll send me links to places in Arizona. I'll say Mom won't leave Duluth. She'll say I'm being unreasonable. I'll fold the conversation up and put it away and nothing will change. The whole thing makes me feel like a coward, which I know isn't the right word, but I can't find a better one. I just don't want to be the person who starts the fight.
sources.nudge_response: Careful, maybe. Or just tired. I don't know. Coward implies I'm scared and it's not exactly that. It's more like I've calculated the cost of every version of this conversation and none of them end well. So I pick the one where at least nobody is yelling. Even if I'm the one absorbing it all. I've been doing that math my whole life.

Got the revised reading response back from Professor Vasquez. B-plus. She wrote "much better -- this is your voice" in the margin. I read that comment three times. Slid the paper into the folder where I keep things. Not sure why I'm keeping a paper folder of graded assignments like a kid bringing home a report card. But I am.

Group turned in the policy brief. Final version was solid. Priya formatted it, Marcus did the executive summary, I did the implementation risks, and our fourth member Aiden did the literature review. It reads like something a real policy shop would produce. I know that because I've read hundreds of those in my career. Nice to be on the writing end for once instead of the filing end.

Karen called. I told her about the conversation with Mom. She said ninety seconds wasn't enough and I needed to be firmer. I told her she was welcome to come to Duluth and be firm herself. There was a long pause. She said that was unfair. I said maybe. But I said it. First time in a long time I didn't just absorb what she threw and move on. Don't know if it changed anything. Probably made next month's phone call harder. But I was tired of calculating the cost of every sentence before I said it. Sometimes the math isn't worth it.
sources.nudge_response: Lighter. Just for a second. Then immediately guilty, like I'd broken a rule I didn't know I was allowed to break. But the lighter part came first. That's new.

sources.journal_entry:
Long day. Drove to Duluth after class because Barb called and said Mom seemed confused about what day it was. Got there at 9pm. Mom was fine, watching Jeopardy, knew every answer in the history category. Made me a grilled cheese without me asking. I sat at the kitchen table and for a second it was like being twelve again.

Had the conversation. Told her Karen was worried, Barb was worried, I was worried. She said she was fine and that people should mind their own business. I said we might need to think about someone coming in during the day, just to help. She said "I don't need a babysitter, Gerald." I said okay. Drove back at midnight. The conversation Karen wanted me to have lasted about ninety seconds. I don't know if I tried hard enough or if trying harder would have just been cruel.
sources.nudge_response: Sitting there longer, I guess. Listing reasons. Making her feel like she can't take care of herself. I don't want to do that to her. She's my mother. There's a difference between helping someone and cornering them.

values.user_phrase: Seeking new experiences and challenges
values.approved_definition: Excitement, novelty, and challenge in life. Derives from the organismic need for variety and stimulation in order to maintain an optimal, positive, rather than threatening, level of activation. This need probably relates to the needs underlying Self-Direction values.

sources.journal_entry:
The end-of-year ceremony was today and I sat through three hours of speeches about commitment and building foundations and putting down roots. The headmaster went on about how teaching is about planting seeds and watching them grow over decades. Decades! I nearly laughed out loud. I've been here two years and already the walls feel like they're closing in. Same classroom, same view of the vineyard, same Tuesday staff meetings where Marie-Claire complains about the photocopier.

I know I'm supposed to feel grateful. The farmhouse is beautiful, the students are curious, the lavender fields smell like something from a perfume advertisement. But I keep thinking about that email from Kristina asking if I'd consider joining her school project in Kenya next spring. Teaching environmental science to kids who've never seen a glacier, helping build the curriculum from scratch. My heart raced just reading it.

Then I looked at my garden, the tomato plants I actually managed to keep alive this year, and felt this strange guilt. Like I'm betraying something by wanting to leave again. My daughter Elsa called last week and said, "Maman, don't you ever want to just... stay?" And I didn't know what to tell her because the honest answer is no. Not really. The staying is what makes me feel like I'm slowly turning to stone.

sources.journal_entry:
Parent-teacher conference season again. I spent the whole afternoon choosing the right words for each report card comment. Mrs. Tan's son is struggling but she takes any criticism of him personally, so I wrote that he "shows potential for growth with additional practice." Mr. Lim expects detailed feedback, so his daughter got a full paragraph. Different families need different approaches.

Colleague Mei Ling asked why I spend so much time on these when most parents barely read them. I didn't have a good answer for her. I suppose I just feel that if I'm going to put my name on something, it should be done properly. No parent should feel embarrassed or caught off guard at the conference.

sources.journal_entry:
Something happened today that's been sitting with me. During lunch, a student named Darren made a crude joke in the canteen about another teacher, Mr. Goh. The other students laughed. Some teachers nearby pretended not to hear. I was walking past with my tray.

I should have said something. Mr. Goh is a good man, near retirement, a bit old-fashioned but dedicated. Darren's joke was disrespectful. But I kept walking. Sat down at my usual table, ate my noodles, graded papers during lunch like I always do.

The thing is, if I had confronted Darren in front of everyone, it would have become a scene. The other teachers would have had to acknowledge they heard it too. It would have been awkward for Mr. Goh if he found out. Darren's parents are influential in the school community and I don't want to deal with that. So I did nothing.

I keep telling myself it was the practical choice. But Mr. Goh was in the staff room later looking tired in that way that means something happened. Maybe he did hear. Maybe I should have been the one to defend him. I don't know why I'm still thinking about this.
sources.nudge_response: Everyone would have looked at me. The other teachers who ignored it would have felt judged. Darren's parents might have complained. The vice-principal might have gotten involved. And for what? The joke was already made. Mr. Goh's feelings were already hurt. Nothing I could say would undo that. But I still feel like I failed some kind of test.

sources.journal_entry: New vice-principal wants to "shake things up" with the curriculum. Suggested we try project-based learning instead of structured lessons. Everyone at the meeting nodded along. I nodded too.
sources.nudge_response: That the current curriculum has worked for fifteen years. That students need structure and clear expectations. That project-based learning sounds good in theory but creates chaos in practice. But new vice-principals need to feel heard, and nobody else was going to say anything, so why should I be the one.

Sunday. Called Mother at 7pm as usual. She asked about my health, about Mei's school results, about whether I'm eating properly. The same questions every week. I give the same answers. Mei is doing well. Yes I'm eating properly. Yes work is fine.

She mentioned that Cousin Huiying's son just got promoted to senior manager at some company. I said that's wonderful, congratulations to them. She waited a beat, the way she does when she wants me to say something else. I didn't say anything else. After we hung up I sat in the study for a while. The house was quiet, Ling had taken the kids to the mall. I thought about how I've been having the same conversation with my mother for thirty years. The questions change slightly but the shape of it stays the same. I ask nothing of her, she hints at things without saying them directly, we both pretend everything that needs to be said has been said. It's comfortable. Or at least it's familiar.

sources.journal_entry:
Meeting today with the Becker family about their estate commission. Third generation textile money, building a new country house in Baden-Württemberg. They want something for the entrance courtyard. Five meters minimum, abstract but with classical proportions. Budget is essentially open.

Herr Becker junior did most of the talking. Young man, maybe thirty-five, clearly trying to establish himself as the decision-maker now that his father has stepped back. He kept referencing installations he'd seen in Basel and New York. Wanted to know my thoughts on incorporating water features. I told him bronze and water require careful engineering, which adds six months minimum to the timeline.

His wife seemed more interested in the aesthetic conversation. She asked good questions about patina development over decades. I showed them photos of my Frankfurt piece from 2008 and how it's aged. She understood immediately what I was explaining about surface evolution.

Left the meeting feeling solid about the project. Private commissions like this are cleaner. One family, one vision, one contract. No committees, no budget votes, no competing proposals appearing from nowhere. The fee will be substantial. I'm already thinking about how to spend the spring - perhaps extend the Mallorca stay into April this year.
sources.nudge_response: The wife. Herr Becker junior wants to prove he's running things, but she's the one with the eye. He'll defer to her judgment on anything visual. I've seen this dynamic before with these families. The money gives orders, but taste steers the ship. I'll make sure my next presentation speaks to what she responded to.

sources.journal_entry:
The Hamburg project is on hold. The city council voted to delay the commission review until March, citing budget reallocation concerns. I found out through my gallery contact, not from the committee chair who promised to keep me informed directly. That's two months of planning, three revised proposals, and a scale model my team spent five weeks fabricating.

I called Martina, the head of the cultural affairs department, and she said the delay was procedural. No guarantees about the final decision. When I asked about the competing submissions, she went quiet. There are competing submissions now. Nobody mentioned that before.

My assistant Werner suggested we could use the time to refine the proposal further. I told him the proposal doesn't need refining. What it needs is for people to honor their word. The original brief came to me because of my work in Frankfurt and Munich. Now there are suddenly other artists in the conversation.

Spent the evening alone in the studio. Didn't work on anything. Just sat with a glass of Burgundy and looked at the model. It's good work. The proportions are right, the way it catches light from the north side. Should have been straightforward.
sources.nudge_response: Who would I call? Werner just tells me what I want to hear. My ex-wife would say I brought this on myself with my ego. My collector friends would offer sympathy but secretly wonder if I'm losing my touch. The wine was better company.
