sources.journal_entry:
Staff meeting today. The new director gave a presentation about "efficiency metrics" and patient throughput targets. During the Q&A, one of the junior nurses — Fatima, she's been here about eight months — asked a very good question about whether these targets would mean less time per patient for the non-Dutch-speaking patients who need interpreters. The director gave a non-answer about "equitable resource allocation" and moved on.

After the meeting, Fatima looked deflated. She came to me in the hallway and said she felt like nobody supported her question. I told her it was a good question and I agreed with her concern. She asked why I hadn't said anything during the meeting. I said something about it being a big room and timing not being right. She just nodded and walked off.

I've been that young nurse asking the hard question in a room full of people who agree privately and stay silent publicly. I know exactly how that feels and I let it happen to someone else. She needed one senior person to back her up and I didn't do it. The timing excuse is nonsense. I just didn't want to be seen challenging the new director in his first week. Politics over principle again. I should have backed her up.
sources.nudge_response: I think I have to. Not just for her. I need to know I'm still capable of following through.

sources.journal_entry:
Today I drove to work instead of cycling because it was raining hard and I was running late. Sat in traffic on the A20 for forty minutes, engine running, watching the Shell refinery chimneys pump out whatever it is they pump out, and I thought about what a fraud I am. I have a sign on my fridge that says "There is no Planet B" and there I was sitting in a diesel car because I didn't want to get wet.

It's not just the driving. I had a coffee from the machine downstairs in a disposable cup because I forgot my thermos. I ordered something from Amazon last week because it was cheaper and I needed it quickly when I could have waited and bought it from the local shop. Each thing on its own is nothing. But they add up and I'm adding them up and I don't like the total.

I talk to my daughter Lotte about these things and she says I'm too hard on myself, that systemic problems need systemic solutions and individual guilt is a distraction. She's probably right intellectually. But I grew up in a generation that was told every action matters, that you vote with your wallet, that if everyone just did their bit. And now I'm not even doing my bit consistently. The convenience keeps winning and I keep noticing and it's exhausting.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly no. It just makes me tired.

sources.journal_entry: Quiet Sunday. Cycled to the market, bought too much cheese, came home and pottered around the garden pulling weeds. Nothing on my mind for once.

Can't sleep so I'm writing more. Still stuck on the glove thing from earlier but it's connecting to something bigger now. At the ethics panel meeting last month, there was a discussion about end-of-life care guidelines for undocumented patients. The hospital legal team sent someone who basically said we should follow the strict protocol, which in practice means reduced access for people without valid papers. I pushed back in the meeting — I did speak up that time — but when the vote came I abstained because I didn't want to be the only dissenting voice on record. The motion passed.

I told myself abstaining was a form of protest, that it showed I didn't agree. But really I just didn't want my name attached to a losing vote. That's cowardice dressed up as strategy. These are people's lives and I was protecting my position on the panel.

The pattern is clear when I write it all out like this. I care deeply and I act cautiously and there's a gap between the two that keeps growing. I'm fifty-eight years old and I've built a reputation as someone who cares about these things, but when it costs me something — even something small like an awkward moment or a dissenting vote — I back down. I don't know what to do with that.

Been thinking about this all weekend and I need to write it down. Last Tuesday the ward got offered a bulk supply deal on disposable gloves and gowns from a company I know uses factories with terrible labour conditions in Southeast Asia. I've read the reports, I've seen the articles. The alternative supplier is more expensive and our budget is already squeezed. I signed off on the cheaper option because the ward manager was pushing hard and I didn't want to hold up the order for something nobody else seemed to care about.

It's such a small thing in the grand scheme. Nobody dies because of which glove supplier we use. But it's the principle — I spend my weekends at the refugee clinic working with people who've fled exactly these kinds of conditions, and then on a Tuesday morning I quietly approve the purchase order that keeps those conditions going. The hypocrisy of it sits badly.

I keep telling myself I'm one person and I can't fight every fight. But I also know that's what everyone tells themselves and it's how nothing ever changes. Willem says I take too much on and that it's not my job to fix global supply chains. He's probably right practically but it doesn't make me feel less complicit.
sources.nudge_response: Probably just an awkward meeting. That's what bothers me.

sources.journal_entry: Colleague made a joke about the refugee patients "costing us all money" at lunch and everyone laughed. I didn't laugh but I didn't say anything either. I'm not their teacher.

Long week. Thursday and Friday were double shifts because Pieter called in sick and nobody else could cover. By Friday afternoon I was running on automatic. One of my patients, an elderly man with no family contact, was scheduled for a comfort care review. I should have sat with him properly, gone through everything, made sure he understood all the options. Instead I rushed through it in ten minutes because I had three other patients waiting and the ward was short-staffed.

He deserved better than that. Every patient deserves a proper conversation about their care, especially when there's nobody else asking questions on their behalf. But I chose efficiency because I was stretched thin and it was the easier option. Ticked the box, moved on, felt wrong about it immediately.

The system is designed this way — there are never enough people, never enough time, and eventually everyone starts cutting corners. The corners you cut are always on the patients who won't complain. I know this. I've given talks about this. And I still did it. The gap between what I know is right and what I actually do when I'm exhausted is wider than I'd like to admit.
sources.nudge_response: Probably not. And that's the worst part.

sources.journal_entry:
Saturday. Slept in which I almost never do. Made coffee and read the Volkskrant at the kitchen table like I used to when the kids were small, except now the house is quiet and nobody's fighting over the last beschuit.

The paper had a big piece about plastic pollution in the North Sea and it got me going again. They found microplastics in fish at the market in Scheveningen. I remember swimming there as a girl and the water was already dirty then, but at least we weren't eating the pollution. Now it's in everything. I want to feel like individual choices matter — I bring my own bags, I cycle, I sort my recycling obsessively — but these articles make it feel so small against the scale of it. Shell is right there across the river and they're still doing what they've always done.

Went grocery shopping after, argued with myself about buying the organic tomatoes that cost twice as much. Bought them anyway. Had a quiet afternoon fixing the hem on my uniform trousers and listening to a podcast about healthcare in sub-Saharan Africa. Normal day really. Nothing remarkable.
sources.nudge_response: No. It just makes me angrier at the ones who could actually change things and choose not to.

sources.journal_entry:
Spent the afternoon at the refugee clinic. There was a Syrian woman, maybe my age, who came in with chronic back pain that's been ignored for months because she keeps getting shuffled between GP practices and nobody follows through. I got her a proper referral to the physiotherapist and explained everything in simple Dutch, and her daughter translated the rest. When she left she squeezed my hand and said something in Arabic I didn't understand but I could tell what it meant.

Those moments remind me why I do what I do. It's not heroic, it's just basic decency — making sure someone gets the care they should have had weeks ago. The system fails these people constantly and most of the time there's nobody there to catch them. I can't fix everything but I can make sure the ones who come through my door don't fall through the cracks.

Walked home along the Maas afterwards and the late afternoon light on the water was beautiful. Felt like myself for the first time all week. Made a simple stamppot for dinner and sat in the garden with a glass of wine and the radio on. Days like this keep me going.

Had a terrible shift today and I can't stop going over it. We had a team meeting about the new triage protocols and someone — one of the younger consultants — made a comment about how we should be "more selective" about which patients get palliative referrals because the ward is overstretched. He was basically implying we should deprioritise patients who don't have family pushing for it, which in practice means the homeless patients, the migrants, the people nobody's advocating for. I sat there and I knew exactly what he meant and I said nothing. A few people nodded. Anke looked uncomfortable but she didn't speak up either.

I've been doing this work for thirty years and I just let it slide. I told myself it was because the meeting was already running long and tempers were short, but honestly I think I was just tired. Tired and afraid of being that older nurse who's always making everything political. But those are real people he was talking about, people I've held hands with while they died. Nobody should have to earn the right to a dignified death by having relatives who make enough noise.

I'm angry at myself. I keep rehearsing what I should have said and it's making my stomach hurt. Willem would tell me to let it go and pick my battles, but this feels like exactly the kind of battle I should have picked.
sources.nudge_response: I think I was just exhausted and didn't want to be the difficult one again.

sources.journal_entry: They said yes. Contingent on finishing the holiday release first, but yes. I start on Jennifer's team in January. I have been studying Go tutorials at night, feeling like a student again.

I finally did it. I proposed to my manager that I move to Jennifer's team for the Go rewrite project. Not as a lead, not as an architect. Just as a developer. Someone who writes code and learns the new language and maybe remembers what it felt like to not know everything about a codebase.

He looked at me like I had asked for a demotion. Which, technically, I had. He said he would need to think about it, talk to HR, consider the implications. He asked if everything was okay at home. I said yes, everything is fine, I just want to learn something new before I am too old to learn.

I do not know why I said it like that. I am not too old. But something in me wanted to say it out loud, the fear underneath. Like naming it would make it less powerful.

Elena was proud of me when I told her. She said she has been waiting for me to do something like this for years. I did not know she was waiting. I thought I was hiding the restlessness well enough. Apparently I was only hiding it from myself.

Now I wait to see what they decide. Maybe they say no and I stay in my maintenance role forever. Maybe they say yes and I flounder in a new language at 57. Both possibilities feel more alive than certainty.

December sprint started with three people out sick and a scope increase nobody agreed to. I have been working ten-hour days trying to keep us on track for the holiday release. Jennifer is frustrated because her Go rewrite keeps getting deprioritized. I am frustrated because I am the one who has to explain why to her without making leadership look bad.

Had dinner with Elena's cousin Miguel who is visiting from Monterrey. He runs a small construction company there. He asked me about my job and I tried to explain sprint planning and stakeholder management and he just laughed and said it sounds like I spend a lot of energy managing people's feelings about work instead of actually working. He did not mean it unkindly but it stuck with me. Maybe he is right. Maybe that is what corporate software engineering becomes after a while.
sources.nudge_response: Building something. Seeing it run. Not writing status reports about why it is not done yet. But that is not realistic at my level, I suppose.

sources.journal_entry:
Back from the conference for a week now and people at work keep asking how it was. I say it was great, very inspiring, lots of good ideas. Which is true. But when they ask what I am going to do differently, I do not have a good answer. Learn Go? Propose a rewrite? Those feel like someone else's moves.

My manager suggested I do a lunch-and-learn to share what I learned. I said I would think about it. I probably will not do it. Public speaking was never my thing, and honestly, the sessions that meant most to me were the ones I cannot really present in a corporate setting. Nobody wants a slide deck about existential uncertainty in late-career engineers.
sources.nudge_response: Some business card contacts. A reading list. The usual conference stuff.

sources.journal_entry:
Flew to San Francisco yesterday for the unconference. Staying at a hotel near the Embarcadero with a view of the bay. Weather is cold and gray but I brought my good jacket.

The conference format is interesting. You show up in the morning, people pitch sessions on index cards, everyone votes with stickers, and then the schedule emerges. No predetermined speakers, no approved slides. Someone proposed a session on rebuilding legacy systems with LLMs. Someone else wanted to discuss leaving tech after 50. I almost proposed something about maintaining software versus maintaining yourself, but I did not have the index card ready in time.

I attended four sessions. The legacy systems one was good, practical advice I could use. The leaving tech one was harder to sit through. A woman around my age talked about how she realized she had optimized her whole life for a company that laid her off in an afternoon. She cried a little. Everyone was respectful.

Tonight I walked along the waterfront instead of joining the dinner group. Watched the ferries come and go. Called my mother. She asked if I was eating well and I said yes, even though I had skipped lunch. Some lies are kindness.

Tomorrow is the last day. I feel different here. Not better or worse. Just different.
sources.nudge_response: I was still figuring out what I wanted to say. It felt too personal for a room of strangers. Maybe next time.

sources.journal_entry: The morning after a bad night is always strange. Everything looks normal. Coffee tastes the same. I just feel like I am watching myself go through the motions from somewhere slightly outside.
sources.nudge_response: The usual routine. Checking Slack before I get out of bed. Reviewing the overnight alerts. Logging into the standup. Answering questions I have answered a hundred times. It is not bad, exactly. It is just automatic. Like I am not really needed there, just my pattern.

sources.journal_entry:
Long day. Production incident at 3 AM, the payment gateway again. Not the part Jennifer wanted to rewrite, ironically, but the legacy integration with the bank's SFTP server. I was on call so I got the page. Took four hours to trace it to a certificate expiration that nobody had on their calendar.

By 7 AM I had fixed it and documented everything. By 8 AM I was in the standup explaining what happened. By 9 AM I was getting messages from the VP asking how we let this happen. Not thank you for catching it. Not good job on the quick fix. Just how did we let this happen.

I did not let anything happen. I inherited this system. I have been asking for budget to modernize the certificate management for two years. But I did not say that either. I just said we would add better monitoring and put the renewal dates in a shared calendar. Safe answer. Team player answer.

Elena asked me at dinner why I looked so tired. I said work was busy. I did not tell her about the VP message because then she would get angry on my behalf and I would have to either agree with her anger or defend the company that made me feel small today. Both options felt exhausting.

I need to sleep but my mind keeps rehearsing the incident like I missed something. I did not miss anything. The certificate was not in any documentation I had access to. But I keep checking anyway.
sources.nudge_response: Maybe I do. It is easier than the alternative. Every time I push back, I become the difficult one, the senior engineer who cannot adapt, the old guy who thinks he knows better. So I absorb it. I fix things quietly. I make myself small so the team can function. It is what my father did at his factory job for forty years. I used to think he was weak for that. Now I understand he was just tired.

sources.journal_entry:
Elena surprised me with tickets to a tech conference in San Francisco next month. Not the corporate kind with vendor booths and networking bingo, but one of those unconference events where people just propose sessions in the morning and see what happens. She said she noticed I have been looking at conference websites lately but never registering for anything.

I should be excited. Five years ago I would have booked the flight before she finished her sentence. Now I am already thinking about the sprint commitments, about whether Marcus can handle the on-call rotation alone, about what my manager will say when I request the days off. The conference is on a weekend. I would only need to take Friday off. Still, I hesitated.

What bothers me most is not the hesitation itself. It is that I used to make decisions faster. Move to Austin? Two weeks to decide. Take the startup job over the stable bank position? One evening with Elena and a bottle of wine. Now I research, I weigh, I consider all stakeholders. My mother would say I finally grew up. But it feels more like something got dimmer.

I will go to the conference. I already told Elena yes. I just wish the yes had come easier.
sources.nudge_response: Maybe around the time my father got sick. 2018. Suddenly there were consequences everywhere I looked. Every choice felt connected to whether I would be there, whether I was reliable. He passed in 2019 and I thought it would lift, but it did not. The weight just found new things to attach to.

sources.journal_entry:
The new architect they brought in, Jennifer, she wants to rewrite the payment gateway from scratch. Using Go instead of Java. Everyone in the room looked at me like I was supposed to object, since I built the original thing in 2019. But honestly? Part of me wanted to say yes, let us do it, let me learn something new instead of patching the same codebase forever.

I did not say that though. I said we should consider the timeline and the risk to the December release. Which is true. The business needs stability. But I walked out of that meeting feeling like I had swallowed something heavy.
sources.nudge_response: It is not that simple. Jennifer does not know what she does not know about the regulatory requirements. Someone had to be the adult.

sources.journal_entry: Another sprint planning meeting where they want me to estimate the same maintenance tickets I have been doing for three years. I know exactly how long everything takes now. That is maybe the problem.

Not the corporate kind with vendor booths and networking bingo, but one of those unconference events where people just propose sessions in the morning and see what happens. She said she noticed I have been looking at conference websites lately but never registering for anything.

I should be excited. Five years ago I would have booked the flight before she finished her sentence. Now I am already thinking about the sprint commitments, about whether Marcus can handle the on-call rotation alone, about what my manager will say when I request the days off. The conference is on a weekend. I would only need to take Friday off. Still, I hesitated.

What bothers me most is not the hesitation itself. It is that I used to make decisions faster. Move to Austin? Two weeks to decide. Take the startup job over the stable bank position? One evening with Elena and a bottle of wine. Now I research, I weigh, I consider all stakeholders. My mother would say I finally grew up. But it feels more like something got dimmer.

I will go to the conference. I already told Elena yes. I just wish the yes had come easier.
sources.nudge_response: Maybe around the time my father got sick. 2018. Suddenly there were consequences everywhere I looked. Every choice felt connected to whether I would be there, whether I was reliable. He passed in 2019 and I thought it would lift, but it did not. The weight just found new things to attach to.

sources.journal_entry:
The new architect they brought in, Jennifer, she wants to rewrite the payment gateway from scratch. Using Go instead of Java. Everyone in the room looked at me like I was supposed to object, since I built the original thing in 2019. But honestly? Part of me wanted to say yes, let us do it, let me learn something new instead of patching the same codebase forever.

I did not say that though. I said we should consider the timeline and the risk to the December release. Which is true. The business needs stability. But I walked out of that meeting feeling like I had swallowed something heavy.
sources.nudge_response: It is not that simple. Jennifer does not know what she does not know about the regulatory requirements. Someone had to be the adult.

sources.journal_entry: Presented the Q3 roadmap to the leadership team today. Kept it to seven slides, used business metrics instead of technical specs. VP nodded twice. Small win.

Quarterly review feedback came in. My manager said I have strong technical skills but need to demonstrate more "executive presence." I asked what that meant specifically. She said it's about how I communicate upward—being more concise in leadership meetings, framing problems in terms of business impact rather than technical detail.

I've always believed that doing excellent work should speak for itself. That's what my father taught me—results matter, not showmanship. But apparently that's not how it works here. The people who get ahead are the ones who know how to package themselves.

Spent the evening reading articles about executive communication. Downloaded a book on stakeholder management. I don't like that I have to play this game, but I've never failed at something I committed to learning. If this is what they want, I'll figure it out.

What frustrates me is that nobody told me the rules changed. At IIT, you studied hard, you got the marks, you got the placement. Clear metrics. Here it's all subjective—"presence," "influence," "visibility." How do you measure that? How do you know if you're winning?
sources.nudge_response: Then everything I was taught about how success works would be wrong. My father worked for the same company for thirty years and retired as a senior manager—never played politics, just delivered results. But maybe that's why he stayed senior manager. Maybe there was a ceiling I didn't see. I don't want that ceiling.

sources.journal_entry: Three nights of on-call rotations. The junior devs can't seem to handle basic incident triage without escalating to me. I don't mind being the one they depend on, but I need sleep.
sources.nudge_response: Indispensable means they can't function without you. Needed just means they prefer having you around. I'd rather be indispensable, even if it costs me sleep. Nobody promotes the guy who's easily replaced.

sources.journal_entry: Priya asked when I'm taking her to meet my parents. I said after Diwali, maybe. We both know I'm stalling but she didn't push.

Vikram got promoted to Staff Engineer today. Everyone's congratulating him on Slack, and yes, fine, he deserved it. But let's be honest—he's been here six months longer than me and his scope was smaller until Q2. I'm not bitter. I'm just aware of where I stand. My manager keeps telling me my time will come, but I've heard that before at my last company. You have to make your time come.

Called Appa tonight. He asked about work, and I told him everything was progressing well. No point worrying him with the details. He mentioned the temple renovation fund and I sent extra this month. These things matter. You take care of your family, you do what's expected—that's not a burden, that's just how it should be.
sources.nudge_response: Visibility. I need to be leading cross-functional initiatives, not just delivering my own sprint work. I've already started attending product roadmap meetings even when I'm not required. When the reorg happens in Q4, I want my name to come up naturally for the platform team lead role.

sources.journal_entry:
Bad week. The delivery app lowered the per-trip rate again, no warning, no explanation. Just opened the app Monday morning and the numbers were different. I did the same twelve deliveries I always do on a weekday and came home with almost twenty percent less. Twenty percent. That's not nothing. That's a week of groceries, that's Negrita's vet visit I've been putting off.

The handyman side is slower too because people are tightening up. I had three jobs lined up this week and two of them canceled last minute — one lady said she'd "wait until next month" to fix her bathroom faucet and the other one just stopped responding. So now I'm sitting here Thursday night with the calculator app open, moving numbers around like I'm playing some kind of sad puzzle game, trying to figure out where the motorcycle payment comes from.

The thing that really gets to me is the feeling. It's not just about the money, it's the not knowing. Every month is a guess. Every week I wake up and I don't know what I'm going to make. I used to think that was the trade-off for not having a boss breathing down my neck. Lately I'm not so sure the trade-off is worth it. But what am I supposed to do, crawl back and prove Graciela right? No. I'll figure it out. I always figure it out.

My sister Graciela keeps calling to tell me I should go back to a regular job. She doesn't get it. I'm not going to sit in some warehouse again answering to a guy ten years younger than me who treats people like furniture.
sources.nudge_response: It's not impossible, I just don't want to. There's a difference. Look, I know what I'm doing. I've been managing fine for five years this way. Graciela worries because she's Graciela. She married an accountant, everything in her life has a line item. Not everyone lives like that.

sources.journal_entry:
Started doing the math again tonight. If I keep the delivery app running five days a week and pick up at least two handyman jobs on the weekends, I can cover everything with about twelve thousand pesos left over. That leftover is supposed to be for the motorcycle insurance renewal in May. I wrote it on a sticky note and put it on the fridge next to the old one that says "DO NOT touch savings."

Funny thing is, I spent Saturday at the parrilla with Cacho and Pocho like always, and the bill came out heavier than usual because we ordered that tira de asado. I didn't blink. Six hours of good food and good talk, what am I going to do, skip it? Some weeks the numbers work, some weeks they don't. But I'm not going to stop living just because the spreadsheet says I should.

sources.journal_entry: Don Alfredo recommended me to his daughter for some painting work at her new apartment. Three rooms, good rate, she even offered to pay half upfront. I bought Negrita the fancy wet food she likes to celebrate.

Picked up the motorcycle from Raul this morning. It rides clean now, brakes feel solid. That's something. But I'm running on maybe four hours of sleep from the last few days and I can feel it in my eyes, in the way I'm slow to react at intersections. Almost clipped a bus mirror on Corrientes.

Saturday is coming and Cacho already texted about the parrilla. Part of me wants to skip it this week, save the money. But another part of me — the louder part — says that's the one thing that keeps me sane. You take away the asado with friends and what do I have left? A cat, a calculator, and a leaking faucet in my own bathroom that I haven't even bothered to fix.
sources.nudge_response: It's the only time during the week where I'm not counting anything. Not counting deliveries, not counting pesos, not counting hours. I sit down, the meat comes, somebody pours the wine, and for a few hours I'm just Roberto having a good time with his friends. Nobody's asking me to fix something or deliver something or be somewhere in fifteen minutes. It's the closest thing I have to feeling like my life is actually mine.

sources.journal_entry: Couldn't sleep. Opened the app at 1am to see if there were any late-night delivery runs. There were two. I took them both, rode the bicycle I borrowed from my neighbor. Came home at 3am with barely enough to cover tomorrow's gas.

Motorcycle started making a noise yesterday. A grinding thing when I brake. I took it to Raul's shop and he looked at it and said the brake pads are gone and the disc is warped, it needs replacing. He quoted me a number that wiped out everything I'd saved from the Alfredo job. Every peso.

I stood there in Raul's shop and felt my stomach just drop. Because it's not optional — the motorcycle is how I make deliveries. Without it I'm on foot or taking the subte, which means fewer trips, which means less money, which means next month's rent gets tight. It's like this chain where one thing breaks and everything behind it starts wobbling. I told Raul to do it, because what choice do I have. But I walked home and I couldn't even eat dinner.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly, I was thinking about my old man. He worked at the same factory for thirty-two years. Hated it, but every month the check came in. He never had to wonder if the floor was going to fall out from under him. I used to think that was a sad way to live. Now I'm not so sure. He always had a little envelope in the dresser drawer with cash for emergencies. I don't have that envelope. I don't have anything between me and the next bad surprise. And that thought — that I'm one broken motorcycle or one bad month away from not being able to pay rent — that sat on my chest the whole walk home.

sources.journal_entry:
Painting job at Don Alfredo's daughter's place is done. She was happy with it, paid the balance, even tipped me a little extra. So the money situation is stable for the moment. Rent is covered, motorcycle payment is covered, Raul is paid. There's a small cushion again, not much, but it's there.

Went to the parrilla Saturday like always. Pocho brought his nephew, a kid of about twenty-five who does the same delivery app I do but also drives for a rideshare service on the side. He was telling me about his "strategy" — how he works the surge hours, how he tracks which neighborhoods tip best, how he's saving for a down payment on his own place. The whole table was impressed. I just sat there eating my chorizo and feeling old.

It's not jealousy exactly. The kid has energy and optimism and a plan, and good for him. But I was that kid once. I had the energy to work sixteen-hour days and still go dancing with my ex-wife on Saturday night. Now I do eight hours of deliveries and my back locks up. I eat the asado and drink the wine and it's still good, it's always good. But there's this thin layer underneath the enjoyment now, like a film on old coffee. Like I'm enjoying it because I know this might not last. Like I should be saving what I'm spending here but I can't bring myself to stop because this is the part of my life that doesn't feel like survival.

Graciela came over unannounced today while I was between deliveries. She brought empanadas, which was nice, except then she sat at my kitchen table and started doing that thing she does where she looks around the apartment cataloguing everything that's wrong. The peeling paint above the window, the chair with the broken leg, the fact that I still don't have a proper desk and eat on the couch.

Then she said — and I quote — "Roberto, you're almost fifty, you can't live like a college student." And I just stood there holding an empanada feeling like I was fourteen again getting lectured. She doesn't see that I actually like my life most of the time. I like picking my own hours. I like riding through Palermo on a Tuesday morning with the sun out and nobody telling me where to be. But she looks at this apartment and she sees failure. And the worst part is that sometimes, when she leaves, I start seeing it through her eyes too.

sources.journal_entry:
Sprint deadline tomorrow and I'm at the office late. The PM asked me to cut corners on the data validation layer for the remittance feature, the same one Ravi flagged weeks ago. She said we'll circle back to it after launch. I know what "circle back" means. It means never.

I said okay. I could have pushed back, could have said the validation matters because real people's money is on the line and if we ship it broken the ones who suffer are the ones who can least afford it. But the deadline is real and I'm tired and sometimes you just want to go home. Chose what was easy for me. The people affected won't even know my name.

Worker center morning. Helped two new guys file their claims. One of them brought me a packet of murukku his wife made. Sat on the bench outside eating it and feeling grateful for this strange second life I have on Saturdays.

Long week but today felt different. Took Xiao Yu to East Coast Park and she spent an hour picking up shells and bits of plastic from the sand. She didn't separate them at first, just collecting, and then she looked at her bucket and said the plastic ones aren't pretty. I asked what we should do with them and she said throw them away properly. We spent another thirty minutes walking to find recycling and trash bins.

It's a small thing. A kid picking up beach trash. But watching her make that distinction on her own, without being told, reminded me of why Mei Ling and I try to live the way we do. Not because we're going to fix the ocean or the climate or anything so grand, but because the habits matter. The noticing matters.

Came home and cooked dinner together, the three of us. Xiao Yu was in charge of washing vegetables. She takes the job very seriously, inspecting each leaf. Mei Ling and I exchanged a look over her head, the kind of look that says we might be doing okay at this. It's been an exhausting few weeks but tonight I feel settled in a way I haven't for a while.

Team dinner tonight. Quarterly thing, company card. The conversation turned to hiring and someone made a comment about how candidates from certain countries need more "handholding." A few people laughed. I didn't laugh but I also didn't say anything. Just moved the ice around in my glass.

The thing is I know exactly what that comment means. I've been on the receiving end of it, the assumption that because you come from a certain place you're somehow less. And I've watched the guys at the center deal with far worse versions of the same attitude every day. But at the table I just sat there because it was a team dinner and I didn't want to make it awkward. I'm so tired of choosing comfort over what I actually think.
sources.nudge_response: I don't know. Probably both. It's easier to blame it on not wanting confrontation than to admit I'm scared of being seen differently by people I work with every day.

sources.journal_entry: Rainy morning. The uncle at the kopi stall asked about my daughter. Drank my coffee and watched the wet road for a while before heading to the MRT.
Same day, later. Ordered from Grab because I was too tired to cook. While eating I scrolled past an article about plastic waste in the Java Sea. Closed it, kept eating from the styrofoam container.

Normal Monday. Dropped Xiao Yu at school and she asked me why some of her classmates' parents drive them and we take the bus. I told her we like the bus. Which is half true. We can afford a car, we just choose not to, but explaining that to a seven-year-old is its own project.

Work was the usual sprint backlog. Nothing exciting, nothing soul-crushing. Had lunch with a colleague and we talked about the new condo launches. Everyone around me seems to be upgrading something, their flat, their car, their phone. I don't feel the pull the way I used to, but I notice it like background noise you can't quite tune out.

Went to the worker center this morning. There was a new guy, Suresh, from Tamil Nadu. Fell from scaffolding three weeks ago and his employer hasn't filed the injury report. He showed me the bruises on his back, purple-yellow, still swelling around his ribs. I helped him draft a letter to MOM. My Mandarin-accented English and his Tamil-accented English, both of us stumbling through legalese neither of us was built for.

But we got it done. He shook my hand with both of his and said thank you in a way that made me want to cry in the stairwell afterward. I held it together. Barely.
sources.nudge_response: It felt undeserved. All I did was help write a letter. He's the one living through it, sleeping on a bunk bed with broken ribs because he can't afford to stop working.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a team standup today and Ravi brought up that our payment processing pipeline is rejecting a disproportionate number of transactions from certain Southeast Asian corridors. The data was right there in the dashboard. Mostly remittance flows, the kind migrant workers use to send money home. Something about the fraud model flagging certain patterns that are just... normal behavior for people sending small amounts frequently.

I knew what I was looking at. I've sat across the table from guys at the worker center who tell me how hard it is to send money back to their families, the fees they pay, the delays. And here's our system making it worse. But when Ravi raised it, the lead just said we'd revisit the thresholds next quarter and moved on. I could have pushed. I had the context, the stories, the data to make a case. But I just nodded and typed something in the chat about checking the logs.

Part of me says it wasn't the right moment, that I need to build a proper case first. But honestly I think I was just worried about being the guy who derails standup with a soapbox moment. My parents always told me not to stick out, keep your head down and do good work. Maybe that advice served them well in a factory town in Fujian. I'm not sure it serves me well here, sitting on information that could change something.
sources.nudge_response: Probably something about how the people on the other end of those rejected transactions aren't abstractions. They're the same guys I see on Saturday mornings trying to figure out medical claims. But saying that out loud at work feels like crossing a line I can't uncross.

sources.journal_entry: Worker center morning. Helped two new guys file their claims. One of them brought me a packet of murukku his wife made. Sat on the bench outside eating it and feeling grateful for this strange second life I have on Saturdays.

Long week but today felt different. Took Xiao Yu to East Coast Park and she spent an hour picking up shells and bits of plastic from the sand. She didn't separate them at first, just collecting, and then she looked at her bucket and said the plastic ones aren't pretty. I asked what we should do with them and she said throw them away properly. We spent another thirty minutes walking to find recycling and trash bins.

It's a small thing. A kid picking up beach trash. But watching her make that distinction on her own, without being told, reminded me of why Mei Ling and I try to live the way we do. Not because we're going to fix the ocean or the climate or anything so grand, but because the habits matter. The noticing matters.

Came home and cooked dinner together, the three of us. Xiao Yu was in charge of washing vegetables. She takes the job very seriously, inspecting each leaf. Mei Ling and I exchanged a look over her head, the kind of look that says we might be doing okay at this. It's been an exhausting few weeks but tonight I feel settled in a way I haven't for a while.

Team dinner tonight. Quarterly thing, company card. The conversation turned to hiring and someone made a comment about how candidates from certain countries need more "handholding." A few people laughed. I didn't laugh but I also didn't say anything. Just moved the ice around in my glass.

The thing is I know exactly what that comment means. I've been on the receiving end of it, the assumption that because you come from a certain place you're somehow less. And I've watched the guys at the center deal with far worse versions of the same attitude every day. But at the table I just sat there because it was a team dinner and I didn't want to make it awkward. I'm so tired of choosing comfort over what I actually think.
sources.nudge_response: I don't know. Probably both. It's easier to blame it on not wanting confrontation than to admit I'm scared of being seen differently by people I work with every day.

sources.journal_entry: Rainy morning. The uncle at the kopi stall asked about my daughter. Drank my coffee and watched the wet road for a while before heading to the MRT.
Same day, later. Ordered from Grab because I was too tired to cook. While eating I scrolled past an article about plastic waste in the Java Sea. Closed it, kept eating from the styrofoam container.

Normal Monday. Dropped Xiao Yu at school and she asked me why some of her classmates' parents drive them and we take the bus. I told her we like the bus. Which is half true. We can afford a car, we just choose not to, but explaining that to a seven-year-old is its own project.

Work was the usual sprint backlog. Nothing exciting, nothing soul-crushing. Had lunch with a colleague and we talked about the new condo launches. Everyone around me seems to be upgrading something, their flat, their car, their phone. I don't feel the pull the way I used to, but I notice it like background noise you can't quite tune out.

Went to the worker center this morning. There was a new guy, Suresh, from Tamil Nadu. Fell from scaffolding three weeks ago and his employer hasn't filed the injury report. He showed me the bruises on his back, purple-yellow, still swelling around his ribs. I helped him draft a letter to MOM. My Mandarin-accented English and his Tamil-accented English, both of us stumbling through legalese neither of us was built for.

But we got it done. He shook my hand with both of his and said thank you in a way that made me want to cry in the stairwell afterward. I held it together. Barely.
sources.nudge_response: It felt undeserved. All I did was help write a letter. He's the one living through it, sleeping on a bunk bed with broken ribs because he can't afford to stop working.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a team standup today and Ravi brought up that our payment processing pipeline is rejecting a disproportionate number of transactions from certain Southeast Asian corridors. The data was right there in the dashboard. Mostly remittance flows, the kind migrant workers use to send money home. Something about the fraud model flagging certain patterns that are just... normal behavior for people sending small amounts frequently.

I knew what I was looking at. I've sat across the table from guys at the worker center who tell me how hard it is to send money back to their families, the fees they pay, the delays. And here's our system making it worse. But when Ravi raised it, the lead just said we'd revisit the thresholds next quarter and moved on. I could have pushed. I had the context, the stories, the data to make a case. But I just nodded and typed something in the chat about checking the logs.

Part of me says it wasn't the right moment, that I need to build a proper case first. But honestly I think I was just worried about being the guy who derails standup with a soapbox moment. My parents always told me not to stick out, keep your head down and do good work. Maybe that advice served them well in a factory town in Fujian. I'm not sure it serves me well here, sitting on information that could change something.
sources.nudge_response: Probably something about how the people on the other end of those rejected transactions aren't abstractions. They're the same guys I see on Saturday mornings trying to figure out medical claims. But saying that out loud at work feels like crossing a line I can't uncross.

sources.journal_entry:
Monday. Staff meeting went long because Thomas wanted to discuss the new reporting structure again. I'd already decided on it two weeks ago and communicated it clearly, but apparently some people need to re-litigate everything. Let them talk for ten minutes, then moved on.

Lotte asked how work was over dinner. I said fine. She gave me that look, the one that means she knows I'm not actually answering. I wasn't trying to be evasive, I just genuinely didn't have the energy to translate the day into something she'd find interesting. Watched the football afterward, fell asleep on the couch again.
Routine day. Back-to-back calls, budget reconciliation, nothing unusual. Grabbed a broodje kroket from the canteen and ate it at my desk between meetings.

Needed sign-off from Legal on the new supplier contract. Straightforward, or so I thought. Sent it Thursday, followed up Friday morning, got told Anke was "reviewing priorities" and would get to it when she could. Meanwhile the supplier's deadline is Tuesday and I'm the one who'll look like I dropped the ball.

It's not even about the contract, really. It's that I had to sit there refreshing my inbox like some junior waiting for permission. I run a forty-three person division and I can't move a standard supplier agreement through because someone in a different department decides the timeline. I almost went to the CEO directly but thought better of it. Probably should have.

Ran the quarterly review myself today, no slides from anyone else, just my numbers, my narrative. The room was quiet in that good way where people are actually listening. Felt like the division is finally mine in the way I wanted it to be.

Pieter talked right over me in the steering committee today, mid-sentence, and presented the container routing proposal like it was his. I just sat there. Too tired to fight it, too angry to let it go, and now it's midnight and I'm still turning it over.

sources.journal_entry: Can't sleep. Keep thinking about how easily I let things go at work. Tomasz caught my eye in the hallway today and just nodded and I felt like a fraud.

Grocery run after work. Standing in Edeka staring at the coffee shelf. Fair trade option is almost double the price of the store brand. I know what the price difference means — it means someone down the supply chain is getting squeezed. I know this. I've read about it. I've shared articles about it.

Bought the store brand anyway. Forty euros left until payday and I'm not going to pretend that doesn't matter. But it's the same calculation I keep making. The flight to Lisbon. The compliance thing at work. There's always a reason to pick the easier option and the reason is always money or comfort or not wanting to be the difficult one.

I'm exhausted by the gap between what I think matters and what I actually do when it comes down to it. It's not even big moral failures. It's coffee. It's a budget airline. It's staying quiet at lunch. But it's all the same muscle and I keep not using it. And I'm too tired tonight to figure out what to do about that. Going to bed.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly can't tell anymore. Some weeks smaller, some weeks it swallows everything.

sources.journal_entry:
Had a one-on-one with my manager Katharina. She asked how I was finding the team culture and I actually said something. Told her the comment during Tomasz's onboarding bothered me and that I think we could be more careful about that kind of thing. She nodded and took a note and said she'd "keep an eye on it."

Not exactly a revolution. But I said it. Out loud. To someone with authority to do something. I've been replaying the conversation all evening trying to figure out if she took it seriously or just filed it under "Lukas is being sensitive." Probably overthinking it. The point is I didn't let it pass this time.

People at work probably think I'm easygoing because I don't argue in meetings. But easygoing and silent aren't the same thing. I've just been choosing silent for too long. Katharina's response wasn't dramatic — no promises, no action items — but she heard me. And I can live with that being the starting point.

Part of me wants to dismiss this as barely doing anything. Like, congratulations, you mentioned something mildly uncomfortable in a private meeting, what do you want, a medal? But no. I know what it cost me to say it and I know I wouldn't have done it two months ago.

Weird day in a good way. The nonprofit had their summer meetup at the Englischer Garten, just food and talking, nothing structured. I ended up sitting with this Syrian family I'd helped with their paperwork back in March, the Haddads. The dad, Marwan, was telling me about his daughter's school report — she got top marks in maths and he was so proud he was practically vibrating.

And there was this moment where he grabbed my arm and said something in Arabic to his wife and she smiled and he turned back to me and said "she says you are part of the story now." I didn't really know what to say to that. Just sat there eating my Falafel feeling like, okay, this is something real. Not a dashboard metric. Not a compliance tolerance. An actual family doing better because a few people showed up consistently.

I think about the work stuff — the carbon numbers, the things I don't say in meetings — and then I think about this afternoon and it's hard to hold both at the same time. But today was just good. Marwan's daughter got good grades and he wanted to tell me about it. That's enough for one Monday.

New contractor started on the team. Guy named Tomasz, Polish, here on a project-based contract. During onboarding someone made a joke about Eastern European work ethic — meant as a compliment, apparently. Tomasz laughed it off. I didn't say anything.

It's such a small moment. Probably wouldn't even register for most people. But I noticed the way Tomasz's laugh didn't quite reach his eyes and I thought about saying something after the meeting and then I didn't. Went back to my Jira tickets instead.
sources.nudge_response: Maybe just that I noticed. That he doesn't have to laugh at stuff like that here. But saying that out loud feels presumptuous, like I'm deciding what should bother him.

sources.journal_entry:
The carbon audit thing. I finally got a response from Stefan in compliance. He said the numbers I flagged were "within acceptable reporting tolerances" and that the methodology was approved by their external auditor. End of conversation, apparently.

So I looked into it more. The tolerance band they're using is laughably wide — basically you can underreport by fifteen percent and still be compliant. It's technically legal. But the whole reason I pushed for the audit was because I thought the company would want to know the real numbers. Turns out they already know and they're fine with it. The system is designed to allow this.

I could escalate. Take it to the sustainability board or even the Betriebsrat. But I've been here eighteen months and I'm not in a position to make waves. And honestly, part of me is relieved that Stefan shut it down because now I have an excuse to stop. That's the part I don't like admitting. I chose the easier path — I got my answer, I can file it away, and nobody has to be uncomfortable. Including me.

The thing is, when I left the adtech job I told myself I wouldn't do this. I wouldn't just accept things that feel wrong because it's inconvenient to push. And here I am doing exactly that.
sources.nudge_response: That I want someone else to fight this one. Which is exactly the problem.

sources.journal_entry:
Lunch with Felix and Sandra. Sandra was talking about her new apartment in Schwabing and how she's glad the neighbourhood "hasn't changed too much," meaning it hasn't gotten more diverse. She didn't say it outright but the implication was clear. Felix nodded along.

I changed the subject to the upcoming sprint deadline. Could have said something. Should have, maybe. But Sandra is senior to me and she's leading the Q3 roadmap review. There's a calculation that happens in these moments and I went with the safe option. Finished my Kartoffelsalat and went back to my desk.

Booked a flight to Lisbon for August. Budget airline, the one that keeps getting flagged for its emissions record. I know this. I looked at the train option and it was fourteen hours and three times the price and I just couldn't justify it.

I'm tired of every small decision feeling like a referendum. The flight was sixty euros. The train would've eaten half my weekend travel budget. I picked convenience and cost and I'm sitting here feeling vaguely bad about it, which is stupid because one flight isn't going to tip the scales. But it adds up and I know it adds up and that's the part that nags at me.

Team standup today. Felix made a comment about one of our logistics partners using subcontracted drivers with no fixed contracts, basically gig workers with zero protections. He said it casually, like it was just a business fact. I sat there and said nothing.

It's not like I didn't notice. I noticed immediately. But the meeting had twelve people in it and the product lead was driving the agenda and I just... let it slide. Afterwards I thought about saying something to Felix privately but then I got pulled into a deployment issue and the moment passed. I keep telling myself I'll bring it up tomorrow but I probably won't. It's easier to pretend I didn't hear it clearly.
sources.nudge_response: Honestly the room. Twelve people, nobody else flinched.

sources.journal_entry: Helped Amira debug the intake form tonight at the nonprofit. She'd been stuck on a date-parsing issue for two days and we sorted it in twenty minutes. Small thing, but it felt like the right use of a Tuesday evening.
sources.nudge_response: Dunno, just better than watching Netflix again.

sources.journal_entry:
First full week done at Birch Lane. The kids are sweet. One boy, Mateo, already told me he wants to read "chapter books like his sister." That kind of thing is why I'm here. The building is old and the supply closet is basically empty, but I spent the weekend printing worksheets at the library and laminating them myself. Cost me about forty dollars out of pocket, which I noticed when I checked my account this morning.

I set up a reading corner with pillows I found at a thrift store. It looks decent. The other second-grade teacher, Mrs. Okada, lent me a box of leveled readers she wasn't using. I mapped out the first unit already and I feel like I actually know what I'm doing for Monday. Haven't felt that way in a while. Small thing, but it matters. The commute is long and the parking lot has potholes, but I walked into that classroom and the kids were waiting and it just felt like where I was supposed to be.
sources.nudge_response: Because if I don't set this up right from the start, the kids lose momentum and I lose the year. I've seen it happen during student teaching. You can't get that first month back.

sources.journal_entry: People keep asking why I don't just retire and run the foundation full-time. As if it's that simple. The business funds everything — the foundation, my children's projects, the scholarships. Without it there's nothing to give.
sources.nudge_response: Not just income. The ability to actually do something about the problems I see. Money is leverage.

sources.journal_entry:
Flew back from a factory visit in Penang. The new processing line looks good, efficiency is way up, costs are down. Everyone was pleased. On the drive to the airport the plant manager mentioned casually that they'd switched to a cheaper chemical solvent for circuit board stripping. Cheaper and, I suspect, not properly rated for ventilation in that building. I could smell it from the parking lot.

I didn't ask about it. I could have. I had forty minutes in the car and I know enough about chemical handling to ask the right questions. But I was tired and the deal was done and bringing it up would have meant delaying the whole partnership review. I chose convenience. The flight home felt longer than usual.

My son called from Jakarta. His NGO just secured funding to expand their mangrove restoration project into two new provinces. I could hear it in his voice — the energy, the belief that what he's doing actually matters. I told him I was proud. I meant it completely.

After we hung up I transferred some money to the foundation account. Not a huge amount, but enough to cover the clean-water pump installation we've been delaying in Siem Reap because the supplier raised prices. My wife asked why I didn't just wait until next quarter when cash flow is better. I told her some things shouldn't wait. She gave me that look she gives when she thinks I'm being impulsive, but she processed the transfer anyway.
sources.nudge_response: Hearing him talk about the mangroves reminded me why I started the foundation. Sometimes you forget.

sources.journal_entry:
Board meeting for the trade association today. One of the newer members, a woman from a Cambodian labour rights group, raised concerns about working conditions at several member factories — specifically about informal workers who sort e-waste without proper protective gear. She had photos. She had data from a university study. She asked the board to issue a formal statement and require audits before renewing factory memberships.

I didn't say anything. I just sat there. A few other board members started pushing back immediately — talking about how the data was old, how conditions had improved, how public statements would hurt investment confidence in the sector. The usual deflections. And I know they're partly right, some of those factories have made genuine improvements. But the photos were recent. The data wasn't old. I could see the timestamps.

The thing is, two of those factories are long-standing clients of mine. We process their scrap. If I backed the statement, it would put those relationships at risk. Not just financially — personally. I've known these owners for over a decade. We've eaten at each other's homes. It's not as simple as just raising your hand and saying yes, we should hold them accountable. There are layers to this. But I keep replaying her face when nobody supported her motion. She looked like she expected it. That's worse somehow — that she wasn't even surprised.
sources.nudge_response: The relationships. Twenty years of built trust. You don't blow that up in a board meeting.

sources.journal_entry:
Saturday morning, went to the hawker centre near our old Toa Payoh flat. The uncle who runs the wonton noodle stall has been there since my kids were small, must be almost thirty years now. We talked for a while. He's worried about his lease renewal, says the rents keep going up and the younger hawkers can't make it work anymore. Whole stretch of stalls might close.

I started thinking about whether the trade association could do something — not directly but maybe model something. We talk a lot about industry sustainability but it's always about supply chains and compliance frameworks. Nobody talks about what happens to the communities around these supply chains. The hawker uncle isn't e-waste, obviously, but it's the same pattern. Small people squeezed by systems that don't see them. I should bring this up at the next meeting. Or maybe I'll just sit there again. Don't know.
sources.nudge_response: Probably nothing. The agenda is always packed and nobody wants to hear philosophy from the recycling guy.

sources.journal_entry:
Thesis stress is properly hitting now. I was up until two in the morning reading IPCC reports and cross-referencing enforcement data and at some point I just stopped and looked at what I was doing. I'm writing about policy mechanisms that might reduce emissions by some fraction of a percentage point over a decade. And meanwhile the numbers keep getting worse. Every single year. I read a paper last week that said we've already locked in enough warming to make certain Pacific islands uninhabitable. Already locked in. Past tense.

So what am I actually doing. I'm sitting in a well-heated Swedish apartment writing about governance frameworks while people are losing their homes to rising seas right now. My thesis will get graded, filed, maybe cited in another thesis. The policy recommendations I'm writing will be read by my supervisor and two examiners and then forgotten. That's the honest truth of it.

I could have gone into something more direct. Field work. Activism. Legal advocacy. Instead I chose the comfortable academic route where I get to feel smart about the problem without ever getting my hands dirty. My friend Elsa works for an NGO in Bangladesh building flood shelters. She makes a third of what I'll make when I graduate. She's also actually doing something. I chose to write about the problem from a distance because it's safer and it counts toward a degree. That's the choice I made today and every day I sit in that library.
sources.nudge_response: I don't know. I'm too tired to answer that honestly right now.

sources.journal_entry:
Quiet week. Spent most of it in the library working through policy documents for chapter four. The snow has been heavy and cycling has been miserable but the bus is worse, so I keep at it. Had fika with Nils and our other housemate Sara on Wednesday. We talked about summer plans. Nils wants to do a hiking trip in Norway. Sara is going home to Malmö.

Cooked a big pot of lentil soup on Sunday that I've been eating all week. My mum called to check in, asked about the thesis timeline. I told her it's on track for June submission. She sounded relieved. Nothing eventful really. Just the steady rhythm of getting through January.

I told Lindqvist I'd pass on the Vattenfall liaison position. She took it well enough, said she understood, moved on to thesis feedback. I don't think she was surprised.

At the volunteer session on Saturday, one of the newer volunteers, a guy named Anders, made a comment about how some of the refugee families "don't even try to learn Swedish." He said it lightly, like it was just an observation. Two other volunteers nodded. I know for a fact that three of the families he's talking about attend SFI classes four mornings a week. One of the mothers, Amira, practices Swedish vocabulary with her kids at the kitchen table every evening. I've seen her notebook.

I didn't correct him. I thought about it. I opened my mouth and then just said something about how the language courses have long waiting lists, which is true but wasn't really the point. The point was that he was wrong and I sidestepped it instead of saying so directly. I keep doing this thing where I provide context instead of actually challenging what someone says. It feels diplomatic in the moment but afterward it just feels like cowardice dressed up as nuance.

Still thinking about the Vattenfall thing from this morning. Went for a walk along the river after dinner to try to sort it out and I'm not sure I managed. The thing is, I talk a lot about how corporations co-opt well-meaning people. I literally have a slide in my thesis presentation about it. "Institutional capture of reform narratives." That's my phrase. And now I'm being offered a small taste of exactly that.

Convenience is the word I keep coming back to. It would be convenient for my career. It would be convenient to tell myself I'm doing it for the right reasons. It would be convenient to let Professor Lindqvist handle the ethical questions while I just show up and take notes and put Vattenfall on my LinkedIn. That's what most people would do. That's what a practical person would do.

But I keep thinking about Fatima and her daughter from the refugee centre, and the Sámi reindeer herders whose grazing land got destroyed for a mine that Vattenfall then sold off when it became unprofitable. These are not abstract policy questions to me. Or at least they shouldn't be. If I take this liaison position, I become someone who files those things under "complicated" and moves on. And I've always told myself I wouldn't be that person. I just didn't expect the test to come from my own supervisor.

Had a supervision meeting with Professor Lindqvist today. She liked my chapter draft on enforcement gaps but said I need to address the "political feasibility" section more carefully. Fair enough. But then she casually mentioned that the department is being courted by Vattenfall for a research partnership and asked if I'd be interested in being a student liaison. Good for my CV, she said. Good connections.

Vattenfall is state-owned and technically pivoting toward renewables, but they also ran lignite mines in Germany for decades and their track record on indigenous Sámi land rights in the north is awful. I know this because I wrote a case study on it last year. Lindqvist knows I wrote it. She was my supervisor for that paper.

I should have said no on the spot. Instead I said I'd think about it. Because part of me is thinking about what it would look like on a job application. Part of me is doing the math on whether working with them from the inside might actually lead to something useful. And I hate that I'm even calculating like this, because I know that's how everyone justifies it. "Change from within." It's the oldest excuse in the book and I've heard it a hundred times from people I don't respect. But here I am, considering it for myself, because Professor Lindqvist smiled when she said my name and I liked being chosen.
sources.nudge_response: Both. But mostly the second one.

sources.journal_entry:
I'm so tired. Thesis crunch plus volunteering Saturdays plus a seminar on EU regulatory frameworks that runs three hours every Tuesday evening. I barely have energy to cook. Today I ordered Foodora twice. Both times it was from chains I know treat their delivery riders badly. I've seen the articles. I've shared the articles. And then I opened the app and ordered anyway because I couldn't face making pasta.

It's not that I forgot. I just didn't care enough in the moment. Or I cared but my tiredness won. I don't know which is worse. The riders are out there in January cold on bikes so I don't have to walk to my own kitchen. I can dress it up however I want but that's what happened.
Overheard Markus in the department kitchen making a joke about a Somali student's accent during a presentation. A couple of people laughed. I pretended I was busy with the coffee machine.

Spent the morning at Akademibokhandeln buying a new notebook for the semester and ended up at the Espresso House on Svartbäcksgatan after. I ordered a coffee and one of those wrapped sandwiches and then just stared at the packaging. Plastic wrap, plastic tray, a paper sleeve that probably isn't even recyclable. I've been reading about single-use packaging policy for my thesis for months. I know the numbers. I know what this stuff does. And I bought it anyway because I was hungry and didn't feel like walking home first.

It sounds ridiculous to feel bad about a sandwich wrapper. People would laugh. But it's the pattern that bugs me. I write about systemic failures in environmental policy and then I make the lazy choice when it's my own lunch. The gap between what I study and how I actually live keeps showing up in these small ways. I don't buy fast fashion anymore, I cycle, I eat less meat than I used to. But then there's this sandwich in a plastic coffin and I think, what's the point of any of it if I can't even get the small stuff right.

My housemate Nils would say I'm overthinking it. He'd say one sandwich wrapper doesn't matter. And he'd be technically correct. But I think the willingness to say "it doesn't matter" about any single thing is exactly how you end up not caring about anything.
sources.nudge_response: It's about whether I'm becoming someone who just talks.

Same day, later. The Suba committee emailed asking if I'd be interested in a second mural for a park renovation. They mentioned they saw "my recent public work" and want something with that "raw quality." I read the email four times.

On one hand — this is exactly what I wanted. Someone seeing the unfiltered version and asking for more of it. The kind of work where I don't have to translate myself into something palatable. But then I read the rest of the email and there are guidelines, approval stages, a heritage review board. The same machinery. And I started wondering whether they want the rawness or the idea of rawness, something that looks honest but still fits neatly into a park renovation plan.

I haven't replied yet. Part of me wants to say yes and fight for the real version from inside the process. Part of me wants to say no and keep doing the kind of work where I answer only to the paint. And there's a third part — the loudest one, honestly — that says: just be grateful someone asked, don't be difficult, say thank you and show up and do good work within the lines. That voice sounds a lot like my mother. I don't think she's wrong. I don't think she's entirely right either. Going to sleep on it.

The march was last Friday. I spoke. It was short — maybe three minutes — and my voice shook the entire time. I talked about how art can hold what policy reports can't, the texture of a place disappearing, the face of someone losing their home to a decision made in an office they'll never enter. Patricia squeezed my arm when I sat down. The crowd was bigger than I expected.

My mother hasn't mentioned it. Marcela sent a one-word text: "brave." I don't know if that's approval or a warning. Hernando liked a photo of the mural on Patricia's Instagram, which is confusing. The sky didn't fall. The family didn't fracture. I feel lighter than I have in weeks, and also a little raw, like a layer of skin is missing. Not sure if I'd do it again. But I'm glad I did it once.
sources.nudge_response: That nobody was angry. I'd built this whole catastrophe in my head — my mother crying, my uncle calling me irresponsible, the family closing ranks. None of it happened. The worst outcome was silence, and silence turned out to be bearable. The actual surprise was that the shaking in my voice didn't make me less credible. People came up to me afterward and said it made them listen harder. I don't know what to do with that yet.

sources.journal_entry:
Two days until the march. Patricia confirmed I'm on the speaker list. I told her yes three weeks ago and have been quietly hoping she'd forget or the schedule would change. It didn't. So now I'm sitting here at midnight trying to figure out what to say to a crowd when I couldn't even type a paragraph in my family's group chat.

The mural is done. I'm proud of it — really proud. It shows the forest canopy dissolving into ash at the edges, with small figures of families walking along the border between green and grey. It's direct without being preachy, I think. But speaking is a different exposure. My name attached to words, recorded on someone's phone, shared. My uncle could see it. My mother definitely would hear about it. Marcela's voice keeps playing in my head: "be careful what you attach your name to."

I keep going back and forth. One minute I think: this matters more than anyone's comfort, including mine. The next minute I think: who am I to stand on a stage when I can't even push back on a mural committee? Maybe I should just let the painting speak and stay behind it where I'm good. But Patricia asked me specifically because she said artists need to be visible, not just their work. And she's not wrong. I just wish being visible didn't feel like standing in traffic.
Long day prepping supplies for Friday. Shoulders ache. Didn't think about the committee or my mother or the march. Just mixed pigments and cleaned brushes. Sometimes that's enough.

My mother called. Someone told her about the march mural. She didn't yell — she never yells — she just got very quiet and asked "is this going to be a problem for you?" That question does more damage than yelling ever could.
sources.nudge_response: Makes me want to reassure her, mostly. I told her it's just a painting, nothing political, which is not entirely true. But she doesn't need to carry that. She has enough.

sources.journal_entry: Finished the base layer of the march mural today. It's honest work. Stood back and felt something I haven't felt in a while — that the paint is saying exactly what I mean.

Family group chat exploded today. My uncle Hernando posted a news article about the Guaviare deforestation — same issue the march is about — and wrote "sad but what can you do, these people need to eat." I started typing a response three times. Deleted all of them.

It's not that I disagree entirely — the economics of it are real and I've seen the poverty firsthand. But the framing drives me insane. "What can you do" as if there are no choices, no policies, no one responsible. I wanted to write about the logging companies, the lack of enforcement, the families who actually live there being displaced. But Hernando is my mother's brother and I can already picture the awkward silence at Easter dinner if I go off in the group chat.

So I sent a sad emoji and closed the app. Mature. Professional. Utterly hollow. Patricia would have posted a five-paragraph essay with citations. I admire that and also cannot imagine being that person in my own family. The mural for the march — that I can do. Words in the chat where my grandmother can see them — that's different somehow, and I hate that it's different.

The Suba mural committee approved a revised design. I compromised — kept the river but softened the contamination imagery into something more abstract. Flowing blues and greens instead of the murky brown I originally wanted. They loved it. Said it was "inspiring." I nodded and thanked everyone and then sat in my car for ten minutes staring at the steering wheel.

I keep telling myself this is how it works. Public art is negotiation. You serve the community's vision, not just your own. And maybe the abstracted version will still land — maybe someone will look at those blues and sense that something is wrong underneath. That's the hope, anyway. But part of me keeps hearing David's collage in my head, all that directness, no translation required.

Called my cousin Marcela tonight. She's a lawyer in Medellin, very proper, always knows the right thing to say at family dinners. I told her about the march and she got quiet for a long time. Then she said, "Lu, you know how tia Rosa talks. Just be careful what you attach your name to." And I know she means it with love. I know the family worries. But careful has a cost too, and I'm starting to wonder how much it's adding up.
sources.nudge_response: Like a low hum. This background noise of things I chose not to say, images I softened, opinions I kept to dinner with close friends. None of it is dramatic on its own. But when I look at my portfolio from five years ago versus now, the work is technically better but quieter. The edges got filed down somewhere. I'm not sure when it happened exactly.

sources.journal_entry:
Meeting with Patricia from the environmental collective went better than expected. She's organizing a march next month about the deforestation in Guaviare and wants muralists to paint temporary pieces along the route. No committee, no brief, no polite rewrites — just paint what you see and feel. I said yes before I finished my coffee.

Spent the afternoon looking at satellite images of the cleared areas. It's staggering how fast the green disappears between one photo and the next. I started sketching a piece that layers the satellite view underneath a portrait of a family I met two years ago when I traveled there for a residency. They had this small farm at the edge of the forest. I keep wondering if that farm still exists.

The march is February 28. Patricia asked if I'd also speak at the rally beforehand. I told her I'd think about it. Speaking is different from painting — you can't hide behind brushstrokes. My mother would probably tell me to just do the mural and not draw attention to myself. She still worries about artists getting into trouble. But Patricia's right that the work means more when the person behind it shows up.

Good day at the workshop. One of the teenagers, David, showed up with a collage about his neighborhood flooding last year — garbage and river water mixed together. He made it beautiful without sanitizing it. I wish I had his nerve sometimes.
sources.nudge_response: He doesn't have a committee reviewing his work. He doesn't have a landlord or a mother who calls every Sunday asking if the grants are coming through. David just has cardboard and glue and something he needs to say. There's a freedom in that. I used to have it too, I think, before I learned all the reasons to hold back.

sources.journal_entry: Can't sleep. Kept redoing the sketch for the Suba district mural because the committee wants something "uplifting" and every version I draw keeps drifting toward the river contamination. My hand knows what it wants to make but the brief says otherwise.
sources.nudge_response: They'd smile politely and tell me to try again. That's how these things work — you read the room, you adjust, you keep the project alive. It's not about my sketch.
